0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
Luke is the longest book in the New Testament. It is also, in the judgment of many, the most beautiful — a Gospel written by a physician who was also a literary artist, a historian who was also a theologian, a Gentile who understood the Jewish roots of everything he was describing better than most of his contemporaries. When Luke sets out to write an orderly account of the things that have been accomplished among us, he produces something that is at once a careful historical document, a theological masterpiece, and a pastoral letter addressed to a world hungry for good news.

The author never names himself, but the ancient tradition is unanimous: this is Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), the companion of Paul (2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24), the man who stayed with Paul when everyone else had left. He was almost certainly a Gentile — the only Gentile author in the New Testament — and this shapes everything he writes. He sees in Jesus the fulfilment not just of Israel's hopes but of the deepest longings of the whole human race. His Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, probably a Roman official of some standing, and through him to the entire Gentile world. Luke wants the world to know that what happened in Judea was not a local religious event. It was the turning point of all of history.

Luke writes in two volumes: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Together they tell the story of what Jesus began to do (the Gospel) and what he continued to do through his Spirit in the church (Acts). The Gospel ends where Acts begins — with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. This two-volume structure matters for reading Luke: his Gospel is not a self-contained biography but the first act of a larger drama, the story of how the good news of the kingdom moved from a manger in Bethlehem to the centre of the Roman world. The Gospel is movement toward Jerusalem; Acts is movement from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Luke's great themes are the themes of the kingdom come in unexpected ways. He gives more space than any other evangelist to women, to the poor, to Samaritans, to Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners — the people whom polite religious society had written off as beyond the reach of God's grace. He is the Gospel of the outsider welcomed in. He shows Jesus praying at every major turning point of his ministry. He is the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, who appears from the first chapter to the last. And above all, he is the Gospel of joy, because at the centre of everything is the announcement that the Saviour has come, and his name is Jesus.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Chapter 1 of Luke is one of the most carefully constructed passages in all of Scripture. Before a single miracle is performed, before a single sermon is preached, before Jesus has spoken a word in public — Luke gives us seven scenes of annunciation, visitation, and praise that set the theological coordinates for everything that follows. He is telling us, from the very first verse, what kind of Gospel this is going to be: historically grounded, theologically rich, and written to produce the certainty of faith in a world that desperately needs it.

The chapter opens with a prologue that is unlike anything else in the New Testament — a formal literary preface, modelled on the prefaces of great Hellenistic historians like Thucydides and Polybius, establishing Luke's credentials as a careful historian and his purpose as a pastoral one. He has investigated everything carefully; he writes in orderly sequence; his goal is that Theophilus may have certainty about the things he has been taught. This is not mythology. This is history — specific, datable, verifiable history — and Luke wants his reader to know it.

From the prologue, the chapter moves into a world saturated with Old Testament atmosphere. Zechariah and Elizabeth are introduced in language that echoes Abraham and Sarah; the angel Gabriel appears as he did to Daniel; Mary's Magnificat is the New Testament's Psalter. Luke is making the claim that the long story of Israel — the story of promise and longing and waiting — has reached its culmination. The God who made promises in Eden, who called Abraham, who spoke through the prophets, is now fulfilling everything he said. The silence of four hundred years is over. The angel's voice breaks into a world that thought God had gone quiet, and nothing will ever be the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The prologue of Luke is the one place in the Gospels where the author steps out before the story begins and speaks in his own voice about how he wrote it. What he says in four verses establishes the whole intellectual and pastoral framework of what follows. He is writing history — but history in the service of faith. He has predecessors; he has done his own research; he has a named recipient; and he has a stated goal.

The word in v. 1 for what the many compiled is diēgēsis, a narrative that leads a reader through events from end to end. The “orderly” of v. 3 is a different word, kathexēs, meaning in sequence, each thing in its proper place. That need not mean a rigid diary order; Luke sometimes gathers material by theme rather than by date. What he promises is an account with a shape you can follow and trust.

The “many” who had already attempted this were not writing fraudulently, and Luke names their work without a sneer. But he has something to add: his own careful investigation, traced back to the source, from the eyewitnesses themselves. The word in v. 2 is autoptes — those who saw with their own eyes. Luke's history is not rumour at several removes. It is testimony from the people who were there.

Theophilus is greeted as “most excellent,” a formal Roman honorific used of senior officials (cf. Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may be a patron who funded the research, an official investigating the Christian movement, or a recent convert who needs the foundations confirmed. The goal Luke states in v. 4 is asphaleia — the firm ground that comes of knowing that what you believe is true. For Luke, faith is grounded in history or it is not Christian faith at all.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader feels at once: if Luke sifted sources like any careful historian, in what sense is this God's word rather than Luke's book? Scripture's answer is that it is both. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there — guiding the questions, the witnesses, the material kept and the order set (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). God did not bypass Luke's mind; he used it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The prologue's insistence on eyewitness testimony and careful investigation is the New Testament's answer to every form of Christianity that treats the historical details of the gospel as negotiable. Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events — specific, dateable, observable events — and his first act as a historian is to establish their factual grounding.

This rules out from the start any reading of the Gospel as mythology, allegory or spiritual symbol. The incarnation, the miracles, the death, the resurrection: these are things that took place, in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

The goal of certainty (asphaleia) is the pastoral heart of the prologue. Luke is not writing to entertain, nor primarily to persuade the uncommitted. He is writing to confirm the faith of someone already taught the Christian story who needs to know that what he has been taught is true. That is the function of historically grounded preaching in every generation — not to introduce people to a religious experience but to settle them in a historical faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue models what responsible handling of the gospel looks like for any teacher or preacher: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, present the findings in order, and do it all in the service of the hearer's certainty. The person in the pew wrestling with doubt does not need vague spiritual reassurance. He needs the kind of careful, ordered account Luke is about to provide.

The best pastoral response to doubt is rarely “just trust.” It is nearer to “let me show you why trust is reasonable” — which is precisely what the next twenty-three chapters do.

And asphaleia is a gift the gospel gives to those who receive it on its own terms: not the brittle certainty of someone who has never been challenged, but the settled certainty of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid. Theophilus is meant to close this Gospel knowing not only that Jesus is Lord but why that claim can be trusted — and equipped to give the reason to anybody who asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many have undertaken to compile an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word.

The prologue. Luke opens with a single long, carefully balanced sentence (vv. 1–4), in polished literary Greek, like the prefaces of the Greek historians and medical writers of his day. He is announcing that what follows is serious history, researched and reliable. Then, from verse 5, his style changes suddenly to the flavour of the Greek Old Testament: the story belongs to the Bible’s story.

Who was Luke? The early church unanimously named Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), as the author of this Gospel and of Acts, which is its second volume (Acts 1:1). He was a companion of Paul; in Acts, he slips into “we” when he was present (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–28:16). He was probably a Gentile (Colossians 4:10–14 lists him apart from those “of the circumcision”), the only Gentile author in the New Testament. His two books make up over a quarter of the New Testament.

Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative. Others had already written accounts of Jesus. One of them was very likely Mark, much of whose Gospel Luke uses. Luke does not criticise them, but adds his own.

Of the things that have been accomplished among us. “Accomplished” (peplērophorēmenōn): fulfilled, brought to completion. Not just events, but the fulfilment of God’s promises. This is a key theme of Luke: what God promised, he has done (24:44).

Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses. The apostles and others who had been with Jesus from the start (Acts 1:21–22). The Gospel rests on eyewitness testimony, not legend.

And ministers of the word. “Ministers” (hypēretai): servants, attendants. They did not invent the message; they served it. “The word” here is the gospel message, almost a person.

Have delivered them to us. “Delivered” (paredosan): handed down, the technical word for passing on a tradition carefully (1 Corinthians 15:3). Luke places himself in the second generation: he received it from the eyewitnesses.

In a sentence. Luke begins by noting that many had already written accounts of what God had fulfilled, based on what the original eyewitnesses and servants of the word had handed down.

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on the testimony of eyewitnesses, carefully passed on. It is not a myth or a feeling. You can read it with confidence.
verseByVerse.note: Luke did not claim to be an eyewitness himself; he gathered the testimony of those who were.

parallels.desc: Luke’s second volume, also to Theophilus
what we have seen and heard

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus.

It seemed good to me also. A modest statement of purpose. Luke adds his work to the others.

Having followed all things closely for some time past. “Followed” (parēkolouthēkoti): investigated, traced. Luke did research. He had opportunity: he spent two years in Judea while Paul was imprisoned at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), and could have met Mary, James the brother of Jesus (Acts 21:18), and others. Much of Luke’s Gospel is found nowhere else, including the birth narratives, which may come from Mary herself (2:19, 51).

“All things” and “from the beginning”. Thorough research, going back to the very start: the births of John and Jesus.

To write an orderly account. “Orderly” (kathexēs): in sequence, arranged logically. Not necessarily strict chronological order in every detail, but a coherent, ordered narrative.

Most excellent Theophilus. “Theophilus” means “friend of God” or “loved by God”. “Most excellent” (kratiste) was a title for Roman officials and people of rank (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25, used of governors). Theophilus was probably a real person of high social standing, perhaps Luke’s patron who paid for the copying and circulation of the book. He was already instructed in the faith (v. 4). Some have suggested that the name stands for every “friend of God” who reads it; that is not the main meaning, but it is a happy thought.

In a sentence. Having researched everything carefully from the beginning, Luke decided to write an ordered account for Theophilus, a man of rank.

On a Tuesday. Christian faith welcomes investigation. Don’t be afraid to study the evidence for what you believe.
verseByVerse.note: Theophilus means “friend of God.” “Most excellent” was a title used for Roman officials, which suggests a man of rank.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.

That you may have certainty. Key word. “Certainty” (asphaleia): firmness, security, reliability. It comes last in the Greek sentence, for emphasis. Luke writes so that Theophilus will be sure: what he believes is true. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it rests on reliable facts.

Concerning the things you have been taught. “Taught” (katēchēthēs), from which comes “catechism”: instructed by word of mouth. Theophilus had been instructed in the Christian faith, perhaps as a new believer or an enquirer. Luke wants to confirm it with a full, written, ordered account.

The purpose of the whole Gospel. Luke and Acts together aim to give assurance: that Jesus is the promised Saviour, that his death and resurrection fulfilled God’s plan, and that the gospel rightly went from Jerusalem to the Gentiles and to Rome. Assurance is a good thing for believers to seek (1 John 5:13).

In a sentence. Luke wrote so that Theophilus could be sure of the truth of what he had been taught.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels uncertain, read the Gospels. God gave them to make you sure.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With v. 5 Luke moves from the historian's prologue to the historian's narrative, and the contrast could hardly be sharper. From a formal Hellenistic preface he plunges into a world saturated with the Old Testament. Zechariah is a priest; Elizabeth is a daughter of Aaron; and they are described in language almost identical to the description of Abraham and Sarah — both righteous, both blameless, and she barren.

A reader steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures recognises the pattern at once. God is about to do something only God can do. He did it with Sarah, with Rebekah, with Rachel, with Hannah. Now he does it a last time, because the child born of this barren womb will prepare the way for the one who needs no human preparation to be born.

The setting of the announcement is itself a sermon. Zechariah is at work, in his division's week of service, chosen by lot for the incense offering — the one duty most priests never received and no priest received twice (vv. 8-10). The whole multitude is praying outside at the hour of incense. God breaks four hundred years of silence not at a moment of revival but in the middle of an ordinary rota.

Gabriel has not appeared in Scripture since the book of Daniel, and the detail is deliberate. Daniel received angelic revelation about the end of the exile and the coming of an Anointed One; Gabriel's reappearance signals that what Daniel waited for is arriving.

The announcement about John is a mosaic of Old Testament promise: the prohibition on wine and strong drink (echoing the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 and the birth of Samson), the filling with the Spirit from the womb (echoing Jer. 1:5 and Isa. 49:1), and the ministry in the spirit and power of Elijah (fulfilling Mal. 4:5-6). Every detail is a fulfilment of something Israel had been promised and had been waiting for.

Zechariah's response is entirely understandable and entirely insufficient. He asks how he can know — and then supplies his evidence, which is his age. He is asking for proof while the proof stands in front of him. The muteness that follows is as much mercy as discipline: nine months in which he can speak nothing except what God has spoken, and a limit written into the sentence (“until the day that these things take place”).

The chapter does not hurry past what that cost him publicly. The crowd waiting outside expected the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 and did not receive it; a man came out of the Holy Place making signs, and there was no benediction that day (vv. 21-23). And he stayed to the end of his rota, serving out his days in silence.

Elizabeth's response, by contrast, is hidden joy. Her first recorded words are not about the child but about God: the Lord has done this for me, and he has looked on me to take away my reproach among people. She understands what Zechariah will need months to grasp — that this is grace, and grace needs no explanation.
verseByVerse.theology:
The barrenness of Elizabeth, like that of Sarah and Hannah before her, is the Old Testament's persistent symbol of human inability and divine sufficiency. The child of promise is always the child who could not have been born by human power alone. That is not incidental; it is the pattern of grace. God works precisely where human capacity has run out.

The child born to a barren womb, the nation born out of an enslaved people, the Messiah born of a virgin — the pattern holds in every case, and the point is the same in every case: salvation is of the LORD, and not of man.

Gabriel's description of John's ministry — that he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah — identifies John as the fulfilment of Malachi 4:5-6, the last prophecy of the Old Testament. Israel's canonical story ends with the promise of Elijah. It begins again here, with his arrival.

And the four hundred years of silence end not with a king or an army but with a priest's speechless vision in the temple. God's timing is consistently unexpected, and his entry points are consistently the last places power would have chosen.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's request for a sign is the response of a man whose theology was correct and whose faith, in the moment, was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs. He had read the stories and offered the prayers. But when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence.

The gap between what we confess and what we trust in the moment is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about the life of faith. And Gabriel's response is not contempt but the gift of silence: a season of enforced dependence on what God has said rather than on what Zechariah can say.

Elizabeth's instinct to remain in seclusion for five months (v. 24) is the instinct of someone who knows that a gift this size needs to be received before it is announced. A soul that has received extraordinary grace sometimes needs to be quiet with it before it can speak of it.

The rush to publicise every experience of God's goodness can short-circuit the deeper work the grace was given to do. Elizabeth sits with the miracle, lets it form her, and waits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. He had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.

The style changes. From here to the end of chapter 2, Luke writes in a Greek full of Hebrew idiom, like the Greek Old Testament. The story begins as Old Testament stories begin, in the temple, with a priest, a barren wife and an angel. Luke shows us that the story of Jesus continues the story of Israel. The last book of the Old Testament ended with a promise of Elijah coming (Malachi 4:5–6); this Gospel begins with the birth of the one who comes in Elijah’s spirit (v. 17).

In the days of Herod, king of Judea. Herod the Great, who ruled the Jewish land as a client king for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. He was an Idumean (Edomite), not a Jew by descent, a great builder (including the temple), and a cruel, paranoid tyrant who murdered his wife and three of his sons. He died in 4 BC; so Jesus was born before then, probably around 6–5 BC (our calendar, calculated in the sixth century, is a few years out).

A priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. “Zechariah” means “the LORD remembers”, which is what this chapter is about (vv. 54, 72). There were perhaps 18,000 priests in Jesus’ day, organised since David’s time into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). Each division served in the temple for a week, twice a year, and all served at the great feasts.

And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron. Elizabeth was also of priestly descent, which was considered a special blessing. “Elizabeth” (Elisheba) means “my God is an oath”, or “my God is fullness”. Aaron’s wife had the same name (Exodus 6:23).

And they were both righteous before God. “Before God”: not just in the eyes of men. Genuine, godly people.

Walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. Not sinless; Zechariah will doubt (v. 20). But faithful, sincere, upright in their obedience, like Job (Job 1:1) or Noah (Genesis 6:9). Their trouble (v. 7) was not punishment for sin.

In a sentence. In the time of Herod the Great, a godly, faithful priest named Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, both of priestly descent, lived blamelessly before God.

On a Tuesday. Faithful, ordinary obedience over many years, unnoticed by the world, is precious to God. He is about to act through people like this.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC. The priests were organised in twenty-four divisions, each serving in the temple for a week at a time; Abijah’s was the eighth.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.

But they had no child. A deep sorrow. In Israel, children were seen as God’s blessing (Psalm 127:3–5), and childlessness was often a cause of grief and social shame (v. 25), sometimes thought to be a sign of God’s displeasure. For this godly couple, it was a painful mystery.

Because Elizabeth was barren. The Bible’s great births often begin with barrenness: Sarah (Genesis 18), Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 30:1, 22), Samson’s mother (Judges 13), and Hannah (1 Samuel 1). In each case, God opened the womb to give a child who would play a key part in his purposes. The pattern shows that the child is God’s gift and God’s work. Where human hope ends, God begins.

And both were advanced in years. Literally “advanced in their days”. Beyond the age of having children (v. 18), as Abraham and Sarah were (Genesis 18:11). Hope had died. Humanly, it was impossible.

In a sentence. Despite their godliness, Zechariah and Elizabeth had no child, because she was barren and they were both old.

On a Tuesday. Faithful people suffer disappointments that make no sense. That does not mean God has forgotten them. Keep trusting.
verseByVerse.note: Barrenness was a deep sorrow and often a social shame. Scripture’s great births often begin with a barren woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.

He was chosen by lot. With so many priests, the duties of each day were assigned by lot. The highest honour was to offer incense in the holy place, and because there were so many priests, a man was allowed to do this only once in his life; many never did. The lot is not chance: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord (Proverbs 16:33). God chose this day, this man.

To enter the temple of the Lord. The sanctuary building itself (naos), the Holy Place, which only priests could enter.

And burn incense. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar inside the Holy Place (Exodus 30:7–8). The priest would put fresh incense on the coals, so that the fragrant smoke rose before the curtain that hid the Most Holy Place. Incense was a picture of prayer rising to God: Let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).

And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. Probably the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m. The people gathered in the courts to pray while the priest offered incense inside. Prayer outside, incense inside: a picture of the people’s prayers going up to God together.

In a sentence. On the once-in-a-lifetime day when Zechariah was chosen by lot to offer incense in the Holy Place, the people were praying outside.

For worship. Your prayers, offered through Christ our high priest, rise to God like incense. Pray, and pray with God’s people.
verseByVerse.note: With so many priests, the honour of offering incense in the holy place came to few, perhaps once in a lifetime. It was offered morning and evening while the people prayed outside.

parallels.desc: let my prayer be counted as incense

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There appeared to him an angel of the Lord, standing on the right side of the altar of incense. Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.

An angel of the Lord. The silence is broken. There had been no prophet in Israel for about four hundred years, since Malachi. Now God speaks again, through an angel.

Standing on the right side of the altar of incense. The altar of incense stood in the Holy Place, just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place. The right side was the side of favour.

And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. The natural response to the presence of a heavenly being. Fear before divine visitation is a recurring note in Luke (1:29–30, 65; 2:9; 5:8–10; 8:37). It is the right response of sinful creatures to the holy.

In a sentence. An angel of the Lord appeared beside the altar of incense, and Zechariah was terrified.

On a Tuesday. God often comes when we are faithfully doing our ordinary duties. Be faithful where you are.
verseByVerse.note: The altar of incense stood just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to him: do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.

Do not be afraid. The first words of God’s messengers to frightened people throughout Luke (1:30; 2:10; 5:10; 8:50; 12:7, 32). The news is good.

For your prayer has been heard. Which prayer? Perhaps his prayers for a child, long ago, which he had probably given up praying. Or perhaps his prayer as priest that day, for the redemption of Israel. Both are answered: the child he prayed for will be the forerunner of the redemption. God had not forgotten prayers that Zechariah himself may have forgotten.

And your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son. In old age, and barren.

And you shall call his name John. God names him. “John” (Yôḥānān) means “the LORD has been gracious” or “the LORD has shown favour”. The name is the message: God is being gracious to his people.

In a sentence. The angel told Zechariah not to fear, for his prayer had been heard: Elizabeth would bear a son, and he was to be called John.

On a Tuesday. God hears prayers you have stopped praying. Never think a prayer offered in faith has been lost.
verseByVerse.note: John means “the LORD has been gracious.”

parallels.desc: Sarah will bear you a son

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. He must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb.

And you will have joy and gladness. Joy is a theme of Luke’s Gospel from beginning (2:10) to end (24:52).

And many will rejoice at his birth. His birth will matter to the whole people.

For he will be great before the Lord. Not great in the world’s eyes; John was a wilderness preacher, executed by Herod. But great before the Lord. Jesus said no one born of women is greater than John (7:28). But note: of Jesus, the angel will say simply “he will be great” (v. 32), with no qualification.

And he must not drink wine or strong drink. The rule for a Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a vow (Numbers 6:1–4). Samson and Samuel were lifelong Nazirites from birth (Judges 13:4–5; 1 Samuel 1:11). John will be wholly set apart.

And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb. Instead of being filled with wine, he will be filled with the Spirit (compare Ephesians 5:18). From before birth, set apart by God, as Jeremiah was (Jeremiah 1:5). And so he leaps in the womb when Mary arrives with the unborn Jesus (v. 41). The Holy Spirit is a major theme of Luke and Acts.

What it shows. An unborn child can be filled with the Spirit. The child in the womb is a person, known and called by God (Psalm 139:13–16).

In a sentence. John would bring great joy, be great before the Lord, be set apart like a Nazirite, and be filled with the Holy Spirit even before birth.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the unborn children you know. God knows them and can work in them even now.
verseByVerse.note: No wine or strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, someone set apart to God.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.

And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. John’s work: repentance, turning back to God (3:3).

And he will go before him. Before whom? Grammatically, before “the Lord their God”. John goes before the Lord God himself, and the one who comes after John is Jesus. Without saying so, the angel identifies Jesus as the Lord.

In the spirit and power of Elijah. Not Elijah reincarnated, but with the same Spirit-given power and prophetic boldness. Elijah confronted a wicked king and queen (1 Kings 18–21); John will confront Herod and Herodias (3:19–20).

To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. From Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the Old Testament, which promised: I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the Lord comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children. Malachi ended with this promise; Luke begins with its fulfilment. Turning hearts of fathers to children means restoring broken relationships, especially in families, as true repentance always does.

And the disobedient to the wisdom of the just. Turning rebels to the understanding and way of life of the righteous.

To make ready for the Lord a people prepared. The purpose of John’s ministry: a people ready for the Lord when he comes. Isaiah 40:3 (3:4–6).

In a sentence. John would turn many in Israel back to God, going before the Lord in Elijah’s spirit and power, as Malachi promised, to prepare a people for him.

On a Tuesday. True repentance shows itself in restored relationships, especially in families. Is there a relationship your repentance needs to mend?

parallels.desc: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah said to the angel: how shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.

How shall I know this? Zechariah asks for a sign, a proof. Abraham asked a similar question (Genesis 15:8), and Gideon asked for signs (Judges 6:36–40). But Zechariah had an angel of God standing in front of him, in the temple, telling him what God would do, and still asked for proof.

For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years. He looks at the circumstances, not at God. He knows the Scriptures well; he knows about Abraham and Sarah. But he cannot believe it for himself.

The contrast with Mary. Mary will also ask a question (v. 34). But hers is a question of how, not whether. She believes and asks how it will happen; Zechariah doubts and asks for proof. The angel’s different responses show the difference (vv. 20, 35, 45).

In a sentence. Zechariah, looking at his and Elizabeth’s age, asked the angel how he could be sure of this.

On a Tuesday. When God’s promise seems impossible, look at the God who promises, not at your circumstances.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel answered him: I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.

I am Gabriel. Gabriel (“God is my strength” or “man of God”) appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel (8:16; 9:21), where he explained visions about the end and the coming of the Anointed One, the seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24–27). That he should come now signals that the time Daniel spoke of has arrived. He is one of only two angels named in the canonical Scriptures (with Michael).

I stand in the presence of God. One of the highest angels, who serve in God’s immediate presence. The answer to “how shall I know?”: because the one who tells you stands before God.

And to bring you this good news. “Bring good news” (euangelisasthai), the verb from which “gospel” and “evangelise” come. Luke uses it often. The gospel begins here.

You will be silent and unable to speak. The sign he asked for, and a discipline. He could not believe the word, so he will not be able to speak a word. It was also a mercy: a constant reminder for nine months that God’s word would come true. Verse 62 suggests he could not hear either.

Because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time. Unbelief does not stop God’s word. It will be fulfilled anyway; unbelief only robs the doubter of joy. God’s promises have their appointed time.

In a sentence. Gabriel, who stands before God, told Zechariah that because he did not believe, he would be unable to speak until the promise was fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief cannot stop God keeping his word. It only silences your praise. Believe, and speak.
verseByVerse.note: Gabriel appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering at his delay in the temple. When he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realised that he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them and remained mute. When his time of service was ended, he went to his home.

And the people were waiting for Zechariah. The priest who offered incense normally came out quickly and pronounced the priestly blessing over the people from the temple steps: The Lord bless you and keep you (Numbers 6:24–26). A long delay was worrying. The Holy Place was dangerous, and a priest who offended God could die there (Leviticus 16:2, 13).

He was unable to speak to them. The priest could not give the blessing. The old order falls silent; a new blessing is coming. At the very end of Luke’s Gospel, Jesus lifts his hands and blesses his disciples (24:50–51), the blessing the priest could not give.

And they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. Something had happened.

When his time of service was ended, he went to his home. He finished his week of duty, faithful even in his silence. His home was in the hill country of Judea (v. 39).

In a sentence. Zechariah came out of the temple unable to speak or give the blessing, and the people realised he had seen a vision; after his week of service, he went home.

On a Tuesday. Even under God’s discipline, keep doing your duty faithfully. Zechariah finished his service.
verseByVerse.note: The people waited for the priest to come out and pronounce the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying: thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.

His wife Elizabeth conceived. Just as the angel said. God’s word comes true, despite Zechariah’s doubt.

And for five months she kept herself hidden. We are not told why. Perhaps for private worship and thanksgiving. Perhaps because no one would believe her until the pregnancy was visible. Perhaps in obedience to the Nazirite rules. The sixth month will be when Gabriel comes to Mary (v. 26), and her pregnancy will be Mary’s sign (v. 36).

Thus the Lord has done for me. She knows exactly who has done it. Her first words are praise.

In the days when he looked on me. “Looked on”: with favour, with grace. God had seen her all along.

To take away my reproach among people. The shame of barrenness. Rachel said the same: God has taken away my reproach (Genesis 30:23). God lifts the shame of his people.

In a sentence. Elizabeth conceived and stayed in seclusion five months, praising God for looking on her with favour and removing her shame.

On a Tuesday. Whatever shame you carry, God sees you and is able to take it away. Give him the praise when he does.

parallels.desc: Rachel: God has taken away my reproach

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six months after the annunciation to Zechariah, Gabriel is sent again — this time not to a priest in the temple but to a young woman in Galilee. The contrast is everything Luke is about. The gospel does not move from centre to periphery, from the established to the marginal, from the important to the overlooked. It moves the other way.

The temple in Jerusalem is where Gabriel went first; a village in Galilee, to a girl betrothed to a builder, is where he goes next. Nazareth was small and undistinguished — so undistinguished that Nathanael would later ask whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46). The answer, it turns out, is everything.

Gabriel's greeting is without precedent in Jewish literature. Nobody else in the Bible is greeted this way. Mary is “favoured” — the graced one, the one on whom divine favour has freely fallen.

Roman Catholic theology has developed from this greeting the doctrines of Mary's immaculate conception and sinlessness; the Reformed reading takes the word as referring to God's gracious choice of Mary for this specific task rather than to any inherent quality in her. The distinction matters, and Mary settles it herself at v. 47 when she calls God her Saviour. In Luke's account the wonder is never Mary's worthiness. It is God's freedom.

The announcement of Jesus's birth is the most theologically dense passage in the chapter. Gabriel says four things: he will be great; he will be called Son of the Most High; the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father; he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

These claims are simultaneously royal and divine. The throne of David identifies him as the Messiah of Israel's hope; the title Son of the Most High and the endless kingdom move beyond anything a merely human king could claim. Gabriel is announcing the fulfilment of 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and the inauguration of the kingdom of Daniel 7:14. The Messiah Israel expected and the Son of God the disciples would confess are one and the same person.

Mary's question is entirely different in character from Zechariah's request for a sign. She does not doubt; she asks for clarification. The mechanism puzzles her, not the possibility. And Gabriel's answer is the most direct statement of the incarnation in the Synoptic Gospels: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God.

The language of overshadowing recalls the cloud of divine presence that covered the tabernacle (Exod. 40:35) — the presence of God taking up residence. Mary is the new tabernacle, the place where God chooses to dwell. And her response, “Let it be to me according to your word,” is the finest answer to divine grace in the New Testament. Not resignation. Not reluctant compliance. Surrender that is also worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Son of the Most High” places Jesus in direct relationship to the God of Israel's covenant. In Daniel 7:18-27 it is the saints of the Most High who receive the kingdom; here the kingdom is given to the Son of the Most High himself. Gabriel is announcing not merely that Jesus will be the greatest of Israel's kings but that he is the figure Daniel saw receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will not be destroyed.

The Davidic covenant and the everlasting kingdom of Daniel meet in this child — and a thousand years of promise, apparently stalled since the exile, resume in a single sentence spoken in a village house.

The Holy Spirit's role in the conception is the New Testament's clearest statement that the incarnation is a divine act and not a human achievement. Mary supplies the humanity; the Spirit supplies the initiative that makes this birth unlike every other.

The result is not a demigod — a being partly divine and partly human — but a fully human being who is at the same time the eternal Son of God. This is what the church has confessed from the beginning: two natures, one person, without confusion or mixture. Gabriel does not explain the mechanics of the mystery. He announces the reality.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary's “Let it be to me according to your word” is the model response to a divine call that exceeds comprehension. She does not understand how this will happen. She does not know what it will cost. She cannot see Simeon's sword or the hill called Golgotha. She says yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of the word of a God she trusts.

That is what faith is — not the confident feeling that everything will be easy, but the willingness to place yourself in the hands of the One who has spoken.

The contrast between Gabriel's errand to the temple in Jerusalem and his errand to a house in Nazareth is Luke's first great declaration that the gospel is for everyone. The most important conversation in human history took place not in a palace or a sanctuary but in the home of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of.

God's greatest gifts consistently arrive through the most unlikely channels — which means no person, no place and no circumstance is too small or too obscure to be the site of divine grace.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary.

The contrast. Luke sets the two announcements side by side. The first: to an old man, a priest, in the temple, in Jerusalem, about a child born to a barren woman. The second: to a young woman, an ordinary girl, in a small village in despised Galilee, about a child born to a virgin. The first is wonderful; the second is greater. John is great; Jesus is greater.

In the sixth month. Of Elizabeth’s pregnancy.

A city of Galilee named Nazareth. “City” here means a town. Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hills of lower Galilee, perhaps a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament, Josephus or the rabbinic writings. Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46). God chose the insignificant.

To a virgin. Key word. Parthenos, a young unmarried woman who has not had sexual relations. Luke makes this unmistakable: he says “virgin” twice in this verse, and Mary herself says she has not known a man (v. 34). This echoes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:23).

Betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph. Jewish marriage had two stages. Betrothal was a binding agreement, made before witnesses, usually when the girl was perhaps twelve to fourteen. The couple were legally husband and wife, and breaking the betrothal required a divorce (Matthew 1:19). But they did not yet live together or have sexual relations. About a year later came the wedding, when the bride was brought to her husband’s home.

Of the house of David. Joseph was a descendant of King David. As Jesus’ legal father, he gave him the legal right to David’s throne (3:23–31; Matthew 1:1–16).

And the virgin’s name was Mary. Greek Mariam, from Hebrew Miriam, the name of Moses’ sister. One of the most common names among Jewish women of the time.

In a sentence. In the sixth month, Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary, betrothed to Joseph, a descendant of David.

On a Tuesday. God works through obscure places and ordinary people. No village is too small, and no person too ordinary, for his purposes.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee. Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; the couple did not yet live together.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to her and said: greetings, O favoured one, the Lord is with you! But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.

Greetings. Chaire, the ordinary Greek greeting, literally “rejoice”. There may be an echo of the prophets’ calls to the daughter of Zion: Rejoice … the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst (Zephaniah 3:14–17; Zechariah 9:9).

O favored one. Key word. Kecharitōmenē, from charis, grace: “one who has been graced”, “one who has received favour”. The same verb is used of all believers in Ephesians 1:6: his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us (literally “graced us”) in the Beloved. Mary is the recipient of God’s grace, chosen freely by him. She has not earned it.

Where Christians differ: “full of grace”. The Latin Vulgate translated the word gratia plena, “full of grace”, giving the familiar “Hail Mary, full of grace”. Roman Catholic teaching has understood Mary as filled with grace from her conception, and so preserved from original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), and as one who can dispense grace to others. Verdict: the Greek word means one who has been shown favour, not one who is a source of grace. Mary was a sinner saved by grace, who calls God “my Saviour” (v. 47). She is to be honoured as the most blessed of women, the mother of our Lord, and a model of faith and obedience (v. 45). But she is not to be prayed to, and she does not dispense grace. Grace comes from God alone, through Christ alone.

The Lord is with you! The promise given to the great servants of God when he called them: Moses, Joshua, Gideon (Judges 6:12), Jeremiah. God is about to give her a task.

But she was greatly troubled at the saying. Not by the angel (as Zechariah was), but by his words. Why would God’s favour rest on her? Humility.

And tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. “Discern” (dielogizeto): she thought it through, considered it. Mary is thoughtful (2:19, 51).

In a sentence. Gabriel greeted Mary as one favoured by God’s grace and assured her that the Lord was with her, and she was deeply perplexed by the greeting.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you too have been graced (Ephesians 1:6). God’s favour rests on you, not because you deserve it, but because he is gracious.

parallels.desc: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valour”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel said to her: do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

For you have found favor with God. The phrase used of Noah (Genesis 6:8). God’s free choice and grace.

You will conceive in your womb and bear a son. The words echo Isaiah 7:14: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Luke does not quote it, but the echo is clear, and Matthew makes it explicit (Matthew 1:22–23).

And you shall call his name Jesus. Key name. “Jesus” is the Greek form of “Joshua” (Yeshua), meaning “the LORD saves” or “the LORD is salvation”. Matthew gives the meaning: for he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). It was a common name. But this child would fulfil it as no one else. Joshua led Israel into the promised land; Jesus brings his people into God’s eternal rest (Hebrews 4:8–10).

In a sentence. Gabriel told Mary not to fear, for God had shown her favour: she would conceive and bear a son, and name him Jesus, “the LORD saves”.

For worship. The name of Jesus is the gospel in a word: the Lord saves. Call on his name (Romans 10:13).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

He will be great. John was to be great before the Lord (v. 15). Jesus is simply great, without qualification. This is the language used of God himself: Great is the Lord (Psalm 48:1).

And will be called the Son of the Most High. “The Most High” (Hypsistos) is a name for God (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 91:1). “Called” in Hebrew idiom means “will be”: he will be, and be recognised as, God’s Son.

And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David. The fulfilment of God’s covenant with David: I will raise up your offspring after you … and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:12–16; also Psalm 89; Isaiah 9:6–7). Every Jew longed for the Son of David, the Messiah. This child is he.

And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. Jacob was renamed Israel; the house of Jacob is God’s people. And it now includes all who belong to Christ by faith, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:29; 6:16).

And of his kingdom there will be no end. David’s earthly dynasty ended with the exile. This king’s reign is eternal (Daniel 2:44; 7:14). Not an earthly, political kingdom confined to a thousand years, but an everlasting one. He reigns now at God’s right hand, and will reign for ever.

In a sentence. Mary’s son would be great, the Son of the Most High, and God would give him David’s throne, to reign over God’s people for ever in a kingdom without end.

For worship. Jesus reigns now, and for ever. Live today as a subject of the King whose kingdom has no end.

parallels.desc: on the throne of David, no end
a kingdom that shall not be destroyed

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said to the angel, 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said to the angel: how will this be, since I am a virgin?

How will this be. Not doubt, but a sincere question. She does not ask for a sign, as Zechariah did. She asks how God will do it. Gabriel does not rebuke her.

Since I am a virgin. Literally “since I do not know a man”, the Hebrew idiom for sexual relations (Genesis 4:1). She is betrothed, but not yet married, and she understands the angel to mean that she will conceive now, before her marriage to Joseph.

What it does not mean. Not, as some Roman Catholic interpreters have argued, that Mary had taken a vow of lifelong virginity, and so could not imagine having a child even after marriage. Nothing in the text suggests a vow; she was betrothed to be married in the normal way. Her question is simply about how she can conceive now.

In a sentence. Mary asked how she could have a child, since she had never had relations with a man.

On a Tuesday. It is not wrong to ask God how. Faith asks questions; unbelief demands proofs.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel answered her: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.

The Holy Spirit will come upon you. The answer to “how?”: by the direct creative power of God. Not by any human father. As the Spirit hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), the Spirit will bring about a new creation in Mary’s womb. Jesus is the beginning of the new humanity, the second Adam (3:38; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

And the power of the Most High will overshadow you. “Overshadow” (episkiasei) recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence overshadowing the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35, in the Greek Old Testament) and the disciples at the transfiguration (9:34). God’s own presence will rest on her. Mary becomes, in a sense, the tabernacle in which God comes to dwell with his people (John 1:14, literally “tabernacled”).

The virgin conception. This is the teaching of the virgin birth, more precisely the virginal conception: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, without a human father. It is taught plainly by both Matthew and Luke, independently, and confessed by the church in every creed. It matters. It shows that salvation is God’s work, not human achievement. It shows that Jesus is both truly God and truly human: born of a woman, fully human; conceived by the Spirit, the eternal Son taking our nature. And it means that he was not born under the guilt of Adam’s sin, but was holy from conception.

Therefore the child to be born will be called holy. Set apart, sinless (Hebrews 7:26).

The Son of God. Not because the Spirit was his “father” in a physical sense, as pagan myths told of gods fathering children. Luke means that the eternal Son, who already existed (John 1:1–14; Philippians 2:6–7), took human nature in Mary’s womb by the Spirit’s power. The conception does not make him the Son; it is the way the Son became man.

In a sentence. The angel explained that the Holy Spirit would come upon Mary and the power of God would overshadow her, so that her child would be holy, the Son of God.

For worship. The eternal Son of God became a tiny human being in a virgin’s womb, for you. Worship the mystery of the incarnation.
verseByVerse.note: “Overshadow” recalls the cloud of God’s presence overshadowing the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: the cloud settled on the tent

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.

And behold, your relative Elizabeth. A sign, offered without being asked for. Mary could go and see it for herself (v. 39). We are not told exactly how they were related. “Relative” (syngenis) is a general word. Elizabeth was of Aaron’s line; Mary’s ancestry is not stated, though some think Luke’s genealogy is hers.

In her old age has also conceived a son. If God can do this, he can do the greater thing.

And this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. The very thing people called her has been reversed.

For nothing will be impossible with God. Literally “no word will be impossible with God”: no word God speaks will fail. An echo of Genesis 18:14, said to Sarah: Is anything too hard for the Lord? The God who gave Isaac to Sarah has given John to Elizabeth, and will give Jesus to Mary. Jesus will say the same of salvation (18:27).

In a sentence. Gabriel told Mary that her elderly, barren relative Elizabeth was six months pregnant, for no word of God is impossible.

On a Tuesday. What has God promised in his word that seems impossible to you? Nothing he says will fail.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.' And the angel departed from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said: behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word. And the angel departed from her.

Behold, I am the servant of the Lord. “Servant” (doulē): literally “slave”, a female bond-servant. Total submission. She belongs to God, and he may do with her as he wills. Hannah used the same word of herself (1 Samuel 1:11).

The cost. Mary’s yes was costly. An unmarried pregnant girl in a small village faced disgrace, gossip and suspicion that would follow her and her son for life (John 8:41). She might lose Joseph (Matthew 1:19). Under the law, she could even face death for adultery (Deuteronomy 22:20–24). She said yes anyway.

Let it be to me according to your word. Faith and obedience together. She takes God at his word and submits to it. Her response is the opposite of Zechariah’s, and the model for every believer’s response to God. Elizabeth will praise her for exactly this: blessed is she who believed (v. 45). Jesus will later say that those who hear the word of God and keep it are more blessed even than his mother as his mother (11:27–28).

And the angel departed from her. The conversation is over. Now she must live by faith in the word, without the angel.

In a sentence. Mary humbly accepted God’s will as his servant, asking that it be done to her according to his word.

On a Tuesday. Make Mary’s words your own prayer today, whatever it costs: I am the Lord’s servant; let it be to me according to your word.

parallels.desc: let your servant find favour in your eyes

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary leaves for the hill country of Judah “with haste” — the word suggests urgency, even a kind of breathless joy. She has just received the most overwhelming news in history, and the angel has told her that her elderly relative is also pregnant. She goes at once, not to tell the story but to be with somebody who might understand it: someone else visited by grace in a way that makes no human sense.

The moment Mary's greeting reaches Elizabeth, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. John recognises Jesus before either of them has been born. This is not sentimental detail; it is Luke's first testimony to what the Baptist's whole ministry will be. Jesus is the one who is coming, and John exists to point towards him. Even in the womb, before any conscious act of faith, John responds to the presence of the Lord.

The Holy Spirit fills Elizabeth in that moment and she speaks with prophetic clarity. Mary is blessed; the fruit of her womb is blessed; and Elizabeth marvels that “the mother of my Lord” should come to her. That exclamation is the first confession of Jesus's lordship in Luke's Gospel, and it comes from a woman who cannot know it by any natural means. The Spirit has revealed it.

Lord on Elizabeth's lips is the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. She is not saying “the mother of an important person.” She is saying “the mother of the one who is LORD.” The full theological weight of the title is present from the beginning.

And the section does not end with the confession. It ends with a beatitude, and the beatitude is about faith: “blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord” (v. 45). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, does not finally commend Mary's womb, her lineage or her purity. She commends her trust.

That is the section's real climax, and it sets Mary directly against Zechariah, who heard the same angel in the same six months and did not believe. Luke has framed his whole opening around a single question: the word of God has come — will it be received?
verseByVerse.theology:
John's leap at the sound of Mary's greeting is a pre-natal act of recognition that is also a pre-natal act of worship. The Reformed tradition reads this, alongside Jeremiah 1:5 and the Baptist's filling with the Spirit from the womb, as a sign that divine grace and knowledge precede human consciousness. The child does not decide to leap; the Spirit moves him.

This is the grace that goes before us — that calls and shapes and prepares before we are capable of any response. It is not an argument for conscious infant faith. It is a sign of the sovereign grace of God that precedes every human act.

Elizabeth's blessing of Mary — “blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” — applies the Old Testament's blessing language to the New Testament's supreme moment of grace. Mary stands in the line of those through whom God has worked unexpected deliverance.

But she surpasses them all, because the one she carries is not a deliverer of Israel only but the Saviour of the world. And v. 45 keeps even that from becoming a cult of the mother: what the Spirit singles out in her is not her body but her believing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary goes to Elizabeth with haste — not to process her experience alone, not to work things out in private, but to be with somebody who can understand. The instinct is exactly right. The grace of God is not meant to be received and kept in isolation.

The community of the gospel is the community of those who have all, in one way or another, been visited by unexpected grace, and who find in each other's company the confirmation and the joy that private reflection cannot produce. An isolated believer is a believer at risk.

Elizabeth's question — “Why is this granted to me?” — is the question of someone who has not lost the astonishment grace produces. She has been told by an angel that she will bear a child; she is herself six months into an impossible pregnancy; and when she hears Mary's greeting her first response is wonder at the privilege of the moment.

The soul still capable of asking “why me?” in the face of God's gifts is a soul grace is still shaping. The moment we begin to feel we have earned the visit, something essential has been lost. And notice what is entirely absent from Elizabeth: any trace of comparison with the younger woman whose portion is plainly larger than her own.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah. She entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Mary arose and went with haste. Eager to see the sign (v. 36), and to share her news with the one person who would understand.

Into the hill country, to a town in Judah. The highlands around Jerusalem. The town is unnamed; tradition says Ein Karem, about five miles (8 km) west of Jerusalem. From Nazareth it was a journey of 80–100 miles (130–160 km), several days on foot. A young girl would probably have travelled with a group.

And greeted Elizabeth. The ordinary greeting, “peace”.

The baby leaped in her womb. Not just a normal movement. John, filled with the Spirit from the womb (v. 15), recognises the presence of his Lord, himself an unborn child, perhaps only days or weeks after conception. Elizabeth interprets it: he leaped for joy (v. 44). John’s ministry of pointing to Jesus has begun before either is born. An echo of Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah’s womb (Genesis 25:22), and of David leaping before the ark (2 Samuel 6:16).

The unborn. Luke uses the same word for the unborn John here (brephos) that he uses for the newborn Jesus in the manger (2:12, 16) and for infants (18:15). The unborn child is a person. And Jesus was a person, the incarnate Lord, from his conception.

And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. And so she speaks as a prophet.

In a sentence. Mary hurried to visit Elizabeth, and at her greeting, the unborn John leaped in Elizabeth’s womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. When God works in your life, share it with a fellow believer who can rejoice with you.
verseByVerse.note: The hill country of Judea was the highland around Jerusalem, some 80 miles or more from Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: and she exclaimed with a loud cry, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
She exclaimed with a loud cry: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

She exclaimed with a loud cry. Spirit-filled, overflowing joy.

Blessed are you among women. The most blessed of all women, because of the child she carries. Jael and Judith were praised in similar words for delivering Israel (Judges 5:24). Mary will bear the Deliverer.

And blessed is the fruit of your womb! Mary is blessed because her child is blessed. Her honour comes from him.

And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? A remarkable confession. Elizabeth, older, married to a priest, and pregnant with a great prophet, humbles herself before a young girl from Galilee. Why? Because Mary’s child is “my Lord”. “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s own name. By the Spirit, Elizabeth recognises an unborn child as her Lord. This is the first human confession of Jesus as Lord in Luke.

Where Christians differ: Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) gave Mary the title Theotokos, “God-bearer” or “Mother of God”. It was meant as a statement about Christ: the one Mary bore is truly God, one person, not two. Protestants have generally accepted the doctrine while being wary of the title, because it has been used to exalt Mary. Verdict: the doctrine is true and important: the child in Mary’s womb was the eternal Son of God made man, Elizabeth’s Lord. But “mother of my Lord” is the biblical phrase, and Mary’s honour is always derived from her Son.

In a sentence. Filled with the Spirit, Elizabeth blessed Mary and her child, and humbly marvelled that the mother of her Lord should visit her.

For worship. Elizabeth called an unborn child “my Lord”. Is he your Lord?

parallels.desc: most blessed of women be Jael
how can the ark of the LORD come to me?

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.

The baby in my womb leaped for joy. “Joy” (agalliasei): exultation, the joy of the messianic age. The angel had promised joy at John’s birth (v. 14); the joy has already begun.

And blessed is she who believed. Key words. Elizabeth blesses Mary not only for being the mother, but for believing. Her faith is the contrast with Zechariah’s unbelief (v. 20), in Elizabeth’s own house, where her husband still sat silent. Mary is blessed because she trusted God’s word. Faith is what makes anyone blessed (11:28).

That there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord. God’s word will be fulfilled. Faith rests on that.

In a sentence. Elizabeth explained that her baby had leaped for joy at Mary’s greeting, and blessed Mary for believing that God’s word to her would be fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. Blessed are those who believe God’s word. Which of his promises do you need to believe today?

parallels.desc: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–56 — Mary's Song of Praise: The Magnificat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Magnificat — named from the first word of its Latin translation, “My soul magnifies the Lord” — is the New Testament's greatest hymn and one of the most theologically rich passages in Scripture. It is modelled so closely on Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2:1-10 that some have argued Luke originally assigned it to Elizabeth; but the text is clear, and the reasons for it belonging to Mary are overwhelming.

Mary is the New Testament's Hannah — the woman through whom God's greatest act of salvation is brought into the world. And like Hannah she responds not with private gratitude but with public theology: a proclamation of what God is like, what he has done, and what he always does.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 46-50) is personal. Mary sings of what God has done for her: he has looked on the humble estate of his servant; he has done great things for her; his mercy extends to those who fear him. The second (vv. 51-55) is cosmic and historical: God has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty, exalted the humble, filled the hungry, sent the rich away empty, and helped his servant Israel.

Those verbs are past tense — the Greek aorist, expressing completed action — even though none of it has yet visibly happened. Mary sings in the prophetic past: what God is going to do in Jesus is so certain that she sings it as already accomplished. This is the faith that sees the invisible reality and speaks it before it is seen.

The theology of the Magnificat is the theology of the great reversal — the consistent pattern in which God works through what the world considers weak, low, foolish and despised, to accomplish what power and wisdom cannot. The proud are scattered; the mighty brought down; the humble exalted; the hungry filled; the rich sent away empty.

This is not a manifesto for violent revolution — every verb has God as its subject — but the testimony of a God whose ways are not our ways, who chooses the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Mary has understood it because she has lived it: she is herself the lowly servant God has honoured beyond imagining.

And the song ends where the story began, with Abraham (vv. 54-55) — the reversals are not God changing his policy but God keeping an old appointment. Then, with no transition at all, Luke notes that Mary stayed three months and went home (v. 56). She walked back to Nazareth visibly pregnant, to a fiancé who would decide to divorce her. The extraordinary is set down in the middle of the ordinary, and the ordinary is where it has to be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Magnificat's use of the past tense for events that have not yet occurred — he has scattered the proud, he has brought down the mighty — is the linguistic form of prophetic certainty. The prophets of Israel consistently spoke of future events in the past tense when the certainty of God's word made the outcome as sure as if it had already happened.

Isaiah 53 does exactly this, narrating the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense centuries before either occurred. Mary's song places her in that prophetic line — not as one who has received a vision of the future but as one who has received the seed of the future in her own body and understands what it means.

The “humble estate” of Mary is a condition of insignificance and social unimportance. God has looked upon it — deliberately noticed — not despite it but through it. This is the theology of election that runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem and Mary over every princess in Israel.

God's choices consistently invert the world's criteria. The reason is not that the lowly are inherently virtuous. It is that the glory of a grace which chooses them cannot possibly be confused with a favour granted on the basis of merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship since the earliest centuries — in the evening prayer of the church, in the liturgies of East and West, in the hymns of the Reformation — and set to music by composers from Monteverdi to Bach. It is not merely a beautiful poem. It is the church joining Mary's song, declaring that the God who did great things for her is doing great things still.

Every Christian who sings it stands in the line of Mary's witness: scattering the proud, filling the hungry, keeping covenant with his people, is what he is still doing.

It is also among the most politically subversive texts in the New Testament — not because it calls for revolution but because it announces a King whose reign will outlast every human empire, whose justice will overturn every human injustice, and whose mercy will outlive every human cruelty.

The church that sings this song is the community that knows how the story ends, and that knowledge shapes how it lives now: not grasping for power, not trusting in the mighty, not filling itself with the world's goods, but living in the pattern of the God who scatters the proud and exalts the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said: my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour.

The Magnificat. Mary’s song is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin (“magnifies”). It has been sung in Christian worship for centuries. It is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer at the birth of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and the Psalms. Mary was a young village girl, but she knew her Scriptures deeply, and her heart overflowed in their words. The song has four movements: what God has done for Mary (vv. 46–49), his character (v. 50), what he does in the world (vv. 51–53), and what he has done for Israel (vv. 54–55).

My soul magnifies the Lord. “Magnifies” (megalynei): makes great, declares the greatness of. Not making God greater than he is, but seeing and declaring how great he is, as a magnifying glass makes small things visible. “Soul” and “spirit” are parallel: her whole inner being. Hannah began: My heart exults in the Lord (1 Samuel 2:1).

And my spirit rejoices in God my Savior. “Savior” (sōtēr). Mary needed a Saviour. She calls God her Saviour, acknowledging that she was a sinner in need of salvation, like everyone else. This is important for the doctrine of Mary. She was not sinless; she rejoiced in the God who saves sinners, through the Son she would bear (Habakkuk 3:18).

In a sentence. Mary began her song by declaring the greatness of the Lord and rejoicing in God her Saviour.

For worship. Magnify the Lord today. Look at his greatness until you can sing about it, and rejoice in him as your Saviour.
