verseByVerse.note: Mary’s song, known as the Magnificat, is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.

For he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. “Humble estate” (tapeinōsin): lowliness, low social position. Mary was poor, young, unknown, from an insignificant village. God chose her because of her lowliness, not despite it. Hannah prayed: if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant (1 Samuel 1:11). This is God’s way: he chooses the lowly (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

From now on all generations will call me blessed. A prophecy that has come true. Every generation of Christians has called her blessed. Not that she will be worshipped, but that she will be honoured as the one God blessed. Leah said something similar at the birth of Asher (Genesis 30:13).

For he who is mighty has done great things for me. The reason for her blessedness: not her own merit, but what the Mighty One has done for her. The focus is on God.

And holy is his name. God’s name is God himself, as he has revealed himself. He is holy: set apart, utterly pure, majestic. Psalm 111:9: holy and awesome is his name. Mary’s blessedness leads her to worship God’s holiness.

In a sentence. Mary praised God for looking on her lowliness, foretold that all generations would call her blessed, and gave the glory to the Mighty One, whose name is holy.

On a Tuesday. God looks on the lowly. If you feel insignificant, remember that he chose a poor girl from Nazareth for the greatest privilege a human being has ever had.

parallels.desc: look on the affliction of your servant
holy and awesome is his name

verseByVerse.quote: And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.

And his mercy. Mary moves from what God has done for her to who God is. “Mercy” (eleos) translates the Hebrew ḥesed, God’s steadfast, covenant love: loyal, faithful, kind.

Is for those who fear him. To fear God is not to be terrified of him, but to revere him, take him seriously, trust and obey him. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Psalm 103:17: But the steadfast love of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him.

From generation to generation. His mercy does not run out. What he did for Abraham, he does for Mary, and for everyone who fears him, in every generation, including ours.

In a sentence. God’s steadfast mercy rests on those who revere him, in every generation.

For worship. The mercy shown to Mary is the same mercy available to you. Fear God, and trust his mercy.

parallels.desc: the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him

verseByVerse.quote: He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.

The past tense. All the verbs are in the past tense (the Greek aorist). Mary speaks of what God will do through her Son as if it had already happened, because it is certain. Or she describes what God has always done, and is now doing again. Prophetic certainty.

He has shown strength with his arm. God’s arm is a picture of his power in action, especially at the exodus: with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Deuteronomy 26:8; Isaiah 51:9; 52:10; 53:1).

He has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts. The proud plan in their hearts, and God scatters their plans, as at Babel (Genesis 11).

He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate. The great reversal. Hannah sang: The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts (1 Samuel 2:7–8). This is a major theme of Luke’s Gospel: the first will be last and the last first (13:30), the humble exalted and the exalted humbled (14:11; 18:14), blessings on the poor and woes on the rich (6:20–26). Herod sits on his throne; Mary’s son lies in a manger. But God will reverse it.

He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. Psalm 107:9. Hunger here is both physical and spiritual: those who know their need, and hunger for God (6:21; Matthew 5:6). The rich are those who are self-satisfied and need nothing from God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25). God fills empty hands.

What it does not mean. Not a political manifesto, or a call for revolution, as some liberation theologians have read it. Nor does it mean that all poor people are saved and all rich people lost. But it does show that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), that he cares about the poor and the oppressed, and that his kingdom overturns the world’s values. These are real social realities as well as spiritual ones, and the church should reflect them.

In a sentence. Mary sang of the God who by his mighty arm scatters the proud, topples the powerful, lifts up the lowly, fills the hungry, and sends the self-satisfied rich away empty.

On a Tuesday. On which side of the great reversal are you: the proud and self-sufficient, or the humble and hungry? Come to God empty, and be filled.

parallels.desc: he brings low and he exalts

verseByVerse.quote: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring for ever.

He has helped his servant Israel. Isaiah 41:8–9: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham. God has come to the aid of his people.

In remembrance of his mercy. God has not forgotten. Through centuries of silence, oppression and exile, he remembered. The name Zechariah means “the LORD remembers” (v. 5), and Zechariah will sing the same (v. 72).

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever. God’s promise to Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). This is the root of the whole story. Jesus is the offspring of Abraham, the one through whom the blessing comes to the nations (Galatians 3:16, 29). God keeps his promises, even two thousand years later.

In a sentence. Mary ended her song by praising God for helping his people Israel, remembering the mercy he promised to Abraham and his descendants for ever.

For worship. God keeps his promises, however long it takes. Thank him for his faithfulness to the promises that now include you.

parallels.desc: Israel, my servant, offspring of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.

About three months. Until near the time of John’s birth, since Elizabeth was in her sixth month when Mary arrived (v. 36). Whether Mary stayed for the birth Luke does not say; he tells us she returned home, and then turns to John’s birth, rounding off Mary’s part of the story first, as he often does.

And returned to her home. To Nazareth, now visibly pregnant, to face Joseph, her family and her village. Matthew tells how an angel came to Joseph in a dream (Matthew 1:18–25).

In a sentence. Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months and then went home.

On a Tuesday. Time spent with mature believers strengthens you for what lies ahead. Mary had three months with Elizabeth before she faced Nazareth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–66 — The Birth of John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of John is narrated with characteristic Lukan brevity — one verse for the birth itself, and then immediate attention to what matters most, which is the naming. In Jewish custom the name was given at circumcision on the eighth day, and was normally taken from the father's family. The community assumes the child will be called Zechariah.

Elizabeth insists that he will be called John. The community is astonished — there is nobody in the family by that name — and they turn to Zechariah himself. He calls for a writing tablet and writes: his name is John. And immediately his mouth is opened, his tongue is loosed, and he speaks.

The sequence is telling. Zechariah does not begin to speak until he has first obeyed. The muteness that fell at his unbelief is lifted not when he privately makes up his mind but when he publicly and irrevocably acts on the word Gabriel gave him. The name John was not Zechariah's choice; it was God's command (v. 13).

By writing it without qualification he is doing what Mary did in a different register: surrendering his own preference and his family's expectation to the word of God. And the moment he does, the word God gave him is restored to his own mouth.

A small detail in v. 62 fills out the whole nine months. The family made signs to him, which suggests he could not hear either. He had been sealed inside his own head since the day at the altar, with nothing in there but Gabriel's sentence.

The neighbours and relatives are filled with fear, and they laid up all these things in their hearts — a phrase that will appear again of Mary after the shepherds' visit (2:19) and after the temple episode (2:51). Luke's Gospel is full of people who receive these events and hold them, turning them over, not fully understanding but refusing to let go.

That is the posture the gospel consistently produces: not an immediate confident grasp of everything, but the faithful keeping of what has been received, waiting for the understanding that comes in its own time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The crowd's question — what then will this child be, for the hand of the Lord was with him — is the question the rest of Luke-Acts will answer. John will be the voice crying in the wilderness, the preparer of the way, the greatest among those born of women (7:28).

He will baptise Jesus, proclaim the coming kingdom, confront Herod, and die in prison before Jesus's ministry reaches its climax. He is the last and greatest of the prophets, the hinge between the old covenant and the new. The hand of the LORD that the community perceives is the hand that has been shaping him for this purpose since before his birth.

The motif of a whole community sharing in the response to God's action — neighbours and relatives rejoicing, all who heard wondering, everyone laying these things up in their hearts — reflects Luke's consistent understanding that the gospel is not a private transaction between an individual and God. It is a public event that transforms communities.

The birth of John affects not only Zechariah and Elizabeth but the entire social network of their neighbourhood. The ripple of grace always extends further than the point of impact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's obedience at the naming — writing “his name is John” without qualification, against the family's expectation — is the delayed obedience of a man whom nine months of silence have changed. He came into the temple a man of correct theology and insufficient trust. He emerges from the silence a man who writes the word of God on a tablet before he says a word of his own.

The discipline has done its work. The man who needed a sign is now content to be one — the father who names his child what God chose, regardless of what the neighbours think.

The fear that falls on the community is the biblical response to the nearness of the holy. This is not terror but the awe that the presence of God in human history always produces. They sense that something larger than ordinary life is moving through the birth of this child, and they are right.

The instinct to hold that sense carefully — to lay it up in the heart — is exactly the right response to grace that exceeds our comprehension. Not analysis, not immediate explanation, but faithful keeping: holding what has been received until it is better understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.

Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Exactly as the angel said. God’s word fulfilled.

And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her. Literally “that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her”. Everyone recognised that God had done it.

And they rejoiced with her. The angel had promised: many will rejoice at his birth (v. 14). Fulfilled. Rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15).

In a sentence. Elizabeth gave birth to a son, and her neighbours and relatives rejoiced with her at the Lord’s great mercy.

On a Tuesday. When God blesses someone you know, rejoice with them wholeheartedly, without envy.

parallels.desc: everyone who hears will laugh over me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered, 'No; he shall be called John.' And they said to her, 'None of your relatives is called by this name.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. They would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered: no; he shall be called John. They said to her: none of your relatives is called by this name.

And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign God gave to Abraham (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). John is born into the covenant people and receives its sign. Jesus will be circumcised too (2:21).

And they would have called him Zechariah after his father. Naming at circumcision was customary (as with Jesus, 2:21). Naming a son after his father or grandfather was common.

No; he shall be called John. Elizabeth knew the name, either from Zechariah writing it, or by the Spirit. She stands firm against family custom.

None of your relatives is called by this name. The name breaks with family tradition. Something new is beginning. John belongs not to his family’s line, but to God’s purpose. His name says: the Lord has been gracious.

In a sentence. At the child’s circumcision, the relatives wanted to name him after his father, but Elizabeth insisted he be called John, a name no one in the family had.

On a Tuesday. Obeying God sometimes means breaking with family expectations. Do it graciously, but do it.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the name was often given then.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, 'His name is John.' And they all wondered. And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made signs to his father, asking what he wanted him to be called. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote: his name is John. And they all wondered. Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.

And they made signs to his father. Which suggests he was deaf as well as mute (v. 20, where the word kōphos can mean both).

And he asked for a writing tablet. A wooden board coated with wax, written on with a stylus.

His name is John. Not “his name shall be”, but “his name is”. It was settled by God; Zechariah simply obeys. Nine months earlier he had not believed the angel’s word. Now he obeys it exactly.

And they all wondered. Elizabeth and Zechariah, who could not have consulted each other in words, agreed.

And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed. At the moment he obeyed, the discipline was lifted, as Gabriel had said (v. 20).

And he spoke, blessing God. His first words after nine months of silence were praise. No complaint about the discipline. The silence had done its work: the doubter has become a worshipper. His song follows (vv. 68–79).

In a sentence. When asked, Zechariah wrote that the child’s name was John, and at once he could speak again, and his first words were praise to God.

For worship. Let God’s discipline turn you to praise. When he opens your mouth, use it to bless him.
verseByVerse.note: A writing tablet was a wooden board coated with wax.

verseByVerse.quote: And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, 'What then will this child be?' For the hand of the Lord was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear came on all their neighbours, and all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea. All who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: what then will this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.

And fear came on all their neighbors. Awe at the evident work of God.

And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea. The news spread. Some of those who heard it would remember it thirty years later, when John appeared preaching in the wilderness.

And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts. They kept thinking about it, as Mary did (2:19, 51).

What then will this child be? The question everyone asked. The answer: the greatest of the prophets, and the forerunner of the Lord.

For the hand of the Lord was with him. Luke’s comment. God’s power and favour were on him from the beginning (Acts 11:21).

In a sentence. Awe spread through the hill country, and everyone who heard wondered what this child would become, for the Lord’s hand was clearly on him.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the children you know: that the hand of the Lord would be with them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zechariah's song — called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin, “Blessed” — is the longest prophecy in Luke's first chapter and in many ways its theological climax. Where Mary's Magnificat looked back at what God has done throughout Israel's history, the Benedictus looks forward to what God is now doing through the two children, and across the whole sweep of the covenant from Abraham to this moment.

It is the song of an old priest who has spent nine months in silence, and who opens his mouth for the first time not with relief or apology or explanation but with praise and prophecy.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 68-75) is about Jesus: the God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people, has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and has fulfilled the oath he swore to Abraham, so that his people might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all their days.

The second (vv. 76-79) is about John: the child will be called the prophet of the Most High, will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, and will give knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of God by which the sunrise will visit them from on high. The two movements map exactly onto the two births — the greater to Jesus, the preparatory to John.

Verse 77 is the interpretive key to the whole song, and it answers the objection a modern reader raises at v. 71. Rome was never overthrown; Jerusalem fell within a lifetime. But the salvation Zechariah means is defined by Zechariah himself: knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins. The enemies in view are deeper than any empire.

The image of the sunrise from on high is among the most beautiful in Luke's Gospel. Zechariah the priest knows his prophets — the great light dawning on a people in darkness (Isa. 9:2), the sun of righteousness rising with healing (Mal. 4:2) — and the image he chooses reaches back through centuries of longing.

The Sunrise — the one who gives light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, and who guides their feet into the way of peace. Nine months of silence have filled this man's mouth with something far better than anything he said before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Benedictus is covenant theology at its most compact. Zechariah identifies the coming of Jesus as the fulfilment of three overlapping promises: the Davidic covenant (the horn of salvation in the house of David, vv. 69-70), the Abrahamic covenant (the oath sworn to Abraham, vv. 73-75), and the prophetic promise (the forerunner going before the Lord, vv. 76-77).

All three lines of God's covenant faithfulness converge in the two children born in this chapter. The God who made promises to Abraham two thousand years earlier is fulfilling them — not approximately, not symbolically, but specifically, in the births of two real children at a datable moment in history.

The purpose of that salvation is stated with remarkable precision in vv. 74-75: that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. Salvation is not merely rescue. It is freedom for a particular kind of life.

The one delivered from the enemy's hand is freed not for autonomous self-determination but for worship — for service before the face of God, in holiness and righteousness, without the crippling fear that guilt and condemnation produce. This is the goal of redemption: a people who serve God freely because they have been freely saved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's first words after nine months of silence are praise and prophecy — not self-vindication, not explanation, not a word of reproach for the community that doubted him. The discipline of the long silence has produced a man who, when he opens his mouth, speaks entirely about God and about what God is doing.

That is the fruit of involuntary silence used well: what comes out at the end is not our own words. Preachers, teachers and parents forced into seasons of silence — made to listen rather than speak, to receive rather than give — often find that what finally emerges is purer and truer than anything they said before it.

The Benedictus ends with John: the child grew and became strong in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel. The wilderness is both his geographical home and his spiritual formation. He is being shaped in hiddenness for the public ministry that will announce the Coming One.

Every major figure in redemptive history has had a wilderness — Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, and the Lord himself. The wilderness is not the failure of the plan. It is the formation of the messenger, and it cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people.

The Benedictus. Zechariah’s song is called the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin (“blessed”). Like Mary’s, it is woven from the Old Testament. It has two halves: praise for what God has done through the Messiah of David’s line (vv. 68–75), and a prophecy about John’s role (vv. 76–79). Notice: Zechariah, a priest, praises God first for the Messiah, not for his own son. John is secondary; Jesus is the centre.

Filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied. The priest who doubted now speaks as a prophet. The Spirit, silent for centuries, is active again.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. A traditional Jewish blessing (Psalm 41:13; 72:18; 106:48).

For he has visited. “Visited” (epeskepsato): come to look after, care for. In the Old Testament God “visited” his people to rescue them, as in Egypt (Exodus 4:31). God himself has come to his people, in the person of Jesus (7:16; 19:44).

And redeemed his people. Literally “made redemption for his people”. Redemption is release by payment of a price, from slavery or captivity. The exodus was God’s great act of redemption in the Old Testament (Exodus 6:6). Now God has acted to bring a greater redemption, which Jesus will accomplish by giving his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45). Again the past tense: it is as good as done, though the Messiah is not yet born.

In a sentence. Filled with the Spirit, Zechariah blessed the God of Israel for coming to his people and bringing them redemption.

For worship. God has visited and redeemed his people in Jesus. Bless him for it.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah’s song, known as the Benedictus, celebrates God’s faithfulness in terms of the Old Testament promises.

parallels.desc: blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
he sent redemption to his people

verseByVerse.quote: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
verseByVerse.commentary:
And has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.

And has raised up a horn of salvation for us. A horn was a symbol of strength, like the horns of a wild ox or bull (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:10). A “horn of salvation” is a mighty Saviour. David called God “the horn of my salvation” (Psalm 18:2). Psalm 132:17: There I will make a horn to sprout for David.

In the house of his servant David. The Messiah comes from David’s line, as promised (v. 32). Zechariah was from Aaron’s line, but he praises God for the king from David’s line, not the priest from his own. Mary’s child, not yet born, is the horn.

As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old. Everything happens according to Scripture. The prophets spoke God’s word (Acts 3:21).

That we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us. Psalm 106:10. Zechariah would have thought first of Israel’s political enemies, the Romans. But the deeper enemies are sin, death and Satan (Hebrews 2:14–15; Colossians 2:15). Jesus came to deliver from these.

In a sentence. God has raised up a mighty Saviour from David’s line, as the prophets foretold, to rescue his people from their enemies.

On a Tuesday. Christ is your horn of salvation, stronger than every enemy you face. Trust his strength.
verseByVerse.note: A horn was a symbol of strength, like a bull’s horns.

parallels.desc: I will make a horn to sprout for David

verseByVerse.quote: to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

To show the mercy promised to our fathers. God’s covenant love, promised long ago (Micah 7:20).

And to remember his holy covenant. God “remembers” his covenant: not that he had forgotten, but that he now acts on it (Exodus 2:24; Psalm 105:8–9). Zechariah’s name, “the LORD remembers”, is fulfilled; and Elizabeth’s name contains the word “oath”.

The oath that he swore to our father Abraham. Genesis 22:16–18, after Abraham offered Isaac: By myself I have sworn … I will surely bless you … and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. God swore by himself, because there was no one greater (Hebrews 6:13–18). His promise cannot fail.

That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear. The purpose of redemption is not simply freedom, but service. Freed from slavery to sin and fear, we are free to serve God, as Israel was freed from Egypt to worship God (Exodus 4:23). “Serve” (latreuein) means worship as well as serve. “Without fear”: without fear of enemies, and without fear of God’s judgement, because we are forgiven (Romans 8:15; 1 John 4:18).

In holiness and righteousness before him all our days. The life of the redeemed: holiness toward God and righteousness toward others, every day of our lives (Ephesians 4:24; Titus 2:11–14). Salvation produces a changed life.

In a sentence. God has kept the covenant oath he swore to Abraham, rescuing his people so that they can worship and serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness, all their days.

On a Tuesday. You were redeemed in order to serve. Serve God today, not in fear, but as one set free, in holiness and righteousness.

parallels.desc: the covenant he made with Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins.

And you, child. Now Zechariah turns to his eight-day-old son, perhaps holding him in his arms.

Will be called the prophet of the Most High. Jesus will be called Son of the Most High (v. 32); John is the prophet of the Most High. A great title, but not the greatest. The first true prophet in Israel for four centuries.

For you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways. Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3. John goes before “the Lord”, and the one he goes before is Jesus. Again, Jesus is identified as the Lord God.

To give knowledge of salvation to his people. Not to save them himself, but to tell them what salvation is and where it is found (John 1:29).

In the forgiveness of their sins. Key words. Here is what salvation really is. Not first freedom from Rome, but forgiveness of sins. Zechariah, and Luke, make clear that the enemies of verse 71 are, above all, our sins and their consequences. John will preach a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (3:3). Jesus will send his disciples to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (24:47).

In a sentence. Zechariah prophesied that John would be the prophet of the Most High, preparing the way for the Lord and teaching God’s people that salvation means the forgiveness of sins.

On a Tuesday. Salvation, at its heart, is the forgiveness of your sins. Have you received it? Tell someone else where to find it.

parallels.desc: a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins

verseByVerse.quote: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the sunrise shall visit us from on high, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

Because of the tender mercy of our God. Literally “the bowels of mercy”, from the inner organs, the seat of the deepest emotions. The source of salvation is God’s deep, heartfelt compassion. Not our merit.

Whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high. “Sunrise” (anatolē) means the dawn, the rising of the sun. It is also used in the Greek Old Testament to translate “Branch”, a title for the Messiah (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). The Messiah is like the dawn breaking. Malachi 4:2: for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. Isaiah 60:1–3; Numbers 24:17 (a star shall come out of Jacob). “From on high”: from heaven. The Messiah comes from God.

To give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. Isaiah 9:2: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone. Isaiah wrote this of Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1), where Jesus would minister. Darkness is ignorance, sin and despair; the shadow of death hangs over every human life. Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12). And Isaiah 42:6–7; 49:6 speak of the servant as a light for the nations: the light is for Gentiles too (2:32).

To guide our feet into the way of peace. Peace (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is the fullness of well-being that comes from being right with God: peace with God (Romans 5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. The angels will sing of it at Jesus’ birth (2:14).

In a sentence. Through God’s tender mercy, the Messiah will dawn on us like the sunrise from heaven, bringing light to those in darkness and death, and guiding us into peace.

For worship. The sun has risen. If you live in shadow, look to Christ, the dawn from on high, and let him guide your feet into peace.

parallels.desc: the sun of righteousness shall rise
light on those in the land of deep darkness

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

And the child grew and became strong in spirit. Similar words are used of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:21, 26) and of Jesus (2:40, 52). Growth in body and in spirit, by the Spirit with whom he was filled.

And he was in the wilderness. The wilderness of Judea, the barren desert between the hill country and the Dead Sea. Zechariah and Elizabeth were old and probably died while John was young. The wilderness was where Israel had been formed, where Elijah had fled, and where the prophets had said God would make a way (Isaiah 40:3). Some have suggested that John was raised by the Essene community at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, who took in boys; this is possible but unproved.

Until the day of his public appearance to Israel. About thirty years later (3:1–2). Years of hidden preparation for a short public ministry. God is not in a hurry.

In a sentence. John grew strong in body and spirit and lived in the wilderness until the day he appeared publicly to Israel.

On a Tuesday. God prepares his servants in hidden places, often for many years. Don’t despise your wilderness years.

parallels.desc: the word of God came to John in the wilderness

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Chapter 2 of Luke is the world's most familiar story — and precisely because of that familiarity, it is the story most easily received without being heard. We have heard the angels and the manger and the shepherds so many times that the shocking strangeness of the events has been smoothed away by repetition. Luke is a careful historian, and he intends these details to be astonishing: the Emperor of Rome issues a decree, and the decree unwittingly fulfils a prophecy he knows nothing about. The Son of God is born not in a palace but in the place where animals feed. Heaven's armies appear not to priests or rulers but to shepherds — the lowest of the low in first-century Jewish society. The incarnation is not a dignified event. It is a scandal.

The chapter moves through four scenes: the birth in Bethlehem (vv. 1–7), the angels and the shepherds (vv. 8–20), the presentation in the temple with Simeon and Anna (vv. 21–40), and the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple (vv. 41–52). Together they establish three things about the child: he is born in the line of David and in fulfilment of Scripture; he is recognised by the Spirit-filled as the one Israel has been waiting for; and he understands himself, from the earliest age, as defined by a unique relationship with the Father that supersedes even the claims of family.

The presentation in the temple (vv. 21–40) is one of Luke's most theologically dense passages. In Simeon's song — the Nunc Dimittis — the scope of the child's significance is made explicit for the first time: he is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” He is not merely the Messiah of Israel; he is the fulfilment of the universal promise of Isaiah (42:6; 49:6), the Servant who is to be the light of the nations. And the shadow of the cross falls even here: Simeon tells Mary that a sword will pierce her soul, that this child is set for the falling and rising of many, that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed. The manger casts the shadow of the cross from the very beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of Jesus is introduced by one of the most politically freighted sentences in the New Testament: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus.” Augustus was the most powerful man in the world — the man who had ended a century of Roman civil war and inaugurated the Pax Romana. He called himself divi filius, son of the deified Julius. The Roman world hailed him as saviour, as lord, as the bringer of peace and of good news.

Luke places that decree at the head of the story of the one who is the true Son of God, the true Saviour, the true Lord, the true bringer of peace and good news. The contrast is not accidental. Luke's Gospel is, among other things, a counter-narrative to the propaganda of Rome — and it never once raises its voice to say so.

Augustus's census serves God's purposes without Augustus knowing it. He orders a registration for taxation; God uses it to bring a Galilean couple to Bethlehem, where Micah had said the ruler of Israel would be born (Mic. 5:2). The most powerful man on earth is, unwittingly, the instrument for keeping a seven-hundred-year-old promise.

This is the biblical theology of providential history. God works through the ordinary and sometimes brutal machinery of human politics to accomplish his purposes, and neither the emperor's ignorance nor his indifference can obstruct it. Nor does God remove the cost: the couple still walk ninety miles, and Mary still walks them at the end of a pregnancy.

The manger is the detail that has shaped two thousand years of Christian imagination, and rightly. Mary wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no place for them in the inn. The word rendered “inn” (katalyma) more often means the guest room of a private house — it is the word used of the upper room at the Last Supper (22:11) — and the likeliest picture is a crowded family home whose guest room was already full.

Either way the scene is the same: the one who is the bread of life is laid in the box the animals eat from; the one who made every star has nowhere to be put. The incarnation is the ultimate act of self-emptying, and Luke communicates it not with theological abstraction but with the concrete detail of the trough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The juxtaposition of Caesar Augustus and the infant Jesus is a statement about the nature of true power. Augustus commanded armies, controlled the Mediterranean, and issued decrees that moved millions across the empire. The child in the manger will command no army for thirty years, will spend his public life in a small region of a minor province, and will die as a criminal.

And yet it is the child, not the emperor, who is worshipped two thousand years later — whose kingdom, as Zechariah sang, has no end. Luke is asking his reader to see, from the first chapter onward, that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.

The swaddling cloths are not merely a practical detail; they are a sign. When the shepherds are told they will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger, the cloths are part of the identifier. They say: he is truly human, wrapped as every newborn was wrapped, indistinguishable at a glance from any other child in Bethlehem.

The manger says the other half: that his humanity is received in the most vulnerable and dependent form imaginable. The eternal Son of God becomes a baby who cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, and cannot survive an hour without his mother.
verseByVerse.examples:
The census that brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem is a reminder that God uses inconvenient, uncomfortable, even oppressive circumstances to accomplish his purposes. Joseph and Mary did not choose to travel ninety miles at the end of a pregnancy. The Roman state imposed it. And in the imposition, the plan of God was fulfilled.

The Christian who finds himself in circumstances he did not choose — a redundancy that opens a door, a move that leads to an unexpected church, a disruption that turns out to have been an appointment — is living in the pattern of the incarnation. Being in the centre of God's will has never meant being outside other people's decisions.

The manger has been the comfort of every Christian who has ever felt overlooked, marginalised, or without a place. The Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation. He took what was available, in the circumstances Providence had arranged, and made it holy.

No circumstance is too humble, and no situation too undignified, to be the place where God chooses to be present. The God who was born in a stable is found in the most improbable places — which is exactly where his people most often need to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration, when Quirinius was governor of Syria.

Setting. Luke sets the birth of Jesus on the stage of world history. The most powerful man in the world issues a decree, and without knowing it, moves a poor couple to the very town where the prophet Micah said the Messiah would be born (Micah 5:2). God rules the emperors.

Caesar Augustus. Octavian, the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar, who ended Rome’s civil wars and became the first Roman emperor, ruling from 27 BC to AD 14. The Senate gave him the title Augustus, “revered one”. He was hailed in inscriptions as “saviour” and “god”, and his birthday was called “the beginning of the good news (euangelia) for the world”, and he was credited with bringing peace (the Pax Romana). Luke’s readers would notice the contrast: the angels announce good news of a true Saviour, Christ the Lord, and true peace (vv. 10–14), born in a feeding trough.

That all the world should be registered. “All the world” (oikoumenē) means the Roman Empire. A registration, or census, was taken for taxation and military purposes. Augustus ordered several censuses in various provinces during his reign.

This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria. A well-known historical puzzle. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius is known to have been governor of Syria from AD 6, when he conducted a census in Judea after it came under direct Roman rule (Acts 5:37 mentions the revolt it provoked). But Jesus was born before Herod died in 4 BC. Several solutions have been proposed. Quirinius may have held an earlier office in Syria, perhaps as a military commander, during which an earlier census began; there is some evidence he was active in the region then. Or the Greek may be read, as the ESV footnote allows, as “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria”, distinguishing it from the famous later census. Luke was a careful historian (1:3), who knew about the later census (Acts 5:37), and is unlikely to have confused them. The puzzle is not settled, but it is not a proof of error.

In a sentence. The emperor Augustus decreed a census of the empire, the first, when Quirinius was governor of Syria.

On a Tuesday. The decisions of governments, however powerful, serve God’s purposes. He is working even through what seems like bureaucratic inconvenience.
verseByVerse.note: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14. The ESV notes that verse 2 can also be read “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria” — the dating of this census is debated.

parallels.desc: the revolt “in the days of the census”

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone went to be registered, each to his own town. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.

Each to his own town. The town of his family’s origin, or where he held property. An Egyptian census edict from AD 104 similarly required people to return to their home districts.

And Joseph also went up from Galilee. “Up” because Judea is higher, and Jerusalem is always “up”.

To the city of David, which is called Bethlehem. Bethlehem, about five miles (8 km) south of Jerusalem, was David’s home town (1 Samuel 16:1; 17:12). The name means “house of bread”: the Bread of Life is born there (John 6:35). Micah had prophesied: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2). Jerusalem was usually called the city of David; Luke gives the title to humble Bethlehem.

Because he was of the house and lineage of David. Jesus’ legal descent from David came through Joseph (1:27).

With Mary, his betrothed, who was with child. Still “betrothed”: Matthew tells us Joseph had taken her as his wife but had no union with her until the child was born (Matthew 1:24–25). Why did she go? Perhaps she was also required to register, or perhaps Joseph would not leave her alone in Nazareth to face gossip. The journey of about 80–90 miles (130–145 km) would have taken several days, hard for a woman near the end of pregnancy.

In a sentence. Because of the census, Joseph, a descendant of David, travelled from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s town, with Mary his betrothed, who was pregnant.

On a Tuesday. God fulfilled a prophecy seven centuries old by means of a tax census. He is faithful to his word in ways you would never expect.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth to Bethlehem is a journey of roughly 80–90 miles.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were there, the time came for her to give birth. She gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.

And while they were there. We do not know how long they had been there. The tradition that she gave birth on the night they arrived is not in the text.

She gave birth to her firstborn son. Told with the greatest simplicity. The eternal Son of God was born as a human baby. “Firstborn” carries the meaning of legal rights and of being consecrated to God (v. 23; Exodus 13:2). It also implies that Mary had other children afterwards, though it does not require it (Matthew 13:55–56). And Christ is “the firstborn of all creation” and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:15, 18).

And wrapped him in swaddling cloths. Strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn, to keep the limbs straight and warm. Normal care, done by Mary herself, without a midwife, it seems. He was not neglected (Ezekiel 16:4). Solomon was swaddled too (Wisdom of Solomon 7:4–5): even the greatest king began like this.

And laid him in a manger. A feeding trough for animals, perhaps of stone or wood. The tradition of a stable or a cave (from the second century) comes from the manger. Many houses had an area at the lower end, or a cave beneath, where animals were kept at night, with mangers.

Because there was no place for them in the inn. “Inn” (katalyma) is not the word for a commercial inn (that is pandocheion, 10:34). It means a lodging place or guest room, the same word as the upper room of the Last Supper (22:11). The guest room of the house where they stayed was probably full, perhaps with other relatives in town for the census, so they were given the lower level, among the animals. Either way, the point stands: the Lord of glory was born in the humblest circumstances. No room. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). He who was rich, for your sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In a sentence. In Bethlehem, Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in strips of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the guest room.

For worship. The Son of God began his human life in a feeding trough. Worship him for his humility, and make room for him.
verseByVerse.note: Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. A manger is a feeding trough. The word for “inn” can mean a guest room — the same word used for the upper room in 22:11.

parallels.desc: though he was rich, he became poor

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The announcement of the birth is made not to the emperor, not to the high priest, not to the Sanhedrin, not to the scholars who could have quoted the prophecy from memory — but to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in a field at night.

In first-century Jewish society shepherds occupied the lowest rungs of the ladder. Their work made ritual purity nearly impossible to maintain; later rabbinic rulings counted their testimony unreliable; and the settled respectable classes regarded them with suspicion. It is to these men, in this field, at this hour, that the glory of the Lord appears — the same glory that had filled the tabernacle and had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple.

The angel's announcement is one of the most compressed theological summaries in the New Testament: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.” Three titles in seven words. Saviour — the one who rescues; a title Caesar also claimed and could not fulfil. Christ (Christos) — the Anointed One, the fulfilment of Israel's whole prophetic tradition. Lord (kyrios) — the title Israel's Scriptures give to God himself. All three at once, all three together, all three true.

The sign given to confirm it is the inverse of every sign of power in human history: a baby, wrapped as every baby was wrapped, lying in a feeding trough. Kings are found in palaces and gods in temples. This one is identified by the humblest container in the village.

Then the sky fills. The heavenly host is a military picture — the armies of heaven drawn up over a hillside, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.”

That last phrase is sometimes rendered “peace, good will toward men,” following a variant reading behind the older English versions. The better-attested text is the one the ESV follows: the peace comes to the people of God's good pleasure. That is not a colder reading but a warmer one — a goodwill announced to everyone in general is guaranteed to no one in particular, whereas this peace rests on the sovereign choice of God, which does not move.

The section ends where it must. The shepherds go with haste, find exactly what they were told they would find, tell everybody, and go back to work — glorifying and praising God, with the sheep still to be watched and nothing whatever in their circumstances altered.
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is Luke's first major instance of the great reversal that runs through his whole Gospel: the last are first, the humble are exalted, and those the world dismisses are the ones God chooses to honour. God shows here, in advance, the design he later carried out when he chose poor and uneducated fishermen for apostles.

The good news comes first to those who have nothing — no status, no ritual purity, no legal standing — because the good news is precisely that God's grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things.

The sign given to the shepherds requires a different kind of looking than a sign of glory would have required. A God who appears in unexpected humility can be walked past. The shepherds do not go looking for what they would have expected; they go looking for exactly what they were told to expect, and they find it.

And Luke is careful about the response of everyone else. The neighbours wondered — a word he uses often and never confuses with faith. Wonder is a doorway and not a destination. Mary, in the same room, does something different with the same information (v. 19), and the contrast is the point of the paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples:
The shepherds' response — “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened” — is the model of responsive faith. They do not debate the vision. They do not wait for a second confirmation. They do not propose considering the matter carefully before acting. They go with haste, and they find exactly what they were told they would find.

The gap between hearing the word of God and acting on it is where faith most often quietly dies — not by a decision to disobey, but by a perfectly reasonable delay that becomes permanent. The shepherds closed the gap in about ten seconds.

They then became the first evangelists of the New Testament. Fishermen would follow; a tax collector would follow; a persecutor would follow. But the first to announce the birth of the Saviour were men whose word counted for little and who had nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen.

That is the pattern of Christian witness in every generation: not credentials, not eloquence, not social standing, but the testimony of those who have met God and cannot keep quiet about it. And note what they proclaimed — not their experience of the light and the fear, but “the saying that had been told them.” The message, not the sensation.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. An angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.

Shepherds out in the field. Shepherds were humble working men. In the rabbinic writings they were often looked down on, regarded as unreliable and unable to keep the ceremonial law, because their work kept them away. Their testimony was not accepted in court. Yet God sent his first announcement of the Messiah’s birth to them, not to the high priest or to Herod. The good news is for the lowly (1:52). And David, the shepherd king, was from Bethlehem; Jesus is the Good Shepherd (John 10:11).

Keeping watch over their flock by night. Taking turns to guard against thieves and wild animals. Flocks were kept in the open from spring to autumn, and sometimes all year in the milder Judean climate. The date of 25 December was chosen centuries later; we do not know the time of year. Some suggest these flocks near Bethlehem were raised for temple sacrifices.

And the glory of the Lord shone around them. The shining brightness of God’s presence, the shekinah, which filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). It had departed from the temple before the exile (Ezekiel 10). Now it appears again, in a field, to shepherds.

And they were filled with great fear. Literally “they feared a great fear”.

In a sentence. To shepherds keeping watch over their flock at night near Bethlehem, an angel appeared and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.

On a Tuesday. God came first to working men on the night shift. However ordinary your work, he can meet you there.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel said to them: fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.

Fear not. Again, the first word is comfort.

I bring you good news. The verb euangelizomai, from which comes “gospel”. This is the gospel.

Of great joy. Joy is the response to the gospel throughout Luke.

That will be for all the people. “The people” (laos) usually means Israel in Luke. But the joy will spread beyond (v. 32).

For unto you is born. “Unto you”: for shepherds. For you.

This day. “Today” (sēmeron) is a key word in Luke: today salvation has come (4:21; 19:9; 23:43).

In the city of David. Bethlehem, as promised (Micah 5:2).

A Savior. The title the empire gave to Augustus. But this is the true Saviour, who saves from sin (Matthew 1:21; Acts 5:31). The only time in the Gospels Jesus is called Saviour at his birth.

Who is Christ the Lord. Three titles in one breath. “Christ” (Christos): the Anointed One, the Messiah, the promised king from David’s line. “Lord” (Kyrios): the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name, Yahweh. A newborn baby is the Saviour, the Messiah, and the Lord God. The unique combination “Christ the Lord” appears only here in the New Testament. The baby in the manger is God.

In a sentence. The angel announced the good news of great joy: in Bethlehem a Saviour had been born that day, the Messiah and Lord.

For worship. Unto you is born a Saviour. Receive the news as good news, for you, today, and rejoice.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah; “Lord” was the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

parallels.desc: he will save his people from their sins
to us a child is born
the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.

And this will be a sign for you. A way to recognise him.

A baby wrapped in swaddling cloths. That was normal. Every newborn was swaddled.

And lying in a manger. That was not. No one laid a baby in a feeding trough. This would identify him among all the babies of Bethlehem.

The sign is the opposite of what you would expect. The Saviour, Christ the Lord, will be found not in a palace in silk, but in an animal’s feeding trough. That is the sign: his lowliness. It points to the whole shape of his life and death. And it meant the shepherds could come. They would not have been allowed into a palace; they could go into a place with animals.

In a sentence. The sign by which the shepherds would recognise the Saviour was a newborn baby lying in a feeding trough.

On a Tuesday. God’s greatest work is often found in the lowliest places. Look for Christ among the humble.

parallels.desc: the LORD himself will give you a sign

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!

A multitude of the heavenly host. “Host” (stratia) means an army. The armies of heaven, the angels who serve the Lord of hosts (1 Kings 22:19), have come not to fight but to sing. The armies of heaven announce peace.

Glory to God in the highest. In Latin, Gloria in excelsis Deo, sung in Christian worship for centuries. The birth of Jesus brings glory to God, in the highest heavens. The first purpose of the incarnation is God’s glory.

And on earth peace. Peace with God, reconciliation, the end of hostility between the holy God and rebellious humanity (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17). And the shalom that flows from it. Not the political peace of the Pax Romana, imposed by armies, but the peace Christ makes by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20).

Among those with whom he is pleased! Literally “among men of his good pleasure” (en anthrōpois eudokias). “His good pleasure” is God’s: those on whom God’s favour rests, whom he has chosen in his grace (Ephesians 1:5, 9 use the same word). The peace is not for all people indiscriminately, nor for those who are good enough to please God, but for those whom God, in his sovereign grace, has chosen to favour.

Textual note. The King James Version, following later manuscripts, reads “on earth peace, good will toward men”. The difference is one letter in Greek (eudokia or eudokias). The earliest and best manuscripts have eudokias, giving the ESV’s reading. The old reading is familiar from carols, but the better text points to God’s good pleasure.

In a sentence. A vast army of angels praised God, giving him glory in the highest and announcing peace on earth for those on whom his favour rests.

For worship. Join the angels: give glory to God for the birth of Christ. If you have peace with God, it is because his good pleasure rests on you, by grace.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV’s “among those with whom he is pleased” follows the better manuscripts; older translations read “good will toward men.”

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us. They went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.

Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened. “Thing” is literally “word” (rhēma), meaning both the event and the message. They act on the word at once. They do not doubt like Zechariah, but obey like Mary.

Which the Lord has made known to us. They knew the angel’s message came from the Lord.

And they went with haste. Leaving their flocks.

And found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger. Exactly as the angel said. The sign was fulfilled. Every word of God comes true.

In a sentence. When the angels left, the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found Mary, Joseph and the baby in the manger, just as they had been told.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks, respond at once. Go and see for yourself what he has done in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.

They made known the saying that had been told them. The shepherds became the first evangelists, telling what they had heard and seen. Men whose testimony would not be accepted in court were God’s first witnesses to the birth of Christ, as women would be to the resurrection.

And all who heard it wondered. “Wondered” (ethaumasan): were amazed. A frequent response in Luke. But wonder is not the same as faith; we do not hear of what became of them.

In a sentence. Having seen the child, the shepherds told everyone what had been said about him, and all who heard were amazed.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need credentials to tell others about Jesus. Tell what you have heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.

But Mary. A contrast with the general amazement. Mary goes deeper.

Treasured up all these things. “Treasured up” (synetērei): kept carefully, preserved, held on to. “Things” is again rhēmata, words and events. She kept them in her memory. This is probably one of Luke’s hints at his source: who else could have told him these things, but Mary herself (1:2–3)?

Pondering them in her heart. “Pondering” (symballousa): putting together, comparing, thinking through, seeking the meaning. The angel’s words, the shepherds’ story, the manger, the prophecies. She did not understand everything (v. 50), but she reflected on it. Mary is a model of meditation on God’s word and works.

In a sentence. Mary carefully kept all these things and kept thinking them over in her heart.

On a Tuesday. Don’t just be amazed by Christ. Treasure and ponder what God has said and done. Take time today to reflect on a passage of Scripture.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.

And the shepherds returned. To their flocks, to their ordinary work. Their circumstances were the same; they were not.

Glorifying and praising God. They join the angels’ song (v. 14).

For all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them. Heard (from the angel) and seen (the child): everything matched. The word of God and the facts agreed.

In a sentence. The shepherds went back to their work praising God for all they had heard and seen, exactly as they had been told.

For worship. Go back to your ordinary work today glorifying and praising God. Christ is born, and everything is as he said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice and waiting encounters the one the whole system had been pointing at.

Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem for two duties, both required by the law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Lev. 12:1-8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exod. 13:2, 12-15; Num. 18:15-16). They bring the offering of the poor — two birds rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us plainly what the family's circumstances were. The King of heaven and earth was raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in the language of the faithful remnant: righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him. That phrase, the consolation of Israel, comes from Isaiah 40 — “Comfort, comfort my people” — the promised end of exile and return of God to his people. Simeon has been waiting inside that chapter his whole life, and the Spirit has promised him he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ.

Now, as a young couple with the offering of the poor come into the courts, the Spirit moves him. He takes the child into his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is a warm weight in his hands.

His song — the Nunc Dimittis — is among the most moving passages in Luke. The verbs are those of a sentry being stood down after a long watch. He can go now: his eyes have seen God's salvation, and the salvation he is holding is not for Israel only but “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” — the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs (42:6; 49:6) and the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun.

And then the shadow falls. The child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed; and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel. They are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected, and the one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees all of it.

Anna is the second witness the law required (Deut. 19:15) — a daughter of Asher, one of the tribes long written off as lost, who has given decades of widowhood to fasting and prayer in that building and who arrives at exactly the right hour. And the section closes with the family's return to Nazareth and a single sentence covering the boy's whole childhood: he grew, became strong, was filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological seed of the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, Luke's Gospel contains within it the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world.
