This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile reader, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal reach of the good news. The trajectory is established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has waited his whole life to say what he now says and who is ready to die.

Simeon's warning to Mary — that a sword will pierce her own soul — has been understood in the tradition as pointing to her presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25-27). The word is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, and Simeon does not soften it. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves.

But the clause “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” shows a wider purpose. The coming of Jesus forces a crisis of decision in every heart; he does not leave people neutral. He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” — the stone of Isaiah 8:14 laid in the middle of the road. His presence divides, and in dividing it discloses what was already there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of a man who has given up, but the discharge of a sentry who has received what he was waiting for. And notice what his peace does not rest on: not on achievement (we are told nothing of what he accomplished), not on longevity, but on what his eyes have seen.

The Christian who has seen that same salvation — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith, and has taken hold of it — has precisely what Simeon had, and may face death on precisely the same terms. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Christ known in life.

Anna is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She had been waiting most of her adult life — decades of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She did not give up, did not grow cynical, and did not stop praying because the answer had not come. When it came, she was exactly where she had always been.

Her years were not the waiting room for her ministry; they were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when everyone around her saw a queue — and who knew, by name, everyone in Jerusalem who was waiting to be told. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous. It is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

When he was circumcised. On the eighth day, as the law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), like John (1:59). Jesus was born under the law (Galatians 4:4), and from the beginning he fulfilled it perfectly, on our behalf (Matthew 5:17). Circumcision was the sign of the covenant, and the first shedding of his blood.

He was called Jesus. “The LORD saves” (1:31).

The name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. Mary and Joseph obeyed exactly. The name was not their choice but God’s.

In a sentence. On the eighth day Jesus was circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel had commanded before he was conceived.

On a Tuesday. Jesus kept God’s law from his first week of life, for you. His obedience is counted as yours.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord) and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

Two ceremonies. Luke combines two separate requirements of the law.

The time came for their purification. After giving birth to a son, a mother was ceremonially unclean for forty days, and then brought an offering to the priest: a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove for a sin offering. If she could not afford a lamb, she could bring two doves or pigeons instead (Leviticus 12:1–8). “Their” purification may include Joseph, or the family, or simply be loose phrasing.

To present him to the Lord. Every firstborn son belonged to God, because God had spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). The firstborn had to be redeemed, bought back, by a payment of five shekels to a priest (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke does not mention the payment, but speaks of presenting him, as Hannah presented Samuel to the Lord for his service (1 Samuel 1:22–28). Jesus is truly holy to the Lord, given wholly to God.

A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8). Mary and Joseph could not afford a lamb. Jesus was born into a poor family. And the irony: they could not afford a lamb, but they brought the Lamb of God (John 1:29). A sin offering was brought by Mary, as for every mother; she too was a sinner needing atonement.

In a sentence. Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple to present their firstborn to the Lord and to offer the poor family’s sacrifice for Mary’s purification.

On a Tuesday. Jesus grew up in a poor family. He understands financial hardship. And everything you have, including your children, belongs to God.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

A man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. Not said to be a priest; an ordinary godly man. Tradition makes him old, though Luke does not say so (v. 29 implies it).

Righteous and devout. “Righteous” toward God’s law; “devout” (eulabēs), careful, reverent, conscientious in religion.

Waiting for the consolation of Israel. “Consolation” (paraklēsin): comfort, encouragement. Isaiah 40:1: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. The comfort God had promised his people, the coming of the Messiah to end their suffering and exile. Simeon was one of the faithful remnant who were waiting, like Anna (v. 38) and Joseph of Arimathea (23:51).

And the Holy Spirit was upon him. The Spirit, who had been silent in Israel, is now active: on Elizabeth, Zechariah, Mary, John and Simeon. Three times in three verses Luke mentions the Spirit in connection with Simeon (vv. 25, 26, 27).

That he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. A personal promise. “The Lord’s Christ”: the Messiah who belongs to God, God’s anointed one (Psalm 2:2).

In a sentence. Simeon, a righteous and devout man in Jerusalem waiting for God’s promised comfort, had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would see the Messiah before he died.

On a Tuesday. Waiting on God is not wasted time. Wait faithfully, as Simeon did, for what God has promised.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms, blessed God and said:

And he came in the Spirit into the temple. Led by the Spirit at exactly the right moment. God’s timing is precise.

When the parents brought in the child Jesus. Into the temple courts, perhaps the Court of the Women. One poor couple among many, with a baby. No one else noticed.

He took him up in his arms. The old man takes the baby in his arms. The long wait ends in an embrace.

And blessed God. Praise is his first response.

In a sentence. Led by the Spirit into the temple just as Jesus’ parents brought him in, Simeon took the child in his arms and praised God.

For worship. Simeon held God’s salvation in his arms. By faith you can hold Christ too. Bless God for him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.

The Nunc Dimittis. Simeon’s song is called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin (“Now you dismiss”). It has been sung at evening services for centuries.

Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace. “Lord” (despota), Master, the word a slave used of his owner. “Depart” (apolyeis): release, dismiss, as a master releases a slave from duty, or as a watchman is relieved at the end of his shift. Simeon had been on watch for the Messiah. Now he has seen him, and he can be released: he can die in peace. A man who has seen Christ is ready to die.

According to your word. The promise of verse 26 has been kept.

For my eyes have seen your salvation. Simeon looks at a baby and says: I have seen your salvation. Salvation is not a thing, an idea or a system. It is a person. To see Jesus is to see God’s salvation. Isaiah 52:10: all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

That you have prepared in the presence of all peoples. Not only for Israel. Prepared by God, in the sight of all the nations.

A light for revelation to the Gentiles. Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. In the temple of Israel, at the presentation of a Jewish baby, under the law of Moses, an old Jewish man announces that this child is salvation for the Gentiles. This is the theme of Luke and Acts: the gospel goes from Jerusalem to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8; 13:47, where Paul quotes the same verse).

And for glory to your people Israel. The Messiah is Israel’s greatest glory, the one in whom all her history and hope are fulfilled (Romans 9:5).

In a sentence. Simeon praised God that he could now die in peace, for he had seen God’s salvation, a light to reveal God to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

For worship. If you have seen Christ by faith, you can face death in peace. Pray Simeon’s prayer at the end of the day.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father and his mother marvelled at what was said about him.

His father. Luke calls Joseph Jesus’ father, as Mary does (v. 48). He was his legal father, who raised him, though not his biological father (3:23: as was supposed).

Marveled at what was said about him. Even after angels and shepherds, they were amazed. Perhaps especially by the words about the Gentiles. They were learning, step by step, who this child was.

In a sentence. Joseph and Mary were amazed at what Simeon said about Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The more you learn about Christ, the more there is to marvel at. Never lose your wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.

And Simeon blessed them. The parents. He does not bless Jesus; the child is the source of blessing.

And said to Mary his mother. Not to Joseph, perhaps because Joseph would not live to see what follows.

This child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel. Now a darker note. Jesus will divide Israel. Some will fall because of him, stumbling over him; others will rise, be raised up, through faith in him. He is the stone that some stumble over and others build on (Isaiah 8:14–15; 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–8; Luke 20:17–18). No one can be neutral toward him.

And for a sign that is opposed. A sign spoken against. Jesus will be rejected, opposed, contradicted, and finally killed.

And a sword will pierce through your own soul also. A personal prophecy for Mary. She will suffer deep grief. Her son will be rejected and misunderstood, even by his own family (8:19–21). And she will stand at the cross and watch him die (John 19:25). The joy of the angels’ song is not the whole story. The salvation of the world will cost her the agony of seeing her son crucified.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. Jesus reveals what is in people’s hearts. How people respond to him exposes what they really are (5:22; 6:8; John 3:19–21). He is the great revealer.

In a sentence. Simeon prophesied that Jesus would cause many in Israel to fall and rise, would be opposed, would reveal people’s hearts, and that Mary’s own soul would be pierced as by a sword.

On a Tuesday. How you respond to Jesus reveals your heart. And following him may bring grief as well as joy. That is not a sign that God has failed.

parallels.desc: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. Coming up at that very hour, she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

A man and a woman. Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, and many others in the Gospel. Two witnesses, as the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15).

A prophetess. Like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah in the Old Testament (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9). God spoke through her.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, “grace”, the name of Samuel’s mother, whose prayer Mary echoed (1:46–55). Phanuel is the same name as Peniel, “face of God”, where Jacob wrestled with God (Genesis 32:30).

Of the tribe of Asher. One of the northern tribes of Israel, scattered by Assyria in 722 BC. Some families had kept their genealogies. The “lost” tribes were not lost to God. The Messiah comes for all Israel.

Having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin. Married young, widowed young.

And then as a widow until she was eighty-four. Or, as the ESV footnote has it, a widow for eighty-four years, which would make her over a hundred. Either way, a very long widowhood. Widows were among the most vulnerable people in Israel. Anna did not remarry, but devoted herself to God (1 Timothy 5:5).

She did not depart from the temple. Perhaps she lived in one of the rooms in the temple courts, or was there at every service.

Worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. A life of prayer, for decades, waiting.

And coming up at that very hour. Again, God’s timing.

She began to give thanks to God. Literally to confess, acknowledge, praise.

And to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. “Redemption” (1:68): the liberation God had promised (Isaiah 52:9: he has redeemed Jerusalem). There was a circle of faithful people waiting, and Anna told them all: he has come. She was one of the first to preach Christ.

In a sentence. Anna, an aged widow and prophetess who spent her life in the temple in prayer and fasting, arrived at that moment, thanked God, and told everyone waiting for redemption about the child.

On a Tuesday. A life of prayer is never wasted, however long and unseen. And older believers can be among the most effective witnesses of all.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.

And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord. Luke stresses (vv. 22, 23, 24, 27, 39) that Jesus’ family kept the law carefully. The Saviour came from an obedient, devout Jewish home.

They returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. Luke does not record the visit of the wise men, the flight to Egypt and the massacre at Bethlehem (Matthew 2), which happened between the presentation and the return to Nazareth. Each Gospel writer selects.

And the child grew and became strong. Jesus grew as a normal child. His humanity was real. He learned to walk, to talk, to read.

Filled with wisdom. Not born knowing everything, in his human mind, but filled with wisdom as he grew (v. 52).

And the favor of God was upon him. “Favor” (charis): grace. God’s delight rested on him.

In a sentence. After fulfilling the law, the family returned to Nazareth, where Jesus grew strong and full of wisdom, with God’s favour on him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent nearly thirty years in an ordinary town, growing up. Faithfulness in ordinary life is God’s will for most of us, most of the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one: Jesus at twelve, in the temple, sitting among the teachers, leaving the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement. Before the public ministry begins, Jesus is already defined by a relationship with his Father that supersedes every other claim on him — including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The apocryphal gospels of later centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus working wonders and settling scores. In the one childhood story Scripture preserves, he performs no miracle at all. He asks questions, and then goes home and does as he is told.

The setting is Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, commemorating the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood. Jesus is twelve, the year before a Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments, and this is the last Passover of his childhood. The irony Luke intends is deep: the Passover Lamb has come up to keep the Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover him missing from the caravan and search three days, her question is entirely natural and entirely human: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Scripture lets her say it, and does not correct her tone.

Jesus's answer contains the first recorded words of his life, and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word must (dei) is one of Luke's great theological words, marking the divine necessity that drives the whole redemptive plan. And the Father he names is not Joseph. He distinguishes — gently, but unmistakably — between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.

He had not run away, and he had broken no commandment; his surprise is genuine that after twelve years they had to be told where he would be. And then, having said it, he goes down with them to Nazareth and is subject to them for another eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei — “it is necessary,” “I must” — runs through Luke and Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time.

This is not a child defying his parents. It is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of that single must, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission after the episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents: not one act of compliance but a settled condition sustained for eighteen years.

And he genuinely grows (v. 52). The one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom is hidden grows in wisdom. This is the mystery of two natures in one person, and it means the incarnation was never a costume. It was real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter Luke shows her holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to arrive.

This is one of the most honest and most encouraging pictures of faith in the Gospel. The mother of the Son of God did not always understand what he was doing. But she did not discard what she could not explain. She kept it, turned it over, and waited — and she was still carrying this one twenty years later when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began to make sense.

The closing verse is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years: Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins — of growing, learning, working, and being formed in a village nobody wrote about.

The God who could have compressed everything into three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty in ordinariness. That is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. Anyone impatient to skip the hidden years has not yet understood how God shapes the people he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.

The only story of Jesus’ boyhood. The Bible tells us nothing of Jesus between infancy and about thirty, except this one episode. Later legends (the “infancy gospels”) invented miracles from his childhood, such as making clay birds fly. The canonical Gospels are restrained. This story, probably from Mary, gives a single window into his growing self-awareness.

Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. The law required every Jewish man to go to the sanctuary for three feasts each year: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Those who lived far away often went only once, at Passover. Women were not required to go, but Mary did. A devout family.

And when he was twelve years old. At thirteen, a Jewish boy became a “son of the commandment” (bar mitzvah), responsible to keep the law. The year before, he would begin to be prepared, and perhaps taken to the feast to learn.

They went up according to custom. Families travelled together in large caravans, with relatives and neighbours from their towns, for safety and company. The journey from Nazareth took about four days.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem every year for Passover, and when he was twelve, they took him as usual.

On a Tuesday. Regular worship with God’s people shaped Jesus’ childhood. Make worship a habit of your family’s life.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group, they went a day’s journey. Then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.

When the feast was ended. Passover and Unleavened Bread lasted eight days. Some pilgrims left after the first two days; Jesus’ parents stayed for the whole feast.

The boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Deliberately, as his answer shows (v. 49). Not disobedience: his parents had not told him to stay with them, and assumed he was with the group. A twelve-year-old in that culture had considerable independence.

Supposing him to be in the group. In a large caravan, children ran among relatives and friends. Men and women may have travelled in separate groups, and each parent may have thought he was with the other. It was not neglect.

They went a day’s journey. About 20 miles (30 km). Then, at the evening camp, they discovered he was missing.

And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him. Any parent can imagine the fear: a child lost in a city crowded with pilgrims.

In a sentence. After the feast, Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without his parents knowing; after a day’s travel they discovered he was missing and went back to search for him.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ godly parents assumed too much. Don’t assume Christ is with you; seek him (Jeremiah 29:13).

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.

After three days. One day out, one day back, and a day searching. Some see a foreshadowing of the three days before his resurrection, after which he was again found, in a sense, about his Father’s business.

They found him in the temple. In the temple courts, probably in the colonnades where teachers met.

Sitting among the teachers. The teachers of the law sat with their pupils, teaching by question and answer, especially during and after the feasts. Jesus sat as a student among the rabbis.

Listening to them and asking them questions. Not lecturing them, as later legends imagined, but learning, as a good student did. And yet his questions showed remarkable insight.

And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. “Understanding” (synesei): insight, intelligence. He was asked questions too, and his answers astonished the experts. Twenty years later, the teachers in this same temple would be astonished, and then furious, at his answers (20:26, 40).

In a sentence. After three days of searching, they found Jesus in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and everyone was amazed at his understanding.

On a Tuesday. Jesus listened and asked questions. Learn God’s word humbly, by listening and asking.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his parents saw him, they were astonished. His mother said to him: son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress. He said to them: why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?

They were astonished. To find him there, calmly among the teachers.

Son, why have you treated us so? The natural reproach of a frightened, relieved mother. Mary speaks; mothers often do.

Your father and I. She calls Joseph “your father”.

In great distress. “Distress” (odynōmenoi): anguish, pain. A foretaste of the sword that would pierce her soul (v. 35).

Why were you looking for me? Not rudeness, but surprise. Why search everywhere? You should have known where I would be.

Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? These are Jesus’ first recorded words, and they are full of meaning. “My Father”: Mary said “your father”, meaning Joseph; Jesus says “my Father”, meaning God. At twelve, he is aware of his unique relationship to God as his Father. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the word Jesus will use of his destiny of suffering (9:22; 24:26). Even as a boy, he knows he is under his Father’s purpose. “In my Father’s house”: literally “in the things of my Father”, which can mean his Father’s house, the temple, or his Father’s affairs, his Father’s business (as the King James has it). Both meanings fit.

In a sentence. When his distressed mother reproached him, Jesus answered, in his first recorded words, that they should have known he must be in his Father’s house.

For worship. Jesus called God “my Father” from his youth. Through him, you too can call God Father (Galatians 4:6).
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.

They did not understand. Even Mary and Joseph, after the angels and the prophecies, did not understand. The mystery of who Jesus was, and what his relationship to his Father meant, was too great to take in at once. Luke is honest about it. Mary is not portrayed as all-knowing; she too had to learn.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents did not understand what he meant.

On a Tuesday. It is all right not to understand everything about God at once. Keep treasuring and pondering, as Mary did.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was submissive to them. His mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man.

And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. The Son of God, conscious of his unique relationship with his Father, went home and obeyed his parents. “Submissive” (hypotassomenos): continually subject, obedient. He kept the fifth commandment perfectly, for us. His awareness of his heavenly Father did not lead him to despise his earthly parents. And this obedience continued for perhaps eighteen years, working as a carpenter (Mark 6:3).

And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. As in verse 19. And probably told Luke.

And Jesus increased in wisdom. Growth in understanding. In his human nature, Jesus really learned and developed (Hebrews 5:8). This does not deny his deity, but affirms the reality of his humanity. He was not a divine being pretending to be a child, but a real child, growing up.

And in stature. Or “in years”, or “in maturity”. Physical growth.

And in favor with God and man. Words used of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26). Loved by God and by people. A balanced, whole development: intellectual, physical, spiritual and social. This is the model of godly growth. And it covers silently the “hidden years” in Nazareth, ordinary years of work, family, synagogue and prayer.

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Nazareth and obeyed his parents, while Mary treasured these things, and he grew in wisdom, in stature, and in favour with God and people.

On a Tuesday. If you are a child or a teenager, Jesus obeyed his parents; you can too. And at any age, aim to grow as he did: in wisdom, in body, and in favour with God and others.

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man

<sup>3</sup> And all went to be registered, each to his own town. <sup>4</sup> And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, <sup>5</sup> to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child. <sup>6</sup> And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. <sup>7</sup> And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn. <sup>8</sup> And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. <sup>9</sup> And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear. <sup>10</sup> And the angel said to them, “Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. <sup>11</sup> For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord. <sup>12</sup> And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.” <sup>13</sup> And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, <sup>14</sup> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!” <sup>15</sup> When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” <sup>16</sup> And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger. <sup>17</sup> And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. <sup>18</sup> And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them. <sup>19</sup> But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart. <sup>20</sup> And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them. <sup>21</sup> And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. <sup>22</sup> And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord <sup>23</sup> (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, “Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”) <sup>24</sup> and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” <sup>25</sup> Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. <sup>26</sup> And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. <sup>27</sup> And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, <sup>28</sup> he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said, <sup>29</sup> “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; <sup>30</sup> for my eyes have seen your salvation <sup>31</sup> that you have <sup>35</sup> (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.” <sup>36</sup> And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, <sup>37</sup> and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. <sup>38</sup> And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. <sup>39</sup> And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. <sup>40</sup> And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him. <sup>41</sup> Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. <sup>42</sup> And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom. <sup>43</sup> And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, <sup>44</sup> but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, <sup>45</sup> and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him. <sup>46</sup> After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. <sup>47</sup> And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. <sup>48</sup> And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” <sup>49</sup> And he said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” <sup>50</sup> And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them. <sup>51</sup> And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. <sup>52</sup> And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Seven named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Seven officials are named: Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas.

This is the world into which the word of God intrudes: Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and a compromised religious leadership. And the word comes to none of them. It comes to John, in the wilderness, the son of a village priest. The contrast is pointed. All the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing; the word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not trouble to look.

The names are also checkable, and they have been checked. Lysanias of Abilene was long cited as proof of Luke's carelessness until an inscription from the reign of Tiberius turned up near Damascus honouring exactly that man in exactly that office.

John's message has three parts. First, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — a rite John did not invent, but radically reapplied. Jewish practice may already have had a baptism for Gentile converts entering the covenant people; John baptised Jews, which said out loud that being born inside the covenant was not enough and that Israel itself needed converting. It was scandalous, and it was meant to be.

Second, a demolition of presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is no substitute for personal repentance, and the axe is already at the root.

Third, practical instruction to three specific groups who ask the same question — what shall we do? The crowds are told to share a spare tunic and their food. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than the authorised figure. Soldiers are told not to extort, not to lay false charges, and to be content with their pay. Notably, neither the tax collectors nor the soldiers are told to leave their work. Repentance in John's mouth has hands and feet, and all three answers land on money.

The climax is not John's own proclamation but his announcement of another: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The one who follows is not an improved John; he is of a different order altogether. And Luke calls the whole of this preaching — vipers, axe, unquenchable fire and all — good news (v. 18).

The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced immediately before the Word begins to speak. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance.

This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely his biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit — the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Spirit is the agent of new birth and renewal, the fulfilment of Ezekiel's new heart and Joel's outpouring. Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away dross, and the thresher's fire that consumes chaff.

John does not separate these two; they are two sides of one coming. For those who receive him the fire purifies; for those who reject him it consumes. Everyone who meets Christ is touched by fire. The only question is which kind.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of direction that shows. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly.” It is “share your tunic and your food.”

The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting; the soldier's looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from — and in both those cases it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real financial cost, alongside colleagues who would not.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage (v. 19) — knowing what it would cost him — is the model of prophetic courage before political power. He did not reserve his hard message for crowds who could do him no harm; he took it to the palace, where it was entirely unnecessary and entirely dangerous.

The man who tells the crowd hard truths and comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. And John's own end is worth facing honestly: he did everything he was sent to do, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

Luke the historian. Luke dates John’s ministry the way ancient historians dated great events, with a list of rulers. Seven names: one emperor, three Roman-appointed rulers, one more minor ruler, two high priests. The whole political and religious world of the day. And then the word of God bypasses them all, and comes to a man in the desert.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14. His fifteenth year was about AD 28–29 (depending on how the years were counted, and whether from his co-regency with Augustus, which began in AD 11–12). Jesus’ ministry began shortly after.

Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea. Prefect from AD 26 to 36, who would condemn Jesus (23:1–25).

Herod being tetrarch of Galilee. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. “Tetrarch” originally meant ruler of a quarter of a kingdom, then any minor ruler under Rome. He would imprison and behead John (v. 20; 9:9) and mock Jesus (23:6–12).

His brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. Another son of Herod the Great, who ruled the territory north-east of Galilee from 4 BC to AD 34. He rebuilt Caesarea Philippi.

And Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. A region north-west of Damascus. Critics once claimed Luke was wrong, because the only known Lysanias died in 36 BC. But an inscription has since been found naming a Lysanias as tetrarch in the time of Tiberius. Luke was right.

During the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. There was officially one high priest. Annas held the office from AD 6 to 15, when the Romans deposed him. But he remained the power behind the office; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (AD 18–36) held it after him. Jews may have regarded Annas as still the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life. Jesus was taken first to Annas (John 18:13).

The word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. The language of the Old Testament prophets: the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:2), Hosea, Joel, Jonah. After four hundred years of prophetic silence, a prophet is called. Not in Rome, not in Jerusalem, not in the palace or the temple, but in the wilderness, to the son of a country priest. God’s word does not depend on the powerful.

In a sentence. In about AD 28, under Tiberius, Pilate, the Herods and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, God’s word came to John in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is rooted in real history, with real dates and rulers. And God still bypasses the powerful to speak through the humble.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

parallels.desc: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the days of…

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

Into all the region around the Jordan. The Jordan valley, north of the Dead Sea, a hot, low-lying region. A place of crossing: Israel had entered the promised land by crossing the Jordan (Joshua 3). Elijah was taken up near there (2 Kings 2:6–11).

Proclaiming a baptism of repentance. A baptism that expressed repentance. “Repentance” (metanoia) means a change of mind leading to a change of life: turning from sin to God. Jews were used to ritual washings for purification, and Gentiles who converted to Judaism were baptised. John’s baptism was shocking because he called Jews, God’s own people, to be baptised like Gentiles: you too need to start again.

For the forgiveness of sins. John promised forgiveness to those who truly repented. Not that the water itself forgave, but that it was the sign of a repentance God would honour. And John’s baptism pointed forward to the one who would actually win forgiveness, by his death (1:77; 24:47).

As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah 40:3–5. Isaiah 40 begins the second half of Isaiah, the great prophecies of comfort and return from exile: Comfort, comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1).

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. John is the voice. Not the Word, but the voice that announces it.

Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. When a king was to visit a region, roads were repaired and straightened before him. In Isaiah, it is the Lord God himself who is coming, to lead his people home. John prepares for Jesus, so Jesus is the Lord God who is coming. The preparation is moral and spiritual: repentance.

In a sentence. John preached throughout the Jordan valley a baptism expressing repentance for the forgiveness of sins, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of a voice preparing the way of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. What in your life needs straightening to make way for the Lord? Repentance is the road on which he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. Road-building language. But also a picture of the reversal Mary sang of (1:52): the lowly lifted up, the proud brought down. The humble are raised; the proud are humbled.

And the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways. Crooked lives made straight: the tax collectors and soldiers of verses 12–14.

And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. Only Luke continues the quotation this far, because this is his great theme. “All flesh” means all humanity, Gentiles as well as Jews. Simeon had seen God’s salvation in the baby (2:30–32). The whole world will see it. Luke’s Gospel ends with repentance and forgiveness of sins proclaimed to all nations (24:47), and Acts ends with Paul in Rome declaring that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

In a sentence. Isaiah’s prophecy promised the levelling of every obstacle, the straightening of the crooked, and the revelation of God’s salvation to all humanity.

For worship. Praise God that his salvation is for all flesh, for people of every nation, including you.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptised by him: you brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?

He said therefore to the crowds. Matthew says he addressed this to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7); Luke applies it to the crowds in general. Many came out of curiosity or because it was the thing to do.

You brood of vipers! A shocking way to greet people who came to be baptised. Vipers are poisonous snakes. When a fire swept through the dry scrub of the wilderness, snakes would flee before it. These people were fleeing the coming judgement like snakes running from a fire, without any change of nature. And “brood of vipers” recalls the serpent of Genesis 3: children of the devil, not of Abraham (John 8:44).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? “The wrath to come”: God’s judgement, the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; Zephaniah 1:14–18; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). John was not ashamed to preach the wrath of God. Without it, the good news makes no sense. The question is sarcastic: do you think a dip in the river is enough to escape?

In a sentence. John confronted the crowds as snakes fleeing a fire, asking who had warned them to escape God’s coming wrath.

On a Tuesday. The wrath of God is real. Don’t treat religious ritual as fire insurance. Flee to Christ with a changed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, we have Abraham as our father. For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. Repentance is not only an inner feeling, or a ritual. True repentance shows itself in a changed life, as a healthy tree shows itself by its fruit (6:43–45). Paul preached the same (Acts 26:20).

And do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father. Many Jews believed that being physical descendants of Abraham guaranteed God’s favour. Some rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of hell to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you. Neither will your church background or your parents’ faith.

For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. There may be a pun in Aramaic between “children” (banayya) and “stones” (abnayya). God does not need you. He could make children of Abraham out of the rocks lying by the river. And he will: Gentiles, as dead to God as stones, will become Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7, 29). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12).

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. The axe is already in position, lying at the root, ready to strike. Judgement is near. The fig tree has had its time (13:6–9).

Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Fruitless trees are firewood. The fire is God’s judgement.

In a sentence. John demanded that repentance be shown in changed lives, warned that descent from Abraham would not save them, and declared that God’s judgement was ready to fall on every fruitless tree.

On a Tuesday. What fruit of repentance can be seen in your life? Don’t rely on your background; rely on Christ, and bear fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds asked him: what then shall we do? He answered them: whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.

What then shall we do? The right response to preaching (Acts 2:37; 16:30). Three groups ask the same question (vv. 10, 12, 14). Only Luke records this section.

Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none. The tunic was the inner garment, worn next to the skin. A second one was a spare, a luxury for the poor. Repentance is practical: share what you have with those in need. The fruit of repentance includes generosity.

And whoever has food is to do likewise. The same with food. Love your neighbour as yourself (1 John 3:17–18; James 2:15–16).

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by giving things away. Nor a political programme of enforced equality. But a heart that has truly turned to God will turn toward the needy.

In a sentence. When the crowds asked what to do, John told them to share their spare clothing and food with those who had none.

On a Tuesday. Look in your wardrobe and your cupboard. What do you have two of, that someone else needs?
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tax collectors also came to be baptised and said to him: Teacher, what shall we do? He said to them: collect no more than you are authorised to do.

Tax collectors also came to be baptized. Tax collectors were among the most despised people in Jewish society. Rome sold the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder, who paid in advance and then collected what he could, keeping the surplus. They were seen as traitors, working for the occupying power, and thieves, overcharging their own people. They were barred from synagogues and their testimony was not accepted. Yet they came to John, and later to Jesus (5:27–32; 15:1; 19:1–10). The despised were often more ready to repent than the respectable.

Teacher. They recognised John’s authority.

Collect no more than you are authorized to do. Not “leave your job”. John does not tell them to stop being tax collectors; the state has the right to taxes (20:25; Romans 13:6–7). He tells them to be honest in their work. Repentance does not usually mean leaving your calling, but living differently in it. For a tax collector, honesty would mean a dramatic loss of income.

In a sentence. When tax collectors asked what they should do, John told them to collect only what was required, nothing extra.

On a Tuesday. Repentance shows itself at work. Be scrupulously honest in your dealings, even when it costs you.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers also asked him: and we, what shall we do? He said to them: do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.

Soldiers also asked him. Probably Jewish soldiers in the service of Herod Antipas, or perhaps police who protected the tax collectors. Possibly some Gentiles. They had power, weapons and poor pay, and the temptations that go with them.

Do not extort money from anyone by threats. “Extort by threats” (diaseisēte): literally “shake down”, intimidate, use violence to get money.

Or by false accusation. Sykophantēsēte, from which comes “sycophant”: to accuse falsely, to blackmail. Threatening to report someone for a crime unless they paid.

And be content with your wages. The root of their sins was discontent and greed. Contentment is the cure (Philippians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5). Again, John does not tell them to leave the army. Soldiering is a legitimate calling (7:1–10; Acts 10). But do it justly.

In a sentence. John told soldiers not to use their power to extort money by violence or blackmail, and to be content with their pay.

On a Tuesday. Whatever power you have, at work or at home, never use it to take from others. And be content with what God has given you.
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all: I baptise you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

As the people were in expectation. Messianic hope was intense. Many were waiting for the promised Messiah, and here was a prophet like Elijah.

Whether he might be the Christ. John could have claimed it. Many did.

I baptize you with water. John’s baptism was only water, an outward sign.

But he who is mightier than I is coming. John points away from himself. Throughout his ministry, he made himself small, to make Christ great: He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals and washing his feet was the job of the lowest slave. Rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher that a slave would do, except untie his sandals; that was too degrading. John says: I am not even worthy to do the lowest slave’s task for him. The greatest of the prophets (7:28) considers himself unworthy to be the Messiah’s slave.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. The great promise. John’s baptism was outward; the Messiah’s will be inward. The prophets had promised that God would pour out his Spirit in the last days (Joel 2:28–29; Ezekiel 36:25–27). Jesus will do this, as God does. Fulfilled at Pentecost, when tongues of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:1–4; 1:5). “Fire” has a double meaning: purifying fire for those who repent (Malachi 3:2–3), and the fire of judgement for those who do not (v. 17). One baptism of Spirit and fire: purifying the wheat, burning the chaff.

Where Christians differ: the baptism of the Spirit. Pentecostal teaching holds that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues. Verdict: in the New Testament, all believers are baptised by the Spirit into Christ at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9). Pentecost was the unique, once-for-all outpouring at the beginning of the new age. Believers are commanded to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), but not to seek a second baptism.

In a sentence. When people wondered if John was the Messiah, he said the coming one was far greater than he, and would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Christ. And thank God that if you belong to Christ, you have his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. After harvest, grain was threshed (beaten to loosen the husks) on a hard, flat threshing floor, often on a hilltop to catch the wind. Then it was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork or shovel. The heavy grain fell back; the light chaff blew away, and was swept up and burned. The fork is already in his hand: the separating is about to begin.

To clear his threshing floor. To clean it completely.

And to gather the wheat into his barn. The repentant, the true people of God, will be gathered safely. The Messiah will save.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. The unrepentant will be judged, with fire that cannot be put out (Mark 9:43, 48). The Messiah is not only Saviour but Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Notice: it is his threshing floor, his wheat, his barn. Everything belongs to him.

In a sentence. The coming one will separate humanity like a farmer winnowing, gathering the wheat into his barn and burning the chaff in unquenchable fire.

On a Tuesday. Everyone will be either wheat or chaff. There is no third category. Make sure you belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.

With many other exhortations. Luke gives us only a sample of John’s preaching.

He preached good news to the people. “Preached good news” (euēngelizeto): evangelised. After all the warnings of wrath, the axe and the fire, Luke calls it good news. Why? Because the warnings are part of the good news. The coming one is near. Escape is possible. Forgiveness is offered. The bad news makes the good news necessary and precious. A gospel without warning of judgement is not the gospel.

In a sentence. With many other appeals, John proclaimed the good news to the people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to warn people of judgement. It is part of the good news, because it makes Christ’s salvation precious.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by John for Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all: he locked up John in prison.

But Herod the tetrarch. Herod Antipas.

Who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother’s wife. Herodias had been married to Herod’s half-brother (called Philip in Mark 6:17; not the tetrarch Philip of v. 1). Herod divorced his own wife, a Nabatean princess, to marry her, and she divorced her husband. The marriage broke God’s law (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John told Herod to his face that it was unlawful (Mark 6:18). A prophet confronting a king, like Nathan with David (2 Samuel 12) and Elijah with Ahab (1 Kings 21).

And for all the evil things that Herod had done. His sins were many.

Added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. Instead of repenting, he silenced the preacher. Josephus tells us John was imprisoned in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Herod later had him beheaded (9:9; Mark 6:17–29).

Luke’s order. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, before Jesus’ baptism (v. 21), though it happened later. He rounds off John’s story before turning to Jesus, so that the stage is clear for him. John decreases; Jesus increases.

In a sentence. When John rebuked Herod for marrying his brother’s wife and for his other sins, Herod added to his evil by imprisoning him.

On a Tuesday. Faithful preaching may cost you dearly. And beware of silencing those who confront your sin; it only adds to the sin.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event; the baptism itself is a participle, almost an aside. What he focuses on is what happens while Jesus is praying afterwards.

This is characteristic. Luke consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre of the scene; the prayer is. And what happens during it is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water; the Spirit descending in bodily form like a dove; the Father's voice from heaven.

Why is Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's answer: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

He is baptised not because he needs what the water signifies but because he is identifying himself with the people he came to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The Jordan is the first public act of the substitution that ends at Golgotha.

The Father's voice weaves two Old Testament texts together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the royal psalm of the Davidic king. “With you I am well pleased” is Isaiah 42:1, the opening of the first Servant Song. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will reign and the Servant who will be crushed. Both identities are laid on him at the outset, and the whole ministry is the working out of what it costs to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an inward impression but something anyone standing on the bank could have seen.

The dove carries a layered background: the dove of Noah signalling that the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12); the dove of the poor person's offering (Lev. 5:7; and 2:24 in this Gospel); and, most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Gen. 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. A new creation is beginning.

The Father's declaration comes before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, preached a single sermon, or won a single crowd. The pleasure of the Father in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the love that existed between them before the foundation of the world (John 17:24).

That is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything. And the Christian who is in Christ shares the status — not earned but given, not provisional but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus praying at his baptism is the first instance of a pattern that runs through the whole Gospel. The implication is not that prayer is a mechanism that causes the Spirit to descend. It is that prayer is the posture of one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources.

The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power, but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before decisions and transitions is not following a technique. He is following his Lord.

The Trinity is present at the Jordan in a way impossible to mistake and impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously directed towards one redemptive event.

The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils. It is the description of what happened at the Jordan. The church was simply trying to find words adequate to what the evangelists reported.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the people were baptised, and when Jesus also had been baptised and was praying, the heavens were opened.

Now when all the people were baptized. Jesus is baptised among the crowd, one of the people. Luke tells it briefly, without naming John.

And when Jesus also had been baptized. Why was the sinless Son of God baptised with a baptism of repentance? Matthew records John’s objection, and Jesus’ answer: to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15). He identified himself completely with the sinners he came to save, taking his place among them, as he would on the cross, numbered with the transgressors (22:37). He began his ministry as he would end it: standing in the place of sinners.

And was praying. Only Luke notes this. Prayer marks every turning point of Jesus’ life in Luke: here, before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter’s confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28–29), in Gethsemane (22:41–44), on the cross (23:34, 46). The Son of God depended on his Father in prayer.

The heavens were opened. As Isaiah prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). The barrier between heaven and earth is opened. God is about to speak.

In a sentence. After Jesus was baptised along with the people, while he was praying, heaven opened.

For worship. Jesus took his place among sinners at the start of his ministry. Thank him that he stood where you stand, so that you could stand where he stands.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

The Trinity. The Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends. One of the clearest revelations of the Trinity in Scripture: one God, three persons, each distinct and each active.

And the Holy Spirit descended on him. Anointing him for his ministry. He is now the Christ, the Anointed One, in the fullest sense: anointed with the Spirit (4:18; Acts 10:38). Isaiah had foretold it: the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

In bodily form, like a dove. Only Luke says “in bodily form”: a visible appearance, not just a feeling. The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), as a new creation begins; or the dove returning to Noah after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12), signalling a new beginning after judgement. Doves are gentle (Matthew 10:16).

You are my beloved Son. Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed king: You are my Son. Jesus is the messianic King and the eternal Son. “Beloved” may also echo Genesis 22:2, Isaac, Abraham’s beloved only son, who was to be sacrificed.
