With you I am well pleased. Isaiah 42:1: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. Jesus is the Servant of the Lord, who will suffer and die for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). In one sentence, the Father declares Jesus to be both the Son-King and the suffering Servant. And he is pleased with him before he has done any public ministry. The thirty years of hidden obedience in Nazareth pleased the Father.

For believers. Because we are in Christ, the Father’s words to him are true of us: in him, we are God’s beloved children, and God is pleased with us, not because of our performance, but because of his (Ephesians 1:6).

In a sentence. The Spirit descended visibly on Jesus like a dove, and the Father declared from heaven that Jesus is his beloved Son, in whom he delights.

For worship. Father, Son and Spirit are at work together for your salvation. Worship the triune God.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward, from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus; it is placed after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative; and it extends past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God.

These are not inconsistencies but theological choices. Matthew writes for a Jewish readership and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham. Luke writes with the world in view and presents Jesus as the answer to the human story, beginning at the Jordan — where his identity has just been declared by the Father — and tracing his lineage to the first man.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in many of the names between David and Joseph. Some hold that Luke traces the line through Mary; others that one evangelist follows legal succession and the other physical descent; others appeal to the complexities of levirate marriage. No solution is free of difficulty, and the church has lived with the two lists for two thousand years without resolving every detail.

What is clear is that the difference does work. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings — the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and also the line under the curse pronounced on Jeconiah, that none of his offspring would prosper sitting on David's seat (Jer. 22:30). Luke's runs through Nathan, a son of David who never reigned and whose descendants never came under that word. On one common reading, the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child.

Most of the names between David and Joseph are otherwise unknown — dozens of men of whom Scripture records nothing except that the line ran through their houses. Further back the list passes through Ruth the Moabite, through Perez the son of Tamar, through Abraham who twice lied about his wife. God ran the promise straight through a family history containing foreignness, deception and disgrace, and did not clean it up first.

The placement after the baptism gives the list its frame. The Father has just said “You are my Son”; the genealogy answers the question whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph as registered; the son of David, which is his royal credential; the son of Abraham, which is his covenantal one; the son of Adam, which is his human solidarity. And at the end of the list — the son of God.

He is the Son of God who has become the son of Adam, so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived.

He did not merely appear in human form. He entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history — which is what Paul means by “born of woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Fully embedded in the situation he came to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit here becomes explicit in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience constitutes many righteous.

Luke's genealogy does not spell out that typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise on which the typology stands: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means Adam's story is part of his story, and his story is the answer to Adam's.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy is one of the portions of Scripture readers habitually skip — a long list of unfamiliar names that looks like a necessary but uninspiring prelude. But it is the gospel in miniature. It announces that the salvation of the world came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real families making real choices.

Every name in the list is a person whose life contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan, and almost none of them had any idea of it. Providence is not abstract. It is as specific as a name — including the many names in this list about whom history has kept nothing else at all.

The final phrase, “the son of Adam, the son of God,” is the summary of everything the Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human and fully divine, and the two cannot be separated without destroying the gospel.

A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us, because he cannot represent us. A Jesus who is only human cannot save us, because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden, and named by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph.

Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age. Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Priests began at thirty (Numbers 4:3); Joseph stood before Pharaoh at thirty (Genesis 41:46); David began to reign at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). “About” thirty: an approximate figure.

Being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph. Luke guards the virgin birth. People supposed he was Joseph’s son; he was legally Joseph’s son, but not biologically.

Why the genealogy is here. Matthew puts his genealogy at the very beginning, tracing Jesus forward from Abraham, to show that he is the son of Abraham and of David, the Jewish Messiah (Matthew 1:1–17). Luke places his after the baptism, just before the temptation, and traces it backward all the way to Adam, “the son of God” (v. 38). The voice from heaven has just called Jesus “my Son”. The genealogy shows him as the true Son, the new Adam, who will succeed where Adam failed, as the temptation (4:1–13) immediately shows.

The son of Heli. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob (Matthew 1:16). The two genealogies differ between David and Joseph. Several explanations have been offered. One: Luke gives Mary’s line, and Heli was Mary’s father, Joseph being his son by marriage (Joseph is then “son of Heli” as son-in-law). Two: Matthew gives the royal, legal line of succession through Solomon, and Luke the physical descent of Joseph through Nathan. Three: levirate marriage, where one man was the legal and another the biological father. The ancient historian Julius Africanus (about AD 220) gave this explanation from Jesus’ own family relatives. Any of these is possible, and both Gospels trace Jesus to David.

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry at about thirty, supposed to be Joseph’s son, and Luke traces his ancestry back from Joseph.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent thirty years in preparation for three years of ministry. God’s timing in your life may be slower than you would like. Trust it.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum … the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel … the son of Nathan, the son of David.

Names we do not know. Most of these names are otherwise unknown. Ordinary people, faithful or unfaithful, in whose line, generation after generation, God was working toward the birth of his Son. God remembers every one of them.

The son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Zerubbabel led the first return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, and rebuilt the temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2). Haggai prophesied that God would make him like a signet ring (Haggai 2:23). Both genealogies include him and his father Shealtiel, perhaps because the two lines crossed there.

The son of Nathan, the son of David. Luke’s line runs through Nathan, a son of David by Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5), not through Solomon, as Matthew’s does. Jeremiah had pronounced a curse on King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), Solomon’s descendant, that none of his offspring would sit on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Jesus, physically descended through Nathan (if Luke gives the physical line), escapes the curse, while inheriting the legal right to the throne through Joseph. However the details are explained, both lines meet in David.

In a sentence. The genealogy continues back through the exile’s leader Zerubbabel to David’s son Nathan and to David himself.

On a Tuesday. You may never be remembered in the history books. But God is working through ordinary faithful generations. Your faithfulness matters.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor.

The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz. The line of the book of Ruth (Ruth 4:18–22). Boaz married Ruth, a Moabite, a foreigner. Matthew names her (Matthew 1:5); Luke does not, but she is there. God’s plan included Gentiles from the beginning.

The son of Nahshon. The leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7).

The son of Perez, the son of Judah. Perez was born to Judah by Tamar, in a shameful story (Genesis 38). God worked even through human sin. Jacob had prophesied that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). Jesus is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5).

The son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham. The patriarchs, to whom God made the promises (Genesis 12:1–3; 22:18). Matthew begins here; Luke goes further back.

The son of Terah, the son of Nahor. Abraham’s father and grandfather, idol-worshippers in Ur (Joshua 24:2). God called Abraham out of a pagan family.

In a sentence. The genealogy goes back through David’s family, including Boaz and Ruth, to Judah and the patriarchs, and to Abraham’s pagan ancestors.

On a Tuesday. God’s grace runs through families with foreigners, scandals and idolaters. No family history is beyond his redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

Beyond Abraham. Luke takes the line back past Israel’s father to the father of all humanity, following Genesis 11 and Genesis 5. Jesus is not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of the whole human race. This fits Luke’s great theme: all flesh shall see the salvation of God (v. 6).

The son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad. This Cainan (v. 36) is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, but appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which Luke used. Ancient genealogies were not always complete; they could skip generations, since “son of” can mean “descendant of”.

The son of Noah. Through whom the human race was preserved through the flood.

The son of Enoch. Who walked with God, and God took him (Genesis 5:24).

The son of Seth. Born after Abel was murdered and Cain went out from God’s presence. In Seth’s days people began to call on the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26).

The son of Adam, the son of God. The climax. Adam had no human father; he was created directly by God, and so called God’s son. Jesus also had no human father; he is the eternal Son of God made man. Adam, the first son of God, failed the test in a garden and plunged humanity into sin and death. Jesus, the true Son of God, is about to be tested in the wilderness (4:1–13), and will succeed. He is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49). As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

In a sentence. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through Noah and Seth to Adam, the son of God, presenting Jesus as the new Adam and Saviour of all humanity.

For worship. In Adam you were born into sin and death. In Christ, the last Adam, you can be born into new life. Thank God for the second Adam.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam — Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

3.text: <sup>1</sup> In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, <sup>2</sup> during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. <sup>3</sup> And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>4</sup> As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. <sup>5</sup> Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, <sup>6</sup> and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’” <sup>7</sup> He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup> Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>9</sup> Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” <sup>10</sup> And the crowds asked him, “What then shall we do?” <sup>11</sup> And he answered them, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.” <sup>12</sup> Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” <sup>13</sup> And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” <sup>14</sup> Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.” <sup>15</sup> As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, <sup>16</sup> John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>17</sup> His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>18</sup> So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people. <sup>19</sup> But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, <sup>20</sup> added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. <sup>21</sup> Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened, <sup>22</sup> and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>23</sup> Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, <sup>24</sup> the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, <sup>25</sup> the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, <sup>26</sup> the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, <sup>27</sup> the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, <sup>28</sup> the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, <sup>29</sup> the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, <sup>30</sup> the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, <sup>31</sup> the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, <sup>32</sup> the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, <sup>33</sup> the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, <sup>34</sup> the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, <sup>35</sup> the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, <sup>36</sup> the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, <sup>37</sup> the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, <sup>38</sup> the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation follows immediately on the baptism: the Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate. The Father's declaration of sonship — “You are my beloved Son” — is at once followed by the devil's challenge to it: “If you are the Son of God…”

The wilderness is where the identity given at the baptism is tested, and where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use divine power for his own relief? Will he take the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he force the Father to prove his care? The answer each time is no — and the no is spoken not by supernatural force but with the word of Scripture.

The three assaults correspond to Israel's three great wilderness failures. Israel hungered and grumbled (Exod. 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stone into bread. Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exod. 32); Jesus is offered the kingdoms for an act of worship. Israel tested God at Massah (Exod. 17:1-7); Jesus is urged to throw himself from the temple. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus stands — and he does it by the means available to every Israelite: the word of God, believed and obeyed. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy, the book Moses gave Israel before they entered the land.

The final offer is the subtlest, because it comes with chapter and verse. The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately, so far as it goes. But he stops the quotation at “to guard you” and omits the psalm's own qualifier, “in all your ways.” The promise covers the paths of obedience; it does not cover a stunt. The temptation is not to misread a promise but to use one as leverage — to demand that the Father demonstrate his care by preventing the consequences of a chosen folly.

Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16 and the memory of Massah. The difference between trust and testing is the difference between resting in God's faithfulness and requiring him to prove it on our terms. The person who says “I will believe God loves me if he does this specific thing” is not trusting God. He is testing him.

The section ends with a phrase Luke intends to be remembered: the devil departed “until an opportune time.” The wilderness was the opening exchange, not the war.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation establishes Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness of deprivation and stands. Adam's failure brought sin and death into the human story; Jesus's obedience begins the reversal.

This is the logic Paul unpacks in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: what the first Adam lost, the second Adam wins back. And the victory is not won by raw divine force but by the very means God made available to Adam — the word of God, and the decision to trust it rather than the alternative on offer.

The devil's departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) signals that the conflict continues through the ministry — in the demons, in the religious leaders, in the crowd's wish for a political king. The appointed opportunity is the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53).

And at the cross the wilderness temptations return almost verbatim — save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews. What looks there like Satan's victory is the moment of his defeat, because the Son who refused every shortcut in the desert walked the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's weapon against every temptation is Scripture — received, remembered, and spoken with precision. He does not argue philosophically, does not marshal feelings, and does not reach for resources unavailable to ordinary disciples. He quotes the word of God.

That is not a pastoral cliché but a pattern with hard practical consequences. The Christian who has stored up Scripture has the weapon Jesus used. The Christian who has neglected it is left to improvise arguments in the moment, which is not a fair fight.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, and with a clause removed. The most dangerous misuse of Scripture is never the obviously wrong use; it is the superficially plausible one — a true promise lifted out of its context and used to license what the context forbids. Every cult and every proof-texted disaster has this shape.

Which is the argument for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. A man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. A man who knows what God is doing across the whole of Scripture can recognise a true verse being turned against its own purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were ended, he was hungry.

Setting. The genealogy has just ended with “Adam, the son of God” (3:38). Now the new Son of God faces the test the first Adam failed. Adam was tested in a garden, with every tree to eat from, and fell. Jesus is tested in a wilderness, starving, and stands. He is also the true Israel: God’s son (Exodus 4:22) who was tested in the wilderness for forty years and failed. All three of Jesus’ answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ words about Israel’s wilderness testing.

Full of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit has just come on him at the baptism (3:22). Being full of the Spirit does not mean being spared temptation; it means being equipped for it.

And was led by the Spirit in the wilderness. The Spirit led him there. Temptation was not an accident or a defeat; it was part of God’s plan. God tests to prove and strengthen; Satan tempts to destroy. The same event is both. The wilderness of Judea, barren and rocky, between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, home of wild animals (Mark 1:13).

For forty days. As Moses fasted forty days on Sinai (Exodus 34:28), as Elijah travelled forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), and as Israel wandered forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2).

Being tempted by the devil. The tense suggests continuous temptation throughout the forty days, coming to a head at the end. “The devil” (diabolos, “slanderer”, “accuser”) is a real, personal being, the enemy of God and man. The temptations were real. Jesus was really tempted, as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. A complete fast. Real hunger, from a real human body, after forty days, near starvation. Satan strikes at the point of greatest weakness.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some say that if he could not have sinned, the temptation was not real. Others say that as God, he could not sin. Verdict: the historic view is that Jesus, being God, could not sin (he was “impeccable”), yet the temptation was real and fully felt. A strong bridge cannot fall, but the weight on it is real. Indeed, only the one who never gave way knew the full force of temptation, because the rest of us give way before it reaches its height.

In a sentence. Full of the Spirit, Jesus was led into the wilderness, where he fasted forty days and was tempted by the devil throughout, and at the end he was hungry.

On a Tuesday. Being full of the Spirit does not mean you won’t be tempted. Expect it, especially when you are weak, and prepare for it with Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil said to him: if you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread. Jesus answered him: it is written, man shall not live by bread alone.

If you are the Son of God. Not doubting it; the Greek form suggests “since you are”. The Father has just said it (3:22). The temptation is: use your sonship for yourself. Use your power to meet your own needs, independently of your Father. Why should the Son of God go hungry?

Command this stone to become bread. Bread was not wrong. Jesus will feed thousands (9:10–17). But to do it now, for himself, at Satan’s suggestion, would be to step out of dependence on his Father, who had led him into the wilderness to hunger. It would also be to refuse the path of humiliation and weakness he came to walk (Philippians 2:7). He would not use his divine power to avoid the human condition he came to share.

It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture. Three times. The Son of God, full of the Spirit, does not argue with Satan or rely on his own wisdom. He relies on the written word, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17). If Jesus needed Scripture to resist temptation, how much more do we.

Man shall not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3. Moses reminded Israel that God let them hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord. Physical bread matters, but life depends ultimately on God and his word. Israel grumbled when hungry; Jesus trusted. His food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

In a sentence. The devil tempted the starving Jesus to use his power as Son of God to make bread for himself, but Jesus answered from Scripture that life depends on more than bread.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to meet a legitimate need in an illegitimate way, remember: life depends on God and his word, not on getting what you want right now.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him: to you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.

The order. Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s, who has the temple second and the kingdoms last (Matthew 4:1–11). Neither says “then” in a way that requires strict sequence. Matthew ends with the kingdoms, perhaps because his Gospel ends with Jesus given all authority on a mountain (Matthew 28:18). Luke ends with Jerusalem and the temple, because Jerusalem is the goal of his whole Gospel (9:51; 24:47).

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. A vision, not a physical view from a mountain. “Kingdoms” (oikoumenē): the inhabited world, the Roman Empire and beyond. All the power and glory of human civilisation, in an instant.

For it has been delivered to me. A half-truth. Satan does have power in this world. Jesus calls him the ruler of this world (John 12:31; 14:30); Paul, the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4); John says the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). Since Adam’s fall, humanity has been under his dominion. But his authority is limited and borrowed; ultimately all authority belongs to God (Daniel 4:17), and Satan is a liar (John 8:44).

If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours. A short cut to the throne. The Father had promised the Son the nations as his inheritance (Psalm 2:8), but by way of the cross. Satan offers the crown without the cross. One act of worship, and the kingdoms are yours, without suffering. The same temptation Peter would put to him (Mark 8:32–33).

In a sentence. In a vision of all the world’s kingdoms, the devil offered Jesus all their authority and glory, claiming they were his to give, if Jesus would worship him.

On a Tuesday. Satan still offers short cuts to success and power, at the price of compromising your worship. No gain is worth bowing to him.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s; Luke ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his whole Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is written, you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.

It is written. Again, Scripture.

You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. Deuteronomy 6:13, from the passage just after the Shema (“Hear, O Israel”), warning Israel not to go after other gods when they enter the land and enjoy its prosperity. Worship belongs to God alone. Israel repeatedly bowed to idols for the sake of prosperity and security; Jesus will not. And notice: Jesus, who is God, worships God. As a man, he gives the Father the worship due to him. Jesus will receive all the kingdoms, but from the Father’s hand, through obedience and the cross (Philippians 2:8–11).

“Only”. The word “only” is not in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13, but it is in the Greek Old Testament, and it is implied by the whole passage (Deuteronomy 6:14–15). There is no room for divided worship.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, quoting the command to worship and serve God alone.

For worship. Who, or what, do you serve? Give your worship to God alone, and trust him for everything else.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took him to Jerusalem, set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you, and, on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

And he took him to Jerusalem. Perhaps in a vision, or physically. Jerusalem, the holy city, the place of the temple.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. “Pinnacle” (pterygion, “little wing”): a high point of the temple complex, perhaps the south-east corner of the outer wall, overlooking the Kidron Valley, a drop of perhaps 450 feet (140 m), or the roof of the royal colonnade.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here. Prove your sonship; force God to act. A spectacular rescue in front of the temple crowds would also prove to everyone that he was the Messiah. A sign from heaven, the very thing the Pharisees would demand (11:16).

For it is written. Now Satan quotes Scripture too. Having been answered twice from Scripture, he tries to use it himself. The devil can quote the Bible.

He will command his angels concerning you … lest you strike your foot against a stone. Psalm 91:11–12. A true promise of God’s protection for those who trust him. But Satan misuses it: he quotes it out of context, leaving out “to guard you in all your ways” (that is, in the ways of obedience), and turns a promise of protection into an invitation to presumption. The psalm also goes on: you will tread on the lion and the adder (Psalm 91:13), the serpent Jesus is about to defeat.

In a sentence. On the temple’s highest point, the devil tempted Jesus to throw himself down to prove he was God’s Son, quoting Psalm 91’s promise of angelic protection.

On a Tuesday. Scripture can be twisted. Read verses in context, and beware of anyone who uses God’s promises to justify doing what God has not commanded.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is said, you shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

It is said. Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture. Scripture interprets Scripture; one verse is not to be set against the rest.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. Deuteronomy 6:16, which goes on: as you tested him at Massah. At Massah, the Israelites demanded water and asked: Is the Lord among us or not? (Exodus 17:7). To test God is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, to manufacture a crisis and force him to rescue us. That is not faith but unbelief. True faith trusts God without demanding proof, and does not presume on his protection by doing what he has not called us to do.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, answering from Scripture that we must not put God to the test.

On a Tuesday. Don’t take reckless risks and expect God to bail you out. Trust him in the path of obedience.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.

When the devil had ended every temptation. Every kind: the three represent the whole range. Appetite (the flesh), power and possessions (the world), and pride and presumption (the devil), as John sums up: the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16). The same three that Eve faced: the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Jesus faced them all, and did not give way. He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

He departed from him. Defeated. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

Until an opportune time. Only for now. Satan will return: through opposition, through Peter (Matthew 16:23), and above all in the passion, when Satan entered into Judas (22:3), and Jesus faced the hour of darkness (22:53). The battle is not over until the cross and resurrection.

In a sentence. Having tried every temptation and failed, the devil left Jesus until a more opportune time.

On a Tuesday. A victory over temptation today does not mean it won’t return. Stay alert. And take comfort: Jesus has already defeated your tempter.

parallels.desc: your hour, and the power of darkness

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns from the wilderness “in the power of the Spirit” — the forty days have not depleted him but concentrated the anointing. He teaches through Galilee and is praised by everyone. Then he comes to Nazareth, where he grew up, and on the Sabbath stands to read.

He is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the place: Isaiah 61:1-2. “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” He reads it, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. And he says: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

The passage is a Jubilee text — the year of the Lord's favour is the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and lost land returned. Jesus announces that the true Jubilee has arrived. And he stops mid-sentence: Isaiah goes on to “the day of vengeance of our God,” and Jesus does not read it. The favour has come; the reckoning waits for a coming still ahead.

The congregation's first response is admiration — they marvel at his gracious words and say “Is not this Joseph's son?” It is simultaneously flattering and dismissive: impressed by the local boy, unprepared for the claim. Jesus reads the room and pre-empts the demand he can see forming: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here also.”

Then he does the thing that turns admiration into fury. He tells two stories from their own Scriptures: Elijah sent past every widow in Israel to a pagan widow in Sidon (1 Kings 17), and Elisha cleansing a Syrian general while Israel's lepers went uncleansed (2 Kings 5). In both, the prophet bypasses Israel and the blessing lands on an outsider.

The congregation hears it perfectly. The year of the Lord's favour is not automatically theirs; they could be the ones passed over. It is a challenge to every form of religious privilege, and the response of privilege threatened is exactly what one would expect. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, intending to throw him off. He passes through the midst of them and goes away — because the hour, and the place, and the manner of his death are not theirs to choose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Isaiah text Jesus reads is a Jubilee text, and the Jubilee was Israel's built-in rehearsal of release: the trumpet, the cancelled debt, the freed slave, the restored land. Jesus announces that the ultimate Jubilee has arrived — not an economic reset but a cosmic one. The debt of sin cancelled, the captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight, the oppressed set free.

This is why he can say “today.” Not soon, not when conditions improve, but today, in your hearing — and the “today” does not depend on the congregation's response. It depends on who has just sat down.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. They wanted a Messiah for Israel who would bless Israel and defeat Israel's enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies themselves.

Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to want Jesus for itself, to treat the gospel as the property of those who already have it, and to be offended when grace reaches people who had been written off. The Nazareth synagogue is the permanent warning against a Christianity that has lost the scandal of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” is the most decisive today in Luke's Gospel — and this Gospel is full of them: “unto you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11); “today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43).

The gospel in Luke is always a present-tense announcement, never merely past-tense history or future-tense hope. The Scripture fulfilled in Jesus is not fulfilled in some spiritual realm remote from the present moment; it is fulfilled now, here, in the hearing of particular people in a particular room.

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched — not because violence is ineffective but because his hour has not come. His death must be the death he chooses, on the terms the Father has set.

And the scene is a warning about familiarity. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus and was the one town where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, those who met him with no prior file: a centurion, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector, a dying criminal.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.

And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit. Full of the Spirit (v. 1), led by the Spirit (v. 1), now in the power of the Spirit. Victorious over temptation, he begins his ministry. Luke stresses that Jesus’ ministry is empowered by the Spirit (v. 18; Acts 10:38).

To Galilee. The northern region, where most of his ministry will take place (4:14–9:50). Luke skips the early Judean ministry that John records (John 1–4).

A report about him went out. His fame spread.

And he taught in their synagogues. Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer, reading and teaching of Scripture, in every Jewish town. They began during the exile, when the temple was destroyed. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak, and Jesus, and later Paul, used them for preaching (Acts 13:15).

Being glorified by all. At first, universal acclaim. It will not last (v. 28).

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and his fame spread as he taught in the synagogues to universal praise.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is fleeting. Jesus was praised by all, and within days, they tried to kill him. Seek God’s approval, not the crowd’s.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written:

The programme of the ministry. Luke places this scene at the start of the Galilean ministry as a kind of manifesto, setting out what Jesus came to do. Mark and Matthew record a similar rejection at Nazareth later (Mark 6:1–6; Matthew 13:53–58). Luke may have brought it forward for its meaning, or it may be a different visit. Verse 23 implies that Jesus had already worked in Capernaum.

He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. His home town, where everyone knew him as the carpenter.

As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day. Regular worship was his habit. If the sinless Son of God needed to worship with God’s people every week, so do we (Hebrews 10:25).

And he stood up to read. A synagogue service included the Shema, prayers, a reading from the Law, a reading from the Prophets, a sermon, and a blessing. Readers stood to read Scripture, out of respect, and sat to teach. A visiting teacher or a respected member could be invited to read and preach.

And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. Books were scrolls, kept in a special cupboard. The attendant (v. 20) handed it to him.

He unrolled the scroll and found the place. He chose the passage himself.

In a sentence. At Nazareth, Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath, as was his custom, stood to read, and found a chosen place in the scroll of Isaiah.

On a Tuesday. Make weekly worship with God’s people your custom, as it was Jesus’.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.

parallels.desc: Paul invited to speak after the readings

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour.

The passage. Isaiah 61:1–2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6 (“to set at liberty those who are oppressed”). In Isaiah, the speaker is the Lord’s anointed servant, announcing the good news of return from exile and restoration. Jesus claims it as his own job description.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. As at his baptism (3:22). The Spirit is the power of his ministry.

Because he has anointed me. “Anointed” (echrisen), from which comes “Christ”. Jesus is the Anointed One, the Messiah, anointed not with oil but with the Spirit (Acts 10:38).

To proclaim good news to the poor. “Poor” (ptōchois): the destitute, the needy, and in the Old Testament especially the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 66:2). The gospel comes first to those who know they have nothing (6:20; 7:22). Both material and spiritual poverty are in view.

To proclaim liberty to the captives. “Liberty” (aphesis) is the same word Luke uses for “forgiveness” (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). Release from captivity and release from sin are the same word. Jesus sets free those bound by sin, Satan and disease (13:16).

And recovering of sight to the blind. From the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 61:1. Jesus will heal the physically blind (7:21; 18:35–43), and open the eyes of the spiritually blind (Acts 26:18).

To set at liberty those who are oppressed. Isaiah 58:6. “Oppressed”: crushed, broken.

To proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor. “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:8–55). Every fiftieth year, debts were cancelled, slaves set free, and land returned to its original families. A trumpet was blown on the Day of Atonement to announce it. Jesus announces the great Jubilee: the age of God’s favour, freedom and restoration has come.

Where he stopped. Jesus stopped in the middle of Isaiah 61:2. He did not read the next words: and the day of vengeance of our God. Why? Because his first coming is for salvation; the day of vengeance is still to come, at his return (21:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

What it does not mean. Not merely a programme of social or political liberation, as some liberation theologians have read it. Nor merely spiritual, with no care for the poor and sick. Jesus’ ministry addressed both: he forgave sins and healed bodies, preached to the poor and fed the hungry. But the deepest captivity is to sin, and the greatest liberty is forgiveness.

In a sentence. Jesus read Isaiah’s words of the Spirit-anointed one sent to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom to the oppressed, and the year of the Lord’s favour.

For worship. Jesus came to set you free. Thank him for your release, and share the good news with the poor and the captive.
verseByVerse.note: “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next words, “the day of vengeance of our God.”

parallels.desc: to let the oppressed go free

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. He began to say to them: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant. The hazzan, the synagogue official who looked after the scrolls.

And sat down. Teachers sat to teach. The congregation knew he was about to preach.

And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. Intense expectation. A dramatic moment, vividly told.

Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. One of the most astonishing sentences ever preached. Not “one day”, but “today”. Not “this is about the Messiah”, but “this is about me, and it is happening now, as you listen”. The prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus. The Jubilee has begun. Isaiah 61 was understood as a messianic prophecy; Jesus claims to be the Messiah. “Today” is a key word in Luke (2:11; 19:9; 23:43).

In a sentence. Jesus sat down to teach and, with every eye on him, declared that Isaiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled that day as they listened.

On a Tuesday. All Scripture finds its fulfilment in Jesus. Read your Bible looking for him.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

parallels.desc: everything written about me must be fulfilled

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All spoke well of him and marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said: is not this Joseph’s son?

And all spoke well of him. Or “bore witness to him”. At first, admiration.

And marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. “Gracious words”: literally “words of grace”. Both his eloquence and the content: grace, favour, release. Psalm 45:2: grace is poured upon your lips.

And they said, Is not this Joseph’s son? The turning point. Admiration turns to doubt. How can this be the Messiah? We know him. He grew up here. He is the carpenter’s son. Familiarity made it impossible for them to accept that God was at work in someone so ordinary. They did not know (as Luke’s readers do, 3:23) that he was not really Joseph’s son. And Matthew and Mark record that they took offence (Mark 6:3).

In a sentence. The congregation admired his gracious words but then asked how this could be, since he was only Joseph’s son.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let familiarity with Jesus blind you to who he really is.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, physician, heal yourself. What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your home town as well. And he said: truly, I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his home town.

Physician, heal yourself. A proverb, found in Greek and Jewish writings. Here it means: prove yourself. Do for your own people what you did elsewhere. If you claim to be the Messiah, show us. They wanted signs, not faith. On the cross, the same taunt: He saved others; let him save himself (23:35).

What we have heard you did at Capernaum. Jesus had already worked miracles there (vv. 31–41 come later in Luke’s order, confirming that Luke has placed this scene first for its meaning).

No prophet is acceptable in his hometown. “Acceptable” (dektos) is the same word as “favour” in “the year of the Lord’s favour” (v. 19). A play on words: Jesus proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord, but he himself is not acceptable to his own. The prophets were often rejected by their own people (Jeremiah 11:21; Acts 7:52).

In a sentence. Jesus anticipated their demand that he prove himself with miracles as he had elsewhere, and observed that no prophet is accepted in his home town.

On a Tuesday. If those closest to you are least willing to hear the gospel from you, you are in good company. Keep faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.

Two examples from Israel’s history. Jesus gives two Old Testament examples, of Elijah and his successor Elisha, the great miracle-working prophets.

Many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah. During the famine God sent in Ahab’s time (1 Kings 17–18). James 5:17 also gives three and a half years; 1 Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year, probably counting from a different point.

Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. 1 Kings 17:8–24. Zarephath was a Gentile town on the coast near Sidon, the very region of Jezebel, Israel’s great enemy. God sent his prophet past all the widows of Israel to a Gentile widow, fed her through the famine, and raised her son from death.

And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. 2 Kings 5. Naaman was the commander of the army of Syria (Aram), Israel’s enemy. He was healed when he humbled himself and washed in the Jordan.

The point. Two Gentiles, an enemy’s widow and an enemy’s general, received God’s blessing, while Israel, in unbelief, did not. God is free to show mercy to whom he will (Romans 9:15). His grace is not limited to Israel, or to Nazareth. If they reject their prophet, his blessings will go to others, to the Gentiles. This is the story of Luke and Acts in miniature (Acts 13:46; 28:28). And it shows that God’s grace is sovereign: not earned by birth or nationality.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that in the days of Elijah and Elisha, God sent his prophets past many in Israel to bless Gentile outsiders, a widow from Sidon and a Syrian general.

On a Tuesday. No one has a claim on God’s grace by birth or background. Thank God that his grace reaches outsiders, including you.
verseByVerse.note: Both of these beneficiaries were Gentiles. Zarephath lay on the coast near Sidon.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. They rose up, drove him out of the town, and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.

All in the synagogue were filled with wrath. From admiration (v. 22) to fury in minutes. Why? Because Jesus suggested that God favoured Gentiles over them. National and religious pride was wounded. The suggestion that God’s grace was for outsiders, enemies even, enraged them. The same reaction met Paul when he mentioned the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

And they rose up and drove him out of the town. On the Sabbath, in the synagogue, the congregation became a lynch mob.

And brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built. Nazareth is built on a hillside, with steep drops nearby.

So that they could throw him down the cliff. Stoning, the penalty for blasphemy or false prophecy, sometimes began by throwing the condemned down a drop. A foreshadowing of the cross: his own people would reject him and try to kill him.

But passing through their midst, he went away. How? Luke does not say: perhaps by his sheer authority, or by a miracle. His hour had not yet come (John 7:30; 8:59). No one could take his life before the Father’s appointed time. He would die in Jerusalem, not Nazareth (13:33). And so he walked away. The rejection at Nazareth sets the pattern for the whole Gospel: grace offered, rejected by his own, and going on to others.

In a sentence. Enraged that God’s grace had gone to Gentiles, the congregation drove Jesus out of town to throw him off a cliff, but he walked through the crowd and went away.

On a Tuesday. Grace offends those who think they deserve it. Receive God’s grace humbly, as an outsider.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth is built on a hillside with steep drops nearby.

parallels.desc: Jesus hid himself and went out

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth, which rejected him, Jesus goes to Capernaum, which will be the base of the Galilean ministry. Within what appears to be a single Sabbath he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a multitude brought to his door.

The contrast with Nazareth is complete. The hometown that had him from childhood loses him; the town that receives him gets a cascade of kingdom power — teaching, healing, and liberation.

The exorcism in the synagogue is Luke's first, and it raises a question that runs through the Gospel: what is the relation between the kingdom of God and the realm of demons? The demon's cry — “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God” — is the first confession of Christ in his public ministry, and it comes from a demon. The powers of darkness identify him before anyone in Galilee does, and their knowledge saves them nothing. The demons believe and shudder (Jas. 2:19); they do not trust and rest.

Jesus silences it and casts it out with a single sentence. No ritual, no incantation, no procedure — which is exactly what a first-century reader would have found astonishing, since contemporary exorcists used elaborate techniques. Luke, the physician, adds that the man was left unharmed.

The healing of Simon's mother-in-law is narrated with the same economy: Jesus rebuked the fever, the same verb used of the demon, and it left her. The response is immediate — she rises and serves. That is the New Testament pattern: what is received is not kept. The restored woman becomes the one who provides.

The healings at sunset, when the Sabbath ended and the sick could lawfully be carried through the streets, are the kingdom in miniature: a whole town at one door, and Jesus laying his hands on every one of them, individually, into the night.

Then, at dawn, he leaves for a desolate place, and refuses the crowd's attempt to keep him: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” The healings are real and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce a kingdom, and he goes to the next town.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demon's address, “the Holy One of God,” appears elsewhere in the New Testament, outside this scene and its parallel (Mark 1:24), only at John 6:69, on Peter's lips. The irony is severe: the demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually and the religious leaders will refuse. The spiritual world sees what the natural eye misses.

But knowledge of who Jesus is, without submission to who he is, is not faith. The demons have impeccable Christology and it does them no good whatever. Right doctrine held in terror is still a lost condition.

Jesus's withdrawal at daybreak to a desolate place, and his answer to the crowd who would have kept him, establishes the missionary imperative of the ministry. The word “must” (dei) appears again — the same divine necessity that took him to the temple at twelve and will take him to Jerusalem.

And this is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel: the kingdom of God. It is not a place or a programme but God's rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King — which is why its arrival looks like demons evicted, bodies mended, and the poor given news.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon's terror — “Have you come to destroy us?” — is the correct reading of what the kingdom of God means for the powers of darkness. Wherever the kingdom comes, the dominion of darkness gives ground.

That is the cosmic dimension of every healing, every exorcism, every act of forgiveness in the Gospels. It is not merely a personal benefit to the recipient; it is territory changing hands. The church that prays for the sick, that names fear and guilt and lies for what they are, and that proclaims forgiveness in the name of Jesus, is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to possess Jesus — to keep him local, to make him the property of one congregation or one tradition — is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. Jesus consistently refuses it.

He came not to be kept but to be followed. The congregation that asks how to keep Jesus to itself has asked very nearly the wrong question. The right one is how to follow him to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. He was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.

Following Mark. From here Luke follows Mark’s account closely (Mark 1:21–39), with his own touches.

And he went down to Capernaum. “Down”: from the hills of Nazareth to the lakeside, about 700 feet (200 m) below sea level. Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, with a customs post, a Roman garrison, and a synagogue. It became Jesus’ base in Galilee (Matthew 4:13). The remains of a later synagogue, built on the foundations of an earlier one, and of a house thought to be Peter’s, can still be seen there.

A city of Galilee. Luke explains for his non-Palestinian readers.

And they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. The scribes taught by quoting earlier authorities: Rabbi so-and-so said. Jesus spoke on his own authority: I say to you (Matthew 7:28–29). His words had divine power, as the next scenes show: they cast out demons and healed diseases.

In a sentence. In Capernaum, Jesus taught on the Sabbath, and people were astonished at the authority of his word.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word still carries authority. Read it as his authoritative word to you, not just interesting advice.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice: ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

A man who had the spirit of an unclean demon. Luke, writing for Gentiles, for whom “demon” could mean a neutral spirit, adds “unclean”: an evil spirit. In the synagogue, on the Sabbath.

Ha! A cry of surprise, anger or dismay. Or “Leave us alone!”

What have you to do with us. Literally “what to us and to you?”, a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common? Why are you interfering with us? (1 Kings 17:18). “Us”: the demon speaks for all the demons. The kingdom of God has invaded Satan’s territory.

Have you come to destroy us? They know their end is coming (Matthew 8:29; Revelation 20:10). Jesus has come to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).

I know who you are—the Holy One of God. The demon knows exactly who Jesus is, better than the people in the synagogue. “The Holy One of God”: set apart by God, sinless, belonging to God (1:35). Perhaps an attempt to gain power over Jesus by naming him, as was believed in ancient magic. But knowing who Jesus is does not save. The demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19).

In a sentence. In the synagogue, a man with an unclean spirit cried out, recognising Jesus as the Holy One of God who had come to destroy the demons.

On a Tuesday. Knowing correct facts about Jesus is not faith. Even demons know who he is. Trust him and follow him.
verseByVerse.note: “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus rebuked him, saying: be silent and come out of him! When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. They were all amazed and said to one another: what is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.

But Jesus rebuked him. A word of command.

Be silent. Literally “be muzzled”. Jesus does not accept testimony from demons. His identity was to be revealed in God’s time and God’s way, and not by evil spirits whose motive was hostile.

And come out of him! No rituals, no incantations, no appeals to other authorities, as Jewish exorcists used. Just a command.

Having done him no harm. A detail only Luke, the physician, records. Though the demon threw him down, he was unhurt.

What is this word? Or “what is this message?” Both his teaching and his command.

For with authority and power. “Authority” (exousia): the right to command. “Power” (dynamis): the ability to enforce it. Jesus has both. Luke often pairs them (9:1).

He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! The kingdom of God has come, and Satan’s power is being broken (11:20).

In a sentence. Jesus silenced the demon and commanded it to come out, and it left the man unharmed, while the people marvelled at the authority and power of his word.

On a Tuesday. No power of evil can stand against Jesus’ word. If you belong to him, you need not fear the devil.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He arose, left the synagogue and entered Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.

And entered Simon’s house. Simon, later called Peter, has not yet been formally called in Luke (5:1–11). Luke assumes his readers know him. Simon was married (1 Corinthians 9:5). The leader of the apostles had a wife and a mother-in-law, which hardly fits later teaching about compulsory clerical celibacy.

Ill with a high fever. Only Luke, the doctor, says “high” (megalō), a medical term used by Greek physicians who distinguished “great” and “small” fevers.

And they appealed to him on her behalf. Intercession. They asked for her.

And he stood over her and rebuked the fever. The same word as for rebuking the demon (v. 35) and the storm (8:24). Jesus confronts illness as an enemy, part of the disorder sin has brought into the world. Not that the fever was a demon, but that Jesus has authority over every power that harms.

And it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. “Immediately”: complete healing, with no weakness or convalescence, as usually follows a high fever. She was well enough at once to serve the meal. Her response to healing is service, the natural response of those Jesus has touched. “Serve” (diēkonei) is the word for ministry.

In a sentence. At Simon’s house, Jesus rebuked the high fever of Simon’s mother-in-law, and she was instantly healed and got up to serve them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick, as Simon’s family asked for her. And when Jesus has blessed you, serve.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, notes that it was a high fever. Simon (Peter) was married.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying: you are the Son of God! But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

Now when the sun was setting. The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules about carrying burdens (Jeremiah 17:21).

All those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him. The whole town.

And he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. Only Luke says “every one”: not mass healing, but individual care. Jesus touched each person personally, however long it took. And he healed every one.

You are the Son of God! The demons know.

But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. Luke links “Son of God” and “the Christ”. Jesus silenced them because testimony from demons would discredit him (11:15), and because the popular understanding of “Messiah” was political and military. He would reveal his identity himself, in his own way, culminating in the cross.

In a sentence. At sunset the whole town brought their sick, and Jesus laid hands on each one and healed them, while silencing the demons who declared him the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares for people one by one. Bring the people you love to him, individually, in prayer.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown; only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. The people sought him, came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them: I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

He departed and went into a desolate place. Mark tells us he went to pray (Mark 1:35). After a night of healing, the Son of God sought solitude with his Father.

And would have kept him from leaving them. They wanted to keep him in Capernaum, for themselves. Nazareth drove him out; Capernaum tried to hold him in. Both wanted him on their own terms.

I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. The first time Luke uses the phrase “the kingdom of God”, the central theme of Jesus’ preaching. The kingdom is God’s reign, his rule breaking into the world through Jesus, to save and to judge.

To the other towns as well. His mission was wider than one town.

For I was sent for this purpose. Sent by the Father. His primary mission was to preach, not to heal. The healings were signs of the kingdom, but the message of the kingdom was the main thing. Healing a body was good, but bodies die again. The word of the kingdom gives eternal life.

In a sentence. When the people tried to keep Jesus in Capernaum, he said he must preach the kingdom of God in other towns too, because that was what he was sent to do.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prioritised preaching the gospel. Don’t let good things crowd out the main thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

In the synagogues of Judea. Some manuscripts read Galilee, which fits the context (Mark 1:39 has Galilee). But the best manuscripts read Judea, and the scribes probably changed it to Galilee to make it fit. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee (1:5; 6:17; 7:17; 23:5; Acts 10:37). So it means: throughout the Jewish land.

And he was preaching. The tense means he kept on preaching. A summary of an extended period of ministry.

In a sentence. Jesus went on preaching in the synagogues throughout the land of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. The good news must go to every town. Pray for preachers, and support the spreading of the gospel to places that have not heard it.
