verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Galilee. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes that together define what it means to encounter Jesus: a miraculous catch of fish that produces not pride but prostration; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; the healing of a paralytic whose friends refused to be stopped by a crowd; the call of a tax collector from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens into the deepest question of the chapter — whether the new thing Jesus is doing can be contained in the old structures of Judaism. The answer is no. New wine requires new wineskins. What Jesus brings is not a reform of the old system; it is something genuinely, radically new.

The call of the first disciples (vv. 1–11) is Luke's fullest account of how Peter, James, and John came to follow Jesus — fuller than the brief summaries in Matthew and Mark, because Luke wants to show not just the what but the why. They did not follow a charismatic teacher because he seemed promising. They followed because they had encountered something that simultaneously exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust. Peter's “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is the most honest response to the presence of holiness in the New Testament — the instinct that knows it cannot stand in the presence of what it has just encountered, and is answered not with departure but with the word: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.”

The chapter closes with a theological dispute about fasting (vv. 33–39) that turns out to be the interpretive key to everything that has come before. The Pharisees and John's disciples fast; Jesus's disciples do not. The question is not merely about religious practice; it is about eschatology. Jesus answers with the image of a wedding: the bridegroom is present. The time of mourning is over; the feast has begun. This is not the time for old wineskins; the new wine of the kingdom — the presence of the Son of God himself — cannot be contained in the structures designed for a world still waiting for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The call of the first disciples is set on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, where Simon Peter and his partners James and John have fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus borrows Peter's boat as a floating pulpit, teaches the crowd from the water, and then tells Peter to put out into the deep and let down the nets.

The instruction is professionally absurd. Fishermen who have worked the prime hours of the night without result do not take advice on technique from a carpenter, in daylight, with the nets already cleaned. But Peter obeys — “at your word I will let down the nets” — and the catch is so large that both boats begin to sink.

The miracle is not primarily about fish. It is about the person who commanded them. Peter, who knows these waters better than almost anyone alive, has just watched something no expertise can produce, and his response is immediate: he falls at Jesus's knees and says “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”

That is the language of Isaiah's vision (“Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips,” Isa. 6:5), of Job before the whirlwind (Job 42:5-6), of John falling as dead at the feet of the risen Christ (Rev. 1:17). It is what happens when a creature with a conscience encounters holiness. Nothing had been said about sin; a boatload of fish had told him who was in the boat.

Jesus's answer to the confession of unworthiness is not agreement and not dismissal but a commission: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” The fear that holiness produces is not the end of the encounter; it is the beginning of the calling — because the calling was never going to rest on Peter's worthiness.

The verb is zōgreō, to take alive. Fishing is bad news for fish; this net means the opposite. The trade is the same and the direction is reversed.

“From now on” is one of Luke's phrases for a hinge. They bring the boats to land, leave everything — including the greatest catch of their lives, lying on the shingle — and follow him.

And this is not the first meeting. Jesus was in Simon's house a chapter earlier (4:38-39), and John records an earlier introduction at the Jordan (John 1:35-42). Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it. Most people are called the way Simon was — not all at once, but finally.
verseByVerse.theology:
The miraculous catch authenticates the call. Jesus does not simply appear on the shore and invite Peter to follow; he first demonstrates, in the domain where Peter's competence is greatest, that Peter's competence is not the final authority over the natural world.

The one who commands the fish is the one who made them. Peter's professional knowledge is real and valuable, and it is relativised — not demeaned. In the presence of the maker of the sea, every human expertise finds its proper place, which is a genuine place and not the top one.

The commission “you will be catching men” describes a rescue rather than an occupation. The disciples are being called to pull people alive out of the water that was drowning them — which is why the calling that begins with a catch of fish reaches its first great haul at Pentecost, when three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41), and has not stopped since.

And the pattern of the encounter is the pattern of every conversion: an approach from Christ's side, a demonstration that leaves the man with nothing to stand on, an honest confession of unworthiness, and a calling that does not depend on the confession being answered with reassurance.
verseByVerse.examples:
“At your word I will let down the nets” — spoken after a night of futile effort, in the daylight hours when fishing is least productive, on the instruction of someone who is not a fisherman — is the model of obedient trust.

It is not blind obedience. Peter states the professional futility of the exercise plainly and is entirely right to state it. But he has heard something that overrides his own competence, and the reason he gives is the only one he has: not that the strategy makes sense, but that the one who commands can be trusted.

“They left everything and followed him” (v. 11) is the most radical vocational change in the New Testament. James and John leave their father in the boat — not just a career but a family business and a family obligation. The “everything” is genuinely everything: livelihood, security, plans, and the future they had imagined.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade; Luke's own Gospel sends several people home. But everyone who follows has a moment when something must be left on the beach — and it is very often the thing that had only just started going well.

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.

Setting. Only Luke tells the story of the great catch at the call of Peter. Mark and Matthew record the call more briefly (Mark 1:16–20). Luke has already shown Jesus in Simon’s house (4:38), so Simon knew him already. This is the moment of decisive commitment.

The crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God. “The word of God”: Luke’s phrase for Jesus’ preaching. They came hungry for it.

The lake of Gennesaret. Luke’s precise name for the Sea of Galilee, from the fertile plain of Gennesaret on its north-western shore. Luke, who had seen the Mediterranean, does not call a lake about 13 miles by 8 (21 by 13 km) a “sea”.

The fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. After a night’s fishing, nets had to be cleaned of weed and debris, mended and dried. Tired men, at the end of a long, fruitless night (v. 5), doing the dull work.

Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s. Jesus chooses Simon’s boat. He borrows what belongs to Simon, as a first step in claiming Simon himself.

And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. A natural pulpit. Water carries sound, and the shore sloped like an amphitheatre. Simon sat in the boat listening, while he held it steady.

In a sentence. With the crowd pressing to hear God’s word, Jesus got into Simon’s boat, asked him to push out a little, and taught from it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus often begins by asking for the use of something ordinary of yours. Let him have it.
verseByVerse.note: The lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee. Nets were washed and mended after a night’s fishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch. Simon answered: Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.

Put out into the deep and let down your nets. “Your” is plural: the whole crew.

Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! “Master” (epistata): a word for one in authority, a commander; used only by Luke, and only by disciples. Simon was a professional fisherman. Fishing on the lake was done at night, when the fish came near the surface, in the shallows. Daytime, in deep water, was the wrong time and the wrong place. A carpenter was telling a fisherman how to fish. Simon’s reply is honest: it makes no sense.

But at your word I will let down the nets. Key words. Obedience against his own experience and expertise, because of who was speaking. This is faith: acting on Christ’s word when it contradicts what we think we know. Not blind faith, but faith in a word, from a person he had begun to trust.

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon to go into deep water and let down the nets, and Simon, though they had caught nothing all night, obeyed because Jesus said so.

On a Tuesday. Where does Christ’s word tell you to do something that seems pointless by your own experience? Say with Simon: at your word, I will.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night; daytime in deep water was the wrong time and place.

parallels.desc: a night of nothing, then a great catch

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.

They enclosed a large number of fish. Not a lucky shoal, but a miracle of the Lord of creation, who commands the fish of the sea (Psalm 8:8; Jonah 1:17).

And their nets were breaking. Literally “were beginning to break”: overwhelming abundance.

They signaled to their partners in the other boat. James and John (v. 10). A small fishing business.

And filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. More than they could hold. God’s generosity overflows. After a night of empty nets, two boats full to sinking. A picture of the harvest of people that the gospel would bring (v. 10; Acts 2:41).

In a sentence. When they obeyed, they caught so many fish that their nets began to tear, and two boats were filled to sinking.

On a Tuesday. Obedience to Christ’s word may bring a blessing far beyond what you expected. Trust him with your empty nets.

parallels.desc: the net full of large fish

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying: depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken.

Simon Peter. The only time Luke uses both names before 6:14, as if to mark the moment Simon became Peter.

He fell down at Jesus’ knees. In the boat, among the fish. Worship.

Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. A surprising response to a miracle of blessing. Not “thank you”, but “go away”. Why? Because Simon suddenly saw who Jesus was. “Master” (v. 5) has become “Lord”. In the presence of divine holiness and power, Simon saw his own sinfulness. This is what happened to Isaiah in the temple: Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips … for my eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts! (Isaiah 6:5). And to Job: now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself (Job 42:5–6). The nearer we come to God, the more we see our sin. Conviction of sin is the beginning of true discipleship.

For he and all who were with him were astonished. “Astonished” (thambos): awe, amazement, fear.

In a sentence. Seeing the miraculous catch, Simon fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man in the presence of the Lord.

For worship. Have you seen Christ’s holiness clearly enough to see your sin? That is not the end, but the beginning. He does not depart.

parallels.desc: woe is me, for I am lost

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon: do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men. When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Business partners in the fishing trade. With Simon, they became the inner three (8:51; 9:28).

Do not be afraid. Jesus does not depart. He does not deny Simon’s sinfulness. He answers it with grace. A sinful man is exactly the kind of man he calls.

From now on you will be catching men. “Catching” (zōgrōn) literally means “catching alive”, taking alive. Fish are caught to die; people are caught by the gospel to live. Simon’s skills, patience and hard work would be redirected to a new purpose. Peter’s first sermon at Pentecost would catch about three thousand (Acts 2:41). “From now on”: a new life begins.

They left everything and followed him. Only Luke says “everything”. At the moment of their greatest catch, the best night’s work of their lives, they left it all: boats, nets, fish, business. Jesus was worth more. This is what following him means (14:33; 18:28).

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon not to fear, for from then on he would catch people, and Simon, James and John left everything and followed him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus calls sinners to follow him and fish for people. What would it mean for you to leave everything and follow him today?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man “full of leprosy” comes to Jesus. The description is Luke's medical precision: this is not an early skin complaint but an advanced case. Leprosy in the ancient world covered a range of chronic conditions, all of which rendered the sufferer ritually unclean (Lev. 13-14).

The consequences were total. He lived outside the settlement, was required to warn others of his approach — “Unclean! Unclean!” (Lev. 13:45-46) — and was excluded from worship. He was the ultimate social and religious exile, and not because of anything he had done. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside.

His approach is itself an act of desperation and faith: he is in a city he may not enter, on his face in public, saying “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt the power. He is uncertain only about the will — which is exactly the right question to bring, and the answer is the most intimate thing in the chapter.

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches him: “I will; be clean.” The touch is the miracle inside the miracle. Any rabbi could have spoken healing from a safe distance; a word would have done it. Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Under the law, contact ran one way: touching a leper made you unclean. Here the direction is reversed. The holiness of Jesus is not contaminated by the leper; the leper is cleansed by the holiness.

The instruction to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Lev. 14) is not legalism but pastoral wisdom. The priest's certificate was the man's ticket back into the community; without it, even a healed leper could not go home. Jesus heals the disease in a second, then walks the man through the process that heals everything else the disease had done to him — and the certificate stands in the temple records as “a proof to them.”

“Tell no one” is the recognition that a reputation as a healer will bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate. It does, immediately. And Jesus's answer to growing fame is the one Luke keeps recording: he withdraws to desolate places and prays.
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch of the leper is the incarnation in miniature. The Son of God who became flesh did not keep a hygienic distance from the contaminated human condition. He entered it, touched it, took on himself what should have made him unclean, and transferred his own wholeness to the sufferer.

This is what Paul means: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:21). The direction of the transaction never varies. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his. The leper's healing is a parable of salvation performed on a real body.

The willingness Jesus expresses — “I will” — is the answer to every theology that doubts the desire of God to save. The leper's “if you will” is the question of everyone who has been told, explicitly or by implication, that God may not want them, that their case may be outside the scope of his grace, that they may be too far gone.

The reply is not merely “I can.” The power was never in question. It is “I will” — the desire, the purpose, the determination to cleanse, as absolute as the power.
verseByVerse.examples:
The leper models the prayer of humility. He falls on his face; he presumes nothing about Jesus's willingness; he makes no claim on his own account — and he comes. The combination of complete certainty about the power (“you can make me clean”) with complete submission about the will (“if you will”) is the posture faith takes before sovereign grace.

It is not the prayer of someone with low expectations. He expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking and knows he cannot command the answer. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he asks.

Jesus's withdrawal to desolate places in the middle of growing popularity (v. 16) is the model of spiritual formation under pressure — and it was a habit, not an episode. The more the ministry succeeded by external measures, the more he went away.

The pattern refuses the assumption that fruitfulness makes prayer less necessary. For Jesus, fruitfulness was the reason to pray more, because fruitfulness creates demands that only communion with the Father can carry. The minister who cuts prayer in order to meet ministry demands has confused the cause with the effect.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.

A man full of leprosy. Only Luke, the physician, says “full”: an advanced case, covered with it. “Leprosy” in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at) covers a range of skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy (Hansen’s disease). Leviticus 13–14 gives the rules. A person with it was ceremonially unclean. He had to live outside the town, wear torn clothes, leave his hair unkempt, cover his upper lip, and cry out “Unclean, unclean!” to warn people away (Leviticus 13:45–46). No one could touch him without becoming unclean themselves. He was cut off from family, worship and society: a living death. The rabbis considered curing leprosy as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7).

He fell on his face. Desperate reverence.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. He has no doubt about Jesus’ power: you can. His only question is Jesus’ will: if you will. Will Jesus want to help someone like him? “Clean”: not just healed, but restored to God’s people and worship.

In a sentence. A man covered in leprosy fell before Jesus, confident that Jesus could make him clean, if he was willing.

On a Tuesday. Never doubt Christ’s power. And bring your request humbly: if you will. He is always willing to cleanse those who come to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: I will; be clean. And immediately the leprosy left him.

And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. The most shocking detail. No one touched a leper. This man may not have felt a human touch for years. Jesus could have healed him with a word, from a distance (7:7). But he touched him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean. But when Jesus touched the leper, the uncleanness did not pass to Jesus; the cleanness passed to the leper. Holiness is contagious in him.

I will; be clean. The answer to his question. Jesus is willing. Two words in Greek (thelō, katharisthēti). His will and his power are one.

And immediately the leprosy left him. Not gradually. Complete, instant cleansing. A sign that the Messiah had come (7:22).

A picture of salvation. Sin is like leprosy: it defiles, isolates, spreads and kills, and no human remedy can cure it. Christ alone can cleanse it, and he does so by touching us in our uncleanness, taking it on himself at the cross (2 Corinthians 5:21).

In a sentence. Jesus reached out and touched the leper, saying he was willing, and commanded him to be clean, and the leprosy left him at once.

For worship. Jesus is willing to cleanse you. Come to him with your sin, however foul, and hear him say: I will; be clean.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He charged him to tell no one, but: go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.

He charged him to tell no one. Jesus did not want to be known mainly as a miracle-worker, and the crowds were becoming unmanageable (v. 15).

Go and show yourself to the priest. Leviticus 14 set out an elaborate ritual for a cleansed leper: an examination by a priest, the offering of two birds, a week’s wait, then sacrifices. Only then could he return to normal life. Jesus respects the law of Moses, and wants the man to be fully restored to society.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests, and to the people, that he was truly clean. And a testimony to the priests that the Messiah had come, since leprosy was rarely if ever cured.

In a sentence. Jesus told the man not to spread the news, but to go to the priest and offer the sacrifice Moses commanded, as proof of his cleansing.

On a Tuesday. Jesus respected the proper process and authorities. Follow through on what God requires, even after a great blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.

Even more the report about him went abroad. Mark tells us the man disobeyed and spread the news (Mark 1:45).

Great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed. Note the order: to hear first.

But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. The tense means it was his habit: he kept on withdrawing. The busier he was, the more he prayed. Only Luke records this here. The more the crowds pressed in, the more Jesus needed to be alone with his Father. Prayer was not a luxury for him but a necessity. If the Son of God needed to pray, how much more do we.

In a sentence. As his fame spread and crowds came to hear him and be healed, Jesus regularly withdrew to lonely places to pray.

On a Tuesday. When life is busiest, you most need to pray. Make time today to withdraw and be alone with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the first confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities in Luke, and it is carefully staged. Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village of Galilee, and from Judea, and from Jerusalem — a gathering with the shape of an inspection. They are seated. And Luke notes, before anything happens, that the power of the Lord was with Jesus to heal.

Meanwhile four men are carrying a paralysed friend, and the crowd has made the door impassable. So they go up on the roof, take it apart, and lower the man on his mat into the middle of the room, through the ceiling, in front of everyone. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order — and Luke calls it faith.

The faith Jesus sees is not the paralysed man's alone. It is “their” faith: the faith of friends who refused to be stopped. The man himself says nothing in the entire passage. His only contribution is to lie there and be carried, and everything that follows happens because other people would not leave him outside.

What Jesus then says is not what anyone came for: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” Not “rise and walk.” The physical healing is four verses away; forgiveness comes first.

The scribes and Pharisees recognise the claim at once: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Their theology is entirely correct — only God can forgive sins against God. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the premise right and the observation right, and instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy.

Jesus's challenge is pedagogical. “Which is easier, to say 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say 'Rise and walk'?” It is easier to say the first, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. The second is the dangerous sentence. So he does the checkable one — as the credential for the claim that cannot be checked: “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”

The miracles are never the message in this Gospel. They are the authentication of it.

And the man rises, picks up the mat he has spent his life lying on, walks out through the crowd, and goes home glorifying God — leaving a room full of people, dignitaries included, filled with awe and saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing establishes the priority of Luke's whole Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. The paralysis is real, the suffering is real, the exclusion from ordinary life is real — and Jesus removes all of it. But he deals first with something that would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

This is not a denigration of physical suffering, and it is emphatically not a suggestion that the paralysis was caused by the man's sin; Jesus explicitly rejects that reasoning elsewhere (John 9:3). It is a statement about what finally matters — the standing before God that sin destroys.

The scribes' objection is the most important theological sentence in the passage, and Jesus does not answer it by denial. He never says they are wrong about the exclusive divine prerogative. He acts on it, and offers the visible miracle as the proof.

“Son of Man” sounds modest in English and is not. It is Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples shall serve. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, that title while forgiving sins was the claim doubled — and “on earth” presses it further still. The authority is here, at ground level, exercised by a man they can see.
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends are the model of intercessory persistence. They could not bring their friend by the normal route, so they found another. They could not get through the door, so they went through the roof. Their determination is not disrespect for the gathering; it is the overflow of confidence that Jesus can and will do what they believe he can.

This is what intercession looks like when it becomes serious: not eloquence, not technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish on somebody else's behalf.

“When he saw their faith” — the faith Jesus responds to is the faith of the group. That is a significant detail for understanding how the church actually works. The person who cannot bring themselves to pray, whose faith is exhausted or paralysed by their suffering, can be carried to Jesus by the faith of those around them.

People do get carried. There are seasons — grief, depression, shame, sheer exhaustion — when a believer will not get themselves into the room, and somebody else has to do the carrying. This passage says the carrying counts.

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. The first appearance of the Pharisees in Luke. Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes (v. 21), experts in the law of Moses. They had come from every part of the country, even from Jerusalem, perhaps an official investigation of this new teacher. The conflict that will run through the Gospel begins here.

And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. “The Lord” here means God. Jesus’ healing power was the power of God, by the Spirit (4:14).

Some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed. Mark says four men (Mark 2:3). A man who could not come himself, carried by friends.

They were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus. They had one aim: to get him to Jesus.

In a sentence. As Jesus taught, with Pharisees and teachers of the law from all over the land watching, some men tried to bring a paralysed friend to him on a mat.

On a Tuesday. Some people cannot come to Jesus on their own. Who can you carry to him in prayer and in friendship?
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes, experts in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst, before Jesus.

Finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd. The crowd was an obstacle, as crowds often are to those who need Jesus most (18:39; 19:3).

They went up on the roof. Houses in Palestine had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase or ladder.

And let him down with his bed through the tiles. Mark describes digging through the roof (Mark 2:4), the typical Palestinian roof of beams, branches and packed clay. Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek and Roman readers knew, translating the scene into terms they could picture. Either way, they made a hole in someone’s roof. Persistent, creative, costly faith.

Into the midst before Jesus. Right in front of him. They got him there.

In a sentence. Unable to get through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof, removed the tiles and lowered the man on his mat right in front of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let obstacles stop you bringing people to Jesus. Be persistent and creative in love.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek readers knew; Mark describes digging through a roof of packed earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw their faith, he said: man, your sins are forgiven you. And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying: who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?

And when he saw their faith. Faith he could see, because it acted. The faith of the friends, and presumably of the man too. Jesus honours faith that brings others to him. Our faith and prayers can matter for others.

Man, your sins are forgiven you. Not what anyone expected. They had brought him to be healed. Jesus deals first with the deeper problem. A man can be healed in body and still be lost; the greatest need of every person is forgiveness. Some Jews believed sickness was caused by sin, and sometimes it is (John 5:14), though not always (John 9:2–3). Jesus goes to the root. The perfect tense means: your sins have been forgiven, and stand forgiven.

Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Blasphemy is speaking against God, or claiming what belongs to him alone. The penalty was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? They are right. All sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). A person can forgive a wrong done to himself, but only God can forgive sins against God. Isaiah 43:25: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake. If Jesus is not God, he is a blasphemer. Their logic is perfect; their conclusion is wrong. He is not a blasphemer, because he is God.

In a sentence. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the paralysed man his sins were forgiven, and the scribes and Pharisees thought this blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins.

For worship. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus does. Hear his word to you: your sins are forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them: why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, your sins are forgiven you, or to say, rise and walk? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (he said to the man who was paralysed), I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.

When Jesus perceived their thoughts. He knew what they were thinking. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Another sign of who he is.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk? In one sense, forgiving sins is easier to say, because no one can see whether it has happened. Anyone can say it. Healing is harder to say, because if it does not happen, everyone can see. In another sense, forgiveness is far harder, because it is a divine act, and would cost Jesus his life. Jesus will now do the visible, “harder to say” thing, to prove the invisible one.

That you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The healing is evidence. “The Son of Man”: Jesus’ favourite title for himself, from Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure given everlasting authority. The first time Luke uses it. “On earth”: God forgives from heaven; Jesus forgives on earth, as God in human flesh.

Rise, pick up your bed and go home. Three commands, impossible for a paralysed man. The word of Jesus gives the power to obey.

In a sentence. Knowing their thoughts, Jesus healed the paralysed man before their eyes, so that they would know that he, the Son of Man, has authority on earth to forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ visible works prove his invisible authority. If he can heal, he can forgive. Trust him for both.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately he rose up before them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went home, glorifying God. Amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying: we have seen extraordinary things today.

And immediately he rose up before them. In front of everyone, including the sceptics.

And picked up what he had been lying on. The bed that had carried him, he now carried.

And went home, glorifying God. Only Luke records his praise. Forgiven and healed.

And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God. “Amazement” (ekstasis): being beside oneself. Even, perhaps, some of the Pharisees.

We have seen extraordinary things today. “Extraordinary” (paradoxa), from which comes “paradox”: things contrary to expectation, beyond belief. “Today”: again, Luke’s word (4:21).

In a sentence. The man got up at once, carried his mat home praising God, and everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying they had seen incredible things.

For worship. Have you seen extraordinary things in Christ? A forgiven sinner is the greatest of them. Glorify God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the crowded house Luke moves straight to one of the most understated calls in the Gospel. Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says “Follow me.” And Levi left everything and followed him.

The form is identical to the call of Peter, James and John (v. 11) — an encounter, a bare imperative, and complete abandonment. But Levi's “everything” carries a different weight. Tax collectors in the Roman system had purchased the franchise; leaving the booth meant writing off a substantial investment with no prospect of return, and no possibility of going back. The fishermen could have returned to fishing. Levi could not return to a tax booth.

He was also, by the reckoning of every devout person who walked past him, beyond the pale: a collaborator with Rome, a legally protected extortioner, ritually unclean, inadmissible as a witness. Jesus called him without an assessment, a probation, or an interview.

Levi's first act as a disciple is to throw a great banquet and fill it with the only people he knows — a large company of tax collectors and others. He has no theology and no method. He has a house and a contact list, and he puts Jesus in the middle of them.

The Pharisees and their scribes complain, and they complain to the disciples rather than to Jesus: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” The objection is not mere snobbery. Table fellowship in that world was a public declaration of acceptance and solidarity — closer to a signed statement than a meal — so this is a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God.

Jesus's answer is the programmatic statement of the whole ministry: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.”

The word “righteous” is ironic. Everyone in that house is sick; the difference between the two groups is entirely in what they know about themselves. A man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor, however available the doctor makes himself. And the last two words are not decoration — he called sinners to repentance. The table at Levi's house is a doctor's visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease.
verseByVerse.theology:
The call of Levi is Luke's announcement that the kingdom of God comes to the most unexpected people. Matthew's Gospel tells us this is Matthew himself (Matt. 9:9). The author of one of the four Gospels is a man whom the respectable religious society of his day considered beyond the reach of God's grace.

And of the four apostle lists in the New Testament, the only one that attaches “the tax collector” to his name is the one he wrote (Matt. 10:3). He never got over it.

“I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” is not a statement about two classes of people — the righteous who do not need Jesus and the sinners who do. Scripture is unambiguous that there are no righteous: “none is righteous, no, not one” (Rom. 3:10).

It is a statement about two self-perceptions. The “righteous” are the self-righteous, whose assessment of their own spiritual condition is so favourable that they see no need of a physician. The tragedy of the Pharisees is not their theology, most of which was sound. It is their self-knowledge. They could not be called to repentance because they did not believe they needed to repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi's banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace and immediately wants the people he loves to meet the one who gave it. No training, no method, no strategy — he invites his friends to his house and invites Jesus to the same room.

The criticism this drew is the criticism grace-shaped evangelism has always drawn: it happens in the wrong places, with the wrong people, without sufficient concern for the reputation of those involved. Jesus's presence at that table is the answer to every objection of the kind.

“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” is the perennial complaint of those who would like the church to be more selective in its welcome. The instinct to keep the table clean — to eat only with the already acceptable — is deeply human, and it rests on a real principle: that holiness is preserved by separation.

What it has not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round, which the same chapter has already shown at a leper's skin. Jesus's table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well gather to congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. He said to him: follow me. And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.

A tax collector named Levi. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); perhaps he had both names, like Simon Peter. Tax collectors were despised (3:12). Levi probably collected tolls on goods passing along the trade route through Capernaum, for Herod Antipas.

Sitting at the tax booth. At work. The place of his sin.

Follow me. Two words in Greek. Jesus calls a sinner, as he had just forgiven one. The Pharisees had complained about forgiveness; now Jesus makes a tax collector a disciple.

And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. Like the fishermen (v. 11). But for Levi it was more costly. A fisherman could go back to his boat (John 21:3). A tax collector who left his post could not get it back. He gave up a lucrative career for good.

In a sentence. Jesus called Levi, a despised tax collector, from his booth to follow him, and Levi left everything and followed.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond Christ’s call. He calls people from the middle of their sin, and he calls you to leave whatever holds you.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew’s Gospel calls Levi “Matthew.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying: why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?

And Levi made him a great feast in his house. A celebration. Levi’s first act as a disciple: invite his friends to meet Jesus. A rich man, he gave a banquet.

A large company of tax collectors and others. Levi’s friends were tax collectors and other outcasts; respectable people would not associate with him. He introduced them to Jesus. The natural evangelism of a new believer.

Reclining at table with them. In that culture, sharing a meal was a sign of acceptance, friendship and fellowship. To eat with someone was to accept them.

And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled. “Grumbled” (egongyzon): murmured, the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27). They do not speak to Jesus directly, but to his disciples.

Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? The Pharisees kept themselves separate from “sinners”: those who did not keep the law as they interpreted it, and the openly immoral. Eating with them would make you unclean. To the Pharisees, holiness meant separation from sinners. For Jesus, it meant going to them. The charge will come again (7:34; 15:2; 19:7).

In a sentence. Levi held a great feast for Jesus with many tax collectors and outcasts, and the Pharisees grumbled to the disciples about eating with sinners.

On a Tuesday. Introduce your non-Christian friends to Jesus. And don’t let fear of criticism keep you from friendship with outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb, especially apt from Luke the physician. A doctor goes to the sick. That is his job. He does not catch their disease; he heals it. Jesus is the doctor; sinners are the sick. Where else should he be?

I have not come to call the righteous. Irony. There are no righteous (Romans 3:10). But the Pharisees thought they were, and so did not think they needed him. Jesus cannot help those who think they are well.

But sinners to repentance. Only Luke adds “to repentance”. Jesus does not accept sinners to leave them as they are, but calls them to change. His welcome is not approval of sin, but the beginning of transformation. Grace receives sinners and changes them.

In a sentence. Jesus replied that, like a doctor who goes to the sick, he came to call not those who think they are righteous but sinners to repentance.

On a Tuesday. You qualify for Jesus only by admitting you are sick. Come to him as a sinner, and he will heal you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question about fasting is deceptively simple — why do Jesus's disciples not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees? — and the answer, in two images and an observation, reframes the whole relationship between the old covenant and the new.

The bridegroom image is the most significant, because it is a claim about identity. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God: “Your Maker is your husband” (Isa. 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hos. 2:19; cf. Jer. 2:2). Israel is the bride, and every apostasy is described as adultery. To explain his disciples' behaviour by saying the bridegroom is present is to say who has arrived — and John the Baptist had already made the same identification, placing himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre (John 3:29).

The disciples do not fast because this is not the season for it. Fasting at a wedding is not more serious; it is out of time.

Then the shadow: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” It is the first hint of the cross in Jesus's own teaching in Luke, dropped without warning into an argument about religious observance. Nobody at that table could have understood it.

The garment and the wineskin press the same point. A patch cut from a new coat ruins the new and does not match the old; new wine in a hardened skin bursts the skin and is lost. The kingdom Jesus inaugurates is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfilment — and fulfilment is not the same as continuation.

The new covenant is organically connected to the old; Jesus keeps the law, goes to the synagogue weekly, sends the leper to the priest. But what has arrived could not be contained by what preceded it, not because the old was worthless but because it was never designed to hold this.

And the last line is the sharpest: “no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good.'” It is not a compliment to the old wine. It is a description of a palate — and of the men in the doorway, who refused Jesus not because they had examined him and found him wanting but because they were comfortable, and he did not taste of what they were used to.
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language is one of the most significant implicit claims to deity in the Synoptic Gospels. In the prophets, the husband of Israel is the LORD himself, and the relationship between God and his people is consistently described in bridal terms.

Revelation carries the image to its conclusion — the marriage supper of the Lamb, the new Jerusalem coming down as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 19:7-9; 21:2-9). The fasting question in Luke 5 is a thread that runs all the way to the last page of the Bible.

The observation in v. 39 is not a sociological aside about wine preferences. It is a precise description of the spiritual condition of people who have grown comfortable in the old forms: they feel no need of new wine, because what they have is satisfying.

That is the condition of the Pharisees, and it was not a moral failure. The old wine of the law and the tradition was genuinely good — God gave it. This is the most dangerous spiritual position there is, because it requires a good thing to settle into: contentment with something genuinely good, in the presence of something better.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom's presence is the reason for the disciples' joy, and it remains the reason for Christian joy. The resurrection did not remove the bridegroom; it confirmed that he is alive and with his people until he returns.

So Christian fasting is not the fast of the men who asked the question. Jesus assumes his people will fast — “they will fast in those days,” and those days are these — but it is the fast of people who have known him, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God's attention. A body saying what the heart already knows: that the best thing is still ahead.

The new wineskins are a standing challenge to every Christian tradition, and the question has to be asked honestly. Not “is this old?” — age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

This is not a call to theological novelty. The wine is always the same wine, the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, and it is the oldest thing there is. But a wineskin's only job is to hold wine, and the moment it begins to be valued for itself it has started to fail at the one thing it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: the disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink. Jesus said to them: can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.

The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers. The law commanded only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). But devout Jews fasted more. Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (18:12). John’s disciples, following his austere life, fasted often.

But yours eat and drink. As they had just been doing at Levi’s feast.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? A wedding feast lasted up to a week, and was a time of joy; wedding guests were excused from religious duties such as fasting. Fasting expressed mourning, sorrow and longing. But while Jesus is here, the time of longing is over. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus calls himself the bridegroom: another claim to be God. The messianic wedding feast has begun.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them. “Taken away” (aparthē): snatched, removed by force. The first hint in Luke of his violent death (Isaiah 53:8).

And then they will fast in those days. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Fasting is right for Christians now, as we long for his return. But it is no longer a mark of mourning without hope, nor a means of earning favour.

In a sentence. When asked why his disciples did not fast, Jesus answered that wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is present, but they will fast when he is taken away.

On a Tuesday. The Christian life has times of feasting and times of fasting. Rejoice in Christ’s presence, and long for his return.
verseByVerse.note: The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement. A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: no one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.

He also told them a parable. Three short parables (vv. 36–39) explain why Jesus’ disciples do not follow the old patterns.

No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Luke’s version is slightly different from Mark’s (Mark 2:21). In Luke, you ruin the new garment by cutting a patch out of it, and the patch doesn’t match the old one anyway. Both are spoiled.

The point. What Jesus brings is not a patch to mend the old system of Judaism. It is something entirely new: the new covenant, the kingdom of God. It cannot be stitched onto the old ways of fasting and rule-keeping without ruining both. The gospel is not a supplement to religion; it is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

In a sentence. Jesus said that no one cuts a patch from a new garment to mend an old one, since that ruins the new and does not match the old.

On a Tuesday. Don’t treat Jesus as a patch on your old life. He makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.

Wineskins. Wine was stored in goatskins, sewn up with the hair inside. New wine is still fermenting, giving off gas and expanding. A new skin stretches with it. An old skin has already stretched and become brittle; it would burst under the pressure, and both wine and skin would be lost.

The point. The new wine is the life of the kingdom that Jesus brings: joy, grace, the Spirit, the new covenant. The old wineskins are the old forms of Judaism, the Pharisees’ traditions and rituals. They cannot contain the new life; they would burst. The new life needs new forms: the church, with its new covenant worship.

But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. “Must” (blēteon): it is necessary.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is bad or useless. Jesus came to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). But the old covenant’s forms, the sacrifices, food laws, priesthood and temple, were shadows that pointed forward to Christ, and give way to the reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 8:13).

In a sentence. Jesus said new wine must go into new wineskins, because old ones would burst, meaning the new life of his kingdom cannot be contained in the old forms.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith so tied to familiar forms that you resist anything new God is doing? Hold to the gospel; hold forms loosely.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says: the old is good.

Only Luke adds this saying. A wry, almost humorous comment on human nature.

No one after drinking old wine desires new. Old wine is smooth and mellow; new wine is raw and harsh. People who are used to the old prefer it, and will not even try the new.

For he says, The old is good. Some manuscripts read “the old is better”, but the best read “good”: the old is good enough. Why change?

The point. Jesus explains why the Pharisees and many others reject him. It is not that they have tried the new and found it wanting. They are content with the old, comfortable in their religion, and do not want anything new. They do not feel the need for what Jesus brings. Self-satisfaction is a great obstacle to faith.

In a sentence. Jesus observed that those who are used to old wine do not want new, because they think the old is good enough, explaining why many rejected him.

On a Tuesday. Being content with your religion can keep you from Christ. Ask whether you are truly drinking his new wine, or just the old.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke adds this saying — a wry comment on those content with the old ways.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is Luke's equivalent of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount — shorter, sharper, and structurally parallel, though not identical. Before the sermon comes the choosing of the twelve and two Sabbath controversies that frame the sermon's radical ethics with a theological question: by what authority does Jesus define what is lawful, and what kind of community does that authority create? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) is the charter of the kingdom community — the description of what it looks like to live under the reign of God when that reign runs against every instinct of the natural self.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) are the most direct statement in the chapter: the kingdom reverses the world's value system. The poor are blessed; the rich are warned. The hungry are filled; the full are emptied. Those who weep now will laugh; those who laugh now will mourn. This is not a promise that poverty is virtuous or that comfort is sinful; it is a statement about the direction of the kingdom. God's attention, God's blessing, God's purposes consistently run toward those whom the world has left behind — and consistently challenge those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from anyone, including God.

The ethical core of the sermon (vv. 27–45) — love your enemies, do not judge, produce good fruit — is the most demanding teaching in Luke's Gospel, and it rests entirely on the character of God. Love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and evil. Do not judge because you will be judged by the measure you use. Bear good fruit because the tree is known by its fruit. The final image — the house on the rock — is the sermon's warning: hearing these words is not enough. The one who hears and does not do is building on sand. The storm will come, and only the house that is built on hearing and doing will stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes everything in the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

The first is about disciples plucking grain as they walk through fields. Plucking ears from a neighbour's standing grain was expressly permitted (Deut. 23:25), so the objection is not theft; it is that plucking counts as reaping and rubbing as threshing, both forbidden on the Sabbath by the scribal fence built around the commandment.

That fence did not begin in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment. And it had become unbearable — a gift turned into an audit, a day given to relieve working people now governed by case law only the leisured could master.

Jesus's response reaches back to 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run and hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which the law reserved for priests, and shared it with his men — and Scripture records it without a word of censure. The point is not that rules do not matter. It is that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. Jesus is not appealing over the head of Scripture; he is appealing to Scripture against a reading of it.

The choice of precedent is not accidental either. Of all the cases available, he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, rejected and on the run, with his own small band of followers, doing what the authorities called unlawful.

Then the conclusion: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” He does not argue that the Sabbath is unimportant. He claims that he is the one who determines its meaning — which, given that the Sabbath is rooted in creation, enshrined in the Ten Commandments, and named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel, is a claim about who he is.

The Pharisees are not wrong to take the Sabbath seriously. They are wrong to think their authority over it exceeds the authority of the one who instituted it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” is a divine claim in Jewish ears. The Sabbath is God's own institution — rooted in creation (Gen. 2:2-3), enshrined in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:8-11), and described as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exod. 31:12-17).

To be Lord of the Sabbath is to exercise authority over the covenant sign of God himself. Jesus is not relativising the day; he is claiming to be its author. This is among the most compact and most decisive of the implicit claims to deity scattered through the Synoptic Gospels.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7:13-14 — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds modest in English and was not.

What is worth adding is what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest, but to give it back. The day always pointed at a person, and the person has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples:
The complaint about grain-plucking is a case study in confusing the purpose of a law with the law itself. The Sabbath was given as a gift — a day of rest for those who worked, and a sign of trust that God would provide without their constant labour.

The Pharisees' elaborate hedge of regulations (the Mishnah tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters) had turned that gift into a burden. When a law loses contact with the grace and wisdom that gave it, it becomes oppression. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he liberates it from the accretion that had buried what it was for.

The sequence is worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and does not require bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of the point.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said: why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?

The Sabbath controversies. Two conflicts over the Sabbath (vv. 1–11) follow the conflicts of chapter 5. The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest (Exodus 20:8–11), was one of the great marks of Jewish identity, along with circumcision and the food laws. The Pharisees had built a vast fence of rules around it, defining 39 categories of forbidden work, including reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food.

His disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. Only Luke mentions rubbing them in their hands, to remove the husks. Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field while walking through was explicitly allowed by the law (Deuteronomy 23:25). The disciples were hungry.

Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? The objection was not theft but the day. By the Pharisees’ rules, plucking was reaping, and rubbing was threshing and winnowing. They had turned a day of rest and delight (Isaiah 58:13) into a burden of regulations.

In a sentence. When Jesus’ disciples picked and rubbed some grain to eat as they walked through a field on the Sabbath, Pharisees accused them of breaking the Sabbath law.

On a Tuesday. Human rules can turn God’s good gifts into burdens. Make sure the rules you live by are God’s, not just tradition’s.
