verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?

Have you not read. A pointed question to experts in Scripture. Jesus answers from the Bible.

What David did when he was hungry. 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came to the priest Ahimelech at Nob, where the tabernacle then stood, and asked for food. The only bread was the holy bread.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on a golden table in the Holy Place before the Lord each Sabbath, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). Only priests could lawfully eat it.

The argument. Scripture records without criticism that David, God’s anointed king, and his men ate the holy bread in a time of need. The ceremonial law gave way to human need. If David could do that, then the Son of David, the greater anointed king, and his followers can do much more. And if Scripture itself shows that ceremonial rules yield to need and mercy, the Pharisees’ rules certainly must. God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 12:7).

In a sentence. Jesus answered from Scripture that David and his men, when hungry, ate the holy bread that only priests could lawfully eat.

On a Tuesday. God’s law is for human good. Use it to show mercy, not to load burdens on others.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. An enormous claim. God instituted the Sabbath at creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and gave it in the Ten Commandments. To be lord of the Sabbath is to have authority over God’s own law, to determine its meaning and use. Only God could claim that. Jesus is not breaking the Sabbath; he is its Lord, who gives its true interpretation. Mark adds: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians must keep Saturday. Many Reformed and Puritan Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday, the “Christian Sabbath”, to be kept by resting from work and recreation and devoting the day to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10); Christians are not bound to its ceremonial regulations (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5). Yet the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, is the church’s day of gathering for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). It is a privilege and a gift, not a burden, and the principle of a regular day of rest and worship remains wise and good. This is held charitably toward those who keep a stricter Sabbath.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath, with authority over God’s own law.

For worship. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, and he gives true rest. Use the Lord’s Day as a gift: rest in him, and worship with his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second Sabbath controversy involves a man with a withered right hand — which, in a manual economy, meant an inability to earn a living. Luke the physician notes which hand.

The scribes and Pharisees are watching to see whether Jesus will heal, “so that they might find a reason to accuse him.” The watching is calculated and hostile, and it is worth registering how ugly it is: they are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. His hand interests them only as evidence.

Jesus knows exactly what they are doing, and he does not avoid the confrontation — he creates it. He tells the man to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and puts a question to the room: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?”

That question is the interpretive key to his whole Sabbath theology, and it is why they cannot answer. They came prepared to argue that healing is work and that a hand withered for years can wait until sundown — a reasonable position on their own terms. Jesus refuses the terms. He removes the neutral square marked “wait until tomorrow”: to be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction but a choice, and it belongs in the other column.

The Sabbath is not a day of inaction. It is a day defined by the character of its author — and the God who rested on the seventh day is the God who sustains life on every day. Their silence answers the question for them.

Then he heals without touching. The man is simply told to stretch out the hand he cannot stretch out, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. There is nothing to accuse.

And the response is fury — the first time in Luke that the religious leaders plot against him. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The hardness that sets in at this point — “they were filled with fury” — begins the trajectory that ends at the cross. The fury is not primarily moral; it is theological. Jesus has publicly claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their interpretation, and refused to be intimidated by their watching.

Every confrontation confirms what they most fear: this man is either a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided he is a blasphemer, and from that decision every subsequent action follows with a terrible logic.

Their fury is a rage that has stopped thinking. It is what a framework does when it has been exposed in public and its owners are unwilling to revise it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So these Sabbath controversies are not peripheral disputes about religious practice. They are the opening moves of the confrontation that will define history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man with the withered hand is told to stand up and come out into the middle — to be visible, exposed, in front of everyone. He obeys, knowing his disability will be on display, and Luke records that he rose and stood there.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. The person who keeps their need hidden, who manages a difficulty from the edge of the community, does not receive what the one standing in the middle receives. Jesus consistently calls his healings into the light.

And the command he gives is the one thing the man cannot do — stretching out that hand is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first so that obedience becomes possible. He is told to do the impossible thing, and discovers in the doing that it is possible.

That is very often the order in the Christian life. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of following Christ feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. The scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand: come and stand here. And he rose and stood there.

A man was there whose right hand was withered. Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand: the working hand. Without it, a labourer could not earn a living. “Withered”: shrunken, paralysed.

The scribes and the Pharisees watched him. “Watched” (paretērounto): watched closely, spied on. They were there not to worship but to catch him out.

To see whether he would heal on the Sabbath. By the rabbis’ rule, healing counted as work, and was allowed on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand could wait until tomorrow.

But he knew their thoughts. As in 5:22.

Come and stand here. Literally “stand in the middle”. Jesus does not avoid the confrontation. He makes the healing public, in full view of his critics.

In a sentence. In the synagogue on another Sabbath, with scribes and Pharisees watching to accuse him, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, called a man with a withered right hand to stand in front of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let fear of critics stop you doing good openly.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it? After looking around at them all he said to him: stretch out your hand. And he did so, and his hand was restored.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm. Jesus reframes the question. Not “is healing work?”, but “what is the Sabbath for?” To fail to do good when you can is to do harm. There is no neutral option. And the irony: Jesus is doing good on the Sabbath, while his critics are plotting to destroy him on the Sabbath (v. 11).

To save life or to destroy it? “Life” (psychē) can also mean “soul”.

And after looking around at them all. A long, searching look. Mark says with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5).

Stretch out your hand. The very thing he could not do. The command brings the power to obey. Jesus did no “work” that could be charged: no touch, no medicine. Just a word.

And his hand was restored. Made whole, as it had been.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or destroy it, and then told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored.

On a Tuesday. Failing to do good when you can is not neutral. Look for the good you can do today.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.

But they were filled with fury. “Fury” (anoias): literally “mindlessness”, a senseless rage. Not joy that a man was healed, but anger that their rules had been broken. Their religion had made them blind to mercy.

And discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. The plotting begins. Mark says they began to plot with the Herodians how to destroy him (Mark 3:6). Luke’s wording is milder at this stage, but the direction is clear.

In a sentence. The scribes and Pharisees were filled with senseless rage and discussed what they could do to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Religion without love can make people furious at the very goodness of God. Examine your reactions when God blesses people in ways you don’t expect.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before choosing the twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer on the mountain. This is characteristic of Luke: the major decisions of the ministry are set in the context of prayer. And the placing is deliberate — Luke has just recorded the first plot against Jesus, and the next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

The choice of twelve from a larger body of disciples is not made lightly or impulsively. Luke gives the two stages precisely: he called the disciples, and from them he chose twelve.

The number is not convenient; it is theological. Israel had twelve tribes named for twelve sons, and no Jew could hear the number accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and at the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations bearing these men's names (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke — apostoloi, sent ones. They remain disciples, learners; but a disciple who has been given an errand is something more.

The list itself is a study in unlikely combinations. Peter, who a chapter ago asked Jesus to leave because he was a sinful man. Matthew, the tax collector from the booth. And Simon the Zealot — a man whose title points to zeal for Israel and the law, and very possibly to sympathy with armed resistance to Rome. In ordinary life Matthew and Simon would not have shared a road. They shared a purse and a mission for three years.

Several of the twelve are almost unknown — James the son of Alphaeus above all, of whom the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists.

And the list ends with Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached, and the wording matters: not who was a traitor but who became one. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the others, and heard and saw everything they did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are distinguished from disciples by a specific function: they are sent ones, commissioned witnesses rather than merely learners. Their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus will be the foundation of the church's proclamation.

Paul will later say the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). The night of prayer before the choice establishes that this foundation is not a human selection but a divinely guided one, even though the divine guidance works through a human process.

Luke's parenthesis on Judas — chosen deliberately, after a night of communion with the Father, and yet becoming a traitor — is a weight the reader is not permitted to set down. Election to office is not the same as salvation, and proximity to Christ is no protection.

He handled the money, was sent out with power like the rest, and heard every word of the sermon that follows. The verb Luke chooses describes a process, not a category — which should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.
verseByVerse.examples:
The night of prayer before the choice models the principle that consequential decisions belong to God before they belong to us. Not every decision requires a night of prayer — but every decision that will shape the community of God's people belongs first to the Father.

The Jesus who spent a whole night praying before choosing twelve men puts a question to every leader, every elder board, every appointment committee: have we prayed as long and as seriously as this decision actually deserves?

And the composition of the twelve is a standing rebuke to congregations divided along political lines. Whatever holds a church together, it is not agreement about Rome, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be.

If a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man called the Zealot could eat from the same bag for three years, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. When day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles.

He went out to the mountain to pray. Only Luke records this night of prayer. At a time of growing opposition (v. 11), and before a crucial decision, Jesus prays.

And all night he continued in prayer to God. The whole night. The only time the Gospels record this before Gethsemane. The choice of the Twelve was so important that Jesus spent the night seeking his Father’s will. Even Judas was chosen after a night of prayer (John 6:70).

He called his disciples and chose from them twelve. “Disciples”: a larger group of followers. From them he chose twelve, an inner circle. Twelve, matching the twelve tribes of Israel: Jesus is reconstituting the people of God around himself. The Twelve will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (22:30), and their names are on the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14).

Whom he named apostles. “Apostle” (apostolos) means “one who is sent”, an envoy, an authorised representative. They would be sent with his authority to preach (9:1–2), and after his resurrection, to be his witnesses to the world (24:48; Acts 1:8). Luke uses the title more than the other Gospels.

The apostles’ unique role. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22), commissioned directly by him, and laid the foundation of the church through their teaching, which we have in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). There are no apostles in this sense today. Their teaching, in Scripture, is our foundation.

In a sentence. After spending the whole night in prayer on a mountain, Jesus chose twelve of his disciples and named them apostles.

On a Tuesday. Pray before big decisions. If Jesus spent all night in prayer before choosing, how much more do you need to?
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

Four lists. The Twelve are listed four times in the New Testament (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). The order varies, but Peter is always first and Judas Iscariot always last. They fall into three groups of four, each headed by the same name (Peter, Philip, James son of Alphaeus).

Simon, whom he named Peter. “Peter” (Petros, Aramaic Kēphas) means “rock”. Not what he was, but what he would become (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42).

Andrew his brother. Who first brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:40–42).

James and John. Sons of Zebedee, fishermen (5:10). James was the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John wrote the Gospel, letters and Revelation.

Philip, and Bartholomew. Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Bartholomew (“son of Tolmai”) is probably the Nathanael of John 1:45–51, since he is paired with Philip.

Matthew. The tax collector Levi (5:27).

Thomas. “The twin” (John 11:16), remembered for his doubt and his great confession: My Lord and my God! (John 20:28).

James the son of Alphaeus. Possibly “James the younger” (Mark 15:40).

Simon who was called the Zealot. “Zealot” may mean zealous for the law, or a member of the nationalist movement that wanted to overthrow Rome by force. If so, he and Matthew, the tax collector who worked for Rome’s client, were political enemies, now united in Christ.

Judas the son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark; the same man with two names. Also called “Judas (not Iscariot)” in John 14:22.

And Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. “Became”: he was not chosen as a traitor, but became one. Chosen after a night of prayer, with the same privileges as the others, yet he betrayed his Lord. A sobering warning that outward closeness to Jesus is no guarantee of a true heart.

In a sentence. The twelve apostles were Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

On a Tuesday. Jesus chose ordinary, very different, flawed men: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot. He can use you. And he unites people who would otherwise be enemies.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sermon on the Plain begins with a declaration that sounds like a mistake on first reading: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Luke's beatitudes are addressed directly to the disciples — “blessed are you” — unlike Matthew's more generalised forms. And they are paired with woes Matthew does not include. The poor are blessed and the rich are warned; the hungry are promised satisfaction and the full are warned of hunger; those who weep now will laugh, and those who laugh now will mourn.

The poverty is not romanticised. Luke does not say “poor in spirit” but simply “poor” — the destitute, those with nothing of their own who depend entirely on what others give. This is not a spiritualisation of poverty; it is the announcement that the kingdom belongs to those whose condition leaves no room for self-sufficiency. Not because poverty is virtuous, but because the poor have no resources to trust except God.

Set beside Matthew's “poor in spirit,” the two hold opposite ends of one truth, and neither is safe alone. Luke without Matthew makes an empty purse a ticket. Matthew without Luke lets “poor in spirit” be quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing. Matthew names the poverty God blesses; Luke names the room such people are usually standing in.

The woes are the other edge of the same blade. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets' word, carrying grief as much as warning (Isa. 5:8-23; Amos 6:1-7). It is not a wish for harm but a declaration that those who have “received their consolation” have been paid already and have nothing further outstanding.

The last woe is the most searching: “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.” Israel's true prophets were consistently unwelcome; the popular ones were the ones who told the king what he wanted to hear.

And the final beatitude (vv. 22-23) is the only one about something the disciples bring on themselves. Four escalating forms of social death — hated, excluded, reviled, name thrown out as evil — and the command attached is not endurance but leaping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes together express the eschatological reversal — the biblical pattern in which the last days invert the present order. Mary sang it in the Magnificat: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty.

This is not a programme of economic analysis; it is a prophetic announcement about the direction of God's kingdom. Those whose present condition drives them to dependence on God are in the right position to receive what the kingdom gives; those who can be self-sufficient are in the wrong one.

Read through the whole gospel, these blessings and woes are far more than social reversal — they are anchored in Christ himself, who entered the very conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept real tears, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us.

The great reversal is therefore no abstract law of history but a sure thing purchased in him. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the One who was made poor that we might be made rich, and who fills the empty out of his own fullness. And the woes are not cruelty but mercy raising its voice — a warning to the comfortable to loosen their grip on thin, passing riches before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples:
The beatitudes are often preached as comfort to those who suffer, and they are that. But they are also diagnosis and invitation. The question they put to every hearer is: in which column do you find yourself? The sermon does not allow a neutral answer; it creates a crisis of self-knowledge.

And the woes have to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading them is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. The question is not whether you enjoy good things but where your consolation actually comes from — what steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

“Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy” (v. 23) is the response Jesus commands to persecution — not stoic endurance, not grim determination, but leaping joy. The verb is the one used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41).

This is eschatological joy: the joy that knows how the story ends and can afford to leap because the future is secure. It is what Paul means in Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. The leap is only possible if the landing is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. Those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.

The Sermon on the Plain. What follows (vv. 20–49) is Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon, shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), with much of the same material. Matthew’s is given on a mountain; Luke’s on a level place. Either they are two occasions (Jesus surely preached similar sermons many times), or Luke’s “level place” was a plateau on the mountain. Luke omits material about the Jewish law, which would interest his Gentile readers less, and adds the woes.

And he came down with them. Like Moses coming down from the mountain with the law. But Jesus brings the law of the kingdom.

From all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. Jews from the south, and people from the Gentile coastal cities of the north. A foretaste of the gospel to all nations.

Who came to hear him and to be healed. Again, hearing first.

For power came out from him and healed them all. The power of God (5:17), flowing from him (8:46).

In a sentence. Jesus came down with the Twelve to a level place, where crowds from Judea, Jerusalem and the Gentile coast came to hear him and be healed, and power went out from him and healed them all.

On a Tuesday. Come to Jesus to hear him, as well as to receive from him.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples. The sermon is addressed to disciples, though the crowd hears it. It describes the life of those who follow him.

The Beatitudes. Luke gives four blessings (vv. 20–23) and four matching woes (vv. 24–26). Matthew gives nine blessings and no woes (Matthew 5:3–12). Luke’s are in the second person (“you”), direct and personal; Matthew’s in the third (“those who”).

Blessed. Makarioi: not “happy” in a shallow sense, but fortunate, in a good position before God, approved by him. The Hebrew equivalent opens the Psalms: Blessed is the man (Psalm 1:1). It is God’s verdict, not a feeling.

Are you who are poor. Matthew says “poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3). Luke speaks of the poor as they actually were. Many of Jesus’ disciples were literally poor, having left everything (5:11, 28). But in the Old Testament, “the poor” were also the humble, who had no one to depend on but God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2). Poverty is not itself a virtue, and not every poor person is blessed. But the poor are often more ready to receive the kingdom, because they know their need. The two readings come together: the blessed poor are those who come to God empty-handed.

For yours is the kingdom of God. Present tense: it is yours now. They have no earthly security, but they have God’s kingdom, the greatest wealth of all (12:32). This fulfils Jesus’ mission: to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that they who are poor are blessed, because the kingdom of God belongs to them.

For worship. Come to God as one who is poor, with nothing to offer. The kingdom belongs to such people.

Where it applies: An elderly widow in your church lives on very little, and trusts Christ. Do not pity her as one who has missed out. She is rich in the kingdom, and you may learn more from her than she from you.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks poverty in itself makes a person right with God, or uses this verse as a reason not to help the poor, since they are blessed already. The poor Jesus blesses are those who look to God (Matthew 5:3), and the same Lord commands us to open our hands to them (1 John 3:17).

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.

Blessed are you who are hungry now. “Now” is important, and only Luke has it. Present hunger, future satisfaction. Real hunger, physical (the poor often went hungry), but also hunger for God and righteousness (Matthew 5:6). Mary sang: he has filled the hungry with good things (1:53).

For you shall be satisfied. Future tense. At the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15; Isaiah 25:6), and in a measure even now. Satisfied completely: the word is used of animals fed full.

Blessed are you who weep now. Those who grieve over suffering, over their own sin, and over the world’s rebellion against God. Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4).

For you shall laugh. Joy will come. God will wipe away every tear (Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 21:4). Psalm 126:5: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Psalm 30:5).

The pattern. The present is not the whole story. The kingdom reverses present conditions. Those who suffer now with Christ will rejoice with him later. This is the logic of the cross and resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced blessed those who are hungry and weeping now, because they will be filled and will laugh.

On a Tuesday. If you are weeping now, take heart: Jesus promises you will laugh. Your present sorrow is not the end.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.

When people hate you and when they exclude you. Four kinds of persecution. Hatred. Exclusion: being cut off from the synagogue, from family, from community (John 9:22; 16:2). Reviling: verbal abuse. Spurning your name as evil: your name, or the name “Christian”, treated as a curse (Acts 11:26; 1 Peter 4:14–16).

On account of the Son of Man! Not for being obnoxious, but for Christ’s sake. Suffering for wrongdoing has no blessing (1 Peter 4:15).

Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy. Not just endure it, but rejoice, even leap, like a lamb in spring, or like John in the womb (1:41, the same word). An astonishing command. The apostles did exactly this (Acts 5:41).

For behold, your reward is great in heaven. The reason for joy: God sees, and will reward. Not that we earn heaven by suffering, but that God honours faithfulness.

For so their fathers did to the prophets. Persecution puts you in the company of the prophets. It is a mark of belonging to God’s true servants (11:47–51; 13:34).

In a sentence. Jesus called his disciples blessed when they are hated, excluded and insulted for his sake, and told them to leap for joy, because their reward in heaven is great, as the prophets’ was.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or excluded for following Christ, rejoice. You are in the company of the prophets, and God will reward you.

Where it applies: You are left out of a family group chat because you became a Christian. Do not answer with bitterness. Rejoice: you are in the company of the prophets.

Where it would be wrong: You are left out because you lecture everyone at family meals. That is not being hated for the Son of Man’s sake. Ask first whether the offence is Christ or your manner (1 Peter 3:15–16).

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.

Woe. Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings. “Woe” (ouai) is a cry of grief and warning, used by the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1). Not a curse, but a lament: how terrible for you.

Woe to you who are rich. Not that wealth is sinful in itself; Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich. But wealth tends to make people self-sufficient, satisfied with this world, and blind to their need of God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25). It is a great danger.

For you have received your consolation. “Received” (apechete) is a business word, used on receipts: paid in full. You have had your comfort already. There is nothing more to come. Abraham said the same to the rich man: you in your lifetime received your good things (16:25).

Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Those who are satisfied with this world’s goods, and feel no spiritual hunger.

Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Not innocent laughter, but the careless laughter of those who do not take God or sin or suffering seriously (James 4:9).

In a sentence. Jesus warned that the rich, the full and those who laugh now have had their comfort already, and will hunger and weep.

On a Tuesday. If you are rich, full and laughing, examine yourself. Is your comfort in this world, or in God? Hold your blessings with humility and generosity.

Where it applies: You have plenty. Give generously this month to someone who has little, and give thanks for what you have, holding it loosely.

Where it would be wrong: You look down on wealthy Christians, or feel guilty over every good meal. The woe is on those whose comfort is in their riches instead of God. Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia were wealthy and faithful (Genesis 13:2; Matthew 27:57; Acts 16:14–15). Paul tells the rich not to hope in riches but to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.

When all people speak well of you. Universal popularity is a danger sign. A faithful witness to Christ will always offend some (v. 22). If no one ever objects to what you say, perhaps you are saying only what people want to hear.

For so their fathers did to the false prophets. The false prophets of Israel were popular because they told people what they wanted: Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 1 Kings 22:13; Isaiah 30:10). The true prophets were persecuted; the false ones were praised.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should try to be unpopular, or that being well thought of is always wrong (Acts 2:47; 1 Timothy 3:7). But seeking everyone’s approval will lead to compromising the truth.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that being praised by everyone is a danger, because that is how people treated the false prophets.

On a Tuesday. Are you more concerned about pleasing people than pleasing God (Galatians 1:10)? Speak the truth in love, even when it is unpopular.

Where it applies: Your friends all approve of something Scripture calls sin, and expect you to cheer. Gently say what you believe, even if it costs you their good opinion.

Where it would be wrong: You take being disliked as proof that you are faithful, and do not care what outsiders think of you. Unpopularity proves nothing on its own. An elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Christians are to commend the gospel by honest, kind lives (1 Peter 2:12).

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is probably the most demanding ethical command in the New Testament, and it is not an aspiration but an imperative, repeated in four parallel forms.

All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling — which matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings; he commands treatment. And the four escalate in cost: do good can be done at a distance; bless requires words; pray for is hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long.

The natural instinct is reciprocity — love those who love you, do good to those who do good to you. Jesus points out that reciprocal love proves nothing: “even sinners love those who love them.” It requires no faith and no change of heart; self-interest produces it unaided. The question the passage forces is whether anything in a Christian's life could not have been produced by ordinary human decency.

The ground of the command is not the worthiness of the enemy. There is no suggestion that the enemy deserves love. The ground is the character of God, “for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.” The disciple who loves enemies is not performing an act of heroic willpower; he is showing a family resemblance.

The concrete instructions in vv. 29-30 — the cheek, the cloak, the beggar, the goods taken — have been read both as absolute commands and as radical illustrations of a disposition. What is certain is their subject: a backhanded blow was an insult to honour, and the cloak is taken by force. These are about personal affront and personal loss, and what is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of one's own dignity.

They are not, and have never been, a command to remain within reach of violence. Jesus walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30); Paul invoked his citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37).

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36) is the summary — and mercy presupposes a real debt and then declines to collect it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is the most radical expression of grace in the New Testament — and it is exactly what God has done towards his own. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:8, 10).

The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies. The disciple who loves an enemy is not doing something beyond what God has done; he is doing what has already been done to him, and doing it because he received it. The ethics of the sermon flow from its gospel: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Luke's “be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” is a different formulation from Matthew's “be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), and the difference is instructive. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific attribute this whole section reflects. In a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And the order can never be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all — which is also why the sentence begins “your Father,” addressed to people who already hold the position they are being asked to display.
verseByVerse.examples:
The command to love enemies has been the most transformative teaching in Christian history — the basis of martyrdom (Stephen dying while forgiving, Acts 7:60), of peacemaking, of every real reconciliation in the church's story.

It has also been the teaching most frequently domesticated into something manageable: being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, or to former enemies who are now friends. The test is not whether we are kind to the kind. It is what we do with the person who is actively hostile, who has genuinely wronged us, and who continues to wish us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) has parallels in nearly every ethical tradition — and almost all of them state it negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. A man can keep that rule perfectly by doing nothing at all.

Jesus states it positively, which cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative, imagination, and going towards somebody at your own cost without being asked. And there is a mercy in how he frames it: he does not ask for an abstract theory of the good but for the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — how you would want to be treated — applied in the other direction.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say to you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.

But I say to you who hear. Those who are really listening. The woes were to outsiders; now Jesus turns back to his disciples.

Love your enemies. Key words. The heart of the sermon. Not just your neighbour, but your enemy. The love Jesus means (agapē) is not a feeling of liking, but a commitment to seek someone’s good, whatever they deserve. No ancient religion or philosophy taught this so radically. And it is exactly how God loved us: while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).

Four commands. Love is shown in action, in four rising steps. Love (attitude). Do good (deeds). Bless (words): speak well of them, wish them well, even when they curse you. Pray for them (prayer): bring them before God. Jesus did all four on the cross: Father, forgive them (23:34). So did Stephen (Acts 7:60).

Those who abuse you. “Abuse” (epēreazontōn): mistreat, insult, harass.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded his followers to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them.

On a Tuesday. Who is your enemy, the person who has hurt or opposed you? Do one good thing for them today, speak well of them, and pray for them by name.

Where it applies: A former friend is spreading unkind things about you online. Do not reply in kind. Pray for him by name, and do him good when you have the chance.

Where it would be wrong: The lie is serious: it accuses you of a crime, or it will lose you your job and hurt your family. Loving an enemy does not mean letting a damaging falsehood stand. Correct it calmly and truthfully, and if need be ask the platform or the law to deal with it. Paul defended himself against false charges more than once (Acts 24:10–21; 25:8–11).

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.

To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. A slap on the cheek was more an insult than an injury, a calculated humiliation. Don’t retaliate. Don’t return insult for insult (1 Peter 2:23; 3:9). Absorb the wrong, rather than escalate it.

From one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one. If someone takes your coat, don’t fight to get it back; let him have your shirt as well. Put people before possessions.

Give to everyone who begs from you. Generosity without discrimination.

And from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. Hold possessions loosely. Don’t live for revenge or recompense.

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Some (Anabaptists, Quakers, Tolstoy) take these words literally and absolutely: Christians may never use force, serve in the army or police, go to court, or defend themselves. Verdict: these commands govern personal relationships and the disciple’s heart: no personal revenge, no retaliation for insult, generosity rather than grasping. They do not abolish the God-given role of the state to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), nor the duty to protect others, nor all legal redress (Paul appealed to Caesar, Acts 25:11). Jesus himself, when struck, did not offer the other cheek literally but protested the injustice (John 18:22–23). The principle is: never repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Giving to everyone who asks is to be exercised with wisdom, for their real good (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

In a sentence. Jesus called his followers not to retaliate when insulted, not to cling to their possessions when wronged, and to give freely to those who ask.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you today, resist the urge to hit back. Overcome evil with good.

Better to let it go: A friend borrowed your drill years ago and never gave it back. Let it go. You do not need to demand it back, or let it sour the friendship.

Wrong to let it go: Your house is burgled, or your employer stops paying your wages. Jesus forbids personal revenge and a grasping heart, not justice through proper means. Report the burglary to the police; pursue your wages, for withholding a worker’s pay is a sin God hears (James 5:4). And if others depend on you, you owe it to them.
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.

The Golden Rule. One of the most famous sayings of Jesus. Others had stated it negatively: Rabbi Hillel said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Confucius and others said similar things. Jesus states it positively, which is much more demanding. Not just “don’t harm others”, but “do for others all the good you would want done for you”. It requires active, imaginative love.

As you wish. We know what we want: to be treated with kindness, patience, respect, generosity and forgiveness. That is the measure of how we should treat others. Matthew adds: for this is the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 7:12).

What it does not mean. Not “treat others well so that they will treat you well”, as a self-interested bargain. The motive is love, not return (v. 35).

In a sentence. Treat others in every way as you would want them to treat you.

On a Tuesday. In every conversation today, ask: how would I want to be treated if I were them? Then do it.

Where it applies: You would want your manager to tell you plainly, but kindly, where your work falls short. Do that in your next review of someone else.

Where it would be wrong: A friend asks you for a glowing reference that you know is not true. The golden rule does not mean giving people what they ask for. The employer who will read the reference is also someone you must treat as you would want to be treated. Write honestly and kindly.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.

What benefit is that to you? “Benefit” (charis): grace, credit, thanks. What is there about that which deserves God’s thanks? What is gracious about it?

For even sinners love those who love them. Love that is returned is just an exchange. Everyone does it. It shows nothing distinctively Christian.

Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. Lending that expects repayment is business, not grace.

The point. Disciples are to be different. Their love goes beyond what is natural and expected. It loves the unlovable, gives without expecting return, and does good to those who cannot or will not repay. That is grace. And it is the kind of love that shows the family likeness of God (v. 35).

In a sentence. Loving, doing good to and lending to those who will repay you is nothing special, since even sinners do it.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything about your love that could not be explained by self-interest? Do something today for someone who cannot repay you.

Where it applies: A single mother in your church cannot cover this month’s bills. Lend her what she needs, without setting a date, and be ready never to see it again.

Where it would be wrong: A relative wants you to co-sign a loan you could not repay, or keeps borrowing to cover gambling. Lending that feeds a destructive habit, or that puts your own family at risk, is not love (Proverbs 22:26–27; 1 Timothy 5:8). Give what you can afford to lose, and help in ways that actually help.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. The opposite of verses 32–34. Love, do good and lend, without hope of return. In a society without banks, lending to the poor was a major act of charity, and the law forbade charging interest to fellow Israelites (Exodus 22:25).

And your reward will be great. You will not lose by it. God will repay (14:14).

And you will be sons of the Most High. You will show that you are God’s children by acting like him. A son resembles his father. Not that loving enemies makes you a child of God (that comes by grace through faith), but that it shows it.

For he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Common grace. God sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). He gives life, food and countless blessings to people who never thank him and who hate him. And supremely, he gave his Son for enemies (Romans 5:8). His children must be like him.

In a sentence. Love your enemies, do good and lend without expecting return, and you will be rewarded and will show yourselves children of God, who is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

For worship. God has been kind to you when you were ungrateful and evil. Thank him, and be like him toward others.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.

Be merciful. The summary of everything Jesus has said about love. “Merciful” (oiktirmones): compassionate, full of pity, feeling for others in their need and acting to help. Matthew has: You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). Luke shows that the perfection of God is seen above all in his mercy.

Even as your Father is merciful. God is the Father of mercies (2 Corinthians 1:3), merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). The standard is not other people, but God himself. And the motive: you have received mercy; show it (Matthew 18:33). This verse introduces the next section about judging.

In a sentence. Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.

For worship. Reflect today on the mercy God has shown you. Let it overflow in mercy to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The teaching on judging (vv. 37-42) and on fruit (vv. 43-45) form one unit held together by the theme of discernment: how we assess others and ourselves.

“Judge not” is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, taken to mean that no moral assessment of anyone is ever permitted. It cannot mean that. Four verses later Jesus tells his hearers to remove the log from their own eye so that they will see clearly to remove a brother's speck — an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified oneself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one.

What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but condemnation — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning their final worth and destiny. That work belongs to a court, and there is only one. The difference is felt easily enough: “that was a lie” assesses an act; “he is a liar” delivers a summary of a life, and requires access to motives and history that no human being has.

The image of the measure in v. 38 is from a grain market: filled, pressed down to compact it, shaken so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills over into the fold of a man's garment. It is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

The blind guide and the log-and-speck follow, and the comedy is deliberate. A man with a plank in his eye leaning in to extract a splinter is an optical impossibility, and the audience can see it. Note that Jesus does not say “leave the speck alone.” The brother is still to be helped; what is corrected is the order. “First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly.”

The tree-and-fruit teaching is the positive counterpart: character produces conduct. This is not moralism — it does not say “try harder to produce good fruit.” It is a statement about the direction of causation. The fruit reveals the tree; what a person does consistently reveals what they are.

And the source is the treasury of the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” — out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say; it is what spills when the container is full and nobody is watching.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of v. 38 recurs across both testaments (Matt. 7:2; Rom. 2:1; Jas. 2:13). It is not mechanical karma but a reflection of God's character — the God who shows himself merciful to the merciful and severe to the severe (Ps. 18:25-26).

The warning is not that God will be unkind to those who judge. It is that a person who approaches God without mercy will meet his justice applied with the rigour they themselves used. Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has fundamentally misunderstood what grace is.

The word “hypocrite” at v. 42 needs care. In ordinary English it means a conscious fraud. But the man Jesus describes genuinely does not see the log — it is stated twice. The hypocrisy is not deliberate pretence but a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best — and the blind guide of v. 39 is in the same condition, sincerely certain he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log-and-speck has a sharp application for every relationship involving authority: parents with children, leaders with congregations, employers with employees, elders with members. The right to speak into another person's life is not conferred by position; it is earned or forfeited by the quality of one's own self-examination.

The mentor who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better about himself. There is a practical test before speaking: ask what this conversation will cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

“Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (v. 40) is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. Formation works. The ceiling of what you become is set by the person you follow, whether or not you intend it.

And “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (v. 45) is the most usable diagnostic Jesus gave. Not what a person says when trying to impress, but what comes out when they are tired, unobserved, or talking about people who are not in the room. That is the overflow, and it is a straight readout of the treasury. Nor can it be fixed by monitoring speech — that produces a careful hypocrite. What must change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.

Judge not, and you will not be judged. Not a ban on all judgement. Jesus will tell us to recognise trees by their fruit (vv. 43–44), and to rebuke a brother who sins (17:3). Christians must discern right and wrong, and the church must exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What Jesus forbids is a censorious, fault-finding, self-righteous spirit, that judges others harshly while excusing oneself, assumes the worst, and takes God’s place as judge (Romans 2:1; 14:4, 10–13; James 4:11–12).

Condemn not, and you will not be condemned. Don’t pronounce the final verdict on others. That belongs to God.

Forgive, and you will be forgiven. “Forgive” (apolyete): release, let go. A forgiving spirit is the mark of those God has forgiven (11:4; Matthew 6:14–15).

Give, and it will be given to you. Generosity is repaid by God’s generosity.

Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. A picture from the grain market. Grain was measured into a container, or into a fold of the robe used like an apron (the “lap”). A generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle the grain, and heaped it until it overflowed. God gives like that: generously, more than we could hold.

For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you. A principle of God’s dealings. The way you treat others is the way God will treat you. Harsh judgement brings harsh judgement; generous mercy brings generous mercy (James 2:13).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by forgiving or giving, nor a “prosperity gospel” promise that giving money guarantees getting more money back. But God is no one’s debtor, and he repays generosity in his own way and time.

In a sentence. Don’t judge, condemn, or withhold forgiveness, but forgive and give, and God will treat you with the same measure, generously, overflowing.

On a Tuesday. Are you quick to judge others? Choose today to assume the best, to forgive and to give, and trust God to repay.

Where it applies: A family leaves your church, and rumours begin about why. Refuse to assume the worst. Think the best of them, and if you have reason to, ask them kindly.

Where it would be wrong: An employer must evaluate staff, a parent must decide which friends are safe, and a church must deal with open sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus forbids condemning and harsh judgement, not discernment or right decisions. And give, and it will be given to you is not a promise of money in return for giving: God repays in his own measure and his own way.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.

Can a blind man lead a blind man? A judgemental person is blind to his own faults (vv. 41–42), and cannot guide others. Jesus applied this especially to the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14), who claimed to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19).

Will they not both fall into a pit? Teacher and follower alike come to ruin. Choose your teachers carefully. And if you teach, make sure you can see.

A disciple is not above his teacher. Students cannot rise higher than their teachers. Follow a blind guide, and you will be blind.

But everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. “Fully trained” (katērtismenos): equipped, completed, mended (the word for mending nets). A disciple becomes like his teacher. So follow the right teacher, Jesus, and you will become like him: merciful, non-judgemental, loving even enemies (Romans 8:29).

In a sentence. Jesus warned that a blind guide leads his followers into a pit, and that disciples become like their teachers.

On a Tuesday. Who are you learning from? You will become like them. Make sure your teachers lead you to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye, when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye.

The speck and the log. A comic exaggeration, perhaps from the carpenter’s workshop. A tiny speck of sawdust, against a beam of timber. A man with a beam sticking out of his eye offers to remove a speck from his friend’s eye.

The point. We are very good at seeing small faults in others and very bad at seeing large faults in ourselves. The critic is often guilty of a greater sin than the one he criticises, often the sin of judging itself.

You hypocrite. An actor, pretending to a righteousness he does not have.

First take the log out of your own eye. Deal with your own sin first. Self-examination comes before correction of others.

And then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye. Notice: Jesus does not say leave your brother’s speck alone. Once you have dealt with your own sin, you are able, and responsible, to help your brother, gently and humbly (Galatians 6:1). Removing a speck from an eye requires great care and gentleness.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against criticising others’ small faults while ignoring our own great ones, telling us to deal with our own sin first, so we can then help others clearly.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone today, ask God to show you the log in your own eye.

Where it applies: Before you speak to your teenager about time on the phone, look honestly at your own.

Where it would be wrong: You never correct anyone, because you are not perfect either. Jesus does not say leave the speck; he says take out the log first, then you will see clearly to take out the speck (v. 42). Humility makes correction gentle; it does not make it silent.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.

For no good tree bears bad fruit. The nature of the tree determines the fruit. What a person does flows from what he is.

For each tree is known by its own fruit. You can tell a tree by its fruit. And you can tell a person, and a teacher, by the fruit of their life (Matthew 7:15–20). This is right judgement, the discernment Jesus approves.

Figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. Common plants of Palestine. You cannot get good fruit from a bad plant.

The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good. The heart is a storehouse. What is stored there comes out.

For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. Words especially reveal the heart. What overflows from your mouth shows what fills your heart (James 3:10–12).

The implication. To change the fruit, the tree must be changed. Outward reform cannot produce good fruit from a bad heart. A person needs a new heart, which only God can give (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 5:17). Then good fruit follows.

In a sentence. As a tree is known by its fruit, so a person’s words and deeds show what is stored in their heart.

On a Tuesday. Listen to what comes out of your mouth today. What does it reveal about your heart? Ask God to fill it with good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses, and one storm — and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

It is preceded by the question that makes the parable necessary: “Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?” Jesus does not doubt that they call him Lord, or suggest they are insincere; the doubled address is the language of warmth. The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter — and to call a man Lord while deciding independently what to do with his instructions is a contradiction in terms.

The parable is not a contrast between a man who heard and a man who did not. Both come to Jesus. Both hear his words. Both build. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. The wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” — two verbs describing the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

Then the flood, and Luke is precise: the same stream breaks against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is weather, and it comes to everyone — which rules out the reading in which the obedient are protected from trouble. Both are hit equally. What differs is what happens next.

“Immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” There is no gradual subsidence and no chance to shore it up. A life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm is unspecified, and the vagueness is the point: bereavement, illness, betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Something always comes.

And the rock is not a set of principles. Jesus has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The eschatological note — the house that falls, and “the ruin of that house was great” — places the sermon's ethics in the context of final judgement. This is not moralism; it is eschatology.

The commands of the sermon are not useful guidelines for a better life. They are the description of the life that will stand on the day when every life is tested — which is why the sermon cannot be domesticated into a programme of self-improvement. It describes a life that is only possible through the transformed heart the kingdom produces, which is exactly what the tree-and-fruit teaching has just said.

And it is why the question at v. 46 is not an attack on assurance. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says. Every command in this chapter is checkable, and not one of them can be kept by admiring it.

The rock, finally, is not the sermon. It is the one who preached it. To hear these words and do them is to build on Jesus himself, and he is what the digging reaches.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the two builders has been used in Christian preaching from the earliest centuries as the description of the difference between nominal and genuine faith. Both builders heard Jesus; both began to build; both appeared to be doing the same thing. The difference was invisible until the storm came.

This is Jesus's own warning against the self-deception that hears the word, feels its power, admires its truth, and then returns to a life built on other foundations. The church in every generation has members who have heard much and built little.

The wise builder “dug deep” — the effort of foundation-laying is not passive. It requires excavation, the removal of everything covering the rock, the work of getting down to what will hold. That is spiritual formation: not merely hearing but digging, through prayer and Scripture, through accountability, through obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood and circumstance and social approval.

The digging is unglamorous and nobody sees it. The house is what people see. But the digging is what determines whether the house stands — and the way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?

Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord’. The repetition shows fervour, perhaps in worship. To call Jesus “Lord” is to acknowledge his authority, and in the full sense, his deity.

And not do what I tell you? A contradiction. A lord is someone you obey. To call Jesus Lord and ignore his commands is hypocrisy. Words of worship without obedience are empty (Matthew 7:21–23; James 1:22). The test of whether Jesus is really your Lord is whether you do what he says, including everything in this sermon: love your enemies, don’t judge, give.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why people called him Lord but did not do what he said.

On a Tuesday. Which of Jesus’ commands in this sermon are you not doing? Don’t just call him Lord; obey him.

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.

Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them. Three steps: come, hear, do. Not hearing alone; doing.

He is like a man building a house, who dug deep. Only Luke says “dug deep”. Hard work, below the surface, where no one sees, through the soil to the bedrock.

And laid the foundation on the rock. The rock is Jesus and his words, received and obeyed. The foundation is invisible once the house is built, but it determines everything.

And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it. In Palestine, wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season, with devastating force. The flood is any crisis: suffering, temptation, persecution, death, and finally the judgement of God.

But the one who hears and does not do them. He has heard the same sermon. The difference is not in hearing but in doing.

Is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. Easier, quicker, and in fair weather it looks just the same.

When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great. The end of the sermon is a warning. Hearing Jesus without obeying him leads to ruin. The difference between the two houses is only revealed when the storm comes.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works. The foundation is Christ himself (1 Corinthians 3:11). But true faith in Christ shows itself in obedience. Faith that does not obey is not saving faith (James 2:17).

In a sentence. Jesus ended by comparing those who hear and obey him to a man who built on rock and survived the flood, and those who hear and do not obey to a man whose house without foundations was swept away.

On a Tuesday. Storms are coming. Dig deep today: hear Jesus’ words and put one of them into practice.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season.

6.text: <sup>1</sup> On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. <sup>2</sup> But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?” <sup>3</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup> how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>6</sup> On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. <sup>7</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. <sup>8</sup> But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come and stand here.” And he rose and stood there. <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to them, “I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?” <sup>10</sup> And after looking around at them all he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” And he did so, and his hand was restored. <sup>11</sup> But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. <sup>12</sup> In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. <sup>13</sup> And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles: <sup>14</sup> Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew,
