<sup>15</sup> and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, <sup>16</sup> and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. <sup>17</sup> And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, <sup>18</sup> who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. <sup>19</sup> And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all. <sup>20</sup> And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. <sup>21</sup> “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. <sup>22</sup> “Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! <sup>23</sup> Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets. <sup>24</sup> “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. <sup>25</sup> “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. <sup>26</sup> “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets. <sup>27</sup> “But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, <sup>28</sup> bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. <sup>29</sup> To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. <sup>30</sup> Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. <sup>31</sup> And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. <sup>32</sup> “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. <sup>33</sup> And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. <sup>34</sup> And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. <sup>35</sup> But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. <sup>36</sup> Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful. <sup>37</sup> “Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; <sup>38</sup> give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.” <sup>39</sup> He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? <sup>40</sup> A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. <sup>41</sup> Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>42</sup> How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye. <sup>43</sup> “For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, <sup>44</sup> for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. <sup>45</sup> The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. <sup>46</sup> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? <sup>47</sup> Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: <sup>48</sup> he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. <sup>49</sup> But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is one of the richest chapters in Luke's Gospel — four scenes that together compose a portrait of the grace of God operating at the edges of what respectable religion thought was possible. A Roman soldier sends word to Jesus about his dying servant; a widow's dead son is raised in a small village; the imprisoned John the Baptist sends messengers to ask if Jesus is really the one; and a woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus's feet with her tears and her perfume at a Pharisee's dinner table. In every scene, the expected is reversed: the Gentile soldier has greater faith than anyone in Israel; the dead man walks; the greatest prophet struggles with doubt; and the sinner, not the Pharisee, demonstrates the love that flows from forgiven debt.

The chapter's theological centre is the exchange between Jesus and John's disciples (vv. 18–35). John's question — “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” — is the most honest expression of faith-under-pressure in the Gospels. The forerunner who announced the Coming One from the womb, who saw the Spirit descend at the Jordan, who proclaimed the axe at the root of the trees — is now in prison, and the Coming One is not doing what John expected. Jesus's answer is not an argument but a recital: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them. He is, in other words, doing exactly what Isaiah promised the Servant would do. Blessed is the one who is not offended by him — even when he does not do what you expected.

The sinful woman at Simon's house (vv. 36–50) is the chapter's most searching scene. She comes uninvited, she weeps, she wipes Jesus's feet with her hair, she anoints them with perfume. Simon, the Pharisee host, draws the obvious conclusion: if Jesus were really a prophet, he would know who was touching him, and he would not allow it. Jesus's response is the parable of the two debtors — one forgiven a small debt, one a large one; which loves more? And the answer overturns Simon's entire moral framework. The woman's extravagant love is not the cause of her forgiveness; it is the evidence of it. She loves much because she has been forgiven much. Simon's cool hospitality reveals that he considers himself forgiven little — which means he considers himself to owe little, which means he loves little.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The centurion whose servant is sick is the first Gentile whose faith is commended in Luke's Gospel — and it is commended in the strongest possible terms: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

He is a Roman military officer, commander of a hundred men, the local face of the occupying power in a garrison town. He has also built the local synagogue — an extraordinary act of generosity towards a community he was not part of, and towards a God who was not his. And Luke's first fact about him is that a dying slave was “highly valued by him,” which in a world that classified slaves as speaking tools tells you a great deal before the man opens his mouth.

The Jewish elders who come on his behalf argue from merit: “He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” That is how human beings naturally think about who deserves help. The centurion contradicts every word of it.

“Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.” The elders said he was worthy; he says he is not. Nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Then the reasoning, and it is the most penetrating theology anyone has produced in the Gospel so far: “For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me.” Note the first phrase. Not a man with authority but a man under it. He knows exactly why his orders are obeyed — when he speaks, Rome speaks — and that such authority operates through words, at any distance the words can travel.

He applies the framework to Jesus and concludes that illness is in the same position as a legionary: under orders. He is right, and he worked it out from his life in the army.

This is the faith the church has lived on since the ascension. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and received: the word, spoken at a distance, by one whose authority is not limited by where his feet are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The centurion's analogy is more profound than it first appears. He is not merely saying that Jesus is like a commanding officer. He is recognising that authority over illness has the same character as authority in a chain of command — it operates through words, at a distance, on the basis of what stands behind the speaker.

He knows that a soldier who refuses his order is refusing the emperor whose authority he carries. He perceives that the illness Jesus commands is in the same position, and he is right. The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Creator, and creation obeys its Creator.

Jesus's amazement — “he marvelled at him” — is one of only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel; the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth (Mark 6:6). Faith where none was expected, and unbelief where all was.

How the eternal Son can be surprised is answered the way Luke answered it at 2:52: two whole natures in one person. According to his divine nature he knows all things and learns nothing; according to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man and was genuinely moved. The wonder was real. He was not acting.
verseByVerse.examples:
“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof” is the model of the humility that genuine faith produces. By every external measure this man is among the most impressive people in the narrative — authority, resources, a reputation for generosity — and he is the one who says he is not worthy. The elders say he is; he says he is not.

It is not false modesty. It is the accurate perception of a man who has understood who he is asking for help, and the awareness of that distance is precisely what Jesus names as great faith.

And there is a quieter thing worth taking from him. Everything remarkable he says about authority he learned at work, in the army, in the ordinary business of command — not from the prophets and not in a synagogue. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

The centurion never came in person and received everything he asked for. The word of Jesus is not constrained by geography, and the authority he trusted across the streets of Capernaum is the same one trusted across continents in every generation of the church's praying.

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. A centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.

After he had finished all his sayings. The Sermon on the Plain is over. Now Jesus shows in action what he taught: the kingdom comes to outsiders (a Gentile soldier), to the grieving (a widow), to the doubting (John), and to sinners (a woman of the city).

A centurion. A Roman army officer commanding about a hundred soldiers, the backbone of the army. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas, whose forces were organised on the Roman model, stationed at Capernaum to keep order on the frontier and protect the customs post. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (23:47; Acts 10:1–2; 27:3, 43).

Had a servant. “Servant” (doulos): a slave. Matthew uses a word that can mean “boy” (pais).

Who was highly valued by him. Or “dear to him”. In the Roman world, a slave was property. This officer genuinely cared for his slave, an unusual compassion.

In a sentence. In Capernaum, a Gentile centurion’s slave, whom he valued dearly, was sick and about to die.

On a Tuesday. How do you treat those under your authority? Care for them as this officer cared for his slave.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. When they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying: he is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.

He sent to him elders of the Jews. Leaders of the local Jewish community. Luke tells us he sent messengers; Matthew compresses the story, as if he came himself (Matthew 8:5–13), as we might say a king built a palace, meaning he had it built. What a person does through representatives, he does himself.

He is worthy to have you do this for him. The elders’ view: he deserves it, because of his good works.

For he loves our nation. Some Gentiles were attracted to the God of Israel and to Jewish morality and worship, without becoming full converts: “God-fearers” (Acts 10:2; 13:16). This centurion was probably one.

And he is the one who built us our synagogue. At his own expense. A wealthy and generous man. The remains of a white limestone synagogue from the 4th century stand at Capernaum, built on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, possibly the very one he built.

The contrast. The elders say he is worthy (axios). He himself will say he is not worthy (v. 6). The elders think in terms of merit; the centurion knows grace. And it is his humility, not his merit, that Jesus will praise.

In a sentence. The centurion sent Jewish elders to ask Jesus to heal his slave, and they urged Jesus to help because the man deserved it, loving the Jewish people and having built their synagogue.

On a Tuesday. No one deserves God’s grace because of their good works. But good works can open doors for others to speak for you.
verseByVerse.note: Luke tells us he sent elders; Matthew compresses the story as if he came himself. Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him: Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.

And Jesus went with them. At once, without hesitation, to a Gentile’s house.

Lord, do not trouble yourself. Don’t go to the effort.

For I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. “Worthy” again (hikanos, sufficient, fit). A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house, because it would make him ceremonially unclean (Acts 10:28). The centurion knew this and spared Jesus the embarrassment. But it is more than that: he recognises Jesus’ greatness and his own unworthiness. A powerful Roman officer humbles himself before a Jewish teacher.

Therefore I did not presume to come to you. He did not consider himself worthy even to approach Jesus.

But say the word, and let my servant be healed. A word is enough. He believes that Jesus’ word has power at a distance, without contact, without presence. No one in Israel had shown this kind of faith.

For worship. The centurion’s words have entered Christian worship before the Lord’s Supper: Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof; but only say the word.

In a sentence. As Jesus approached, the centurion sent friends to say he was not worthy to have Jesus enter his house, and asked him simply to speak the word of healing.

On a Tuesday. Come to Jesus as one unworthy, trusting the power of his word. That is the faith he honours.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, go, and he goes; and to another, come, and he comes; and to my servant, do this, and he does it.

For I too am a man set under authority. He understands authority from his military life. He is under authority (his commanders, ultimately the emperor), and therefore has authority over others. His orders carry the weight of Rome behind them.

With soldiers under me. When he gives a command, it is done. He does not have to be present; his word is enough.

The reasoning. If my word, backed by Caesar, is obeyed by soldiers and slaves, then your word, backed by God, is obeyed by sickness and death. Jesus stands under God’s authority and therefore has God’s authority over every power. The centurion grasped what even the disciples were slow to understand: that Jesus’ word is the word of God, which does what it says (Isaiah 55:11).

In a sentence. The centurion explained that, as a man under authority whose commands are obeyed, he knew Jesus’ command would be obeyed too.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word has authority over every situation you face. Trust his word as the centurion did.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard these things, he marvelled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said: I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith. And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.

He marveled at him. Only twice in the Gospels does Jesus marvel: at this Gentile’s faith, and at the unbelief of his own home town (Mark 6:6). Jesus was truly human and could be astonished.

Not even in Israel have I found such faith. Israel, with the law, the prophets and the promises, should have had the greatest faith. Instead, a Gentile soldier outshines them all. A foretaste of the Gentile mission in Acts (Acts 10–11; 28:28). Matthew adds the saying about many coming from east and west to sit at table with Abraham (Matthew 8:11).

And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. Healed by a word, at a distance. Jesus never saw him or spoke to him. The only other healing at a distance in the Synoptic Gospels is also of a Gentile (Mark 7:24–30). The Gentiles receive the blessing of Christ without seeing him, as believers have done ever since (John 20:29).

In a sentence. Jesus marvelled, declaring that he had not found such faith even in Israel, and the messengers returned to find the servant healed.

For worship. You have not seen Jesus, yet his word reaches you. Trust him as this Gentile did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The raising at Nain is one of the most tender scenes in Luke and one of the most deliberately crafted. Two crowds meet at the town gate: the crowd following Jesus, and a funeral coming out.

At the centre of the funeral is a widow carrying out her only son, and Luke underlines both facts because both are load-bearing. A woman's economic and legal standing ran through a man — father, then husband, then son. She has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son, and there is no fourth name on the list. This is not only the worst grief there is; it is destitution.

Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart. She has not prayed and does not know who he is. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

“And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her.” Two things in that sentence. This is the first time Luke himself calls Jesus the Lord in his own narration — not a title on somebody's lips but the evangelist's own description, and he uses it in front of a coffin. And the compassion is something involuntary and physical — Luke uses the same words of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33).

He touches the bier, which under the law makes a man unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11) — and, as with the leper in chapter 5, the traffic runs the wrong way. Then one sentence to a corpse: “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

Luke, the physician, records the result in two clinical stages: he sat up, and he began to speak. And then the sentence that is the point of the whole scene — “and Jesus gave him to his mother” — which is almost word for word what is said of Elijah at Zarephath: he delivered him to his mother (1 Kgs. 17:23).

The crowd's response is fear, and then two acclamations: “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” Both are true, and both fall short. Elijah prayed three times and God raised the boy; this man gave an order.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising of the widow's son is a sign of the kingdom with both an immediate and an ultimate reference. Immediately it is the reversal of the most final of all reversals, accomplished by the one who will himself die and rise. Ultimately it points forward to the general resurrection, when the dead will rise at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25-29; 1 Thess. 4:16).

Jesus does not raise this young man permanently; he will die again. What the miracle demonstrates is not the abolition of biological death but authority over death as a power — the authority that reaches its final expression in Jesus's own resurrection.

The echo of Elijah is deliberate, and Luke has been preparing it since 4:26, when Jesus preached about the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth and the town tried to kill him. Both prophets meet a widow whose only son has died; both speak; both give the son back to his mother in almost the same words.

The echo establishes Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophetic tradition rather than its continuation. Where Elijah stretched himself over the boy and cried out to the LORD three times, Jesus simply speaks. The authority has been concentrated. The prophet gives way to the Lord of the prophets.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's compassion for the widow, unprompted and unsolicited, is the model of the grace that sees before it is asked. She did not pray. She did not seek him out. She was lost in her grief, and he saw her.

He was not the only person at that gate who could see her — the whole town was there. He was the one who looked at the woman rather than the coffin. The posture of compassion begins with seeing, and the Christian who prays to notice what God notices is asking to become like the man who walked into Nain and saw a widow in a crowd.

“Do not weep” — said to a woman at her only son's funeral — would be an outrage from anybody else. It is not a denial of her grief and not a rebuke; he wept himself at a friend's tomb. He says it because he is about to remove the reason.

That is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he was standing in. Nobody else may say it. He may — and one day, to everybody, he will (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon afterwards he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.

A town called Nain. A village about 6 miles (10 km) south-east of Nazareth, on the slope of the hill of Moreh. Only Luke records this miracle. Nain is near Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37), and Elijah raised a widow’s only son at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:17–24). The crowd will draw the connection (v. 16).

As he drew near to the gate of the town. Two crowds meet at the gate: one following the Lord of life into the town, one following a corpse out of it.

A man who had died was being carried out. Burial took place on the day of death, outside the town, because of the heat and because the dead made people unclean. The body was wrapped and carried on an open bier.

The only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A double tragedy. She had already lost her husband; now her only son. In that society, a widow without a son had no one to support or protect her, and no one to carry on the family name. She faced poverty and destitution, as well as grief.

And a considerable crowd from the town was with her. Mourners, including probably hired flute players and wailing women, as was customary.

In a sentence. At the gate of Nain, Jesus and his followers met a funeral procession carrying the only son of a widow.

On a Tuesday. Jesus meets people at the gates of their grief. Bring your sorrow to him.
verseByVerse.note: Nain was a village south-east of Nazareth, near Shunem, where Elisha raised a widow’s son. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her: do not weep.

And when the Lord saw her. The first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative, at the moment he is about to show his power over death.

He had compassion on her. Esplanchnisthē: moved in the depths of his being. The word for the deepest compassion. No one asked him. No one expressed faith. He simply saw her grief and was moved. This is pure grace.

Do not weep. In anyone else’s mouth, a cruel thing to say to a widow at her son’s funeral. From Jesus, it is a promise. He has the power to remove the reason for her tears. One day he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

In a sentence. When the Lord saw the widow, he was filled with compassion and told her not to weep.

For worship. Jesus sees your grief and is moved with compassion. He is not distant from your tears.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said: young man, I say to you, arise. And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.

And touched the bier. An open stretcher or plank. Touching it made a person ceremonially unclean (Numbers 19:11, 16). But Jesus is not defiled by death; death is undone by him.

And the bearers stood still. Startled, they stopped.

Young man, I say to you, arise. “I say to you”: on his own authority. Elijah stretched himself three times on the dead boy and prayed (1 Kings 17:21); Elisha prayed and lay on the child (2 Kings 4:33–35). Jesus simply speaks. He does not pray for power; he commands, because he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). He speaks to a dead man as if he could hear, and he does.

And the dead man sat up and began to speak. Proof that he was alive, and well.

And Jesus gave him to his mother. Exactly the words of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah gave the boy to his mother. A tender detail. The miracle was for her. Jesus restores him to her, and her future with him.

What it shows. Jesus has power over death. This young man would die again; it was a restoration, not the resurrection of the last day. But it was a sign of the final resurrection, when all the dead will hear his voice (John 5:28–29).

In a sentence. Jesus touched the bier, commanded the dead young man to rise, and he sat up and spoke, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.

For worship. The one who spoke to the dead at Nain will speak to the dead on the last day. Worship the Lord of life, and do not grieve as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
verseByVerse.note: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day. Touching it made a person unclean.

parallels.desc: he gave him to his mother

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: a great prophet has arisen among us! and: God has visited his people! And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.

Fear seized them all. Holy awe.

A great prophet has arisen among us! They think of Elijah and Elisha, who raised the dead. Perhaps the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). True, but not the whole truth. Jesus is more than a prophet.

God has visited his people! The words of Zechariah’s song (1:68, 78). They speak more truly than they know. God has visited his people in person.

Through the whole of Judea. The whole Jewish land (4:44).

In a sentence. Everyone was filled with awe and praised God, saying a great prophet had arisen and God had visited his people, and the news spread everywhere.

On a Tuesday. God has visited his people in Jesus. Tell others what he has done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is in prison — Herod arrested him for confronting the tetrarch's marriage (3:19-20) — and the imprisonment has raised the question that was always implicit in his ministry. He sends two disciples with it: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

Take in who is asking. The man who leapt in the womb at Christ's approach (1:41), who saw the heavens open and the Spirit descend, who said “Behold, the Lamb of God” — this man, in a cell, in the dark, wondering whether he had been wrong. If he could come to the edge of that question, the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

Jesus's answer is neither a rebuke nor a reassurance but a demonstration. First he works, in that very hour, in front of the messengers. Then: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them.”

The list is a mosaic of Isaiah — 26:19, 29:18, 35:5-6, 61:1 — the texts describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save. John knew every one by heart. Jesus is answering doubt not with an argument but with evidence, and the evidence is the Scriptures John built his life on, now enacted in front of his own men.

“And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” is a gentle warning that names John's actual difficulty without embarrassing him. He had announced an axe at the root and a winnowing fork (3:9, 17); what he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties. Everything promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

After the messengers leave — and only after — Jesus tells the crowd what he thinks of John: not a reed shaken by the wind, not a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1. “Among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

The section ends with the children in the marketplace. John came fasting and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and they called him a glutton. The objections were mutually exclusive, which proves the objections were never the reason.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's doubt from prison is the New Testament's most honest portrait of faith under pressure, and it is treated with complete respect. Jesus does not rebuke him, question his faith, or withdraw the commendation he is about to give. He answers the question with careful evidence.

That is the pastoral heart of the passage. Genuine doubt, honestly expressed, receives a genuine answer. A Christian tradition that treats doubt as a mark of spiritual failure has missed the model of Jesus himself. Honest wrestling with “is it really true?” is not the absence of faith; it is faith pushed to its limit by circumstance and still asking — and asking the right person.

The saying about the least in the kingdom is not a demotion of John but an elevation of the kingdom. It concerns position in redemptive history, not personal holiness or usefulness. John stood at the threshold: he announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

The least believer in the kingdom has what John did not yet have — an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, and the indwelling Spirit. Not because that believer is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's question is the question of every sincere believer facing a crisis of expectation: I believed this was true; this is not what I expected; am I wrong? And the answer Jesus gives is not “of course you are right, do not worry.” It is “look at the evidence.”

When faith is under pressure the antidote is not reassurance but the careful examination of what has actually happened — the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, the testimony of those who met the risen Christ. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is a step towards evidence that has been examined.

Notice too what John did with his doubt. He did not sit in the dark nursing it, and he did not broadcast it. He sent it to Jesus. That is the one move available to a man in a cell, and it is the right one.

And the parable of the children diagnoses a condition that is not confined to Pharisees. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection — the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated. The test is not whether you have a criticism, but whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples of John reported all these things to him. John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying: are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? When the men had come to him, they said: John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?

The disciples of John reported all these things to him. John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea (3:20).

Are you the one who is to come. “The one who is to come” (ho erchomenos) was a title for the Messiah (Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1; 3:16).

Or shall we look for another? Why did John doubt? He had baptised Jesus, seen the Spirit descend, and pointed him out as the Lamb of God (John 1:29–34). But John had preached a Messiah who would come with the axe and the fire of judgement (3:9, 17). Jesus was healing and preaching to the poor, eating with sinners, and the judgement had not come. And John was in prison, which the Messiah was supposed to open (4:18). Jesus did not fit his expectations. Even the greatest of the prophets had moments of doubt.

What it does not mean. Not that John lost his faith. He brought his doubt to Jesus, which is exactly what to do with doubt.

In a sentence. From prison, John sent two disciples to ask Jesus whether he really was the Messiah, or whether they should wait for someone else.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus doesn’t act as you expected, and doubts come, take them to him. He does not despise honest questions.
verseByVerse.note: John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.

In that hour. Only Luke records that Jesus did these miracles while John’s messengers watched. He answered John’s question not with an argument, but with evidence.

Diseases and plagues and evil spirits. “Plagues” (mastigōn): literally “scourges”, severe afflictions.

And on many who were blind he bestowed sight. “Bestowed” (echarisato): gave as a gift of grace. Sight given freely.

In a sentence. At that very time, Jesus healed many diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and gave sight to many blind people.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt, look at what Jesus has done. The evidence is there.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered them: go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.

Go and tell John what you have seen and heard. Report the evidence, eyewitness testimony.

The blind receive their sight, the lame walk. Jesus answers in the language of Isaiah’s promises about the coming of God to save: Isaiah 35:5–6 (the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer); Isaiah 26:19 (your dead shall live); Isaiah 61:1 (good news to the poor), which Jesus read at Nazareth (4:18). John, who knew his Isaiah, would recognise it at once: these are the signs of the messianic age. Yes, I am the one.

Lepers are cleansed … the dead are raised up. Jesus adds these (5:12–13; 7:11–15), not in Isaiah’s list, but greater still.

The poor have good news preached to them. The climax of the list. Preaching to the poor is placed after raising the dead, as the greatest sign. The gospel itself is the greatest miracle.

Where he stopped. As at Nazareth, Jesus omits the vengeance. Isaiah 35:4 says: your God will come with vengeance. Isaiah 61:2: the day of vengeance of our God. The judgement John expected will come, but not yet. This is the time of grace.

And blessed is the one who is not offended by me. “Offended” (skandalisthē): caused to stumble. A gentle warning to John, and to all: do not stumble because I am not the kind of Messiah you expected. Blessed is the one who trusts me even when I do not fit his expectations.

In a sentence. Jesus told John’s messengers to report the signs Isaiah foretold for the age of salvation, and pronounced blessed the one who does not stumble over him.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus doesn’t meet your expectations, don’t stumble. Trust him as he is, not as you imagined him.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John’s messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings’ courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

When John’s messengers had gone. Jesus does not criticise John in front of his disciples. Once they leave, he praises him publicly. The crowd might have thought less of John for his question; Jesus defends him.

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds grew along the Jordan, bending in every breeze. Was John a man who blew with every wind of opinion? No. He was unbending, a man of conviction, who rebuked a king and went to prison for it. His question did not make him a reed.

A man dressed in soft clothing? John wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (Mark 1:6). He was not a courtier. Those who dress softly and live in luxury are in kings’ courts, like Herod’s, where John was now in a dungeon below.

A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. The first true prophet in four centuries. And more: the forerunner whom the prophets themselves had foretold.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the crowds what they had gone out to see in John: not a wavering reed or a courtier, but a prophet, and more than a prophet.

On a Tuesday. Defend absent fellow believers, rather than criticising them. And be unbending in truth, like John.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is he of whom it is written: behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face. Malachi 3:1, combined with Exodus 23:20. In Malachi, God says: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. Jesus changes “me” to “your”: God speaks to the Messiah about the forerunner who prepares his way. John prepares the way for the Lord, and the Lord is Jesus.

Among those born of women none is greater than John. A remarkable verdict. Greater than Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Isaiah. Why? Because of his unique role: he stood at the turning point of history, pointing directly to the Messiah. The prophets saw Christ from afar; John saw him and pointed: Behold, the Lamb of God (John 1:29).

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. Not greater in character, but in privilege. John belonged to the age of promise; he stood at its threshold. The least believer after the cross and resurrection knows more of Christ and his finished work, and possesses the Spirit and the blessings of the new covenant. John saw the dawn; the least Christian lives in the full day. This shows how great the privilege of a believer is.

In a sentence. Jesus identified John as the messenger Malachi foretold, the greatest person ever born, yet said that the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he.

For worship. You have privileges the greatest prophets longed for (1 Peter 1:10–12). Thank God for them.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptised with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptised by him.)

A comment by Luke. The ESV puts this in brackets, as Luke’s explanation of the crowd’s response.

When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too. The ordinary people and the outcasts.

They declared God just. Literally “justified God”: acknowledged that God was right, in his judgement on sin and in his call to repentance through John. They had admitted their sin and been baptised. They agreed with God about themselves.

But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves. “Lawyers” (nomikoi): experts in the law of Moses. “The purpose of God” (boulēn): his plan, his will for them, the call to repent. They refused it, to their own loss. God’s call can be refused. They thought they were righteous and did not need to repent (5:32).

Not having been baptized by him. Their refusal of John’s baptism showed their refusal of repentance.

In a sentence. The ordinary people and tax collectors, baptised by John, acknowledged God was right, but the Pharisees and lawyers, refusing John’s baptism, rejected God’s purpose for them.

On a Tuesday. Agree with God about your sin. Those who justify God are justified by him; those who justify themselves reject his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another: we played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.

The people of this generation. Especially the religious leaders who rejected both John and Jesus.

Like children sitting in the marketplace. Children played games in the town square, imitating adults: weddings, with music and dancing, and funerals, with wailing. Some children would refuse to play whatever game was suggested. Let’s play weddings! No. Then let’s play funerals! No. Sulky, contrary children whom nothing satisfies.

We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep. The leaders are like that. They found fault with whatever God offered.

In a sentence. Jesus compared his generation to sulky children in the marketplace who refuse to play either weddings or funerals.

On a Tuesday. Are you someone who finds fault with whatever God sends? Beware of a spirit that will never be satisfied.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say: he has a demon. The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say: look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners! Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.

John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine. An ascetic, fasting, living on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6). The funeral song, a call to mourn for sin.

And you say, He has a demon. Too strict. Mad.

The Son of Man has come eating and drinking. At feasts, with sinners (5:29). The wedding music, the joy of the kingdom.

And you say, Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard. Too loose. An echo of Deuteronomy 21:20, where a rebellious son who was a glutton and a drunkard was to be stoned.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant as an insult. It is one of the most beautiful titles of Jesus. He is the friend of sinners. That is the gospel.

The point. They rejected John for being too severe and Jesus for being too relaxed. The problem was not John or Jesus; it was their hearts. People who don’t want God’s message will always find an excuse to reject the messenger.

Yet wisdom is justified by all her children. God’s wisdom, in sending both John and Jesus, is shown to be right by those who respond to it: the people and tax collectors of verse 29, and the sinful woman of verses 36–50. The proof is in the changed lives.

In a sentence. The leaders rejected John as demon-possessed for fasting, and Jesus as a glutton and drunkard for feasting with sinners, but God’s wisdom is proved right by those who respond to it.

For worship. Jesus is the friend of sinners. If you are a sinner, he is your friend. Thank him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepts — which is worth registering, since two verses earlier they were calling him a friend of tax collectors and sinners. He ate with the disreputable and with the respectable, and seems to have refused nobody.

The setting explains the story. Guests reclined on low couches, propped on the left elbow, feet extending away from the table; and such meals were semi-public, with uninvited townspeople free to come in and stand round the walls. That is how she gets in.

She is “a woman of the city, who was a sinner” — no name, no history, and in that context the description almost certainly means she was publicly known for sexual immorality. She comes uninvited, stands behind him at his feet, weeps enough to wet them, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with ointment from an alabaster flask.

Every one of those acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public. The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, and the anointing belonged on the head. She does not appear to notice any of it. She never speaks.

Simon's response happens entirely behind his face: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is.” The logic is tidy, and what he cannot conceive is the third possibility — that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Jesus answers the unspoken thought, which settles Simon's question about prophetic knowledge before the conversation starts.

Then the parable of the two debtors, and Simon walks into it with a hedge that gives him away: “The one, I suppose.” Neither debtor could pay; the lender cancelled both; the one forgiven more loved more.

And then the mirror is turned on the table. No water for the feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for the head — three ordinary courtesies any Galilean host provided without thinking, and Simon omitted all three. Against each, what she did, and each of hers is enormously larger. He withheld the cheap minimum; she gave the costly maximum at the lowest place in the room.

“Your sins are forgiven… Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” Not her love — her faith. The love was the fruit. The faith was what got her through the door.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the two debtors is the theological key to the scene and to the chapter. Forgiveness is the cause; love is the effect. This is the reverse of the moralism that says “love more, and God will forgive you more.” The gospel runs the other way: the more you understand what you have been forgiven, the more you will love.

Her love is extravagant because her sense of her cancelled debt is accurate and large. Simon's love is cool because his sense of his own debt is small — or rather, because he does not yet believe he has one. A man who considers himself basically righteous will never produce the love that flows from a woman who knows she was lost and is not any more.

Verse 47 is regularly misread, and the passage itself supplies three corrections. The parable Simon has just endorsed runs cancellation first and love after. Her forgiveness is what brought her into the house. And three verses later Jesus names what saved her, and it is her faith.

The “for” is the for of evidence, not of cause — as in “it rained last night, for the ground is wet.” The second half of the verse proves it: “he who is forgiven little, loves little.” Forgiveness is the input; love is the output.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman is the chapter's portrait of what it looks like to be genuinely overwhelmed by grace. She is not performing for the guests; she seems unaware of them. She is not observing social convention; she has left it behind. She is not managing her reputation; she forfeited it years ago.

What she is doing is the only thing she can think of in the presence of the one who has forgiven her — giving everything she has left, her tears, her hair, her perfume and her dignity, because what she has received is worth more than all of it together. The question the scene puts to every reader is whether we feel forgiven like that.

Simon's failure is the failure of good morality without grace-shaped self-knowledge. He is not a bad man. He is careful, observant, theologically serious, and he has kept his reputation intact. What he has never seen is the size of his own debt.

A person who does not see the depth of their own sin cannot be overwhelmed by the grace that forgives it, cannot produce the love that flows from it, and cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. The church that produces more Simons than sinful women has failed at the most basic level of gospel communication: it has not helped people grasp what they have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment.

Wisdom’s children. This scene illustrates verse 35: the friend of sinners, and a sinner who responds to wisdom.

One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as with tax collectors (11:37; 14:1). He was friend to all. This Pharisee, Simon (v. 40), was curious, perhaps wanting to evaluate this new prophet.

And reclined at table. At a formal dinner, guests lay on couches arranged around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them. So a woman could stand behind him at his feet without reaching the table. Such dinners were semi-public; uninvited people could come in to watch and listen.

A woman of the city, who was a sinner. Known in the town as a sinner, probably a prostitute. She is not named. She is not Mary Magdalene, as later tradition wrongly assumed (Mary is introduced separately in 8:2), and not Mary of Bethany, whose anointing was a different occasion (John 12:1–8).

When she learned that he was reclining at table. She came on purpose, at great risk of humiliation.

Brought an alabaster flask of ointment. Perfume, expensive. Perhaps used in her trade. Now she will pour it out on Jesus.

In a sentence. When Jesus was dining at a Pharisee’s house, a woman known in the town as a sinner came, bringing an alabaster jar of perfume.

On a Tuesday. No one is too sinful to come to Jesus. And no place is too respectable for sinners to seek him.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so a woman could stand at his feet. Doors were often open at such meals and onlookers could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.

Standing behind him at his feet, weeping. Tears of repentance, and of gratitude. Her tears suggest she had already met Jesus, or heard him preach, and received forgiveness (v. 47). This is a response to grace already received.

She began to wet his feet with her tears. So many tears that they washed his feet.

And wiped them with the hair of her head. A respectable Jewish woman never let down her hair in public; it was shameful, even grounds for divorce. She did not care what anyone thought. Her hair, perhaps her pride and her attraction, became a towel for his feet.

And kissed his feet. Continually (v. 45). Kissing the feet was a sign of deep humility, gratitude and reverence, given to a great benefactor or a king.

And anointed them with the ointment. Perfume on the feet, not the head. She did not consider herself worthy to anoint his head.

In a sentence. Standing behind Jesus, she wept on his feet, wiped them with her hair, kissed them repeatedly, and poured perfume on them.

For worship. When did you last weep at Jesus’ feet in gratitude for his forgiveness? Love that knows it has been forgiven is extravagant.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: if this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner. And Jesus answering said to him: Simon, I have something to say to you. And he answered: say it, Teacher.

He said to himself. He did not say it aloud. But Jesus heard his thoughts.

If this man were a prophet. Some manuscripts read “the prophet”. The people had said Jesus was a great prophet (v. 16). Simon now concludes he is not.

He would have known who and what sort of woman this is. Simon assumes that a true prophet would know she was a sinner, and would push her away, because touching a sinner would make him unclean. Simon thinks holiness means separation from sinners.

The irony. Jesus does know who she is: a forgiven sinner. And he knows who Simon is, and what Simon is thinking, which proves he is a prophet. Simon is the one who does not know what sort of woman she is, or what sort of man he himself is.

And Jesus answering. Answering a question that Simon had not spoken.

Simon, I have something to say to you. A gentle, personal approach.

Say it, Teacher. Polite, but only “Teacher”.

In a sentence. Simon the Pharisee thought to himself that Jesus could not be a prophet if he let a sinner touch him, and Jesus, knowing his thoughts, said he had something to tell him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts, including your judgements about others. Let him speak to you about them.
verseByVerse.note: Simon was a common name; this Pharisee is not Simon the leper of Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more? Simon answered: the one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt. And he said to him: you have judged rightly.

A certain moneylender had two debtors. A simple parable, told to make Simon judge himself, as Nathan made David judge himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. Five hundred denarii was more than a year and a half’s wages; fifty, less than two months’. Both are real debts. Sin is a debt to God (11:4; Matthew 6:12).

When they could not pay. Neither could pay. Both were bankrupt. This is the point Simon misses: he is a debtor too.

He cancelled the debt of both. “Cancelled” (echarisato): forgave freely, graciously, as a gift. The word comes from charis, grace. Free forgiveness of an unpayable debt. That is the gospel.

Now which of them will love him more? Love is the response to forgiveness, in proportion to the sense of how much has been forgiven.

The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt. “I suppose”: Simon answers cautiously, sensing a trap.

You have judged rightly. Simon has condemned himself.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a lender who freely cancelled two debts, one large and one small, and Simon admitted that the one forgiven more would love more.

On a Tuesday. Your debt to God is greater than you can pay. Have you let him cancel it freely?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; five hundred denarii was more than a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon: do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.

Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon. He looks at her, but speaks to him.

Do you see this woman? Simon saw only a sinner. Jesus asks him to see her as she is: a forgiven woman pouring out love.

Three contrasts. Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting, and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to an honoured guest. Simon had given none of them. He had invited Jesus, but treated him with coolness, perhaps deliberate disrespect.

  • Water: you gave me no water for my feet (after a dusty walk in sandals); she washed them with her tears.
  • Kiss: you gave me no kiss of welcome (on the cheek); she has not stopped kissing my feet.
  • Oil: you did not anoint my head with ordinary olive oil; she anointed my feet with costly perfume.

Each time, Simon gave less than the minimum; she gave far more than the maximum.

In a sentence. Jesus contrasted Simon, who had not even given him water, a kiss or oil, with the woman, who washed his feet with tears, kissed them and anointed them with perfume.

On a Tuesday. Are you cool toward Jesus, giving him the minimum? Love him as she did.
verseByVerse.note: Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to a guest.

parallels.desc: let a little water be brought, and wash your feet
you anoint my head with oil

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.

Her sins, which are many, are forgiven. “Are forgiven” (apheōntai): perfect tense: have been forgiven and remain forgiven. Jesus does not deny that her sins are many. He declares them forgiven.

For she loved much. How should “for” be understood? Does her love earn forgiveness, or prove it? The parable answers: the debtor who was forgiven more loved more. Love is the result of forgiveness, not its cause. “For” here means “as you can see from”: her sins have been forgiven, as is shown by her great love. Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price.

Where Christians differ: love and forgiveness. Some Roman Catholic interpreters, following the Latin, have taken this verse to mean that her love (as an act of contrition and charity) merited or brought about her forgiveness. Verdict: the parable (vv. 41–43) makes the order plain: forgiveness first, love second. Jesus will tell her that her faith, not her love, has saved her (v. 50). We are forgiven by grace through faith, and love is the fruit.

But he who is forgiven little, loves little. Aimed at Simon. Not that Simon’s sins were few, but that he thought they were. He did not see himself as a debtor at all. Feeling little need of forgiveness, he felt little love. The person who thinks he needs little forgiveness will love Jesus little. Self-righteousness kills love.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that her many sins were forgiven, as her great love showed, while the one who thinks he has been forgiven little loves little.

For worship. If your love for Jesus is cold, ask God to show you how much you have been forgiven. Love grows from seeing grace.
verseByVerse.note: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price, as the parable shows.

parallels.desc: we love because he first loved us

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to her: your sins are forgiven. Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves: who is this, who even forgives sins? And he said to the woman: your faith has saved you; go in peace.

And he said to her, Your sins are forgiven. Now he speaks directly to her, publicly, so that everyone hears it and she knows it for certain. An assurance of what was already true. She had been condemned by the town; now she is declared forgiven by the Lord, in front of the Pharisees.

Who is this, who even forgives sins? The same question as in 5:21. Only God can forgive sins. The question hangs over the Gospel: who is he? He is the one who forgives sins, because he is God, and because he will pay the debt himself on the cross.

Your faith has saved you. Not her love, not her tears, not her perfume: her faith. She trusted Jesus and came to him. Faith is the empty hand that receives forgiveness. Her love flowed from it.

Go in peace. Literally “go into peace”: into a new life of peace with God and wholeness. The Hebrew blessing shalom. She came weeping; she leaves in peace.

In a sentence. Jesus told the woman publicly that her sins were forgiven, and that her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace, while the guests wondered who could forgive sins.

For worship. Hear Jesus’ words to you: your sins are forgiven; your faith has saved you; go in peace.

parallels.desc: who can forgive sins but God alone?

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.

The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — out of their own money.

So the Galilean ministry was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village for the better part of three years, eating every day, with no visible income — and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

The significance of the passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were excluded from the travelling company of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included them as named, active participants — and it exposed him to precisely the accusation his enemies had already made (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Each woman is identified by what was done for her rather than by what she brought. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising; it is a collection of the rescued.

Mary Magdalene needs rescuing from a long misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the lake, and the name says only where she came from. What Scripture tells us of her past is that seven demons came out of her — which is affliction, not scandal. She is not the unnamed woman of the previous chapter; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs invited that merger, and a sixth-century sermon fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it in the text.
