Joanna is a court wife whose husband managed the estate of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell. Whatever her presence here cost her at home, she is named again at the empty tomb (24:10) — as is Mary Magdalene, who will still be there at the cross when the men have gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The inclusion of women in the travelling band is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous, and Jesus's opponents were already looking for material.

His practice reflects the consistent pattern of including those the religious establishment excluded, and it anticipates the full participation of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17-18; Gal. 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters.

It matters, too, that the women are introduced immediately before the parable of the soils. Luke has just shown a company of people in whom the word took root and bore fruit — and their fruit was that they gave everything they had to keep the sowing going.

These same women are at the cross when the twelve have scattered (23:49), and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1-11). They are not peripheral figures. On the two occasions when the testimony mattered most, they are the witnesses Luke has.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women who supported the ministry “out of their means” are the New Testament's first and clearest model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they paid for it, and they kept paying.

The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Cor. 8-9; Phil. 4:14-19) has its roots here: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it forward. It is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread.

And notice what these women could not do. They could not preach in a synagogue, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and mobility, and they put both under the mission for years, and were named once and then never mentioned in that connection again.

There is a whole doctrine of unglamorous service in that. The four Gospels exist partly because a group of women paid the bills of an itinerant preacher and did not require anybody to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon afterwards he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

Proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. His main work, as he said (4:43). Two verbs: to herald (kēryssōn) and to evangelise (euangelizomenos).

And the twelve were with him. Learning by being with him (Mark 3:14).

And also some women. Only Luke records this. Remarkable in its culture. Rabbis did not normally have women disciples, and some rabbis said it was better to burn the law than to teach it to a woman. Jesus welcomed women as followers, who travelled with him and learned from him. Luke gives special attention to women throughout his Gospel.

Who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Their discipleship was a response to what Jesus had done for them, like the woman of 7:36–50.

Mary, called Magdalene. From Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, south of Capernaum. She stood at the cross (23:49; Mark 15:40), saw the burial (23:55), and was the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:11–18).

From whom seven demons had gone out. A severe case of possession, perhaps over a long time. Seven: complete bondage. And complete deliverance.

What it does not mean. Nothing in Scripture says Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. That idea arose in the sixth century, when Pope Gregory the Great identified her with the sinful woman of 7:37 and with Mary of Bethany. But Luke introduces her here as a new character, freed from demons, not from immorality. She was a woman of means and devotion, and a witness of the resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus travelled through towns and villages preaching the kingdom, with the Twelve and with women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, freed from seven demons.

On a Tuesday. Jesus welcomes all who have been freed by him to follow him. What has he freed you from? Let it lead to devotion.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.

Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager. Herod is Herod Antipas. Chuza was his steward (epitropos), a high official managing the royal household or estates. Joanna came from the court of the man who imprisoned and beheaded John. The gospel reached even into Herod’s household (Acts 13:1 mentions Manaen, brought up with Herod; Philippians 4:22, saints of Caesar’s household). Joanna was also among the women at the empty tomb (24:10). Perhaps she was one of Luke’s sources for the inside story of Herod (9:7–9; 23:8–12).

And Susanna. Otherwise unknown. But known to Jesus, and to Luke’s readers.

And many others. Many women followed Jesus.

Who provided for them out of their means. “Provided” (diēkonoun): served, ministered. They supported Jesus and the Twelve financially, from their own money. Jesus, who fed five thousand, allowed himself to be supported by the gifts of these women. Their giving was ministry. Women of means were the patrons of Jesus’ ministry, as Lydia and others would be of Paul’s (Acts 16:14–15).

In a sentence. Joanna, from Herod’s court, Susanna and many other women supported Jesus and the Twelve from their own resources.

On a Tuesday. Giving your money to support gospel ministry is serving Christ. Do it gladly, as these women did.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why his disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells it publicly (vv. 4-8), then explains it privately (vv. 9-15), with a hard word about the purpose of parables in between.

Note when he tells it. Not to a disappointing turnout, but to a great crowd — and what he says is a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds.

The picture was entirely ordinary. In that agriculture, sowing came before ploughing: a man walked the field broadcasting seed by the handful, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed genuinely did fall everywhere. The sower is not careless; that is simply how the job was done, and it matters — the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

The disciples ask what it means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in the Gospels on parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, the commission given after the vision of the throne — the hardening that follows persistent rejection of revelation.

This should not be softened, and three things hold it together. It is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given; Luke has shown a Nazareth that tried to kill him and a delegation plotting his death. A parable is also a door held ajar, hiding the thing from the casual and rewarding the man who comes back and asks — which is exactly what has just happened in verse 9. And it is mercy as well as judgement: to be told plainly and reject it plainly is a far more terrible position.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God, which settles a great deal. The variable in this parable is never the seed; it is the ground. The path is hardened by ordinary traffic. The rock is shallow soil over limestone, where the fastest growth in the field is the first to die. The thorns are already rooted and simply grow at the same time, for the same water and light. And the good soil holds the word fast in an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

It is not a rigid psychological classification. It is a mirror, and every hearer is invited to hold it up.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark records Jesus saying, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:13). It establishes the principle governing all his teaching: the response to the word determines everything.

The seed does not change. It is the same word in all four soils, and the same generous hand scattering it. What varies is the condition of the heart it lands in — which is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of what has been given.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” — describes a heart that is not simply admirable. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one but the honest one: the heart that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, and does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

And the last word is patience, patient endurance. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable is a diagnostic tool. The question it puts to every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?”

Has it been taken away before it could go in — by distraction, by noise, by a life with no quiet in it? A footpath is not naturally hard ground; it is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent.

The rock soil frightens sincere believers, and it should be handled carefully. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there — not someone who is struggling and worried about it. Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28), and John's own comment on those who left is that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The remedy is never introspection; a plant cannot inspect its own roots. It is to go deeper, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives — because the sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

The thorns are the most dangerous soil, because nothing appears to be wrong. And not one of the three Jesus names is a sin: cares, riches, and the ordinary pleasures of life. The choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things — which is exactly why it is so hard to see, and why the outcome is stated so precisely: their fruit does not mature. Not nothing at all. Perpetually promising, and never actually there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: a sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.

A great crowd. The crowds were large, but how many truly heard? The parable answers.

He said in a parable. A parable is a story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. It reveals truth to those who want to hear, and conceals it from those who do not (v. 10).

A sower went out to sow his seed. Seed was scattered by hand, broadcast over the field as the sower walked. Some say that in Palestine, ploughing came after sowing, so the sower scattered widely, not knowing which ground was good. Only Luke says “his seed”.

Some fell along the path. Hard footpaths ran through and around the fields, trodden by feet. Seed could not sink in.

And was trampled underfoot. Only Luke adds this.

And the birds of the air devoured it. Lying on the surface, it was easy picking.

In a sentence. To a great crowd, Jesus told a parable of a sower whose seed partly fell on the path, where it was trampled and eaten by birds.

On a Tuesday. Being in the crowd around Jesus is not the same as truly hearing him. How are you hearing today?
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. As he said these things, he called out: he who has ears to hear, let him hear.

And some fell on the rock. Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. The seed sprouts quickly, because the soil warms fast, but its roots hit rock.

It withered away, because it had no moisture. Only Luke mentions moisture. No depth, no water, no life.

And some fell among thorns. Thorny weeds, whose roots were still in the ground though not visible. They grow faster and stronger than the grain.

And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. Deep, clean, prepared ground. A hundred grains for one: an extraordinary harvest, beyond normal expectations (Genesis 26:12). The word of God bears abundant fruit in a good heart.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. “Called out”: he raised his voice. A summons to pay attention. Everyone has ears; not everyone truly hears. Hearing in the Bible means listening, understanding and obeying.

In a sentence. Other seed fell on rock and withered, among thorns and was choked, and on good soil, where it yielded a hundredfold, and Jesus called out to those with ears to hear.

On a Tuesday. You have ears. Use them. Listen to Jesus’ word with your whole attention.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said: to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

When his disciples asked him what this parable meant. Disciples ask. The desire to understand marks those who truly hear.

To you it has been given. A gift, by God’s grace. Understanding the kingdom is not achieved by intelligence but given by God (10:21; Matthew 16:17).

To know the secrets of the kingdom of God. “Secrets” (mystēria): mysteries, not puzzles but truths once hidden and now revealed by God, especially that the kingdom has come in Jesus, in an unexpected form, like a seed (Ephesians 3:3–6).

But for others they are in parables. To outsiders who do not believe, the parables remain riddles.

So that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ Isaiah 6:9–10, God’s commission to Isaiah, warning that his preaching would harden a rebellious people. The parables are a form of judgement on those who have already rejected the truth. They hear the stories without understanding, because they do not want to. To those who reject the light, more light is withheld (v. 18). Luke, unlike Mark, omits the end of the quotation (lest they turn and be forgiven), perhaps because he holds it back for the end of Acts (Acts 28:26–27).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to keep people from salvation. He taught in parables also to draw people in, to provoke thought, and to make truth memorable. But for the hard-hearted, they confirm their blindness. The same sun melts wax and hardens clay.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that God had given them to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but for others they remain in parables, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about seeing without seeing.

For worship. If you understand the gospel, it is God’s gift. Thank him, and ask him to give the same gift to those you love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parable is this: the seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.

The seed is the word of God. The gospel message. Its power is not in the sower but in the seed (Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 Peter 1:23). The sower is first Jesus, and then everyone who spreads his word.

The ones along the path are those who have heard. The hard-hearted: the word does not get in. They hear it, but it makes no impression.

Then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts. The birds are the devil. Satan is active in snatching the word away: by distraction, by doubt, by forgetfulness, by the next thing that comes along. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

So that they may not believe and be saved. Only Luke adds this. Satan’s aim: to prevent faith and salvation. And so faith comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17); Satan’s strategy is to stop the hearing from taking root.

In a sentence. The seed is God’s word, and the path represents those whose hard hearts let the devil snatch away the word before they can believe and be saved.

On a Tuesday. When you hear God’s word, don’t let it lie on the surface. Think about it, pray over it, and let it sink in before the devil can take it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.

When they hear the word, receive it with joy. An enthusiastic response. They seem to be converted. But joy is not proof of genuine faith.

But these have no root. No depth. The word has not gone down into their heart and will.

They believe for a while. Only Luke says “believe”. A real but temporary belief: intellectual and emotional, but not a heart transformed by God.

And in time of testing fall away. “Testing” (peirasmou): trial, temptation, or persecution (Matthew 13:21: when tribulation or persecution arises). When following Jesus becomes costly, they give up. “Fall away” (aphistantai): depart, apostatise.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians take this as a believer who loses salvation. Verdict: the parable describes a faith that was never rooted, never the saving faith of the good soil. Its fruit never came. Scripture teaches that those whom God truly saves he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and that those who fall away permanently show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). This is the perseverance of the saints. But the warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people: examine yourselves.

In a sentence. The rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy and believe for a while, but having no root, fall away when testing comes.

On a Tuesday. Enthusiasm is not enough. Let God’s word go deep. When testing comes, it will show whether you have roots.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.

They are those who hear. They hear, and the word grows. But it shares the soil with other things.

As they go on their way. Gradually, over time, not in a sudden crisis.

They are choked. Strangled slowly.

By the cares. Anxieties, worries about daily life, the future, money, health (12:22–31; 21:34).

And riches. The love of money and possessions (12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:9–10).

And pleasures of life. Only Luke adds this. Not necessarily sinful pleasures; good things that crowd out God.

And their fruit does not mature. There is growth, perhaps even the beginning of fruit, but it never ripens. A divided heart cannot bear the fruit of the kingdom. No one can serve two masters (16:13).

In a sentence. The thorny ground represents those who hear, but whose faith is gradually choked by worries, wealth and pleasures, so that it never bears mature fruit.

On a Tuesday. What thorns are growing in your heart: worries, money, or pleasures? Pull them out before they choke the word.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

They are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast. “Hold it fast” (katechousin): keep it, retain it, not letting it go. Mary treasured the word (2:19). The good hearer hangs on to it.

In an honest and good heart. Only Luke has this phrase (kalē kai agathē), which in Greek described a person of noble character. A heart that is genuine and open to God. Such a heart is itself God’s gift; he prepares the soil (Acts 16:14, where the Lord opened Lydia’s heart).

And bear fruit with patience. “Patience” (hypomonē): endurance, perseverance, steadfastness under pressure. The opposite of the rocky ground (v. 13). Genuine faith keeps going. Fruit takes time; it does not appear overnight. The fruit is a changed life: love, obedience, good works, new believers (Galatians 5:22–23; Colossians 1:10).

In a sentence. The good soil represents those who hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and patiently bear fruit.

On a Tuesday. Hear, hold fast, and persevere. Fruit comes with patience. Don’t give up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable, and both apply it.

The lamp saying comes first, and its placing is deliberate. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after saying that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not others. A disciple could easily draw the wrong conclusion: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

“No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Both absurdities are exact: a jar smothers the flame for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed burns the house down. Neither preserves light; both destroy it while pretending to keep it.

And note the purpose clause — so that those who enter may see. Not so the lamp may be admired, and not for the household's benefit. The secrets of the kingdom were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest” cuts both ways. Forward, it is a promise: the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house, and Luke is writing the second volume that proves it. But everything concealed also comes out eventually — which is terrifying for anyone hiding something, and one of the great comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off.

“Take care then how you hear” is the imperative that gathers up the whole chapter. And the principle attached to it — to the one who has, more will be given — is not a cruelty but a description of how understanding actually behaves. Capacity grows by use, and atrophies without it. Luke alone adds the sharpest phrase: “even what he thinks that he has.” The man's holdings were never what he supposed.

Then Jesus's mother and brothers arrive, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” It is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15, six verses on, given a family name — and it is the same hearing-and-doing that ended the sermon at 6:47-49.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying and the redefinition of family are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they received is the lamp; the world they are being sent into is the stand.

The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils. The lamp saying describes what those in whom it took root are to do with it.

And the family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already established about Mary. She is not being demoted; she is the founding member of the category. The woman who said “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38) heard the word of God and did it, and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing — which is why the brothers standing outside at this point in the story, who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5), are outside in more senses than one.
verseByVerse.examples:
The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it.

This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community the ancient world had no category for. It remains the miracle of every congregation that takes hearing-and-doing as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

“Take care then how you hear” is worth turning into a practical question, because the parable has just made hearing the decisive variable. Not what was preached, but what was done with it between the car park and Tuesday.

And “even what he thinks that he has” is aimed precisely at the person who is quite sure they are fine. Both the rock soil and the thorn soil had something, and both would have described themselves as having it, and neither had what they supposed — and each found out at the worst possible moment. There is a mercy in being told now, in a season of quiet, rather than in a season of testing.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.

No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick. You light it to give light, not to hide it.

But puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. The word of God, the light of the gospel, is meant to be seen. Those who have received it must let it shine (11:33; Matthew 5:14–16). The secrets of the kingdom are given to disciples (v. 10) not to be kept secret, but to be spread.

For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest. The truth of the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will be fully revealed. And everything hidden in human hearts will be exposed at the judgement (12:2–3; 1 Corinthians 4:5).

In a sentence. As a lamp is lit to give light, not hidden, so the word must be made known, for everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Don’t hide your faith. Let the light of the gospel be seen in what you say and how you live.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.

Take care then how you hear. Key words, and the conclusion of the parable section. Not just what you hear, but how: with an honest heart, holding it fast, obeying it. Hearing is a moral act, with consequences.

For to the one who has, more will be given. To the one who receives the word and responds, more understanding and blessing will be given. Truth received leads to more truth.

And from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away. Only Luke says “thinks that he has”. The one who does not respond loses even what he seems to have: his superficial knowledge, his religious privilege. Neglected truth is lost. This is a principle of the spiritual life.

In a sentence. Be careful how you listen, because those who receive and respond will be given more, while those who do not will lose even what they think they have.

On a Tuesday. Respond to what God shows you today, and he will show you more. Ignore it, and you will lose even that.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. He was told: your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you. But he answered them: my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.

His mother and his brothers. Mary and Jesus’ brothers: James, Joseph, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3). The most natural reading is that they were Mary and Joseph’s sons, born after Jesus. Mark tells us they had come because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31–35). His brothers did not believe in him until after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7).

But they could not reach him because of the crowd. Even his family had to wait.

My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it. The conclusion of the parables about hearing: the good soil is those who hear and do. Jesus does not reject his family; he is not being rude. He loved his mother (John 19:26–27). But he declares that a new family has come into being, bound not by blood but by obedience to God’s word. This relationship is closer, and more important, than the natural family. Even Mary’s blessedness lies chiefly in hearing and keeping God’s word (11:27–28).

In a sentence. When told his mother and brothers wanted to see him, Jesus said that his true mother and brothers are those who hear God’s word and do it.

On a Tuesday. If you hear and do God’s word, you belong to Jesus’ family. Treat other believers as your family.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake at his own initiative — “Let us go across to the other side.” They are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to get in. The storm is not a consequence of any failure; obedience put them there.

He falls asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where he is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity: he had been preaching all day, and the moment the boat was under way he was unconscious in the stern.

Then a windstorm comes down on the lake. The geography explains it — the lake sits some two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling cold air off the heights into the warm basin without warning. A small, shallow lake goes from flat to lethal in minutes. It still does.

And these are professional fishermen who have worked this water all their lives. When they wake him with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” it is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown — which is worth saying to anyone taught that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is an accurate reading of the instruments.

He “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same verb Luke used of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). There is no prayer. He speaks to the weather in the imperative.

“And they ceased, and there was a calm.” Luke's word is calm, a dead flat calm — and anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When wind drops, the swell runs on. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant.

“Where is your faith?” is gentler than it looks. He does not ask why they have none; he asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some and mislaid it. What was missing was not courage but the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen.

And they were more frightened afterwards than during. The wind had threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. “Who then is this?”
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator over the natural world.

In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea. “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Ps. 107:29). “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Ps. 89:9). “Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther?” (Job 38:8-11).

The disciples' question — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — has only one available answer, and every man in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood. Luke leaves the question hanging; it will not be answered aloud until Peter's confession (9:20).

The sleeping is theologically as significant as the stilling. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned but because he is at peace — the one who will say “do not be anxious” (12:22) practising it in a sinking boat. And it is the fullest possible statement of the incarnation: the Lord of the storm, too tired to stay awake, four feet from men who thought they were dying.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon, seen the healings, received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes they are afraid and amazed.

That is the honest portrait of early discipleship, and of most later discipleship too. Knowing who Jesus is in the abstract is not the same as trusting him in the specific, wet, embodied crisis. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis; it is mislaid — and “where is your faith?” is a search rather than an accusation.

The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure. It is about the one who was in the boat with them. He did not abandon them in the storm and he did not scold them for waking him. He stilled it, and then invited them to examine where their faith had been — not to condemn but to grow.

And the sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these. It heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them: let us go across to the other side of the lake. So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.

Four miracles. Luke now records four great miracles (8:22–56): over nature, demons, disease and death. They show the authority of the one whose word the disciples are to hear.

Let us go across to the other side of the lake. Jesus’ command. He intended them to reach the other side.

As they sailed he fell asleep. A real man, exhausted after a day of ministry. The only time the Gospels describe Jesus sleeping. And at peace, trusting his Father (Psalm 4:8).

And a windstorm came down on the lake. “Came down”: the Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level, ringed by hills. Cold air rushing down the steep valleys from the heights can whip up sudden, violent storms on its warm surface.

And they were filling with water and were in danger. Experienced fishermen, who knew the lake, believed they would die.

In a sentence. As Jesus and the disciples crossed the lake, he fell asleep, and a violent storm struck, swamping the boat and endangering their lives.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus does not keep you out of storms. He sent them into this one.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went and woke him, saying: Master, Master, we are perishing! He awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.

Master, Master, we are perishing! Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s, where they say: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). The double “Master” shows their panic.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves. “Rebuked”: the same word used for rebuking demons (4:35) and fever (4:39). Jesus speaks to the storm as a master to a disobedient servant. In the Old Testament, only God controls the sea: You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Psalm 89:9; also 65:7; 107:23–30). Jesus does what God does.

And they ceased, and there was a calm. Instantly. Normally, even after the wind drops, waves go on for hours. This calm was immediate and complete.

In a sentence. The terrified disciples woke Jesus, and he rebuked the wind and waves, and there was an instant calm.

For worship. The one who sleeps in your boat is Lord of the wind and waves. Cry out to him in your storms.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: where is your faith? They were afraid, and they marvelled, saying to one another: who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?

Where is your faith? They had faith, but where was it in the storm? It had gone missing when they needed it. Jesus’ word, let us go to the other side, should have been enough. And he was in the boat.

And they were afraid, and they marveled. A new fear: not of the storm, but of him. The fear of the storm was replaced by awe at the one who controls it.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him? The question of the Gospel. The answer is in Psalm 107:28–29: Then they cried to the Lord in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still. They are with the Lord himself.

In a sentence. Jesus asked where their faith was, and the disciples, filled with fear and wonder, asked who he could be, that wind and water obey him.

On a Tuesday. Where is your faith today? Put it in the one who commands the wind and water.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore — Gentile territory, east of the lake, with pigs on the hillsides — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet.

The description is harrowing and deliberate. He wore no clothes; he did not live in a house but among the tombs; he had repeatedly broken the chains put on him and been driven into the desert. Stripped of clothing, of community and of self-determination, he is not described as a man with a problem but as a site.

Two puzzles meet a careful reader here. Gerasa lay thirty miles inland, and Gadara six miles off; neither is on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. And Matthew names two men where Mark and Luke name one: Matthew adds a second, he does not subtract one, and the other two follow the man who spoke and who was left with a story to tell.

The demons recognise Jesus at once and their theology is impeccable: “Son of the Most High God” — a title Jews and Gentiles alike used of Israel's God, fitting on this side of the lake. But look at the verb. They beg. Three times in this scene the powers of darkness plead, which is Luke's way of showing how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

“Legion” was nominally six thousand men, and a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force. The word would have had an edge in the Decapolis, where people had watched real ones march. And the answer comes from the occupation rather than the man: asked his own name, there is no I left to reply.

They beg not to be sent to the abyss — the sealed prison of rebel spirits (Rev. 20:1-3) — but into the pigs. Jesus permits it, and it is the demons who stampede the herd, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had done to one man for years. The lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what he had been living under.

The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind, and sitting at the feet of Jesus — the posture of a disciple. And they ask Jesus to leave. The man himself begs to come along; that is the one request in the chapter that is refused. “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.”
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels, and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile herdsmen. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel.

The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the demonised man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33) — both liberated by the same word, with the same authority, and neither able to put up the slightest resistance.

The restored man is “in his right mind” — sober, self-possessed — and he is sitting at Jesus's feet, where a disciple sits (cf. 10:39; Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has not merely been evicted; the ground has been given to somebody else.

That distinction matters, because a deliverance that only removes does not hold. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). The sitting at the feet is not incidental colour. It is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave are the cautionary portrait of a community that values what it can calculate over what it cannot control. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The arithmetic should be straightforward.

But the fear is real, and Luke names it: something has happened here that they do not control. A lunatic in the tombs can at least be chained. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or manage it into something more comfortable — and Jesus does not argue with them. He gets into the boat and goes. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

The man's desire to follow, and Jesus's refusal, is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. That is a harder road than the boat. Everyone who has been converted where their old life is public knowledge understands it.

And he is sent to declare not a doctrine but a testimony — the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority. Then Luke does something quietly enormous and leaves it without comment: Jesus said “declare how much God has done for you,” and the man went and proclaimed “how much Jesus had done for him.” The two sentences sit side by side, and Luke sees nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.

The country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. Some manuscripts read Gadarenes or Gergesenes. The region lay on the eastern shore, in Gentile territory, part of the Decapolis. Luke explains “opposite Galilee” for readers who did not know the geography.

A man from the city who had demons. Matthew mentions two men (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke focus on one, perhaps the more notable.

For a long time he had worn no clothes. Only Luke mentions this. Shame and degradation.

And he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside, unclean places. He lived among the dead, unclean, cut off. Satan’s work: degradation, isolation, uncleanness, death.

In a sentence. On the eastern shore, in Gentile territory, Jesus was met by a demon-possessed man who had gone naked for a long time and lived among the tombs.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far gone, too degraded, too unclean for Jesus to reach.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice: what have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me. For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)

He cried out and fell down before him. The demon recognises his master and submits.

Jesus, Son of the Most High God. “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17). The demons know exactly who Jesus is.

I beg you, do not torment me. The demons know they face judgement (Matthew 8:29: before the time?). They fear Jesus.

For many a time it had seized him. Luke explains the background, as a doctor would describe a case history.

He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles. The townspeople had tried to control him by force. Human methods failed.

And be driven by the demon into the desert. The demon drove him, as a herdsman drives cattle. Bondage, not freedom.

In a sentence. The man fell before Jesus, and the demon in him cried out, recognising him as Son of the Most High God and begging not to be tormented, for it had long controlled the man, defying every chain.

On a Tuesday. No human chain could hold this man. Only Christ could free him. Trust him with the bondages that human methods cannot break.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then asked him: what is your name? And he said: Legion, for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.

What is your name? Perhaps to bring the man to awareness of his condition, or to expose the extent of the possession.

Legion. A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers (about 5,000–6,000). Not necessarily that exact number, but a host, an occupying army. In a land under Roman occupation, the name was vivid.

For many demons had entered him. Luke’s explanation.

And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. Only Luke mentions the abyss. The abyss (abyssos) is the bottomless pit, the place where evil spirits are imprisoned before their final judgement (Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–2; 20:1–3). They know Jesus can send them there.

In a sentence. Asked his name, the man said Legion, because many demons possessed him, and they begged Jesus not to send them to the abyss.

On a Tuesday. However many and powerful the forces of evil, they tremble before Jesus. Take courage.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

A large herd of pigs. Pigs were unclean animals under the law (Leviticus 11:7). This was Gentile territory, where pigs were raised. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13).

So he gave them permission. Even demons need Jesus’ permission. They are completely under his authority.

And the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. Several reasons may be seen. It demonstrated visibly that the demons had left the man, and how many there were. It showed the destructive purpose of the demons: what they did to the pigs, they wanted to do to the man. It showed that a human being is worth more than a whole herd of pigs (12:7). And unclean spirits went with unclean animals into the deep.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about property or animals. He judged that the deliverance of one man was worth the loss. The townspeople judged otherwise (v. 37).

In a sentence. Jesus permitted the demons to enter a large herd of pigs, which rushed down the bank into the lake and drowned.

On a Tuesday. One person is worth more than great wealth. Value people as Jesus does.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. People went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. Those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.

Sitting at the feet of Jesus. Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple (10:39; Acts 22:3). The wild man who roamed the tombs now sits quietly as a learner.

Clothed. No longer naked (v. 27). Someone had given him clothes.

And in his right mind. Sane, self-controlled, at peace. A complete transformation. This is what Jesus does.

And they were afraid. Not glad, but afraid. The power of God at work frightened them.

How the demon-possessed man had been healed. “Healed” (esōthē): literally “saved”. Physical, mental and spiritual salvation.

Then all the people … asked him to depart from them. A tragic response. They preferred their pigs, their peace, and their way of life to the presence of Jesus. The power of God was too disturbing and too costly. Many still ask Jesus to leave, for the same reasons.

So he got into the boat and returned. He does not force himself on people. He left.

In a sentence. The townspeople came and found the man sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and sane, and seized with fear, they asked Jesus to leave, and he did.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you value more than Jesus’ presence, and would ask him to leave rather than lose?
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying: return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you. And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

Begged that he might be with him. The people begged Jesus to leave; the man begged to go with him. The natural desire of the redeemed is to be with their Redeemer.

But Jesus sent him away. Jesus had another plan for him. Not everyone is called to leave home. Some are called to stay and witness where they are.

Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you. The first missionary to the Gentiles of the Decapolis. In Jewish territory Jesus often told people to keep quiet (8:56); here, in Gentile territory, where messianic excitement was less of a danger, he sends the man to tell. His testimony was simple: what God had done for him. Everyone knew what he had been; now they could see what he was.

Proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. Notice: Jesus said “how much God has done”; Luke says the man told “how much Jesus had done”. What Jesus did, God did. Without saying so, Luke equates Jesus with God. When Jesus returned to the Decapolis later, crowds came (Mark 7:31–37).

In a sentence. The healed man begged to follow Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell what God had done for him, and he proclaimed throughout the city what Jesus had done.

On a Tuesday. You are called to tell those around you what Jesus has done for you. Start at home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — a healing folded inside a raising, with each story interpreting the other.

Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue: a lay official who organised the services and carried the community's respect, and a member of the class that had been watching Jesus with hostility since chapter 5. He falls at Jesus's feet in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. His only daughter, about twelve, is dying, and every consideration of position has gone.

Jesus goes with him. The crowd presses. And a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years — exactly as long as the girl has been alive — reaches through the crowd and touches the tassel on the corner of his garment.

Her twelve years had cost far more than health. Leviticus 15:25-27 put a woman in her condition under continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her. Twelve years without the synagogue, without normal contact, very likely without a husband — and none of it her fault. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching: she had spent everything and was no better.

Her approach is furtive because it had to be; by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way. The bleeding stops.

Jesus stops the whole procession to ask who touched him — a question he already knows the answer to. Peter's exasperation is reasonable and Luke lets it stand. But he will not take a transaction where a person is available: she had tried to take the gift and stay invisible, and that would have left her physically healed and socially exactly as she was. He makes her say it out loud, in public — which puts her restoration on the record where her whole town can hear it — and then calls her “Daughter,” the only time in the Gospels he uses that word to a woman.

And while he is still speaking, the message comes: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” From where Jairus stands, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem was attended to first, and his child ran out of time.

“Do not fear; only believe.” Then the mourners are put out, the girl is taken by the hand — “Child, arise” — and her spirit returns. And the first thing Jesus says afterwards is that somebody should get her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman healed on the way to Jairus's house teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for her has more than enough for a dead girl.

Jairus is being taught, at his own cost and in real time, to resist the word that says “it is too late.” The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life, and Jairus had just watched, at close range, what this man does for somebody who ran out of options twelve years ago.

“She is not dead but sleeping” is not a correction of the diagnosis, and Luke — a physician — gives three signals that she was genuinely dead: the professional mourners had arrived, the crowd knew, and “her spirit returned.” Jesus is changing a category, not disputing a fact. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and that is now what death is for those who belong to him (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11).

The woman's touch of the “fringe” may point to the tassels of Numbers 15:38-40, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise “with healing in its wings,” and the Hebrew for wings is the word for the corners of a garment. She may have been reaching, knowingly or not, for exactly that.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years, her exhausted resources, her uncleanness and her invisibility are the conditions in which she finally comes. She did not come while she still had options; she came when she had nothing left.

And Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, calling her “daughter,” declaring her faith in front of everyone — is the public vindication of a person who arrived at the bottom of her resources. Her faith was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it aloud.

Jairus's journey is faith pushed to its absolute limit. He did everything right: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked in time. Then the delay, and then the word that it was over. This has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many lives feel like and pious hurry past it is worthless.

“Only believe” is not a technique, and it is not an instruction to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead — that reading crushes bereaved people. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, asking him to keep hold of the person beside him for another ten minutes.

And the last instruction in the house is the one that could not have been invented. A girl has been raised from the dead, the room is beyond speech, and the Son of God says: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.

The crowd welcomed him. A contrast with the Gerasenes who sent him away.

A man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. A ruler of the synagogue organised its services, invited readers and preachers, and cared for its building. A respected leader in the community. Many synagogue officials were opposed to Jesus. Jairus set aside his dignity and his reputation.

And falling at Jesus’ feet. Humbled by need.

For he had an only daughter. Only Luke says “only”, as with the widow’s son (7:12) and the boy of 9:38. Luke notices the depth of grief when an only child is lost.

About twelve years of age. On the edge of womanhood; old enough to be betrothed. Twelve also links her with the woman who had been ill for twelve years (v. 43): the girl had lived as long as the woman had suffered.

And she was dying. Urgent.

As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. “Pressed” (synepnigon): crushed, nearly suffocated. The same word as the thorns that choked the seed (v. 14).

In a sentence. On his return, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, fell at Jesus’ feet begging him to come to his dying only daughter, aged about twelve, and Jesus went, with the crowd crushing around him.

On a Tuesday. Desperate need levels everyone. Whatever your position, fall at Jesus’ feet.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.

A discharge of blood for twelve years. Probably continuous menstrual bleeding. Under the law, it made her ceremonially unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean too (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been unable to worship at the temple, cut off from normal contact, probably unable to marry or remain married, weak and anaemic. Physically ill, socially isolated, religiously excluded.

Though she had spent all her living on physicians. Some manuscripts omit these words. Luke the physician is gentler than Mark, who adds that she suffered much under many physicians and only grew worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that no one could heal her.

She came up behind him. Secretly. She was not supposed to be in a crowd touching people.

And touched the fringe of his garment. The tassel (kraspedon) that devout Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment, as the law commanded, to remind them of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). Some believed the tassels of a holy man had power (Matthew 14:36). Her faith was mixed with superstition, but it was faith in Jesus.

And immediately her discharge of blood ceased. Luke uses the medical term for a flow stopping. After twelve years, in a moment. And instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his healing passed to her.

In a sentence. A woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years, incurable by any doctor, secretly touched the tassel of Jesus’ cloak and was instantly healed.

On a Tuesday. Even a weak and imperfect faith, if it reaches out to Jesus, finds his power. Reach out to him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: who was it that touched me? When all denied it, Peter said: Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! But Jesus said: someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.

Who was it that touched me? Jesus knew. He wanted her to come forward, for her own sake.

When all denied it. Including, at first, her.

Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! Peter thinks the question is absurd. Everyone is touching you.

Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me. Many touched him; one touched him in faith. There is a difference between jostling Jesus in a crowd and reaching out to him in faith. Many are near Jesus; few touch him. “Power” (dynamis): the power of God, flowing from him (5:17; 6:19).

In a sentence. Jesus asked who had touched him, and when Peter protested that the whole crowd was pressing on him, Jesus said someone had touched him, for he had felt power go out from him.

On a Tuesday. Being in church, near Jesus, is not the same as touching him in faith. Reach out to him personally.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her: daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.

When the woman saw that she was not hidden. She could not escape.

She came trembling. Afraid of being rebuked for touching him while unclean.

And falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people. Only Luke says “in the presence of all the people”. Her public testimony. Why did Jesus make her do this? So that everyone would know she was clean. Her healing had been secret; her restoration had to be public. After twelve years of exclusion, the whole town could now accept her. And so she would know that she had been healed not by magic but by Jesus, through faith.

Daughter. The only time in the Gospels Jesus calls someone “daughter”. An outcast for twelve years, she is welcomed into the family.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken): has saved you. Not the tassel, but faith in Jesus. Body and soul.

Go in peace. As to the sinful woman (7:50). Shalom: wholeness.

In a sentence. Seeing she could not hide, the woman came trembling and told everyone what had happened, and Jesus called her daughter, said her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace.

On a Tuesday. Jesus wants a personal relationship, not just a secret cure. Come to him openly and hear him call you son or daughter.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler’s house came and said: your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. But Jesus on hearing this answered him: do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.

While he was still speaking. The delay. While Jesus stopped for the woman, Jairus’ daughter died. Imagine Jairus’ agony. Jesus’ delays can seem cruel. But he had a greater purpose.

Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. Hope is over. A teacher can heal the sick, but not raise the dead.

Do not fear; only believe. “Only believe”: keep on believing. Fear and faith are opposites. Jairus had seen the woman healed through faith; now he must believe for something greater.

And she will be well. Only Luke adds this. “Well” (sōthēsetai): saved, the same word as v. 48. The promise of Jesus.

In a sentence. Word came that Jairus’ daughter had died, but Jesus told him not to fear but only to believe, and she would be saved.

For worship. When the worst news comes, hear Jesus’ word: do not fear; only believe.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. All were weeping and mourning for her, but he said: do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.

He allowed no one to enter with him except Peter and John and James. The inner three, who would also see the transfiguration (9:28) and Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Witnesses.

And the father and mother of the child. Tender: the parents are included.

All were weeping and mourning for her. Professional mourners, as well as family. “Mourning” (ekoptonto): beating their breasts.

Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. Jesus does not deny that she is dead (v. 53 makes it clear). But for him, death is like sleep: temporary, from which he can wake her. The New Testament speaks of believers who die as having fallen asleep (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). Death is not the end for those Christ will raise.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. Scornful laughter. They knew she was dead. Luke makes it clear that this was a real raising from the dead, not a revival from a coma.

In a sentence. At the house, Jesus took only the three disciples and the parents in, and told the mourners she was not dead but sleeping, and they laughed at him, knowing she was dead.

On a Tuesday. For those who belong to Christ, death is sleep, from which he will wake them. Grieve, but with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand he called, saying: child, arise. Her spirit returned, and she got up at once. He directed that something should be given her to eat. Her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

But taking her by the hand. Touching a corpse made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). But Jesus touches the dead, and death gives way.

He called, saying, Child, arise. Mark preserves the Aramaic: Talitha cumi (Mark 5:41). A tender word: “little girl”. Like waking a child in the morning.

And her spirit returned. Only Luke says this. Her spirit had left her body at death (23:46; Acts 7:59), and came back. A clear statement that she had been dead, and that the human spirit lives on after death.

And she got up at once. Instantly, completely.

And he directed that something should be given her to eat. A practical, caring detail. She was really alive, in a real body, and hungry. After the resurrection Jesus himself would eat to show he was not a ghost (24:41–43).

But he charged them to tell no one what had happened. Of course, everyone would know she was alive. But they were not to spread the story. Jesus did not want to be known as a wonder-worker, attracting crowds for the wrong reasons.

In a sentence. Jesus took the girl by the hand and told her to rise, and her spirit returned and she got up at once, and he told them to feed her and to tell no one.

For worship. Jesus has power over death. He will one day take every believer by the hand and say: arise.

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons.
