For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together, gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Two words, and not synonyms: power (dynamis) is the capacity, authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, and neither is earned.

The instructions are deliberately spartan — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. Between them those five items cover security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away. The messengers are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house first receives them and not moving on to a better one.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a difficulty: Mark records that they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8). Several explanations have been offered, and none is certain; what is plain is that both accounts fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet — the gesture a Jew used at the border when returning from Gentile territory, here applied to Jewish villages that refuse the kingdom's messengers. The old boundary has moved. It now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Luke reports the whole mission in one verse: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere. What is absent is as striking as what is there — no account of the first house, the first refusal, the first demon. The instructions were not an ideal held up for admiration; they were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Herod's perplexity closes the section. He has killed the greatest of the prophets and is now hearing that something greater is happening. The three theories on offer — John raised, Elijah appeared, one of the old prophets risen — are all respectful and all too small. His question, “who is this about whom I hear such things?”, is exactly the right question. And “he sought to see him” is the tragedy: he gets his wish at the trial (23:8), and Jesus does not answer him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sending of the twelve is the first instance of the apostolic mission. The word apostle means simply one who is sent; it says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission.

The authority they receive is delegated — the same authority Jesus has been exercising since chapter 4, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will run through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world.

Note who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), propose incinerating a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready.

And the errand has two halves held together: to proclaim and to heal. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The instructions to take nothing are not a travel policy but a structural embodiment of dependence. The messengers carry no resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to, which creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver, and the receiver depends on the message.

The rule about staying in the first house is more pointed than it looks. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid — and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale.

The shaking of the dust takes a refusal seriously enough to mark it, without bitterness and without a backward argument. Two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing until the gospel becomes an irritation attached to a person, or to shrug it off and privately conclude they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither.

And Herod is the standing warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask exactly the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.

Setting. Chapter 9 is the climax of the Galilean ministry. It moves from the mission of the Twelve, through the question of who Jesus is (vv. 7–9, 18–20), to the first prediction of the cross and the transfiguration, and ends with Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51). From there, the great journey to the cross begins.

And he called the twelve together. Chosen in 6:13, trained by being with him through chapters 6–8, now sent out.

And gave them power and authority. “Power” (dynamis), the ability; “authority” (exousia), the right. Both are delegated from Jesus. They have no power of their own.

Over all demons and to cure diseases. The same works he had done (4:31–41).

And he sent them out. “Sent” (apesteilen), from which comes “apostle”. They were his envoys.

To proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Preaching first, then healing. The healings confirmed the message that the kingdom had come.

In a sentence. Jesus gave the Twelve his power and authority over demons and diseases, and sent them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal.

On a Tuesday. Christ sends his people out with his authority, not their own. Whatever he calls you to, he equips you for.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.

Take nothing for your journey. Travel light, depending entirely on God’s provision through the hospitality of those who receive them.

No staff. Mark says take only a staff (Mark 6:8). Perhaps Mark means take the one you have, while Luke and Matthew mean do not acquire another. The point is the same: no extra provisions.

Nor bag. A traveller’s pack for supplies, or a beggar’s bag. They were not to beg, but to receive what God provided.

Nor bread, nor money. No food, no cash.

And do not have two tunics. No spare clothes.

Whatever house you enter, stay there. Don’t move from house to house looking for better hospitality. Be content with what is offered, and don’t insult your host.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. Later Jesus told them to take a moneybag and knapsack (22:35–36). The instructions fit this short, urgent mission in Galilee. But the principles remain: urgency, simplicity, contentment, and dependence on God.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve to take no supplies or spare clothes, depending on God, and to stay in whatever house welcomed them.

On a Tuesday. Travel light in serving Christ. The more you depend on him, the more you will see his provision.
verseByVerse.note: The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies; a second tunic was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.

Wherever they do not receive you. Some will reject the message. Jesus prepares them for it.

Shake off the dust from your feet. Jews returning to Israel from Gentile lands shook the dust off their feet, so as not to bring unclean soil into the holy land. To do this to a Jewish town was a dramatic act: you are acting like Gentiles, outside God’s people. It was a sign that the town was being left to God’s judgement. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A warning, and a witness at the judgement (10:10–16). Their responsibility has been discharged; the town is accountable.

What it does not mean. Not a gesture of personal contempt or revenge. It is a solemn warning, which might still bring them to repentance.

In a sentence. Where a town rejected them, the Twelve were to shake its dust off their feet as a testimony that it stood under God’s judgement.

On a Tuesday. You are responsible to tell the gospel faithfully, not to make people accept it. Leave the results with God.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

And they departed. They obeyed.

Preaching the gospel. “Evangelising” (euangelizomenoi), Luke’s favourite word.

And healing everywhere. The kingdom’s power at work through them. Jesus’ ministry is multiplied through his disciples, as it will be through the church in Acts.

In a sentence. The Twelve went out through the villages preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ work continues through his people. Where are you taking the gospel this week?

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because some said that John had been raised from the dead, some that Elijah had appeared, and others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said: John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? And he sought to see him.

Herod the tetrarch. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee (3:1). The mission of the Twelve had spread Jesus’ fame even into the palace.

And he was perplexed. “Perplexed” (diēporei): at a loss, unable to make sense of it.

John had been raised from the dead … Elijah … one of the prophets. Popular opinions about Jesus, which the disciples will report again (v. 19). All of them high, none of them right.

John I beheaded. Luke does not tell the story of John’s death, which Mark tells at length (Mark 6:17–29). He records only Herod’s own confession. Herod is haunted by it.

But who is this about whom I hear such things? The great question of the chapter, and of the Gospel. Herod asks it; the disciples will answer it (v. 20); the Father will declare it (v. 35).

And he sought to see him. Out of curiosity, not faith. He wanted to see a sign (23:8). When he finally met Jesus, at his trial, Jesus would not say a word to him (23:9).

In a sentence. Herod, perplexed by reports about Jesus, and haunted by having beheaded John, asked who this could be, and wanted to see him.

On a Tuesday. Curiosity about Jesus is not enough. Herod wanted to see him, but never knew him. Seek him in faith.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Luke records that he later saw Jesus at his trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission and Jesus withdraws with them to Bethsaida for rest. Mark gives his reason in his own words: “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” The crowds find out where the boat is going and get there first.

So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out the destination — and Luke records that “he welcomed them.” The verb means received gladly. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited, and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing, until the day was nearly over.

The disciples' suggestion is sensible and they are right about almost everything: it is late, the place is desolate, thousands need food and lodging, and the villages are the only source of either. Sending away is not wickedness; it is arithmetic, done honestly, by tired men. What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

“You give them something to eat” is emphatic in the Greek — you give them — and there is no reading on which the twelve can obey it. Their answer is what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. Five barley loaves and two fish, which John tells us belonged to a boy. They have even costed the alternative: Mark records two hundred denarii, two-thirds of a year's wage, and even that would not be enough.

They are right. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men — and Luke's andres means adult males specifically, so with women and children (Matt. 14:21) the real number is far higher. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic and Jesus never suggests otherwise. What he does is ask for the loaves. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

The four verbs over the bread — took, blessed, broke, gave — are the ordinary actions of a Jewish householder, and Luke fixes them in the reader's memory because they return twice: at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus, where “their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (24:30-31).

All ate and were satisfied — the satisfaction the Psalms say God gives (Ps. 107:9; 132:15). And twelve baskets of fragments were gathered: one for each man who had done the arithmetic.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle besides the resurrection recorded in all four Gospels, which signals its weight. The typology is dense: a multitude fed in a desolate place, as Israel was fed in the wilderness; the crowd seated in ordered companies of fifty, as Moses set the people in fifties (Exod. 18:25); the one greater than Moses giving bread not prayed down from heaven but broken from his own hands.

It is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast Isaiah promised (Isa. 25:6-9) and Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table it is taking a foretaste of that feast.

And the eucharistic action defines the church's life: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it away. He could have distributed the bread himself. Instead it goes from his hands into the disciples' and from theirs to the people — so that the men who said “send them away” spent the next hour giving away food they did not have.

The twelve baskets left over say what the whole scene says: the kingdom of God does not issue minimum rations. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Send the crowd away” is the reasonable option in far more situations than this one — the pastoral problem genuinely beyond a church's capacity, the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry, the ministry that cannot be staffed.

And notice what had just happened to these men. They had come back that same week from a mission in which they healed the sick with nothing in their pockets, and were still telling him about it two verses earlier. Experience of God's provision has a remarkably short half-life, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

“Bring what you have” can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is to put them in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that they will not do, and see what he does with them.

The rhythm of withdrawal and interruption is worth having by anyone who works with people and has learned, rightly, to guard their time. The guarding is not unspiritual — Jesus withdrew constantly. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when what was properly and prayerfully arranged is taken by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. He took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.

On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. They report back. Ministry is accountable to Christ.

And he took them and withdrew apart. For rest, and private teaching (Mark 6:31).

To a town called Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the lake, just east of where the Jordan flows in, in Philip’s territory, out of Herod’s reach. The feeding took place in a deserted place near it (v. 12).

And he welcomed them. Only Luke says this. His rest was interrupted, and he welcomed them anyway. No irritation. His compassion was greater than his need for rest.

And spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. Word and deed again.

In a sentence. When the apostles returned and reported, Jesus took them away to rest near Bethsaida, but the crowds followed, and he welcomed them, taught about the kingdom and healed them.

On a Tuesday. When interruptions come, welcome people as Jesus did.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day began to wear away, and the Twelve came and said to him: send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (Matthew 14; Mark 6; John 6). It was clearly of great importance to the early church.

Send the crowd away. A reasonable suggestion. The disciples saw the problem, and the solution: let them fend for themselves.

For we are here in a desolate place. A wilderness. As Israel was in the wilderness, needing bread, and God fed them with manna (Exodus 16).

In a sentence. As evening came, the Twelve urged Jesus to send the crowd away to find food and lodging, since they were in a remote place.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to see a problem and send people away. Bring the need to Jesus instead.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them: you give them something to eat. They said: we have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.

You give them something to eat. “You” is emphatic. Jesus puts the responsibility on them. They had just been out preaching and healing in his power; could they not trust him for this?

We have no more than five loaves and two fish. John tells us they came from a boy, and were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9). Small, flat loaves, and small dried or pickled fish. A meal for one person.

Unless we are to go and buy food for all these people. Impossible. Mark says it would cost two hundred denarii, two-thirds of a year’s wages (Mark 6:37).

The lesson. The disciples look at their resources, and despair. Jesus wants them to look at him. Our inadequacy is the starting point for his sufficiency.

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciples to feed the crowd themselves, and they replied that they had only five loaves and two fish.

On a Tuesday. What little do you have? Bring it to Jesus. He does not ask you to supply the need, but to give him what you have.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples: have them sit down in groups of about fifty each. And they did so, and had them all sit down.

About five thousand men. Men (andres); Matthew adds “besides women and children” (Matthew 14:21). Perhaps fifteen or twenty thousand people in all.

Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each. Order, for a large meal. The groups recall Moses organising Israel in the wilderness in thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (Exodus 18:21). Jesus is the new Moses, feeding the new Israel in the wilderness. Literally “reclining”, as at a banquet.

And they did so. The disciples obeyed, before they saw how it would work. Seating thousands for a meal with only five loaves required faith.

In a sentence. There were about five thousand men, and Jesus had the disciples seat them in groups of about fifty.

On a Tuesday. Obey Jesus even before you see how it will work out.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

He looked up to heaven. To his Father, the source of every gift.

And said a blessing over them. Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal: Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. Jesus is the host of this meal.

Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples. Took, blessed, broke, gave: the same four actions as at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus (24:30). Luke’s readers would recognise the shape of the Lord’s Supper.

To set before the crowd. The disciples become the servers, distributing what comes from Jesus’ hands. This is the pattern of ministry: we receive from Christ and give to others. We do not make the bread; we hand it out.

In a sentence. Jesus took the loaves and fish, looked up to heaven and blessed them, broke them and gave them to the disciples to distribute.

For worship. Jesus is the host who feeds his people. Receive from his hands, and pass it on.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Everyone, fully. Psalm 107:9: he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things. The Messiah gives abundantly, as God did with the manna.

Twelve baskets of broken pieces. More left over than they started with. A basket for each apostle. God’s provision is not just enough, but overflowing. Twelve may also point to the twelve tribes: enough for all Israel.

The meaning. John tells us that the next day Jesus explained: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The miracle points to Jesus himself, who gives himself to satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. And it is a foretaste of the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15).

In a sentence. Everyone ate their fill, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered.

For worship. Jesus is the bread of life, and he satisfies completely. Come to him hungry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying — Luke alone tells us so, as he does at every hinge of this Gospel — and out of that prayer comes the question the whole book exists to answer.

“Who do the crowds say that I am?” The answers are the same three that reached Herod's court: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Every one is respectful; every one is wrong in the same way, placing him within the prophetic tradition rather than beyond it.

“But who do you say that I am?” It is a question no survey can answer. Peter says: “The Christ of God.”

And immediately, without celebration, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what the title actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

The silence is not modesty. In Galilee in that decade Messiah meant a son of David who would raise an army and break Rome; John records a crowd trying to make him king by force (John 6:15). The word is embargoed until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it. And the rejection is specified by office — the Sanhedrin, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. The men who had the Scriptures.

The call to discipleship follows on the same terms, and Luke marks the audience: “he said to all.” This is not advanced material for the twelve. “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”

To deny the self is not to deny oneself things. The verb is the one Luke will use of Peter's denials in the courtyard (22:34, 61). And “take up his cross” was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it: crucifixion was a live Roman practice, and the phrase described a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution to the place where he would be nailed to it.

Then “daily,” which is Luke's addition — Matthew and Mark do not have it. It takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom and not reserved for the exceptional.

The section closes with a promise that has troubled readers ever since: “there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” Luke answers it in the very next sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's confession is correct, and Luke records no commendation of it — Matthew's account has the blessing on Peter; Luke, writing for a Gentile church, moves straight to the reframing. The Christ of God is the suffering, dying, rising Son of Man.

“Son of Man” is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying “a human being.” It comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is a claim of enormous weight wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble — which is exactly why he could use it in public.

The word must (dei) is the divine-necessity word Luke uses at every turning point. The cross is not an accident, a miscalculation, or the defeat of the mission. It is the appointment. And he never once announces the death without the rising in the same breath.

On “will not taste death,” three answers are given and they are not equally strong. The weakest strains the words. The second, and much better, takes the kingdom in Luke's usual sense — God's reign breaking in — and points to the resurrection, Pentecost, and the spread Luke describes in his second volume, all within the lifetime of the hearers. But the strongest is the one Luke himself supplies: eight days later, three of them went up a mountain and saw the Son of Man in glory.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Daily” is the word that brings the cross within reach of an ordinary believer. It is not the dramatic act of martyrdom reserved for the exceptional disciple; it is the ordinary Tuesday in which the self is again told it does not rule here.

And self-denial needs guarding, because it can be twisted into something poisonous. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?” is put at the extreme deliberately: if the trade fails at the maximum price it fails at every price below it. Nobody reading this will gain the whole world. The prices most people actually pay are small — a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

And shame is the right word, chosen over “deny” or “reject.” Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ; a great many are embarrassed by him, and by his words particularly. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. He asked them: who do the crowds say that I am? They answered: John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen. Then he said to them: but who do you say that I am? And Peter answered: the Christ of God.

The great omission. Luke moves directly from the feeding to Peter’s confession, omitting a long section of Mark (Mark 6:45–8:26). This places the question “who is he?” immediately after Herod’s question (v. 9) and the feeding.

As he was praying alone. Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi, Mark 8:27) but notes that Jesus was praying, as at every turning point (3:21; 6:12).

Who do the crowds say that I am? The same answers Herod heard (vv. 7–8).

But who do you say that I am? “You” is emphatic. The question every person must answer.

The Christ of God. The Messiah, God’s Anointed. “Of God”: God’s Messiah, the one God has anointed and sent (2:26; 23:35). Peter sees what the crowds do not. Matthew records the fuller confession and Jesus’ blessing (Matthew 16:16–19).

In a sentence. After praying, Jesus asked who the crowds said he was, and then who the disciples said he was, and Peter answered: the Christ of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you the same question. Who do you say that he is?
verseByVerse.note: Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi) but notes that Jesus was praying. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.

He strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one. Popular ideas of the Messiah were political and military. Announcing him now would provoke the wrong response. They themselves did not yet understand what kind of Messiah he was.

The Son of Man must suffer many things. The first passion prediction, immediately after the confession. Yes, I am the Christ, but the Christ must suffer. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the plan of God written in Scripture (24:26, 44–46).

And be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin.

And be killed, and on the third day be raised. Death and resurrection together, always.

Luke’s omission. Luke does not record Peter’s rebuke and Jesus’ “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:32–33). Perhaps to spare Peter, or to keep the focus on the teaching.

In a sentence. Jesus ordered them to tell no one, and explained that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and be raised on the third day.

For worship. The Christ of God had to suffer for you. Worship the crucified and risen Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to all: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.

And he said to all. Not only the Twelve. Every disciple.

If anyone would come after me. “Would”: wants to, wills to. A choice.

Let him deny himself. Not deny himself things, but deny himself: say no to self as the centre and master of life.

And take up his cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Everyone knew the sight. It meant a man going to his death, having lost everything. To take up your cross is to accept rejection, shame and even death for Jesus’ sake.

Daily. Only Luke adds “daily”. Not only in moments of martyrdom, but every day. The cross is a way of life: dying to self in a thousand daily choices, for Christ. For what dying to self does and does not mean, see the note on Philippians 3:10.

And follow me. To Jerusalem, to the cross, and beyond.

For whoever would save his life will lose it. Cling to your life, protect it from the cost of following Jesus, and you lose it eternally.

But whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. Give it up for Jesus, and you find it.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by self-denial; only Christ’s cross atones. And not seeking suffering for its own sake. But the life that belongs to Christ takes the shape of his cross.

In a sentence. Jesus told all who would follow him to deny themselves, take up their cross every day and follow him, because to cling to your life is to lose it, and to lose it for him is to save it.

On a Tuesday. What does taking up your cross today look like? Name one way you can say no to yourself for Christ’s sake.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Only Luke adds “daily.”

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.

What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world. The greatest possible gain: everything.

And loses or forfeits himself? Luke says “himself”, where Mark says “his soul”. The self, the whole person. Nothing in the world is worth losing yourself for.

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words. The pressure on disciples was often not violence but scorn. To follow a crucified Messiah was shameful.

Of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory. Measure for measure. At the judgement, Jesus will disown those who disowned him (12:8–9).

And the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. A threefold glory: his own, his Father’s, and the angels’. Jesus claims to share the Father’s glory. The one about to be rejected and killed will return as the glorious Judge.

In a sentence. Nothing gained in the world is worth losing yourself, and whoever is ashamed of Jesus will be disowned by him when he comes in glory.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to be ashamed of Jesus? Remember the day of his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

Some standing here. Not all.

Who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. Luke leaves out Mark’s “come with power” (Mark 9:1), making it simpler: they will see the kingdom. The fulfilment begins about eight days later, when three of them see Jesus in his glory on the mountain (vv. 28–36), a preview of the kingdom. And it continues in the resurrection, the ascension and Pentecost, when the kingdom comes in power, all within their lifetime.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that some standing there would see the kingdom of God before they died.

On a Tuesday. The cross is not the end. The kingdom is coming, and in Christ you already belong to it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray — and Luke alone tells us that is why he went. It happened while he was praying.

Luke is careful with his words. Mark and Matthew say he was transfigured; Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, describes what was seen: his face became different, his clothing turned a white that flashed. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus becoming something more than he was; it is the covering coming off something always there.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory — the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on the same mountain, Sinai and Horeb; both had asked in their way to see him and been given a back and a whisper. Now they stand in the light, talking with him.

And Luke alone tells us the subject. They “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb, through the sea — is standing there while the word is applied to a death in Jerusalem. It is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens: not a defeat but a deliverance, accomplished by a lamb, on a fixed date, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. And the verb is accomplish, not suffer.

The three were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it — and Luke will find the disciples asleep again in Gethsemane (22:45). Peter's proposal to build three tents comes as Moses and Elijah are leaving: a man trying to stop something ending, and Luke's aside is candid and gentle, “not knowing what he said.” The proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, three equals.

The cloud interrupts him mid-sentence. It is the shekinah — the cloud of Sinai, of the tabernacle, of Solomon's temple, unseen in Israel for centuries — and the verb “overshadowed” is the one Gabriel used to Mary (1:35).

“This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” Then the cloud lifts, and Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is at once christological and eschatological — revealing who Jesus is, and what the coming kingdom will look like. What the disciples see is not a separate divine form he can put on and take off; it is the radiance belonging to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is for a few minutes transparent to it. This is what John means by “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah's conversation is the most extraordinary discussion never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament speaking with the Son of God about the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it.

Some Bibles read “my Beloved” at v.35 rather than “my Chosen One,” and the manuscripts do differ. “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: “my chosen” is Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just discussed his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

“Listen to him” is the only imperative in the scene, and it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tents is the perennial temptation to institutionalise a moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries it. The glory was never given to be housed; it was given for the road down.

And the road down is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Jesus comes off that mountain the next morning into a crowd, a boy in convulsions, and a ministry that has failed. Moses came down Sinai carrying the tablets of God and found a golden calf.

“Listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation, and are told the appropriate response is not to build but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory, though God gives those in his mercy. It is about listening to the voice of the Son, in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith.

And the placing of it is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he will be rejected and killed, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.

About eight days after these sayings. “About eight days” counts inclusively, and Luke says “about”; Matthew and Mark say “after six days”. There is no contradiction.

Peter and John and James. The inner three (8:51).

And went up on the mountain to pray. Only Luke says he went to pray. The transfiguration happened during prayer, as the voice at the baptism came while he was praying (3:21–22).

The appearance of his face was altered. Luke avoids the word “transfigured” (metemorphōthē), perhaps because Greek readers would think of pagan myths of gods changing shape. But the meaning is the same. Matthew says his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). As Moses’ face shone after being with God (Exodus 34:29–35), but Jesus’ glory was his own, shining from within.

And his clothing became dazzling white. “Dazzling” (exastraptōn): flashing like lightning. The glory of heaven.

In a sentence. About eight days later, Jesus took Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray, and as he prayed his face changed and his clothes became dazzling white.

For worship. The Jesus you pray to is this glorious Lord. And as you pray, you are being changed into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.

Moses and Elijah. Moses, who gave the law; Elijah, the greatest of the prophets. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (24:27, 44). Both met God on a mountain; both had unusual ends; both were expected before the end (Malachi 4:4–5).

Who appeared in glory. They share in the glory of the heavenly world.

And spoke of his departure. Only Luke tells us what they talked about. The word for “departure” is exodos, “exodus”. Moses led the first exodus from slavery in Egypt, through the Red Sea, toward the promised land. Jesus will lead a new and greater exodus, through his death, resurrection and ascension, freeing his people from slavery to sin and death and bringing them home to God. The word also means death, departure from life (2 Peter 1:15).

Which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. “Accomplish” (plēroun): fulfil, complete. His death is not something that will happen to him, but something he will achieve. Jerusalem is the goal of the whole Gospel (v. 51; 13:33).

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with Jesus about his exodus, which he would accomplish in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. The whole Old Testament points to the cross. Read it that way.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus — his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus: Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, not knowing what he said.

Heavy with sleep. Only Luke records this. Perhaps it was night. They nearly slept through the glory, as they would sleep in Gethsemane (22:45).

But when they became fully awake they saw his glory. Peter would later write: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty (2 Peter 1:16–18). John wrote: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

As the men were parting from him. Peter wanted to keep them there.

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters, perhaps like those of the Feast of Booths, which looked forward to God dwelling with his people. Peter wants to prolong the glory. But he puts Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah, and he wants to stay on the mountain when Jesus has just told him the way lies through Jerusalem and the cross.

Not knowing what he said. Luke’s gentle comment. Peter spoke from awe and confusion.

In a sentence. The drowsy disciples woke to see Jesus’ glory, and as Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter suggested building three shelters, not knowing what he was saying.

On a Tuesday. We want to stay on the mountaintop. But glory comes through the cross. Follow Jesus down into the valley.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. A voice came out of the cloud, saying: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him! When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

A cloud came and overshadowed them. The cloud of God’s presence, as on Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18) and in the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). “Overshadowed” is the same word used of the Spirit coming on Mary (1:35).

And they were afraid as they entered the cloud. They entered the presence of God.

This is my Son. Not one of three, but the Son, unique. The answer to Peter’s three tents.

My Chosen One. Some manuscripts read “my Beloved”, as in Mark. “Chosen One” echoes Isaiah 42:1: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights. Jesus is the chosen Servant of the Lord, who will suffer (Isaiah 53). The rulers will mock this very title at the cross: if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One! (23:35).

Listen to him! Deuteronomy 18:15: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you … it is to him you shall listen. Jesus is that prophet, greater than Moses. Listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross (v. 22).

And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. Moses and Elijah gone. Jesus only.

And they kept silent and told no one in those days. As Jesus commanded (Mark 9:9), until after the resurrection.

In a sentence. The cloud of God’s presence covered them, and the Father declared Jesus his Son, his Chosen One, and commanded them to listen to him, and then Jesus was alone.

For worship. God’s command to you today: listen to my Son. Open his word and hear him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen
my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only child is seized by a spirit that convulses him — and the disciples who were not on the mountain had tried and failed.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, then flattened exhaustion. So was the boy ill or possessed? Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and he consistently keeps the categories apart: those sick with various diseases, and demons also came out of many (4:40-41); a crowd healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits (6:17-18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm and Luke's care rules out both — that every seizure or darkness of mind is the enemy's work, and that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

“O faithless and twisted generation” is addressed to the whole scene, not the father — the word “twisted” is Moses' word for Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5). And it is followed immediately by “Bring your son here.” He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy anyway.

Luke ends the miracle as he ended the one at Nain: “he gave him back to his father” (cf. 7:15). Not “the boy was healed.” A son handed back to the man who brought him.

Then, at the height of the crowd's enthusiasm, the second passion prediction — “let these words sink into your ears.” They did not understand, it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask. Afraid of the answer, almost certainly; Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32).

And what fills the silence is an argument about which of them is greatest. Jesus takes a child — a person with no legal standing and nothing to offer — and stands the child beside himself. Then John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, and gives his reason: “he does not follow with us.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' failure at v.40, after their success in vv.1-6, raises the question of what changed. Matthew records Jesus naming it as “little faith” (Matt. 17:20). The lesson is what the whole chapter teaches: the authority delegated to them is not their own. It flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him.

“Delivered into the hands of men” — handed over. There is a bitter wordplay the English keeps: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men.

Luke's “it was concealed from them” is a passive without an agent, and probably deliberately so. Two things are true at once: there is a hiddenness God appoints (cf. 19:42; 24:16), and there is a hiddenness they are manufacturing, since the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead.

On “the one who is not against you is for you” — a reader will notice the apparent opposite at 11:23, “whoever is not with me is against me.” The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant's judgement of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child placed beside Jesus is a searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership measured by influence, platform, numbers or reputation. A first-century child had no legal rights, no property, no voice, and no capacity to confer honour on anybody — which is exactly why he was chosen for an argument about greatness.

So the test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats those who cannot advance him, repay him, report him, or do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

“I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” is an honest report of ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. It belongs in the Gospel and it is a comfort of a hard kind: the record of the church's work has always included the things that did not work.

And John's “he does not follow with us” — not “he does not follow you” — names the instinct precisely. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.

When they had come down from the mountain. From glory to need. The mountaintop prepares for the valley.

Teacher, I beg you to look at my son. “Look at” with favour and compassion.

For he is my only child. Only Luke says “only”, as with the widow’s son (7:12) and Jairus’ daughter (8:42). The depth of a father’s grief.

In a sentence. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a crowd and a father who begged him to look at his only son.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus and ask him to look on them with favour.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.

A spirit seizes him. An evil spirit. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the cause was demonic (v. 42).

And shatters him. “Shatters” (syntribon): crushes, bruises, breaks him. Satan’s aim is destruction.

And will hardly leave him. Even between seizures, it barely lets him go.

And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not. The nine disciples who stayed below had failed, though Jesus had given them authority over all demons (v. 1). Mark tells us why: this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer (Mark 9:29).

In a sentence. The father described how a spirit seized and convulsed his son, crushing him, and how the disciples had failed to cast it out.

On a Tuesday. Past success is no guarantee of present power. Every work of God needs fresh dependence on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here. While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marvelling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples:

O faithless and twisted generation. “Twisted” (diestrammenē): perverse, crooked, the word Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5). Addressed to all, including the disciples.

How long am I to be with you and bear with you? The weariness of the holy Son among unbelievers.

Bring your son here. And yet compassion.

The demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. Its last attack.

But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. As at Nain: he gave him to his mother (7:15). The same tender words. Luke tells it more briefly than Mark.

And all were astonished at the majesty of God. “Majesty” (megaleiotēti): greatness, magnificence. They saw God’s greatness in what Jesus did. The same word is used of the transfiguration (2 Peter 1:16). The majesty seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented the faithlessness of his generation, then rebuked the spirit, healed the boy and gave him back to his father, and everyone was astonished at the majesty of God.

For worship. The majesty of God is seen in Jesus’ compassion as much as in his glory. Worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

The second passion prediction. While everyone was marvelling at his power (v. 43), Jesus speaks of his weakness. Popular amazement would not last. The disciples must not be swept up in it.

Let these words sink into your ears. Literally “put these words into your ears”. Pay close attention. Remember this.

The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. “Delivered” (paradidosthai): handed over, betrayed. A play on words: the Son of Man into the hands of men. The one who heals by his hands will be handed into human hands.

But they did not understand this saying. They could not reconcile a suffering Messiah with what they believed.

And it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. Only Luke says this. A divine passive: God concealed it. Not as punishment, but because the time for understanding had not yet come. Their eyes would be opened only after the resurrection (24:16, 31, 45).

And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. Perhaps afraid of the answer.

In a sentence. While everyone marvelled, Jesus told his disciples to remember that he would be handed over to men, but they did not understand, because it was hidden from them, and were afraid to ask.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to ask Jesus about the hard things in his word. Understanding is his gift.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side.

An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. Straight after the prediction of his betrayal. Jesus speaks of being handed over; they argue about rank. Perhaps the choice of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy, or the failure of the nine. The same argument will arise at the Last Supper (22:24).

Knowing the reasoning of their hearts. He knew what they were thinking (5:22; 6:8).

Took a child and put him by his side. Beside himself, in the place of honour. Children had no status in the ancient world.

In a sentence. When the disciples argued about which of them was greatest, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, set a child beside him.

On a Tuesday. Pride is persistent, even in disciples. Watch for the desire to be thought greater than others.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to them: whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.

Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. To welcome a person of no status, for Jesus’ sake, is to welcome Jesus himself. He identifies himself with the least.

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. And so receives God.

For he who is least among you all is the one who is great. Greatness in the kingdom turns the world upside down. The least is the greatest. Not the one who seeks to be great, but the one who becomes small: who welcomes the unimportant and serves without seeking recognition (22:26–27).

In a sentence. Jesus taught that whoever welcomes a child in his name welcomes him and the Father, and that the least among them is the greatest.

On a Tuesday. Welcome someone today who can give you nothing in return. In them, you welcome Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered: Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. But Jesus said to him: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.

We saw someone casting out demons in your name. Successfully, when the disciples had just failed (v. 40).

And we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. “With us”: not one of our group. The same pride as the argument about greatness, now as group pride.

Do not stop him. Jesus corrects their exclusiveness.

For the one who is not against you is for you. A generous principle. Anyone genuinely working in Jesus’ name against Satan is on the same side. Elsewhere Jesus says: Whoever is not with me is against me (11:23). The first is a rule for how to view others; the second, a test for oneself. Don’t exclude genuine fellow workers; but you yourself must be wholly with Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer, or that doctrine does not matter (Matthew 7:22–23; Acts 19:13–16; Galatians 1:8). The issue here is group loyalty, not the truth of the gospel.

In a sentence. When John said they had tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name because he was not one of them, Jesus told them not to stop him, for whoever is not against them is for them.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when Christ is served by believers outside your own circle.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With that sentence Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over, and the journey that runs from here to 19:44 begins. Everything that follows — the parables, the healings, the controversies — happens on the road that leads to the cross.

“Taken up” reaches past the cross to the ascension. Luke has the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, the going home.

“Set his face” is the language of the Suffering Servant: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 50:7) — from a passage whose preceding verse reads, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard.” He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies. He turns and starts walking.

The route runs through Samaria, which some Jewish pilgrims avoided by going round through the Jordan valley. He goes straight through. And the village refuses him precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem — the ancient dispute over Gerizim and Jerusalem. On the first day of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

James and John ask to call down fire, reasoning from Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:10-12), and reasoning badly: Elijah faced armed men sent to seize a prophet, and these two are facing a village that declined to provide beds. Jesus rebukes the disciples, not the Samaritans, and they go on to another village. Samaritan villages like it would be evangelised within a few years (Acts 8:5-8, 25), and no one there was burned.

Three encounters close the chapter. A man volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — a saying that fits the refusal he has just met. A second is called and asks to bury his father first; in that world burial happened the same day, so the request may well mean “let me stay until my father dies,” an indefinite postponement. A third asks only to say goodbye — which is what Elisha was granted (1 Kgs. 19:20) — and is answered with a ploughing image, the difference being that Elisha destroyed his plough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative beginning at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution. Matthew and Mark move quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey. The structure is theological before it is geographical: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of it is lived in the shadow of the set face of 9:51.

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the fifth commandment and of an obligation so weighty that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of judgement (Jer. 22:18-19). It is not an abolition of family duty. It is a refusal of one word, and the word is first. And the saying is wordplay, not cruelty: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life.

“Fit for the kingdom of God” is the language of usefulness. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while facing the wrong way.

And the instinct James and John show — to destroy those who reject Jesus — is answered by the direction he is walking. The one who has set his face toward a cross does not call down fire on those who refuse him; he presses on toward the sacrifice that will make it possible for even Samaritans to receive him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled through stony ground; it had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first. The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

The three would-be disciples represent three ways of not following. The first underestimates the cost — “wherever you go” sounds easy until it means homelessness. The second and third both say first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided. He never does. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. He sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

The journey to Jerusalem. Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins, running to 19:44, ten chapters. Much of Luke’s unique material is here: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus. The whole journey is lived in the shadow of the cross.

When the days drew near for him to be taken up. “Taken up” (analēmpseōs): his ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22), and with it the whole of his departure: death, resurrection and return to the Father. Jesus looks beyond the cross to the glory.

He set his face to go to Jerusalem. A Hebrew expression of fixed determination (Isaiah 50:7: I have set my face like a flint). Jesus knows what awaits him in Jerusalem, and he goes there resolutely. Nothing will turn him aside.

And he sent messengers ahead of him. To arrange food and lodging for a large group.

A village of the Samaritans. Samaria lay between Galilee and Judea. Samaritans were descendants of the northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses, and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem (John 4:20). Jews and Samaritans despised each other. Many Galilean pilgrims avoided Samaria by travelling through Perea.

But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. Because he was going to worship in Jerusalem, the Jewish temple they rejected. Samaritans were often hostile to Jewish pilgrims passing through to Jerusalem.

In a sentence. As the time of his departure approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem, but a Samaritan village refused to welcome him because he was heading there.

For worship. Jesus set his face to go to the cross for you. Nothing could turn him aside from saving you.
