verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples James and John saw it, they said: Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.

James and John. Jesus called them “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). Here we see why.

Do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? They think of Elijah, who called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent by the king of Samaria (2 Kings 1:9–16). They had just seen Elijah on the mountain. And they had been given power (v. 1). Why not use it?

But he turned and rebuked them. Jesus came to save, not to destroy. This is not the time for judgement, but for grace. The day of vengeance has not yet come (4:19). And Jesus would later send his gospel to Samaria (Acts 1:8), where it would be received with great joy (Acts 8:5–8, 14–17), and John himself would go there to lay hands on Samaritan believers so they would receive the Holy Spirit. The fire would come down on Samaria: the fire of the Spirit, not of judgement.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “as Elijah did”, and others add Jesus’ words: You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them. These are probably not original, but they capture the meaning.

And they went on to another village. No revenge. He simply went elsewhere.

In a sentence. When James and John offered to call down fire on the Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them, and they went on to another village.

On a Tuesday. When people reject you or the gospel, resist the desire for revenge. Jesus came to save, and so should you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were going along the road, someone said to him: I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Three would-be followers. Three short encounters about the cost of discipleship (vv. 57–62). Each shows a different obstacle.

I will follow you wherever you go. Enthusiastic, sincere, but perhaps impulsive. Matthew says he was a scribe (Matthew 8:19). Does he know where Jesus is going? To Jerusalem, to the cross.

Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests. Even animals have homes. The Son of Man does not.

But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Jesus had left his home in Nazareth, and had just been refused lodging in Samaria. Following him means giving up security and comfort. Count the cost first (14:28).

In a sentence. To a man who promised to follow him anywhere, Jesus warned that he, the Son of Man, had no home, unlike even foxes and birds.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus may cost you comfort and security. Are you willing?

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another he said: follow me. But he said: Lord, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus said to him: leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.

To another he said, Follow me. Jesus calls this one.

Lord, let me first go and bury my father. Burying a father was a sacred duty in Judaism, so important that it overrode other religious obligations, like reciting the Shema. If the father had just died, he would be burying him that day. But more likely, his father was still alive and the man meant: let me wait until my father dies, and I have my inheritance and have fulfilled my family duty, perhaps years from now. Either way, he puts something else “first”.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead. A shocking, deliberately paradoxical saying. Let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. Those who have not responded to the call of the kingdom can handle the affairs of this world. The kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family duty.

But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God. Your task is greater: to bring life to the spiritually dead.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should neglect their parents or refuse to attend funerals. Jesus condemned the Pharisees for using religion to avoid caring for parents (Mark 7:9–13). But no duty, however sacred, comes before Christ. Whatever you put “first” is your real lord.

In a sentence. When a man called by Jesus asked first to bury his father, Jesus told him to let the dead bury their dead and go and proclaim the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. What do you want to do “first”, before following Jesus fully? Nothing should come before him.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet another said: I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. Jesus said to him: no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. A reasonable request, it seems. When Elijah called Elisha from the plough, Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). But Jesus demands more than Elijah.

No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back. A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward on a fixed point to cut a straight furrow. A light plough was guided by one hand while the other held a goad for the oxen. If he looked back, the furrow went crooked. A divided heart, half looking back to the old life, cannot plough straight for the kingdom. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32).

Is fit for the kingdom of God. “Fit” (euthetos): suitable, useful. Not that he cannot be saved, but that half-hearted discipleship is useless for kingdom work.

The three obstacles. Comfort (v. 58), duty (v. 60), and family affection (v. 61). All good things. But none can come before Christ. Jesus demands undivided loyalty, because he is Lord.

In a sentence. When another man wanted first to say goodbye to his family, Jesus said that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you looking back at your old life while trying to follow Christ? Fix your eyes forward on him.
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

parallels.desc: Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go.

If your Bible says seventy, nothing is wrong: the manuscripts divide almost evenly here and at v. 17, and both figures carry the same symbolism. Moses appointed seventy elders to help carry a burden he could not carry alone (Num. 11:16), and two more prophesied in the camp (Num. 11:26); and the nations listed in Genesis 10 come to about seventy. Either way, the expansion from twelve signals that the mission is wider than the twelve tribes.

They go two by two — the two witnesses the law required (Deut. 19:15) — and they go ahead of him. They are not independent agents but an advance party, and everywhere they arrive he is coming behind them.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” inverts the instinctive picture. The field is not the problem; the field is ready. And faced with a labour shortage, Jesus does not say “go” but “pray” — and he says it to the seventy-two he is about to send out that hour. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the shortage is not finally ours to solve: it is “the Lord of the harvest” and “his harvest,” twice in one sentence.

“Lambs in the midst of wolves” is candid. A lamb among wolves is food; there is no version of that scene where the lamb wins. Jesus does not promise safety, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

The instructions echo those to the twelve, with additions. “Greet no one on the road” is not rudeness but urgency — an Eastern roadside greeting could consume a large part of a day, and Elisha said the same to Gehazi on an errand that would not wait (2 Kgs. 4:29). The “son of peace” is a Semitic idiom for a person already prepared to receive what is being brought; and where there is none, the peace “returns” — nothing is wasted.

“Eat what is set before you” is far more than manners. It sends Jewish men into households whose kitchens were the daily boundary of the covenant, and it plants the seed of Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:14-15).

And the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are among the most severe words in Luke's Gospel — aimed not at pagan cities but at the three villages where most of the ministry had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v.16 — “the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — governs all Christian mission. It rests on the ancient principle that an authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him: insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king.

The comfort in that is enormous. A believer stammering through an explanation to a colleague is not offering a private opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy does not degrade what is carried.

The weight is equally real. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But note the limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant: the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to shield leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. What could not be refused without consequence was a specific announcement: the kingdom of God has come near.

The woes introduce graduated accountability — judgement proportional to light received. Paul develops it (Rom. 2:12-16), and Hebrews applies it to those who have known the covenant (Heb. 10:26-31). The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Chorazin appears in the whole New Testament exactly twice — here and in the Matthew parallel — and not one miracle done there is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though his hearers knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books (cf. John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles no evangelist thought to write down.

“It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town” is not a claim that inhospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near.

And the last word a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated. “Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near” is almost word for word what the receiving towns were told (v. 9). The kingdom came as near to Chorazin as to anywhere — and nearness is not reception.

The principle bites hardest where most has been given (12:48), which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. He said to them: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.

Only Luke. Only Luke records the sending of the seventy-two. The Twelve were sent in chapter 9; now a wider group. The mission is not only for apostles.

Seventy-two. Some manuscripts read seventy; the evidence is evenly divided. The number may recall the seventy (or, in the Greek Old Testament, seventy-two) nations listed in Genesis 10, the whole world. If so, it foreshadows the mission to all nations. Or it may recall the seventy elders who helped Moses (Numbers 11:16–25). Twelve for Israel; seventy(-two) for the nations.

And sent them on ahead of him, two by two. Pairs, for support and credible testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15). They go ahead, preparing for his coming, like John the Baptist.

The harvest is plentiful. The harvest is a picture of people ready to be gathered into the kingdom (John 4:35–38). It is also a picture of the end-time judgement (3:17). There are many people ready to receive the gospel.

But the laborers are few. The problem is not the harvest but the workers.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. The first response to the need is prayer. “Pray earnestly” (deēthēte): beg, plead. God is the Lord of the harvest: it is his, and he sends the workers. Mission begins in prayer.

To send out laborers into his harvest. “Send out” (ekbalē): literally “throw out”, “thrust out”, the word used for casting out demons. God may need to push workers out. And those who pray for workers often find they are the answer to their own prayer.

In a sentence. Jesus sent seventy-two disciples ahead of him in pairs, telling them that the harvest is great but the workers few, and to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for God to send workers into his harvest, and be willing to be sent yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.

As lambs in the midst of wolves. Vulnerable, defenceless, among enemies. Mission is dangerous. But the lambs are sent by the Shepherd, who is with them and will lay down his life for them (John 10:11).

Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals. No money, no supplies, no spare sandals. Total dependence on God.

And greet no one on the road. Not rudeness, but urgency. Travellers’ greetings in the East could be long and elaborate, with embraces, enquiries after families, and invitations to stay. There was no time for that. Elisha told his servant the same (2 Kings 4:29). The mission is urgent.

In a sentence. Jesus sent them out like lambs among wolves, with no money, supplies or spare sandals, and no time to stop for long greetings.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is urgent. Don’t let small things delay what God has given you to do.
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever house you enter, first say: peace be to this house! And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the labourer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.

Peace be to this house! The ordinary greeting, shalom. But on their lips, more than a greeting: the peace of the kingdom, peace with God through the Messiah (2:14).

And if a son of peace is there. A Hebrew idiom: a person open to God’s peace, ready to receive it.

Your peace will rest upon him. The blessing is effective. God’s peace actually comes.

But if not, it will return to you. Like a dove returning to the ark when it found nowhere to rest (Genesis 8:9). Nothing is lost; the blessing comes back.

Eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Those who work for the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve. Paul quotes this saying as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18; also 1 Corinthians 9:14). It is not charity; it is wages earned.

Do not go from house to house. Don’t look for better hospitality. Be content.

In a sentence. They were to greet each house with peace, which would rest on those open to it, and stay where they were welcomed, accepting food as a worker’s due wages.

On a Tuesday. Support those who minister God’s word to you. They deserve their wages.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them: the kingdom of God has come near to you.

Eat what is set before you. Don’t be fussy. Perhaps also, in a mixed area, don’t worry about whether the food meets strict purity rules (1 Corinthians 10:27). This anticipates the gospel going to the Gentiles.

Heal the sick in it. Signs of the kingdom.

The kingdom of God has come near to you. The message. In Jesus, God’s reign is here, at your door. It demands a response.

In a sentence. In towns that welcomed them, they were to eat what was offered, heal the sick, and announce that the kingdom of God had come near.

On a Tuesday. The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus. Tell someone today.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say: even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. A public sign of judgement (9:5): we want nothing of yours; you are under God’s judgement.

Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. Even in rejection, the message stands. They cannot say they were not told. It is a final warning, and still an invitation.

It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. “That day”: the day of judgement. Sodom was the byword for wickedness and judgement (Genesis 19). Yet a town that rejects the gospel will face worse judgement than Sodom. Why? Because judgement is according to light received (12:47–48). Sodom never heard the gospel. To hear the message of the kingdom and reject it is a greater sin.

What it shows. There are degrees of punishment in the final judgement, according to privilege and knowledge (Matthew 11:22–24; Romans 2:12).

In a sentence. In towns that rejected them, they were to wipe off the dust as a sign of judgement, warning that the kingdom had come near, and Jesus said Sodom would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. Hearing the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility. Don’t treat it lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgement for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.

Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum, at the north end of the lake, where Jesus had done many miracles. Chorazin is not mentioned anywhere else in the Gospels; we know of the works only from this verse. The Gospels record only a fraction of what Jesus did (John 21:25).

If the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon. Gentile cities, denounced by the prophets for their pride and wickedness (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28).

They would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth (coarse goats’ hair cloth) and ashes were signs of mourning and repentance (Jonah 3:6). Pagan cities would have responded better than the Jewish towns that saw Jesus’ works. A searching statement: God knows what people would have done in other circumstances.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? Capernaum, Jesus’ own base, the most privileged town of all. An echo of Isaiah 14:13–15, against the king of Babylon: You said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven … But you are brought down to Sheol.

You shall be brought down to Hades. “Hades”, the Greek for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead. Here, the place of judgement. The ruins of Capernaum, Chorazin and Bethsaida still lie empty today.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Galilean towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, saying that pagan cities would have repented and would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. If you have grown up hearing the gospel, you have great privilege. Don’t let familiarity harden you to it.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.

The one who hears you hears me. Christ identifies with his messengers. When they speak his message, he speaks through them. To listen to them is to listen to him.

And the one who rejects you rejects me. Rejection of the messengers is rejection of Christ (Acts 9:4: why are you persecuting me?).

And the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me. And so rejects God himself. The chain: messenger, Jesus, Father.

The authority of preaching. When the word of God is faithfully preached, Christ himself speaks (Romans 10:14–17; 2 Corinthians 5:20). The preacher is not the source of authority, but his message, if true to Scripture, carries Christ’s authority. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) says: the preaching of the word of God is the word of God.

In a sentence. Jesus told his messengers that whoever hears them hears him, and whoever rejects them rejects him and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is faithfully preached on Sunday, listen as to Christ himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return elated: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” The word even gives them away — they expected the preaching to work and did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name.

“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels. It may look back to the primordial fall, or forward to the cross and the final defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9); but the tense and the context favour a comment on what has just happened. They came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw.” He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. The Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work — only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

Then the authority over serpents and scorpions, and the promise that nothing shall hurt them — both of which have been badly misused and both of which the passage itself guards.

And then the redirection: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The joy was not wrong; it was aimed at the wrong thing. Authority is about what they can do, and anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance.

Jesus then rejoices in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places where Luke tells us what he was feeling, and it is exultation. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, and the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

The prayer thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and then makes one of the highest claims in the Synoptic Gospels: all things handed over, and a mutual knowing of Father and Son that admits no third party except by the Son's choosing.

Finally the private beatitude: “blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Not blessed for perceptiveness — blessed for what happens to be in front of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is given in the Spirit and directed to the Father in prayer. The mutual delight of Father, Son and Spirit overflows into the mission and into the lives of those who share in it.

Verses 21-22 have long been called the Johannine thunderbolt, because they drop into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” is not authority in a defined area but everything. And the mutual knowing is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others; it is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. That he opens it is why the prayer is joy rather than terror.

“The wise and understanding” are not scholars in general — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. They are the professionally religious who have watched everything and concluded he is a problem. And the “little children” are the seventy-two. The dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands; learning is no obstacle to that, it simply supplies one more thing to hold onto.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” reorients the worker's identity from achievement to grace. The image is a citizen register — the book of life in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

Every feature of it reverses what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else — and it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

This belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on himself. The Christian who has been ill for two years, can no longer do any of the things he used to do, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

And the beatitude of vv.23-24 is a rebuke to the boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time. Abraham died with one son of the promise and a burial plot. Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown a back. Isaiah described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Every one of them longed for this. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! And he said to them: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

The seventy-two returned with joy. Joy, a Lucan theme.

Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! “Even”: more than they had expected. Jesus had told them to heal (v. 9), not specifically to cast out demons. His name had power.

I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. When? Perhaps in a vision during their mission: as they went out, Jesus saw Satan’s power broken. Or a reference to Satan’s original fall (Isaiah 14:12, the Morning Star fallen from heaven). Most likely the first: their ministry was a sign that Satan’s kingdom was collapsing, suddenly and decisively, like a flash of lightning. The kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of Satan (11:20–22). His final defeat would come at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15; Revelation 12:9–11).

In a sentence. The seventy-two returned joyfully reporting that even demons submitted to them in Jesus’ name, and Jesus said he had seen Satan fall from heaven like lightning.

On a Tuesday. Satan is a defeated enemy. Serve Christ with confidence.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.

I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions. Psalm 91:13: You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot. Serpents and scorpions were symbols of evil powers (Genesis 3:15; Deuteronomy 8:15). The promise is primarily spiritual: authority over the forces of evil.

And over all the power of the enemy. The enemy is Satan.

And nothing shall hurt you. Not that disciples will never suffer; they will be persecuted and even killed (21:16). But no spiritual power can ultimately harm them, separate them from God’s love, or take away their salvation (21:18; Romans 8:35–39).

What it does not mean. Not a licence to handle snakes or seek danger (see Mark 16:18). That would be putting God to the test (4:12).

In a sentence. Jesus gave his disciples authority over all the power of the enemy, so that nothing could ultimately harm them.

On a Tuesday. In Christ, you have nothing to fear from the powers of evil. Nothing can separate you from his love.

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you. Not that it is wrong to be glad at God’s work, but that power and success are not the deepest reason for joy. Spiritual power can lead to pride. And some who did mighty works in Jesus’ name will be rejected at the judgement (Matthew 7:22–23).

But rejoice that your names are written in heaven. The perfect tense: have been written and remain written. The book of life, in which God records his people (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12, 15; 21:27), like a register of citizens. Your salvation is God’s work, settled in heaven. Success in ministry can come and go; your name in God’s book cannot be erased.

Election. The names are written by God. This points to God’s sovereign choice of his people, and their security. Revelation speaks of names written in the book of life before the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8; Ephesians 1:4). Joy rests on grace, not on performance.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice chiefly in their power over spirits, but that their names are written in heaven.

For worship. If you belong to Christ, your name is written in heaven. Rejoice in that today, whatever else happens.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Only Luke mentions the Spirit here. “Rejoiced” (ēgalliasato): exulted, thrilled with joy. A rare glimpse of Jesus’ joy. Father, Son and Spirit: the Trinity in one sentence.

I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Intimacy and sovereignty together.

That you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding. “These things”: the truths of the kingdom, who Jesus is. Hidden from the wise, the scribes and the learned, who were proud of their wisdom.

And revealed them to little children. “Little children” (nēpiois): infants, the simple, the humble disciples. God reveals himself not to the clever but to the humble (1 Corinthians 1:18–31). Not that intelligence is bad, but that pride blinds.

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. “Gracious will” (eudokia): good pleasure, the same word as 2:14. God reveals and hides according to his sovereign good pleasure. Jesus does not complain about it; he thanks God for it. Election is a cause of praise.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father. Total authority and knowledge given to the Son.

No one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son. A unique, mutual knowledge between Father and Son. Only God can know God fully. This is one of the clearest statements in the Synoptic Gospels of Jesus’ deity and unique relationship to the Father, like John’s Gospel.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. The only way to know God is through the Son’s revelation. And the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses. Knowing God is a gift of sovereign grace (John 6:44; 14:6; 17:6).

In a sentence. Rejoicing in the Spirit, Jesus thanked the Father for revealing the truth to the humble rather than the wise, by his gracious will, and declared that only the Son knows the Father and reveals him to whom he chooses.

For worship. If you know God, it is because the Son chose to reveal him to you. Rejoice and give thanks with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning to the disciples he said privately: blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.

Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! The disciples are witnessing the fulfilment of everything the Old Testament promised: the Messiah, the kingdom, the defeat of Satan.

Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56). The prophets searched and inquired about the salvation to come (1 Peter 1:10–12). David, Isaiah, all longed for it. They died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples privately that they were blessed to see and hear what many prophets and kings had longed to see and hear.

For worship. You live after the cross and resurrection, with the whole New Testament. You see more than the prophets. Thank God for your privilege.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer — an expert in the law of Moses — stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” The wording gives him away twice over. What shall I do assumes the answer is an action; and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for, since it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence without noticing.

Jesus answers with two questions. “What is written in the Law?” asks for the text. “How do you read it?” asks for the man — and a reading is never neutral. The examination has quietly moved.

The lawyer's answer is superb: Deuteronomy 6:5 welded to Leviticus 19:18, the spine of the law in a sentence. And Jesus commends it: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

Which is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer. Jesus is using the law as it was meant to be used — not a ladder to climb but a mirror to look into (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24).

And it works. The lawyer does not go home content; he starts negotiating, “desiring to justify himself.” His question — “who is my neighbour?” — sounds like scholarly precision and is a search for a boundary. If neighbour has edges, there are people outside them, and a man can be entirely obedient and still walk past the rest. It was a live question with real answers on offer: neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and the Qumran sect required its members to hate the sons of darkness.

The story refuses him a category from its first line: not a Jew, not a Gentile, just “a man.” Stripped and beaten unconscious, he has lost the two things — clothing and speech — by which anyone could have identified him.

A priest passes. A Levite passes. Every listener now expects the third man to be an ordinary Israelite; that is the shape of the joke. What arrives is a Samaritan — and the hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. It is only a chapter since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it.

Then the reversal: not “who is my neighbour?” but “which of these three proved to be a neighbour?” The lawyer cannot say the word. He says “the one who showed him mercy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made him unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. But note the direction of travel — he was going down, away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, where many priests lived between rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead.

And the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

Luke offers the priest and Levite no mitigation whatever. He simply says they passed by on the other side, and adds of the second that he “came to the place” — he got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

The parable has been read allegorically since Origen: the traveller is humanity, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and prophets that cannot save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the sacraments. The reading is not without insight — Jesus is indeed the one who binds wounds, pays the debt and promises to return. But the surface command is non-negotiable: “Go and do likewise.”
verseByVerse.examples:
“Had compassion” — compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses the word at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and of the Samaritan.

The care is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. Bandages torn from his own clothing; his own oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, now gone; his own animal, which means he walked; a night spent nursing a stranger; two denarii, two days' wages, enough for a fortnight's board; and then an open-ended undertaking — “whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.” A blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despised him.

“Go and do likewise” is not “go and feel compassion,” which is sentiment, or “go and have good intentions,” which are cheap. It is the specific, costly, schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening action of the Samaritan.

Which is unbearable if read honestly — and that is the moment it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road, to where we were lying, when we were in no condition to ask; he paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on (1 John 4:19). The command remains binding — and it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying: Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? He said to him: what is written in the Law? How do you read it?

A lawyer. An expert in the law of Moses, a scribe.

Stood up to put him to the test. Not a sincere question, but a test of Jesus’ orthodoxy. Students stood to ask a teacher a question.

What shall I do to inherit eternal life? The same question as the rich ruler (18:18). The most important question there is. But note again: “do”.

What is written in the Law? How do you read it? Jesus turns the question back. You are the expert. What does Scripture say? Jesus always points to Scripture.

In a sentence. A lawyer tested Jesus by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus asked him what the law said.

On a Tuesday. When you have questions about God, go to his word. What is written? How do you read it?
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbour as yourself. And he said to him: you have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.

You shall love the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 6:5, from the Shema, recited daily.

With all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind. The whole person, nothing held back.

And your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. The lawyer joins them, as Jesus did elsewhere (Mark 12:29–31). A good answer.

You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live. An echo of Leviticus 18:5: if a person does them, he shall live by them. True: if anyone kept these two commandments perfectly, he would have eternal life. But no one does. Jesus is not teaching salvation by works; he is letting the law do its work, showing the lawyer his inability, so that he will see his need of grace (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–12). The lawyer feels the pressure at once (v. 29).

Law and gospel. This is the first use of the law: to convict of sin. The perfect law demands perfect love. Only one man ever kept it: Jesus. And his perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him (Romans 5:19; 10:4–5).

In a sentence. The lawyer summarised the law as loving God with everything and one’s neighbour as oneself, and Jesus told him that if he did this, he would live.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself against these two commands. Have you kept them? If not, flee to the one who did.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus: and who is my neighbour?

Desiring to justify himself. He felt the challenge, and wanted to show he was in the right. Perhaps also to justify his question, since he already knew the answer. Self-justification is the instinct of the human heart: to define God’s law in a way we can keep (16:15; 18:9).

And who is my neighbor? Let us define the terms. If “neighbour” can be limited (to fellow Jews, fellow Pharisees, the righteous), the command becomes manageable. Many Jews understood “neighbour” in Leviticus 19:18 as fellow Israelites; some excluded sinners and enemies. Jesus will not answer the question as asked. He will turn it around.

In a sentence. Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer asked Jesus who his neighbour was.

On a Tuesday. Do you try to limit God’s commands so you can keep them? Let his word define the terms, not you.

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus replied: a man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

The parable of the good Samaritan. Only Luke records it. One of the best known stories in the world.

A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet (900 m) in about 17 miles (27 km), through rocky desert, with caves and bends where robbers hid. It was notoriously dangerous, called “the way of blood”. The man is not described: no nationality, no religion, no status. Just a man, stripped of everything that might identify him.

And he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Unconscious, unable to help himself, perhaps dying.

Now by chance a priest was going down that road. Going down, away from Jerusalem, perhaps after his week of service in the temple. Many priests lived in Jericho.

He passed by on the other side. Why? Perhaps fear: the robbers might still be near. Perhaps ritual purity: if the man was dead, touching him would make the priest unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), though he was going away from the temple. Perhaps simple indifference. Jesus gives no reasons; excuses don’t matter.

So likewise a Levite. Levites assisted priests in the temple. Religious, respectable, knowledgeable about the law. He too came, saw, and passed by.

The point so far. The two men who should have helped, who knew the law about loving one’s neighbour best, did nothing. Religion without love.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man robbed and left half dead on the Jericho road, whom first a priest and then a Levite saw and passed by on the other side.

On a Tuesday. Who have you passed by on the other side? Religious knowledge is no substitute for love.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.

But a Samaritan. The shock of the story. Jesus’ hearers would expect the third man to be an ordinary Jewish layman. Instead, a Samaritan: a hated enemy, a heretic, despised by Jews (9:52–53; John 4:9). Jews would curse Samaritans in the synagogue. The lawyer probably could not even bring himself to say the word (v. 37).

And when he saw him, he had compassion. All three saw. Only one had compassion (esplanchnisthē), the word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the father of the prodigal (15:20). Compassion is the heart of the story.

He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. First aid. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleansed them, the standard treatment. Ironically, oil and wine were also used in the temple sacrifices. The Samaritan offered the true worship (Hosea 6:6).

Then he set him on his own animal. So he himself walked. Taking a risk, in robber country.

And brought him to an inn and took care of him. All night.

Two denarii. Two days’ wages, enough for perhaps two weeks’ lodging. And an open-ended promise to pay more. Without payment, the man could have been held as a debtor.

The cost of love. Time, effort, risk, money, and inconvenience, for a stranger, and an enemy. Love does not calculate.

Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan? From the early church onwards (Origen, Augustine), many read the parable as an allegory of salvation: the man is Adam, the robbers are the devil, the priest and Levite are the law and the prophets, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the church, the two denarii the sacraments, and the return is the second coming. Verdict: the parable’s primary meaning, given by Jesus himself, is ethical: go and do likewise (v. 37). Reading every detail as allegory goes beyond the text. Yet there is a true echo: Christ is the supreme neighbour, who came to us when we were his enemies, half dead in our sins, and gave himself to save us (Romans 5:8–10). The parable both commands love and points to the love that makes it possible.

In a sentence. A despised Samaritan, moved with compassion, tended the man’s wounds, took him to an inn, cared for him, and paid for his ongoing care.

On a Tuesday. Love is costly and practical. Whose wounds can you bind up this week, whatever it costs?
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage — two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbour to the man who fell among the robbers? He said: the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus said to him: you go, and do likewise.

Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor. Jesus has turned the question around. The lawyer asked: who is my neighbour? (whom must I love?). Jesus asks: who proved to be a neighbour? (who loved?). The question is not who qualifies for my love, but whether I will be a neighbour to anyone in need. Neighbourliness is not defined by the other person’s status, but by my compassion.

The one who showed him mercy. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say “the Samaritan”.

You go, and do likewise. The application. Stop asking whom you must love, and start loving whoever is in need, even your enemy. And if the lawyer is honest, he will find that he cannot love like this by his own strength. He needs a new heart. The law drives us to Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of the three had been a neighbour, and when the lawyer answered “the one who showed mercy”, Jesus told him to go and do the same.

On a Tuesday. Don’t ask who your neighbour is. Be a neighbour to whoever is in need, today.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a house in a village — Bethany, though Luke does not name it — and the placing is deliberate. The Samaritan has just poured out his time and money on a road, with “go and do likewise” still in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Martha “welcomed him into her house” — her house, Luke says, which is unusual enough to notice, and she received him as an honoured guest. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching,” and both halves of that would have struck a first-century reader. Sitting at a teacher's feet is the technical posture of a disciple — Paul describes his own training as being brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). And that place was not open to a woman. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and in three verses he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it in a subordinate clause, as though it were ordinary — which, from now on, it is.

Martha is “distracted with much serving” — pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not being busy but being torn. And the thing tearing her is service: she is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for.

Her complaint takes three steps and each goes further. She interrupts his teaching; she accuses her sister in front of the guests; and then she accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed in — and then “tell her,” which does not even ask him to intervene but tells him what to say.

Every word of it is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

“Martha, Martha” is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person: the same register as “Simon, Simon” (22:31), “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34), “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). And the diagnosis is not of her workload but of her interior — “anxious,” the worry he will forbid his disciples (12:22-26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mary sitting at the Lord's feet is the posture of discipleship, and Luke has used the phrase once already of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). In the first century women did not ordinarily receive rabbinic instruction, and the posture of female discipleship was itself a quiet revolution. Jesus does not redirect Mary to help; he defends her right to receive what he is giving.

“The good portion” plays on a word for a share at a meal — and Martha, of all people, would have felt it, since she is in the kitchen dividing portions while Mary has taken the one that matters.

“Which will not be taken away from her” carries the force of a promise. What Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end; the word Mary is taking in is permanent, the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23).

Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one” at v.42; the shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way. What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary defines what must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene speaks to the perennial tension between doing and being. It does not abolish the tension; it orders it. Martha's service is not wrong — her anxiety is. And this is not a rebuke of practical work: Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

“Do you not care?” is worth naming for anyone who has prayed like it, because a good many have. It is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38) — what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord it was all being done for. The cure is not less service. It is the recovery of the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. A woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching.

The placing. After the parable about doing (love your neighbour), a story about listening. The two belong together: loving God by hearing his word, and loving neighbour by serving. Martha and Mary show the balance.

A village. John tells us it was Bethany, near Jerusalem, where they lived with their brother Lazarus (John 11:1; 12:1–3). Luke does not name it, perhaps because in his order of the journey Jesus is not yet near Jerusalem.

A woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. Martha was apparently the head of the household. Hospitality to Jesus and his disciples, perhaps thirteen or more people, was a large undertaking.

Who sat at the Lord’s feet. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple (8:35; Acts 22:3, where Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel). It was a role normally reserved for men. Women were expected to be in the kitchen. Mary took the place of a disciple, and Jesus welcomed it.

And listened to his teaching. The tense means she kept on listening.

In a sentence. In a village, Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and her sister Mary sat at his feet listening to his teaching.

On a Tuesday. Make time today to sit at Jesus’ feet: read his word and listen.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Martha was distracted with much serving. She went up to him and said: Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.

But Martha was distracted with much serving. “Distracted” (periespato): pulled in different directions, dragged away. “Serving” (diakonian), the word for ministry. Her service was good, and necessary. The problem was not her serving but her distraction: it pulled her away from Jesus.

Lord, do you not care. Accusing Jesus, the same words the disciples used in the storm (Mark 4:38). Anxiety turns into resentment, against others and against God.

That my sister has left me to serve alone? Self-pity.

Tell her then to help me. She tries to command Jesus. Busy, worried people often judge others who are not as busy.

In a sentence. Martha, distracted by her many preparations, complained to Jesus that her sister had left her to serve alone and asked him to tell Mary to help.

On a Tuesday. Even good service for Jesus can distract you from Jesus. Notice when busyness turns into resentment.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord answered her: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.

Martha, Martha. The repeated name expresses tenderness and concern (22:31; Acts 9:4). A gentle rebuke, from love.

You are anxious and troubled about many things. “Anxious” (merimnas): worried, the same word as the cares that choke the word (8:14). “Troubled” (thorybazē): in an uproar, flustered. Many things.

But one thing is necessary. Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one”, as if Jesus were saying that a simple meal would do. But the best reading is “one thing”. Not just one dish, but the one thing that matters most: listening to Jesus. The one thing (Psalm 27:4: one thing have I asked of the Lord … that I may dwell in the house of the Lord … to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord).

Mary has chosen the good portion. “Portion” (merida): a share, a helping of a meal. Martha was busy preparing many portions; Mary chose the best one, the food of Jesus’ word (Deuteronomy 8:3; John 4:32–34).

Which will not be taken away from her. Jesus defends Mary. Meals are eaten and forgotten. What she receives from Jesus is eternal.

What it does not mean. Not that serving is unimportant, or that contemplation is better than action. The good Samaritan shows the importance of action. And Martha was not wrong to serve. But listening to Jesus comes first, and is the source of true service. Service without listening becomes anxious and resentful. Hearing his word is the one thing necessary.

In a sentence. Jesus gently told Martha that she was anxious about many things, but only one thing was necessary, and Mary had chosen the best portion, which would not be taken from her.

For worship. What are you anxious and troubled about today? Lay it down, and choose the good portion: sit at Jesus’ feet.

parallels.desc: one thing have I asked of the LORD
the LORD is my chosen portion

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village.
