And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 divides into three movements of escalating intensity. It opens with the disciples' request — “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” — and Jesus's response: the Lord's Prayer and two parables about persistent asking. It continues with the controversy over Beelzebul, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons, and responds with the parable of the strong man, the sign of Jonah, and a warning about the darkness that replaces expelled light. And it closes with the most sustained series of woes in Luke's Gospel — six pronouncements against the Pharisees and lawyers that are simultaneously the most confrontational and the most sorrowful words Jesus speaks in public.

The chapter's movement from prayer (vv. 1–13) to spiritual warfare (vv. 14–36) to religious condemnation (vv. 37–54) is not a random sequence. The prayer section establishes the relationship with the Father that makes spiritual life possible. The Beelzebul controversy shows what happens when the kingdom's power is at work in the world — it provokes opposition, demands decision, and warns against the neutrality that is actually a form of hostility. And the woes reveal what becomes of religious life when it loses the relationship with the Father — when the form of religion remains but the substance has been evacuated, replaced by the performance of piety for the wrong audience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and when he finishes one of the disciples asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” Of everything on offer in three years beside the Son of God — the healings, the stilled storm, the knowledge of men's thoughts — the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Luke's version is shorter than Matthew's (Matt. 6:9-13), and that difference has unsettled readers who learned the prayer by heart as children. Where is “who art in heaven”? Where is “thy will be done”? An older Bible will have them at this very verse and a modern one will not.

There is nothing sinister in it. Luke's prayer was always the shorter of the two, but the version the church actually prayed aloud, week after week for centuries, was Matthew's — and scribes copying Luke knew that fuller wording by heart. Line by line, over generations, they filled Luke out to match what their lips already said. It is one of the most understandable corrections in the history of copying and one of the easiest to detect: the earliest manuscripts of Luke are short, and the additions match Matthew word for word. Nothing was lost. Every phrase you were taught is genuinely the Lord's; it is simply Matthew who recorded it.

And Luke's shorter form is worth having in its own right, because two versions tell us something one could not. Jesus plainly gave this prayer more than once, and not in identical words. Matthew says “pray then like this”; Luke says “when you pray, say.” Set them side by side and the conclusion is unavoidable: this was never handed down as a formula to be recited syllable-perfect on pain of not counting. It is a shape for praying — a floor to build on, not a ceiling.

The prayer opens with one word that was a revolution. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation; what is almost entirely absent is an individual addressing him that way in prayer. The word Jesus himself uses in Gethsemane is the Aramaic Abba (Mark 14:36) — family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of that period addressed God with it in prayer.

Then five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first, then us — and the order is not decoration. A prayer that begins with God's honour can bring every human need afterwards without becoming a list submitted to a dispenser.
verseByVerse.theology:
The address “Father” is the theological revolution of this prayer. Paul will name what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a warmer name for the same relationship; it is a different relationship — the Son's own, opened to people with no natural claim to it.

“Hallowed be your name” asks that God be treated as holy, since his name cannot be made more holy than it is. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known, so the petition asks that he be known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is — first by the one praying, and then by everybody else. It is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

“Your kingdom come” is the central petition and the shortest, and it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he was hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

“Daily” bread — the ESV margin gives “our bread for tomorrow,” enough for the coming day. It is a small request, deliberately: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “for” in “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive” has troubled readers, and it must not become a bargain. God's forgiveness is not purchased by ours; the prayer has just called him Father, which nobody earns.

What the clause does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed — a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour; and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all. Matthew makes the connection explicit (Matt. 6:14-15).

Note the tense, too: “we ourselves forgive,” present and continuing. Not “we forgave, once, years ago.” It is a standing policy.

And “lead us not into temptation” is not a fear that God might try to make us sin, which James forbids (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it — which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.

Now Jesus was praying. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel (3:21; 5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28). The disciples watched him pray, and wanted what he had.

Lord, teach us to pray. A wise request. Prayer must be learned. It does not come naturally to sinners. And the best teacher is the one who prays perfectly.

As John taught his disciples. Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer, which marked them out as a group. The disciples want a prayer that will express who they are as followers of Jesus.

In a sentence. After watching Jesus pray, one of his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, as John had taught his disciples.

For worship. Make the disciples’ request your own today: Lord, teach me to pray.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: when you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.

The Lord’s Prayer. Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13). Jesus probably taught it on more than one occasion, in slightly different forms. Luke’s has five petitions; Matthew’s seven. The ESV notes that some manuscripts expand Luke’s version to match Matthew’s. It is both a prayer to pray and a pattern for all prayer. Notice the order: God’s concerns first, then ours.

When you pray, say. A prayer to be prayed, not only a model. The church has prayed these words ever since.

Father. Key word. Simply “Father”, without “our” or “in heaven”. Behind it is the Aramaic Abba, the intimate word a child used at home, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Jews did not normally address God like this. Jesus invites his disciples to share his own relationship with the Father. We pray as children, adopted by grace (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). This is the privilege of the gospel: the holy God is our Father.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” (hagiasthētō): sanctified, treated as holy, honoured. God’s “name” is God himself as he has revealed himself. The first desire of the praying heart: that God would be known, honoured and worshipped as holy, in my life and in the whole world (Ezekiel 36:23). Not first my needs, but his glory.

Your kingdom come. God’s reign, which has come in Jesus (11:20), is still to come in fullness (22:18). Pray for it to spread now, as people turn to Christ, and to come finally, when Christ returns. The prayer of the early church: Maranatha, Come, Lord (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20).

In a sentence. Jesus taught his disciples to pray to God as Father, first asking that his name be honoured as holy and his kingdom come.

For worship. Begin your prayers with God, not yourself: his name, his kingdom. And call him Father.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.

Give us each day our daily bread. Our physical needs, brought to God. “Daily” (epiousion) is a rare word, whose exact meaning is uncertain: “for today”, “necessary for existence”, or “for the coming day”. The point is clear: daily dependence on God for what we need, as Israel gathered manna day by day (Exodus 16:4). Not riches, but enough (Proverbs 30:8). “Each day”: only Luke. Pray every day. And “us”, “our”: we pray for others’ bread as well as our own.

And forgive us our sins. Matthew has “debts”; Luke “sins”, making the meaning clear for Gentile readers. We need forgiveness as much as bread, every day.

For we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Here Luke keeps the image of debt. Not that our forgiving earns God’s forgiveness. But a forgiven person forgives, and cannot honestly ask for forgiveness while refusing it to others (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35). “Everyone”: no exceptions.

And lead us not into temptation. “Temptation” (peirasmon): trial, testing, the situations that could lead us into sin or cause us to fall away. God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people into trials (4:1). The prayer is: Father, I am weak. Do not let me be put to a test I cannot bear, or let me fall when tested (22:40, 46; 1 Corinthians 10:13). Matthew adds: but deliver us from evil.

In a sentence. Jesus taught them to ask for daily bread, for forgiveness as they forgive others, and to be kept from temptation.

On a Tuesday. Bring your daily needs, your sins and your weaknesses to your Father every day. And forgive whoever you need to forgive before you pray.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two illustrations follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater.

The first is the friend at midnight. To feel it you have to see the house: one room, the family asleep together on a raised platform, a single door barred at night with a beam that cannot be lifted quietly. Getting up wakes everybody. And there is no bread in the house, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily.

The man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. Hospitality in that culture was an obligation with the weight of law, and a traveller arriving at night was the whole village's guest; to fail him was a public disgrace. He asks a friend, at the worst possible hour, for three loaves — enough for one meal — and he asks to borrow them.

The sleeper's excuses are all true. The door is barred, the children are asleep, getting up will wake them. And he gets up anyway, “because of his impudence” — anaideia, shamelessness.

Whose shamelessness has been argued over. The traditional reading takes it as the asker's brazen persistence. A second reading, with a good deal to be said for it, takes it as the sleeper's — he rises to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: if even this man gives, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced.

What the parable licenses is boldness. Most prayer dies of good manners, and this story was told to kill that.

Then “ask, seek, knock” — after that parable, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking — and a promise unconditional in form: “everyone who asks receives.” Which raises the honest problem, because a great many people have read that verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

Jesus answers it with a picture of a father and a child. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion are roughly the same shape. What is described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he asked for and will hurt him — and no father does that.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three imperatives are in the present tense, implying continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. And there is a progression. Asking is words; seeking involves the feet; knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

On the difficulty in v.10, three things have to be said. Scripture itself never treats the promise as a blank cheque and says so in the same breath: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14), and “you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked it — “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). And the next three verses are his own commentary, which is where the weight lies.

A request denied is not a father who is deaf. It is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless, and it is not meant to. What it removes is the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And Luke's ending is his own. Matthew has “how much more will your Father give good things” (Matt. 7:11); Luke has “the Holy Spirit.” Luke's version tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance; it is himself, present, in a person.
verseByVerse.examples:
“You, who are evil” is dropped in without emphasis, as agreed common ground. He is talking to ordinary decent parents and takes it as obvious that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

The parable of the friend at midnight is also worth noticing for what the man needs. He is not asking for himself. He wants bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

And “give us each day our daily bread” has a hard edge for anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, this is where the passage lands. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.

The friend at midnight. Only Luke records this parable. It teaches persistence and boldness in prayer, and the goodness of God.

At midnight. Travellers often journeyed at night to avoid the heat of the day.

A friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him. Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty in that culture. Not to feed a guest would bring shame on the whole village. Villagers baked bread daily, in the morning, and by evening most had none left. Neighbours knew who had baked that day.

Lend me three loaves. Small, flat loaves; a meal for one person.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who went to a friend at midnight to borrow bread because an unexpected guest had arrived and he had nothing to offer.

On a Tuesday. When you have nothing to give others, go to God, who has everything.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he will answer from within: do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.

Do not bother me; the door is now shut. A peasant family slept together in one room, often on a raised platform, with the animals below. The door was barred with a heavy bolt. Getting up, unbarring it, and stepping over sleeping children would wake the whole household.

I cannot get up. I will not.

Because of his impudence. “Impudence” (anaideian): shamelessness, boldness, persistence. The man would not stop knocking. Some interpreters take the word to refer to the sleeper: to avoid the shame of refusing a neighbour’s request, he gets up. Either way, the request is granted.

The point. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater. If a reluctant, sleepy neighbour will get up and give because of shameless persistence, how much more will God, who is not reluctant and never sleeps (Psalm 121:4), give to those who ask him. God is not like the sleeper; he is the opposite. We do not have to wear him down. But we should pray with the boldness and persistence of someone who knows he has a real need and a friend who can meet it (18:1–8).

In a sentence. Even if the friend would not get up out of friendship, he would get up and give everything needed because of the man’s shameless persistence.

On a Tuesday. Pray boldly and persistently. God is not reluctant, but he loves to see his children keep asking.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Ask … seek … knock. Three verbs, rising in intensity. Ask: make the request. Seek: search with effort. Knock: persist at the door, as the man in the parable did. The tense of each means keep on: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking.

And it will be given to you … you will find … it will be opened to you. Three promises. God answers prayer.

For everyone who asks receives. Not a few privileged people, but everyone. Prayer is not reserved for the spiritual elite.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give us anything we want, as if prayer were a blank cheque. God gives what is good (v. 13), according to his will (1 John 5:14). Sometimes his answer is not what we asked for, but something better. A good father does not give his child everything he asks for. But no prayer of his child goes unheard or unanswered.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to keep asking, seeking and knocking, promising that everyone who does so will receive, find and have the door opened.

For worship. What do you need to keep asking God for? Keep knocking. He will answer.

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

What father among you. A second argument from the lesser to the greater: from earthly fathers to the heavenly Father.

If his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent. A fish and a water snake might look similar; an egg and a curled-up white scorpion. No father would play such a cruel trick.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew 7:9. Probably added to match Matthew.

If you then, who are evil. A striking aside. Jesus calls even good fathers “evil”. Human nature is sinful, even at its best (Romans 3:10–12). Yet sinful fathers still give good gifts to their children.

How much more will the heavenly Father. Who is perfectly good.

Give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! Matthew has “good things” (Matthew 7:11). Luke has “the Holy Spirit”, the greatest of all good gifts, the gift that includes all others. Luke and Acts are full of the Spirit. The Father gives his Spirit to his children: to dwell in them, to make them holy, to help them pray (Romans 8:26), and to empower them for witness (Acts 1:8). Every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9). But we may and should keep asking for more of his presence and power (Ephesians 3:16; 5:18).

In a sentence. If sinful fathers give their children good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

For worship. Your Father is better than the best human father. Ask him today for more of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus casts out a demon that has made a man mute, and the crowd marvels. Two responses come from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

The first is the Beelzebul charge — that he works by the prince of demons. Notice what it concedes: nobody disputes that the man is speaking, and nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened.

The second is a demand for “a sign from heaven” — a real one, not this business with a local demoniac. Made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, that is not scepticism; it is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable.

Jesus dismantles the charge twice over. A divided kingdom cannot stand, so Satan casting out Satan is destroying his own operation. And “by whom do your sons cast them out?” exposes a standard applied to him and not to their own exorcists — which means the objection is not the real reason.

Then his own account: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament — Pharaoh's magicians conceding they are out of their depth (Ex. 8:19), and the tablets written by God's own finger (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, in three words. And the verb is “has come upon you” — not near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but arrived.

The parable of the strong man is the interpretation of everything he has done. The strong man is fully armed, on his own ground, and while that holds his goods are safe. Then one stronger attacks, overcomes, strips the armour he trusted in, and divides the spoil. And the goods, in this context, are people.

The section closes with two warnings. Neutrality is abolished — “whoever does not gather with me scatters.” And the swept house: a life cleaned up and left empty is not a neutral state on the way to better. It is a vacancy, advertised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The warning about the returning spirit is the parabolic form of the New Testament's consistent warning against reformation without regeneration. Everything in the description is good news — swept, put in order, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted. One word is missing, and it is the whole point: nobody is living there.

Jesus's assessment of that condition is not “an improvement, as far as it goes.” It is “worse than the first,” because an empty swept house has been made attractive. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation — and Luke has just named who is available, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

“Whoever is not with me is against me” must be read alongside 9:50, “the one who is not against you is for you,” and the two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There the subject is you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here it is me — a person's own standing before Christ. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

And note what Jesus assumes in passing while making his argument: that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. He says it as something too obvious to argue.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's beatitude on Jesus's mother is well meant and entirely ordinary in that culture: praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. Elizabeth said something very like it in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

The word “rather” is doing careful work in the reply. It is not a contradiction but a redirection, and it refuses the assumption underneath the compliment — that blessedness is a matter of proximity. If that were true the whole thing would be closed to everybody else, since there is exactly one womb that bore him.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd: “hear the word of God and keep it” — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. And Mary is the outstanding instance of exactly that: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). The correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

And the swept-house warning is worth turning into a question by anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing. Not “what have you got rid of?” but “who lives there now?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marvelled. But some of them said: he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.

A demon that was mute. A demon that made the man mute. Matthew says he was also blind (Matthew 12:22).

And the people marveled. The common response.

He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Beelzebul is a name for Satan. Its origin is uncertain: perhaps “lord of the dwelling”, or a corruption of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), whose name means lord of flies, which Jews may have mocked as “lord of dung”. They could not deny the miracle, so they attributed it to Satan. Better to call God’s work demonic than to admit Jesus came from God.

While others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. Not enough for them. They wanted something more spectacular, undeniable, on their terms. Jesus will answer this in verses 29–32.

In a sentence. When Jesus cast out a demon that made a man mute, some accused him of doing it by the power of Satan, and others demanded a sign from heaven.

On a Tuesday. People who don’t want to believe will always find an explanation. Don’t demand more evidence than God has given.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them: every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.

Knowing their thoughts. Again, he reads hearts.

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste. The first answer: the charge is illogical. Satan would not destroy his own work. Civil war destroys a kingdom.

If Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? Satan has a kingdom (4:5–6), but it is not divided.

By whom do your sons cast them out? The second answer: inconsistency. “Your sons” means your followers, your people. Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time (Acts 19:13). If you accept their exorcisms as from God, why not mine?

Therefore they will be your judges. Your own people’s practice condemns your double standard.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that Satan would not fight against himself, and that their own exorcists exposed their double standard.

On a Tuesday. Watch for double standards in how you judge others’ ministries.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

By the finger of God. Matthew has “by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy: This is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). God wrote the Ten Commandments with his finger (Exodus 31:18). It means the direct power of God. Jesus’ exorcisms are as clearly God’s work as the plagues of Egypt, and like them, they show God liberating his people from a tyrant.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. “Has come upon you” (ephthasen): has arrived, has overtaken you. The kingdom is not only future; it is present in Jesus. God’s reign has broken in. Satan’s kingdom is being invaded and overthrown. The kingdom has come, though not yet in its fullness: this is the “already and not yet” of the kingdom.

In a sentence. If Jesus casts out demons by God’s own power, then the kingdom of God has arrived.

For worship. The kingdom of God has come in Jesus. Rejoice that God reigns, and that Satan’s power is broken.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armour in which he trusted and divides his spoil.

When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace. The strong man is Satan, guarding his kingdom, holding people captive.

His goods are safe. Satan’s captives, those he holds in bondage, cannot escape by their own strength.

But when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him. The stronger one is Jesus. John had said: he who is mightier than I is coming (3:16). Jesus has come to attack Satan’s kingdom, overpower him, and set his captives free (4:18). This victory began in the wilderness (4:1–13), continued in the exorcisms, and was won decisively at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15).

He takes away his armor in which he trusted. Strips him of his weapons.

And divides his spoil. Isaiah 53:12: he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death. The spoil is the people freed from Satan, who become Christ’s own.

In a sentence. Jesus compared Satan to a strong man guarding his palace, and himself to a stronger one who overpowers him, strips him of his armour and plunders his goods.

For worship. If you are a Christian, you are part of the spoil the stronger one has taken from Satan. Thank him for your freedom.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

Whoever is not with me is against me. In the war between Christ and Satan, there is no neutral ground. You are on one side or the other. Those who stand back and criticise are, in fact, on Satan’s side. Elsewhere Jesus says: the one who is not against you is for you (9:50). The two sayings fit together: be generous in how you view others who serve Christ, but be uncompromising about your own allegiance.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. The picture of a shepherd gathering a flock, or a harvester gathering a crop. Either you work with Christ to gather people into his kingdom, or you scatter them.

In a sentence. There is no neutrality with Jesus: anyone not with him is against him, and anyone not gathering with him scatters.

On a Tuesday. Are you with Jesus, gathering with him? There is no middle ground.

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person. A warning, following the point about neutrality. Deliverance from evil is not enough by itself.

It passes through waterless places seeking rest. Desert places were thought to be the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). Demons are restless; they want a home in a person.

I will return to my house from which I came. “My house”: the demon still thinks of the person as his.

And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Clean and tidy, but empty (Matthew 12:44). Reformed, but not occupied by anyone new. The person has been cleaned up, morally improved, but Christ has not come to live there.

Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven: complete possession.

And the last state of that person is worse than the first. Moral reformation without Christ leaves a vacuum that evil fills. It is not enough to get rid of evil; the heart must be filled with Christ and his Spirit. This applied to the people of Jesus’ generation: they had been stirred by John and Jesus, but without committing to him, they would end up worse (Matthew 12:45). And it applies to anyone who makes a fresh start without Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that a person cleaned of an evil spirit but left empty will be reoccupied by worse spirits, ending worse than before.

On a Tuesday. Self-improvement is not salvation. Don’t just sweep your house clean; invite Christ to live in it.
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him: blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! But he said: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!

A woman in the crowd raised her voice. Only Luke records this. A spontaneous cry of admiration.

Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! A common way of praising a man, by praising his mother: how blessed she must be to have such a son. It is also true: Mary is blessed (1:42, 48).

Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it! “Rather” (menoun): yes, but more than that; or, on the contrary. Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed. But he points to a greater blessedness, open to everyone: hearing God’s word and obeying it. Physical relationship to Jesus, even being his mother, is not what matters most. Mary herself was blessed chiefly because she believed and obeyed God’s word (1:38, 45; 2:19, 51). The same point as 8:21.

Where Christians differ: devotion to Mary. Roman Catholic and Orthodox devotion gives Mary a unique place of honour and intercession: praying to her, and calling her Queen of Heaven and Mediatrix. Verdict: Jesus himself redirects attention from his mother’s physical role to the blessing of obedience, which she shares with all believers. Mary is rightly called blessed, and is a great example of faith. But she is not to be prayed to or venerated. There is one mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. When a woman called Jesus’ mother blessed, he said that those who hear God’s word and keep it are more blessed still.

On a Tuesday. The blessing of hearing and keeping God’s word is open to you today. Read it, and do it.

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowds are increasing — and Luke notes it, because that is when Jesus says “this generation is an evil generation.” Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

They want a sign from heaven, and he refuses; but the refusal is not of evidence. It is of evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain — which is exactly what happened fifteen verses earlier when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

The sign of Jonah works two ways, and they are not rivals. Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh: a foreigner walking into the greatest city of the ancient world with a single sentence of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented (Jon. 3:4-9). And behind that stands what happened before he arrived, which Matthew makes explicit — three days in the belly of the fish, and three days in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). Luke leaves it unstated and lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic.

Two witnesses are then called, and both are chosen to sting. The Queen of Sheba travelled over a thousand miles by camel, on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody's God. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, a byword for a people beyond hope — and it repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there and was furious when it worked.

Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. And twice the refrain: “something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.” Not someone greater but something — broader and stranger. No prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

The lamp sayings close the section. The lamp is not hidden; it has been on a stand in Galilee for three years. So the problem cannot be the lighting — it is the window. “Your eye is the lamp of your body,” and its two conditions are not merely medical: Scripture speaks of “a bountiful eye” for a generous man (Prov. 22:9) and, as the ESV margin renders it, “a man whose eye is evil” for a stingy one (Prov. 28:22; cf. Deut. 15:9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, because both responded to far lesser messengers. It is the graduated-accountability principle of the woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, sharpened: it will not be the ignorant who are condemned by Nineveh, but the well-informed.

“Something greater than Solomon” is worth weighing. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. Jesus does not argue for it; he says “behold,” and leaves it there.

The eye sayings are not about eyesight or intellect. Ancient thinking often understood the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person — so the picture is a house with a window: clear, and the house is bright; blocked, and the house is dark however strong the sun outside.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true — and nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Be careful lest the light in you be darkness” is the warning that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say “be careful in case you are in the dark” — a man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. Be careful — look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

The context names who it is for. The next paragraph is a dinner party with a Pharisee that ends in six woes. The people at greatest risk are not the irreligious but those with the most exposure — long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical.

And then, after the warning, the promise, which is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition — not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut. And the result is not an impressive person but a useful one: “as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowds were increasing, he began to say: this generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.

When the crowds were increasing. Popularity does not impress Jesus. He addresses the crowds with a warning.

This generation is an evil generation. Evil because it does not repent, despite seeing God’s works.

It seeks for a sign. As in verse 16. They had seen many signs. They wanted a sign that would remove the need for faith.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. What was the sign of Jonah? Jonah came to Nineveh as a man who had, in effect, come back from the dead, after three days in the fish (Jonah 1:17). Matthew makes the link with Jesus’ resurrection explicit: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). Luke emphasises Jonah himself as the sign: a prophet sent by God, who preached repentance.

For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh. Jonah himself, and his preaching, was the sign. The Ninevites did not see a miracle; they heard a message, and repented.

So will the Son of Man be to this generation. Jesus himself, his preaching, and above all his resurrection, is the sign. Enough for anyone. No further sign is needed or will be given.

In a sentence. Jesus called his generation evil for demanding a sign, and said the only sign given would be the sign of Jonah: the Son of Man himself, and his resurrection.

On a Tuesday. You have the greatest sign of all: the risen Christ. What more do you need to repent and believe?

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South will rise up at the judgement with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgement with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

The queen of the South. The queen of Sheba, probably from south-west Arabia (modern Yemen), who came to test Solomon with hard questions, and was overwhelmed by his wisdom (1 Kings 10:1–13).

Will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them. At the final judgement, she will be a witness against them. She travelled a vast distance to hear Solomon; they had a greater one in their midst and would not listen.

Something greater than Solomon is here. “Something” (neuter): the kingdom, the wisdom of God, in the person of Jesus. Jesus claims to be greater than Israel’s greatest king and wisest man. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:3).

The men of Nineveh. The capital of Assyria, Israel’s most brutal enemy. Pagans.

For they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Jonah 3:5–10. A reluctant prophet, preaching judgement with no promise of mercy. Yet the whole city repented.

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jesus is greater than any prophet. If pagans repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at his?

The point. Two Gentiles, a queen and a city, will condemn Jesus’ generation. Privilege increases responsibility. Gentiles responded to lesser light; Israel rejected the greatest light.

In a sentence. The queen of Sheba, who travelled far to hear Solomon, and the Ninevites, who repented at Jonah’s preaching, will condemn this generation at the judgement, because one greater than Solomon and Jonah is here.

On a Tuesday. You have far more than Solomon’s wisdom or Jonah’s preaching: you have Christ. Listen, and repent.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.

No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar. The light has been given: Jesus and his preaching, the sign of Jonah. It is not hidden. The problem is not lack of light but lack of sight.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. The eye lets light into the body. If it works, you can see; if not, you are in darkness. Spiritually, the eye is the heart’s ability to perceive God’s truth.

When your eye is healthy. “Healthy” (haplous): single, sincere, generous, undivided. A single-minded focus on God.

Your whole body is full of light. You receive the light and live in it.

But when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. “Bad” (ponēros): evil, diseased. A “bad eye” was an idiom for stinginess, envy or evil desire (Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15). A heart that is double-minded, greedy or hostile cannot see the light, however bright it shines. The crowd’s problem was not that Jesus was unclear, but that their eyes were bad.

In a sentence. The light has been given openly, and a healthy, sincere eye lets it fill the whole person, but a bad eye leaves the whole person in darkness.

On a Tuesday. Is your eye single toward God? Ask him to heal anything in your heart that keeps you from seeing his light.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.

Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. A terrible possibility: thinking you have light, when in fact you are in darkness. The Pharisees thought they saw (John 9:39–41). Self-deception is the worst blindness. Examine yourself.

If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark. Nothing held back, no dark corner.

It will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light. A life fully open to God’s light shines.

In a sentence. Jesus warned them to make sure that what they thought was light in them was not darkness, for a life fully open to the light will shine.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to search you and show you any part of your life you have kept dark (Psalm 139:23–24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and he goes. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel and every one ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked.

He does not perform the ritual handwashing, and the omission may well be deliberate. That washing was not hygiene and it was not in the law of Moses; nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

His answer takes their own debating point about the cleansing of vessels and turns it on them. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup; it is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And the first word for what is inside is greed — the grasping that takes. Something is being taken.

“Give as alms those things that are within” is his prescription, and it is remarkable: they asked how to be clean and the answer is not a better ritual but to give the contents away. The remedy for greed is not scouring the cup; it is giving away what was grasped.

Then six woes — three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers. The word itself needs setting straight: ouai is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict, the sound a man makes watching somebody walk towards a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41).

They tithe mint and rue and neglect justice and the love of God — and “these you ought to have done” refuses to abolish the small duty. They love the best seat and the public greetings. They are unmarked graves. The lawyers load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and have taken away the key of knowledge.

And it hardens them. The chapter ends with respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions to get a sentence they can use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. The law required a tithe of grain, wine and oil (Deut. 14:22-23); it said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. These were not lazy men — they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt. And “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” is regularly ignored: he does not condemn the herb-tithing.

The mechanism is universal. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off — and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The unmarked-grave woe depends on a detail of the law. Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16), so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, conspicuously, so pilgrims could see them and go round. The marking was a public service; it kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite — one a man walks straight over and finds out afterwards, if he finds out at all.

And “the key of knowledge” is the heaviest charge. The knowledge in question is not information about God but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders legitimately — and they did not enter themselves, and they blocked the door for people who were already moving towards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lawyer's interruption — “in saying these things you insult us also” — is wonderfully revealing. He does not say “that is untrue.” He concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, which is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

The burdens woe puts a simple test to anyone who teaches. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself. Set it against “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

The tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet; he has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living one is at the table, and they are about to arrange his death. Every generation of the church admires the awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet requires a subscription; a live one requires repentance.

And the key-of-knowledge woe puts a question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine; he transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test — whether someone who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.

A Pharisee asked him to dine with him. Literally to have the morning meal, the midday meal. Jesus accepted invitations from Pharisees, as from tax collectors (7:36; 14:1).

The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene (Mark 7:3–4). The Pharisees taught that hands must be washed ceremonially, with a special procedure, to remove uncleanness from contact with the world. It was not commanded in the law of Moses for ordinary people; it was the tradition of the elders. Jesus deliberately did not do it, perhaps to provoke the conversation that followed.

In a sentence. Jesus accepted a Pharisee’s invitation to dinner, and his host was surprised that he did not perform the ritual washing first.

On a Tuesday. Be careful about judging others by human traditions rather than by God’s word.
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord said to him: now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.

You Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish. The Pharisees had detailed rules for washing vessels (Mark 7:4). An image: they make the outside of their lives clean, ritually and morally, before people.

But inside you are full of greed and wickedness. “Greed” (harpagēs): plunder, robbery, rapacity. The inside of the cup was dirty, though the outside shone. Their hearts were full of greed. Religion that cares about appearances but not the heart is worthless.

You fools! “Fools” (aphrones): senseless. A strong word.

Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? God made both body and heart. He cares about both. And he sees the inside (1 Samuel 16:7).

But give as alms those things that are within. A difficult phrase. Probably: give from the heart; give what is in the cup, the contents, to the poor, instead of being greedy. A generous heart is a clean heart. Love for the poor is the inward cleanness God looks for (Micah 6:8).

And behold, everything is clean for you. When the heart is right, the ritual rules don’t matter. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while their insides were full of greed, and told them to give generously from the heart, and then everything would be clean for them.

On a Tuesday. God sees your heart. Don’t just look good on the outside; let him clean the inside.

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

Six woes. Jesus now pronounces six woes, three on the Pharisees (vv. 42–44) and three on the lawyers (vv. 46–52). “Woe” is a prophetic cry of lament and judgement.

For you tithe mint and rue and every herb. The law required a tithe (a tenth) of produce: grain, wine, oil, the fruit of the land (Deuteronomy 14:22–23). The Pharisees extended it to garden herbs, the tiniest plants, counting out every tenth leaf. Extremely scrupulous.

And neglect justice and the love of God. The weightier matters (Matthew 23:23). Justice: fair dealing with others, especially the poor. The love of God: loving him with the whole heart. The two great commandments (10:27). Careful about tiny details, careless about the heart of the law.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. Jesus does not condemn tithing; he says they should have done it. But the small things must not replace the great ones. Priorities.

Where Christians differ: the tithe today. Some teach that Christians must give a tenth of their income, as a binding law. Others say the tithe belonged to the old covenant, and the New Testament gives no fixed percentage. Verdict: the New Testament does not command a tithe for Christians, but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate, sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9). A tenth is a wise starting point, and many will give more. The heart matters more than the percentage.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for scrupulously tithing tiny herbs while neglecting justice and the love of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you careful about small religious details and careless about justice and love? Put first things first.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.

You love the best seat in the synagogues. The bench at the front, facing the congregation, where the important people sat.

And greetings in the marketplaces. Respectful greetings, with honorific titles, in public.

The point. Love of prominence and recognition. Their religion served their pride. They wanted to be seen and honoured by people (Matthew 6:1–5; 23:5–7). The problem is not the seat or the greeting, but the love of it.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for loving the places of honour and public recognition.

On a Tuesday. Do you love recognition in church? Seek God’s approval, not people’s honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.

Like unmarked graves. Under the law, touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). Graves were whitewashed each spring, before Passover, so that pilgrims would not accidentally touch them (Matthew 23:27). An unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

The point. The Pharisees thought they were the guardians of purity, keeping people clean. In fact, they were sources of defilement. Their hidden corruption spread to everyone who followed them, unawares. People thought they were being led to holiness, and were being led to death.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees as unmarked graves that unknowingly defile those who walk over them.

On a Tuesday. Your influence affects others. Make sure it leads them to life, not defilement.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the lawyers answered him: Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. And he said: woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

One of the lawyers. An expert in the law of Moses, a scribe. Many lawyers were Pharisees, and the Pharisees followed their interpretations.

Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. He hoped Jesus would distinguish the experts from the Pharisees. Jesus does not back down.

For you load people with burdens hard to bear. Countless rules, built up around the law, which made obedience impossible for ordinary people. Peter would later call the law, as they interpreted it, a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). Contrast Jesus: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30).

And you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. Either they found clever ways to avoid their own rules, or they did nothing to help others carry them. They imposed burdens without compassion.

In a sentence. When a lawyer protested, Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for loading people with impossible burdens while not lifting a finger to help them.

On a Tuesday. Don’t load others with rules God has not given. Help them carry the burdens they have.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.

For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. Honouring the prophets with monuments. It seemed like repentance for their ancestors’ sin. Monuments to prophets and great figures were being built in Jesus’ day.

So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers. Bitter irony. They honour dead prophets, but reject the living ones, as their fathers did. They are completing their fathers’ work: their fathers killed the prophets, and they build the tombs. They will kill the greatest prophet. Honouring dead prophets is easy; listening to living ones costs.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for building tombs for the prophets their fathers killed, because by rejecting God’s messengers they share in their fathers’ guilt.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to honour the great Christians of the past while ignoring the uncomfortable message of God’s word today.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore also the Wisdom of God said: I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute, so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.

The Wisdom of God said. Not a quotation from a known book. Perhaps God, in his wisdom, decreed this. Matthew puts it in Jesus’ own mouth: I send you prophets (Matthew 23:34). Jesus is the Wisdom of God.

I will send them prophets and apostles. “Apostles”: Jesus’ own messengers. Some will be killed (Acts 7:58–60; 12:2).

So that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation. The generation that rejects the Messiah fills up the measure of all its ancestors’ guilt (Matthew 23:32). It is the climax of a long history of rejection.

From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah. Abel is the first murder in Scripture (Genesis 4:8). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court for rebuking the people (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); his is the last murder in the Hebrew Bible, whose final book is Chronicles. So from Genesis to Chronicles, A to Z: the whole of the Old Testament. As he died, Zechariah said: May the Lord see and avenge!

Who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. In the temple court.

It will be required of this generation. Fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24).

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the generation which rejects God’s messengers will be held responsible for the blood of all the prophets murdered from Abel to Zechariah.

On a Tuesday. Rejection of God’s word accumulates. Don’t harden your heart to it today.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.

For you have taken away the key of knowledge. The lawyers were the teachers of Scripture. They held the key to understanding it, which should have opened the way into the kingdom. But by their traditions and false interpretations, they had locked the door. The key of knowledge is the right understanding of Scripture, which points to Christ (24:27, 44–45; John 5:39).

You did not enter yourselves. They did not come to Jesus.

And you hindered those who were entering. They stopped others from coming too, by their teaching and their opposition. The worst of the woes: false teachers who block the way to God.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for taking away the key to understanding Scripture, neither entering the kingdom themselves nor letting others enter.

On a Tuesday. If you teach God’s word, make sure it opens the door to Christ, not shuts it. And pray for faithful teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

The scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard. “Press him hard” (deinōs enechein): to be bitterly hostile, to hold a grudge. The opposition hardens.

And to provoke him to speak about many things. Firing questions at him.

Lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say. Hunting language: like hunters setting traps for an animal. They were not seeking truth, but evidence against him.

In a sentence. After this, the scribes and Pharisees became fiercely hostile, firing questions to trap him in something he might say.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised for faithfulness to Christ, remember that he was too. Speak the truth with wisdom.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body.
