When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most urgent chapters in Luke's Gospel — a sustained call to a particular quality of life in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus addresses a massive crowd (v. 1 — “so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another”) and then moves between the crowd and the disciples in a series of teachings that together form a comprehensive call to undivided allegiance. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Do not covet or stockpile; the rich fool who planned bigger barns died the night he planned them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom first. Be dressed for action, with lamps burning, waiting for the master to return.

The chapter's emotional register is high throughout. Jesus speaks of fire he has come to cast on the earth and a baptism he has to undergo before it — and he is distressed until it is accomplished. He warns that he has not come to bring peace but division — a division that runs through the family. He rebukes the crowd for its ability to read the weather and its inability to read the present moment. And he calls everyone to settle accounts with their adversary before they arrive at the judge — because once you are before the judge, the outcome is fixed. The urgency is eschatological: the crisis of the kingdom's arrival is not a background hum; it is the defining emergency of every human life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled — and in the middle of it Jesus turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful. This is a word for those inside about a temptation specific to religious people.

“The leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Leaven was a lump of soured dough kept back from the last batch: small, invisible once mixed in, working by itself, changing everything it touches. And Luke alone gives us Jesus's own definition. Hypocrisy is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

The argument against it is not moral but practical: “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.” The performance has a fixed run and a closing date. Whether that sentence is the most frightening in the chapter or the most liberating depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The teaching on fear is the application. Do not fear those who kill the body — after that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. What is commanded instead is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror; and the effect is the opposite of paralysis, since a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else. Every tyranny in history has run on the fear of what can be done to a body, and this sentence cuts the supply line.

Which is why “fear him” is followed two verses later by “fear not.” The bridge is a bird nobody wanted: sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, and Matthew's parallel prices them two for a penny (Matt. 10:29), so two pennies buys five — the fifth thrown in free, because it is not worth counting. Not one of them is forgotten.

Then the stakes rise. To acknowledge Christ before men is to be acknowledged before the angels of God; to deny him is to be denied. And then the hardest verse in the chapter — the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — followed immediately by the promise that in the hour of trial the Spirit himself will supply the words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah's worst kings (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it.

The one to be feared is God, not the devil — Scripture never gives the enemy authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. And the whole force of the passage depends on the fact that the one who has authority over death is the same one who does not forget a sparrow and knows a number about you that you do not know yourself.

On the blasphemy against the Spirit, the context is decisive. This saying stands in Matthew and Mark immediately after the Beelzebul accusation — which Luke gave us in the previous chapter (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work in the open and called it the devil, and Mark states the reason plainly: “for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:30).

It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is the settled, eyes-open decision to call the light darkness. And since the Spirit's work is to convict of sin and point to Christ (John 16:8-14), a man who has finally refused that work has stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. The anxiety itself is therefore the disproof: nobody who has committed this sin is afraid of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light” uses the architecture everyone lived in. The “private rooms” are the windowless inner storeroom where valuables were kept — the one place a conversation could not be overheard; the housetops were flat, adjoining, and where public announcements were made. The most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town.

The saying cuts both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost. Much of what Christians say for Christ is said quietly, in rooms with no audience, and looks unrecorded; Jesus says it is being minuted. But the primary force here is the other: everything a man is when nobody is watching is going to be read out. And a man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression — which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him.

The confession sayings must not become a performance requirement, and the safeguard is in the Gospel itself: Peter denied him three times, in public, and was restored on a beach. What is described is a settled position, not a single failure of nerve. Yet it should not be softened into nothing either. Very few Western Christians will stand in a court; the moments that count are the conversation at work, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned.

And “the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour” is not a licence for unprepared preaching — the situation named is arrest and interrogation — nor a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal but that the right words will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.

Setting. Chapter 12 gathers teaching on fearless faithfulness, money and anxiety, readiness for Christ’s return, and the urgency of the present time. Most is addressed to the disciples, with the crowds listening.

So many thousands … that they were trampling one another. Literally “tens of thousands”. Immense popularity, just after his fierce denunciation of the Pharisees (11:37–54). Jesus is not impressed by numbers.

To his disciples first. The warning is for his own followers.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump of dough. A little spreads through everything (1 Corinthians 5:6). Hypocrisy, acting a part, pretending to be what you are not, is like that: it starts small and spreads through a life and a community. The disciples are not immune.

Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed. Hypocrisy is pointless, because God sees everything, and at the judgement everything will be exposed (8:17; 1 Corinthians 4:5). The mask will come off.

In a sentence. With vast crowds around him, Jesus warned his disciples to beware of the spreading influence of the Pharisees’ hypocrisy, because everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to seem more spiritual than you are? Be real before God and people.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; here it pictures hypocrisy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.

Whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light. Private words will be made public. Every careless word will be judged (Matthew 12:36).

In private rooms. Literally “inner rooms”, storerooms in the middle of the house, without windows, where secrets could be shared.

Shall be proclaimed on the housetops. Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them, like a town crier. There are no secrets from God.

A double meaning. A warning: your secret sins will be exposed. And an encouragement: the gospel the disciples now hear privately will be preached publicly to the world.

In a sentence. Everything said in secret will be heard openly and announced from the rooftops.

On a Tuesday. Speak in private as you would if it were broadcast. God hears it all.
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!

My friends. The only time in the Synoptic Gospels Jesus calls his disciples “friends” (John 15:14–15). Tender, as he prepares them for persecution.

Do not fear those who kill the body. Hypocrisy often comes from fear of people. Jesus addresses the root. The worst that human enemies can do is kill the body. That is the limit of their power.

And after that have nothing more that they can do. Death is not the end. They cannot touch the soul.

Fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. God. Not Satan, who has no such authority. “Hell” (geenna, Gehenna): the place of final punishment. God alone has power over eternal destiny. The fear of God drives out the fear of people (Isaiah 8:12–13; Proverbs 29:25). If you fear God, you need fear nothing else.

Yes, I tell you, fear him! Repeated for emphasis. The fear of God is not cringing terror for his children, but reverent awe of the one who holds all power, including over eternity. And this awe is the beginning of wisdom.

In a sentence. Jesus told his friends not to fear those who can only kill the body, but to fear God, who has authority to cast into hell.

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most? Fear God, and you will be set free from the fear of people.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.

Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food, by the poor. Matthew says two for a penny (Matthew 10:29); Luke says five for two pennies: buy four, and get one free. The fifth sparrow was worth nothing at all.

And not one of them is forgotten before God. Not even the one thrown in for free. God’s care extends to the smallest and least valuable creature.

Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. God knows you in the tiniest detail, more than you know yourself.

Fear not. The God to be feared (v. 5) is the God who cares. The same God. Holy fear and trusting confidence go together.

You are of more value than many sparrows. If God cares for sparrows, he cares far more for his children. Even if they kill your body, it is not outside his care. Nothing happens to you that he does not know and allow (Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. God does not forget even the cheapest sparrow, and knows the number of hairs on your head, so do not fear, for you are worth more than many sparrows.

On a Tuesday. You are known and cared for by God in every detail. Face today without fear.
verseByVerse.note: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; Matthew says two for a penny, Luke five for two, as if the fifth came free.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.

Everyone who acknowledges me before men. “Acknowledges” (homologēsē): confesses, openly declares loyalty. In the face of fear of persecution, publicly owning Jesus.

The Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God. At the judgement. Jesus will say: this one belongs to me. Note: Jesus is the judge; his acknowledgement decides eternal destiny.

But the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. Measure for measure (9:26).

What it does not mean. Not that a single failure means final rejection. Peter denied Jesus three times, and was restored (22:61–62; John 21:15–19). The warning is against a settled refusal to acknowledge him. And it is one of the means God uses to keep us faithful.

In a sentence. Jesus will acknowledge before God’s angels all who openly acknowledge him before others, and deny those who deny him.

On a Tuesday. Where can you acknowledge Jesus openly today, at work, with friends, online?

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. Even those who reject and oppose Jesus can be forgiven if they repent. Paul once blasphemed Jesus and persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13). Peter denied him. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (23:34). Many of them were later saved at Pentecost (Acts 2:36–41).

But the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. What is it? In Mark and Matthew, the context is the accusation that Jesus cast out demons by Satan (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32): calling the Spirit’s work the devil’s work. It is a deliberate, settled, persistent rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, in full knowledge, calling God’s light darkness. Why can it not be forgiven? Not because God’s grace is insufficient, but because the Spirit is the one who brings people to repentance. To reject him finally is to cut oneself off from the only way to forgiveness. It is not that someone wants to repent and cannot be forgiven, but that he no longer wants to repent.

Where Christians differ, and a pastoral word. Some have taught that the unforgivable sin is a specific act, such as suicide or a particular blasphemous word. Verdict: it is not a single act or careless word, but a final, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ. Anyone who is worried that they have committed it has not, because the very worry shows the Spirit is still at work in them. Those who have committed it do not care.

In a sentence. Those who speak against Jesus can be forgiven, but those who finally reject the Holy Spirit’s testimony will not be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you are beyond forgiveness, the fear itself shows you are not. Come to Christ, who forgives everyone who comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.

Before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities. Jewish and Gentile courts. Fulfilled in Acts: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Stephen (Acts 7), Paul before governors and kings (Acts 24–26).

Do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself. Not a command to be unprepared in teaching (2 Timothy 2:15; 1 Peter 3:15). A promise for times of persecution.

For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour. The Spirit who is blasphemed by unbelievers (v. 10) helps believers. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly before the council (Acts 4:8–13). Stephen spoke with wisdom they could not resist (Acts 6:10).

In a sentence. When believers are put on trial for Christ, they need not worry about their defence, because the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say.

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians standing trial today, that the Spirit would give them words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man interrupts a discourse on hell and martyrdom to ask for help with a family estate — and it was not an unreasonable request in that world, since rabbis routinely arbitrated inheritance disputes. But notice what he actually asks: not “settle the dispute between us” but “tell my brother.” He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Jesus refuses, and the address is cold — “Man,” not “friend” — with an echo of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 2:14). Then he diagnoses the plaintiff and says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out: “be on your guard against all covetousness.” Not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but every form of it — including the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right.

The parable is not a warning against prosperity or against prudent planning. Notice how it opens: not “a rich man made a fortune” but “the land produced.” He did not do it. The harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange — which is the first thing he forgets.

Then the pronouns. In three verses of soliloquy he says I or my eleven times, and God is mentioned by nobody but God. There is no wife in this man's head, no labourers, no neighbour, and above all no giver. The question “what shall I do?” had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. There were poor people within a mile of that farm.

And then the strangest thing in the parable: he opens a conversation with his own soul, which is what a person does when there is nobody else — and tells it that its needs have been met by grain. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods; many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. He is treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem.

The thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied. And God's first word is “Fool.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“Fool” in Hebrew thought is not an insult about intelligence. The fool of the Psalms is the man who says in his heart “there is no God” (Ps. 14:1) — which is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He simply ran his entire life without reference to anybody but himself.

“This night your soul is required of you” — demanded back, as a lender demands what is his. Which reframes everything he has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time.

And note the timing against his own words: he said “many years,” God says “this night.” The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

“Rich toward God” is the positive alternative and one of the most compact phrases in Luke. It is worth noticing that the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say “so is the one who is rich.” He says “so is the one who lays up treasure for himself” — rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to live in the awareness that every good thing was received and is to be used toward his purposes; the opposite is to treat what one has as one's own achievement, for one's own use, accountable to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man's problem is not the abundance; it is the accounting. He has a genuine agricultural difficulty and his solution is reasonable, practical, and completely self-oriented. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus — distribute it or store it — and he never considers the first. He demolishes serviceable barns to build larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention.

Watch also what happens to the ownership across the parable. It begins as “the land” producing. It becomes “my barns,” “my grain,” “my goods.”

“And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is “somebody else's.” He tore down good barns for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once in five verses.

Which leaves a test that takes about a minute and is uncomfortable. Not “how much have I got?” but: if my accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing?

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone in the crowd said to him: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But he said to him: man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? And he said to them: take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.

Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). Perhaps the elder brother was refusing to divide the estate.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? An echo of Exodus 2:14, where an Israelite asked Moses: Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Jesus refuses the role. He did not come to sort out property disputes, but to deal with the heart. The man’s real problem is not his brother, but his greed.

Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness. “Covetousness” (pleonexias): the desire for more, greed. “All”: every kind, including the respectable kinds. Covetousness is a sin people rarely confess. The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

For one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. Life is not measured by what you own. Possessions cannot give life, or keep it, or satisfy it. True life is found in God.

In a sentence. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus refused and warned against all greed, because life does not consist in an abundance of possessions.

On a Tuesday. Is there a possession or an amount of money you think would make your life complete? Guard your heart against greed.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable, saying: the land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself: what shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?

Only Luke. Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

The land of a rich man produced plentifully. He had done nothing wrong. A good harvest is God’s gift (Acts 14:17). He was already rich, and God gave him more.

And he thought to himself. Literally “he dialogued with himself”. He talks only to himself. Not to God, not to his neighbours, not to the poor.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops? A good question, with a wrong answer. He could have shared with the poor (3:11). Notice: “my crops”. Everything is “mine”.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest, who asked himself what to do with it.

On a Tuesday. When God blesses you with more than you need, ask him what to do with it, not just yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

parallels.desc: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.

I will do this. “I”, “my”: in this short speech, he says “I” or “my” about a dozen times. Utterly self-centred.

I will tear down my barns and build larger ones. More storage for more stuff. His only plan for abundance is to keep it all for himself.

And I will say to my soul. He talks to his own soul, as if it could be satisfied with grain.

You have ample goods laid up for many years. He assumes he has many years. Security in possessions.

Relax, eat, drink, be merry. The philosophy of the world: enjoy yourself, for tomorrow we die (Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Ecclesiastes 2:24 in a godless sense). Retirement as the goal of life.

In a sentence. The rich man planned to build bigger barns to store everything for himself, and then to tell his soul to relax and enjoy itself for many years.

On a Tuesday. Are your plans for the future all about “I” and “my”? Bring God and others into them.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God said to him: fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

But God said to him. He had left God out of his plans. Now God speaks.

Fool! In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1). This man was clever, successful and prudent by the world’s standards. But he planned his life as if God did not exist, and as if he would never die.

This night your soul is required of you. “Required” (apaitousin): demanded back, as a loan is recalled. His life was never his own; it was lent to him by God. He planned for many years; he had one night.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be? He cannot take any of it with him (Psalm 49:16–17; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19; 1 Timothy 6:7). Someone else will get it, perhaps the very inheritance dispute of verse 13.

So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. The application. To be rich toward God is to use what you have for him: for his kingdom, for the poor, for eternal treasure (v. 33; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). Not wealth itself, but wealth hoarded for oneself, is the folly.

In a sentence. God called the rich man a fool, for his life was demanded that very night, and his hoard would go to others, as it does for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.

On a Tuesday. If tonight were your last night, would you be rich toward God? Use what you have for his purposes today.
verseByVerse.note: In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God.

parallels.desc: the fool says in his heart, “There is no God”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not “store less” but “worry less” — aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it; this is for disciples, most of whom had nothing to store. And the two problems are the same underneath: both are attempts to secure a life by managing supplies.

Note what is named — food and clothing, not luxuries. This is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

The ravens are chosen deliberately. They were unclean under the law (Lev. 11:15), they are scavengers, and there is a psalm about exactly this — “he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Ps. 147:9; cf. Job 38:41). The argument is set at the lowest available point. And the ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they lack is a storehouse.

“Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible — the alert mind doing necessary work — and the question exposes the claim. And then the sharper turn: he calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. From where we stand it is not small at all; it is what a person at a bedside would give everything for. He calls it the little end of the problem.

The lilies are probably the wild anemones that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring, and the two activities they do not do — toil and spin — were the two halves of a household's labour. And the argument turns hard on where the grass ends up: gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and burned in a peasant oven within the week. God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will heat somebody's bread.

Then the alternative, and it is not serenity but a different pursuit: “seek his kingdom.” And behind it the tenderest address in the Gospel — “fear not, little flock” — with a gift that is not a wage but the kingdom itself, given because the Father enjoyed giving it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity. The ravens still fly; the lilies still grow; the farmer still plants. What is addressed is not the activity of provision but the anxiety about it — the energy spent worrying about what worry cannot secure.

“O you of little faith” is a name Jesus uses only of disciples. It is never aimed at outsiders; nobody is called little-faith who has none. And the diagnosis is worth noting: not “you have too much to do” and not “your circumstances are difficult,” both of which may be true. The problem named is a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father — which makes anxiety a theological condition rather than a temperamental one.

“Nor be worried” in v.29 names the mind that will not settle — up in the air, unanchored. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture.

“The nations” is not an insult but a description of a real difference. The pagan world had a crowded pantheon of local deities who had to be managed — offerings at the right time, none of them notably fond of you, none reliable. Anxiety in that setting is not a failure of nerve; it is a rational response to the facts as understood. If nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Against which stand seven words: “your Father knows that you need them.” Not a force, not a committee of powers. He knows — so it does not have to be brought to his attention, and a great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying. And the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that anxiety is useless does not cure it. Nobody was ever argued out of worry by being told it achieves nothing; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so the question becomes the right one: not “how do I stop worrying?” but “what am I going to trust instead?”

“Little flock” is an honest name — a small group in an occupied province with the authorities already hunting their teacher. He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is, and the word carries the whole weight of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, where God says “I myself will search for my sheep.” And “good pleasure” means it delighted him.

“Sell your possessions” must be faced, because it is not a metaphor — and Luke supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half and salvation comes to his house that day (19:8-9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they must therefore still have had. And Peter's rebuke to Ananias turns on it: “while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie.

So the command is a transfer of ownership, not a rule about percentages. What it can never mean is a Christian who has settled the matter, drawn a line, and considers the rest his own. Ask not what proportion you have given away, but whether there is anything left that you would refuse him.

And “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” reverses the order everyone assumes. We think the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the heart goes after the treasure — which means the affections can be steered, and that there is a reliable way of finding out what you actually love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to his disciples: therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!

Therefore. The rich fool trusted in his possessions. The poor can be just as preoccupied with possessions, through anxiety. Both are forms of unbelief.

Do not be anxious about your life. “Anxious” (merimnate): worried, divided in mind, distracted (10:41).

What you will eat … what you will put on. The basic needs. For most people in Jesus’ day, these were genuine daily worries.

For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. God gave you life and a body, the greater gifts. Will he not give the lesser ones?

Consider the ravens. “Consider”: look carefully, think about it. Ravens were unclean birds (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers, the least regarded. Yet God feeds them (Job 38:41; Psalm 147:9). Matthew says “birds of the air” (Matthew 6:26).

They neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn. Unlike the rich fool with his barns. Birds don’t plan or store, and God still feeds them.

Of how much more value are you than the birds! If God feeds unclean ravens, how much more his children.

What it does not mean. Not that we should not work or plan. Birds work hard for their food. Paul says: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The point is not idleness but trust: work, but do not worry.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to worry about food or clothing, for life is more than these, and God, who feeds even the ravens, values them far more.

On a Tuesday. What are you anxious about? Consider the ravens. God feeds them; he will feed you.
verseByVerse.note: Ravens were unclean birds — yet God feeds them.

parallels.desc: he gives to the young ravens that cry

verseByVerse.quote: And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?

Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? The ESV notes that this can also be read “a single cubit to his stature”. Either way: worry achieves nothing. It cannot lengthen your life (if anything, it shortens it), or make you taller.

If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? Worry is useless. It does not change tomorrow; it only spoils today. And it forgets God, who controls what we cannot.

In a sentence. Worry cannot add a single hour to your life, so if you cannot do something so small, why worry about anything else?

On a Tuesday. Has worrying ever changed anything? Give your worries to God in prayer instead (Philippians 4:6–7).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.”

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!

Consider the lilies. Probably wild flowers in general, which carpet the Galilean hills in spring with brilliant colours: anemones, irises, poppies.

They neither toil nor spin. Making clothes was hard work: spinning thread, weaving cloth. Flowers do none of it.

Even Solomon in all his glory. The richest, most splendid king in Israel’s history (1 Kings 10). His royal robes were nothing compared with the beauty God gives a wildflower.

The grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Dry grass and wildflowers were used as fuel for clay ovens. They last a day. Yet God clothes them so beautifully.

How much more will he clothe you. You are eternal; they are temporary.

O you of little faith! Anxiety is a sign of little faith. Not no faith, but small faith that does not take God at his word.

In a sentence. If God clothes short-lived wildflowers more beautifully than Solomon, how much more will he clothe his people, who have so little faith.

On a Tuesday. Look at a flower today and remember: your Father clothes it, and he will clothe you.
verseByVerse.note: Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.

Do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink. Don’t make these the goal of your life.

Nor be worried. “Worried” (meteōrizesthe): literally “be up in the air”, suspended, in suspense, like a ship tossed on the waves.

For all the nations of the world seek after these things. The pagans, who do not know God as Father, live for food, drink and clothing. It is all they have. Worry about possessions is pagan, not Christian.

And your Father knows that you need them. The decisive reason. You are not an orphan in a hostile world. Your Father knows, and cares.

In a sentence. Don’t make food and drink your goal or worry about them, as the pagans do, for your Father knows you need them.

For worship. Your Father knows exactly what you need. Thank him today, and trust him with tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. 'Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.

Instead, seek his kingdom. Make God’s reign the goal and centre of your life. Matthew adds: and his righteousness (Matthew 6:33).

And these things will be added to you. Food and clothing, as extras. Not riches, but what you need. God gives the kingdom, and throws the rest in.

Fear not, little flock. Only Luke records this tender saying. A small, weak, vulnerable group, like sheep among wolves (10:3). “Flock”: Jesus is their shepherd, and God is their shepherd (Psalm 23; Isaiah 40:11; Ezekiel 34).

For it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom. “Good pleasure” (eudokēsen): his delight, his gracious will. God is not reluctant. He delights to give. And he gives not just food and clothing, but the kingdom itself, everything. If he gives you the kingdom, will he not give you bread? (Romans 8:32).

In a sentence. Seek God’s kingdom, and he will add what you need, so don’t be afraid, little flock, for your Father delights to give you the kingdom.

For worship. Your Father delights to give you the kingdom. Rest in his good pleasure, and seek his kingdom first today.

parallels.desc: he will tend his flock like a shepherd
the kingdom given to the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. The opposite of the rich fool. Since God gives you the kingdom, you are free to give away earthly things. Some early Christians did this (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–37).

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must sell everything. The rich ruler was told to (18:22); Zacchaeus gave half (19:8); the women of 8:3 used their means to support Jesus. The early church’s sharing was voluntary (Acts 5:4). But every Christian must hold possessions loosely, give generously, and be willing to sell anything for Christ.

Moneybags that do not grow old. Leather purses wore out and got holes.

With a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. What is given to God and the poor is stored up in heaven, safe for ever (1 Timothy 6:18–19). Treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary: kindness, generosity, faithful work and care for others, done for Christ (see the note on Matthew 6:20).

Where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat, or as coins and goods, which thieves could steal.

For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Key words. Your heart follows your treasure. What you spend money on shows what you love, and also shapes what you love. Invest in heaven, and your heart will be drawn there.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to sell their possessions and give to the poor, storing up lasting treasure in heaven, because the heart follows the treasure.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement. Where is your treasure? Give something away today, and see your heart follow.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three parables of readiness, and they describe the church living between the two advents.

“Stay dressed for action” is, as the ESV margin gives it, “let your loins stay girded” — the long outer robe pulled up and tucked into the belt, so that a man could run or work. It has a history: Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened and sandals on, dressed to leave a country that night (Ex. 12:11). And the lamp kept burning through the dark hours required somebody awake to trim the wick — readiness is not a state achieved and possessed but maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

The servants are waiting on the night of somebody else's wedding feast, which could run for days. They have no timetable, and their whole readiness reduces to one small thing: whether the door opens at once. Not whether they achieved anything in his absence. Whether, when he knocked, somebody was still expecting him.

Then the sentence nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for: he will gird himself, sit them at his table, and serve them. That does not happen — the whole architecture of that society rested on the distinction between those who recline and those who serve. And Luke proves it is not a flourish: “I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27), and on the same night John records him tying a towel round himself and washing feet (John 13:4-5).

The watches named are the second and third — roughly ten till two, and two till dawn. Not the early evening when staying up is easy, and not the last hour when the end is in sight. The dead middle, which is where most Christian waiting is actually done.

The thief image changes the register entirely: same arrival, opposite colour, and the difference is wholly in the state of the person inside. The walls were mud brick; a thief had no need to force the door.

Peter asks whether the parable is for the Twelve or for everyone, and gets no answer — only another parable, this one specifically about a man with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, especially you, but not in the direction the question hoped.
verseByVerse.theology:
The returning master who serves his watching servants is the most counter-cultural image of authority in the ancient world. It is the enacted theology of the whole ministry — “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45) — and of the ascended Lord who gives the Spirit, intercedes, and prepares a place. He has never stopped serving those he loves.

The oikonomos of v.42 is a steward, usually himself a slave, placed over the household with the keys and the accounts. He owns nothing and can be dismissed. And his one named duty is not “increase the estate” or “keep order” but “give them their portion of food at the proper time” — which is the same commission Peter himself will receive on a beach: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep (John 21:15-17).

Two adjectives govern it. Faithful — trustworthy with what is not his; and wise — the practical sense to know what the household needs and when. Either without the other is useless.

The reward for faithfulness is startling in its logic: he is set over all the master's possessions. The reward for a job well done is a bigger job — not release from service, not a pension. Which cuts against a picture most people carry without examining it: the New Testament nowhere describes the life to come as retirement. Its images are of reigning, of serving, of being given cities to look after (19:17).

And the unknown hour is the arrangement, not an inconvenience in it. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled — and everyone would schedule it late, which is exactly what the wicked servant does when he concludes the master is delayed.
verseByVerse.examples:
The servant's ruin begins with a private conclusion about a timetable, said “to himself.” There is no moment of rebellion. And the conclusion is not even wrong — the master is delayed. What is wrong is what he does with an accurate observation.

Then two directions, and they are the two ways a leader goes bad. He turns on the household — and these are his fellow servants, not his property. Authority given to feed people is used to hit them, which does not usually involve fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, the discipline that is really about control, the counselling relationship in which one person is always the one who has to change. And he turns to himself: “eat and drink and get drunk,” an echo of the rich fool's “relax, eat, drink, be merry.” The food he was appointed to distribute is going down his own throat.

The two beatings settle something readers often pass over. Scripture does not teach that judgement is a single undifferentiated verdict falling equally on everyone; it teaches degrees (cf. 10:12-14). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion. But note what is not said: the second servant is not acquitted. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence.

And the closing principle falls hardest not on the ignorant but on the well-taught. The wording — “was given,” “they entrusted” — points past the servant to the one who gave, which means every item is a deposit and not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible, a church down the road, forty years of clear preaching. None of them is a reward. Every one raises the bar. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter; it is an account.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.

Readiness for Christ’s return. From possessions, Jesus turns to his return. The two are linked: those who store up treasure on earth are not ready for him.

Stay dressed for action. The ESV notes the literal wording: let your loins stay girded. Men wore long robes, which they tucked into their belts to run or work, as Israel did at the first Passover, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11).

And keep your lamps burning. At night. Ready.

Like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast. A wedding feast could last for days; no one knew when the master would come home. The servants had to be ready at any hour.

So that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. Not keeping him waiting.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to be dressed and ready with their lamps lit, like servants waiting to open the door at once when their master returns.

On a Tuesday. Are you ready for Christ’s return, if he came today?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the literal wording, “Let your loins stay girded” — the long robe tucked into the belt for work.

parallels.desc: your belt fastened, ready to leave

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!

Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake. Faithful, watchful.

He will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. An astonishing reversal. No master would serve his servants; it was unthinkable (17:7–8). But this master will. The Lord of glory will serve his people at the banquet of the kingdom. Jesus already did this when he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), and he came not to be served but to serve (22:27). In heaven, he will still serve them.

If he comes in the second watch, or in the third. The second and third watches covered the middle of the night, roughly 9 p.m. to 3 a.m. The hardest time to stay awake, and the least expected time to come.

In a sentence. Blessed are the servants the master finds awake, for he himself will serve them at table, however late he comes.

For worship. The Lord who will return will serve you at his table. Wait for him with joy.
verseByVerse.note: The second and third watches covered the middle of the night.

parallels.desc: he dressed himself and washed their feet

verseByVerse.quote: But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.

If the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming. A new picture. Thieves don’t announce their arrival.

He would not have left his house to be broken into. Literally “dug through”. Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Not that Christ is a thief, but that his coming will be as unexpected (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 3:3; 16:15). No one can know the date (Mark 13:32). So be ready always.

In a sentence. As a homeowner would guard his house if he knew when a thief was coming, so be ready always, because the Son of Man will come when you do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Live each day as if Christ might return today.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said, 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?' And the Lord said, 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said: Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? And the Lord said: who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?

Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? For the apostles only, or for everyone?

Who then is the faithful and wise manager. Jesus answers with another question, and a parable especially for leaders. A household manager (oikonomos) was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other slaves and the household’s supplies (16:1). The word is used of church leaders (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7).

To give them their portion of food at the proper time. A leader’s task is to feed God’s household: with his word, faithfully and at the right time (John 21:15–17; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2).

In a sentence. When Peter asked whom the parable was for, Jesus described the faithful and wise manager whom the master puts in charge of feeding his household.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who lead your church, that they would be faithful managers, feeding God’s household.
verseByVerse.note: A household manager was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.

Whom his master will find so doing. Not just watching, but working faithfully, when the master comes. Readiness is faithfulness in the task given.

He will set him over all his possessions. The reward for faithfulness is greater responsibility (19:17). In the kingdom, faithful servants will share Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 3:21).

In a sentence. Blessed is the servant the master finds faithfully at work when he comes, for he will put him in charge of everything he owns.

On a Tuesday. What has the Master given you to do? Be found doing it when he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if that servant says to himself: my master is delayed in coming, and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.

My master is delayed in coming. The danger of the delay of Christ’s return. People begin to think he will never come (2 Peter 3:3–4), and live accordingly.

And begins to beat the male and female servants. Abuse of power. A leader who mistreats those in his care.

And to eat and drink and get drunk. Self-indulgence.

The master … will come on a day when he does not expect him. Sudden and unexpected.

And will cut him in pieces. A severe punishment, possibly meaning “cut him off”. The language shows how seriously God judges unfaithful leaders.

And put him with the unfaithful. With unbelievers. He showed himself to be one.

In a sentence. A servant who assumes his master’s delay means he can abuse others and indulge himself will be severely punished when his master returns unexpectedly.

On a Tuesday. The delay of Christ’s return is not a licence for unfaithfulness. He is coming. Live accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.

That servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready. Deliberate disobedience in full knowledge.

Will receive a severe beating. Greater judgement.

But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Ignorance does not excuse; he still did wrong and is punished. But his punishment is lighter. There are degrees of guilt and punishment, according to knowledge (Numbers 15:27–31; Romans 2:12).

Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required. A principle of God’s justice. Privilege brings responsibility. Those who have heard the gospel, those who know the Bible, those who lead in the church, will be judged more strictly (James 3:1). This applies to Christians in wealthy and free countries, who have so much.

In a sentence. Those who knew their master’s will and ignored it will be punished severely, those who did not know, less severely, for much is required of those to whom much is given.

On a Tuesday. You have been given much. Ask what God requires of you in return.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–59 — Fire, Division, and the Urgent Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with three sayings of escalating urgency, and the first is the most emotionally exposed moment in Luke outside Gethsemane.

“I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!” The fire is most likely the one John announced at the start of this Gospel — “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (3:16) — and Luke's second volume opens with tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). It is also the fire of judgement and purifying, and the two are not separable: the same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

“I have a baptism to be baptized with.” To be baptized is to go under — and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Ps. 42:7). He is talking about the cross, and calling it a drowning.

And “how great is my distress” is the cry of a man hemmed in, pressed on every side. Read the two verses together and the shape is precise: the fire cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. Pentecost waits on Golgotha, and he is pressed between them.

Then the division saying, which shocks — not least because angels announced “on earth peace” over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14). Both are true. What he brings is peace with God, which every human being needs and cannot manufacture. What he never promised is the peace of everybody getting along, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked. The household list is quoted from Micah 7:6, where it describes a society coming apart — and every pair is named in both directions.

Finally the weather. West of Israel is the Mediterranean, so cloud coming inland meant rain; a south wind off the desert meant the scorching sirocco. Two confident readings, and Jesus grants they are right. These people are competent. And they will not apply the skill where it matters.
verseByVerse.theology:
“How great is my distress until it is accomplished” is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back — Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment. He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because the pain was unendurable but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

The charge of hypocrisy at v.56 is precise. It is not that the crowd is stupid; it is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite but illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what stands in front of him has made a choice and is pretending it was a limitation.

And the evidence he expects them to have read is not a secret sign. The “present time” is the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor given good news, thousands following, and the authorities plotting a death.

“Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” assumes the resources for the judgement are already in their possession. It needs a guard — Scripture is emphatic that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Prov. 14:12; Jer. 17:9) — so the question is not “why not decide what suits you?” It is narrower: given what you can already read, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something.
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying has real pastoral weight, because someone reading it is living inside it. He does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens — and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case.

Every generation is expert at reading something — markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career — and the skill is genuine. The same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

And “you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny” has carried theological weight it was never built to bear — one of the two verses historically cited for purgatory. But this is practical advice about a lawsuit used to illustrate urgency, and doctrine cannot be quarried from an illustration's scenery. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn, which was the point of the prison; “until you have paid the last penny” is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out. And a doctrine supplying a further opportunity to settle after death removes the urgency of the only sentence that mattered. Settle now, on the road — and know that the settlement is not a schedule of payments but an amnesty, purchased at the judge's own expense (7:41-42; Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptised with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!

I came to cast fire on the earth. Fire can picture judgement (3:9, 17) or purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and the Holy Spirit (3:16; Acts 2:3). Jesus came to bring the fire of God’s judgement and refining, and the fire of the Spirit. All of this would be set alight by his death and resurrection.

And would that it were already kindled! Jesus longs for the completion of his work.

I have a baptism to be baptized with. “Baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed, plunged into suffering, like being submerged in a flood (Psalm 42:7; 69:1–2). His death (Mark 10:38).

And how great is my distress until it is accomplished! “Distress” (synechomai): pressed, constrained, gripped. A glimpse of Jesus’ inner anguish on the road to the cross, anticipating Gethsemane (22:42–44). The fire can only come through his baptism of suffering. He must first be overwhelmed by the judgement of God against sin.

In a sentence. Jesus longed for the fire he came to bring to be kindled, and was deeply distressed until his baptism of suffering was accomplished.

For worship. Jesus felt the weight of the cross long before he reached it, and went on anyway, for you.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.

Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? The angels announced peace at his birth (2:14). Jesus does bring peace: with God, and between those who belong to him. But not the peace of the world, a peace without truth.

No, I tell you, but rather division. The effect of his coming is to divide people by their response to him (2:34–35). Everyone must decide. Families split over him.

Five divided, three against two and two against three. A family of five: father, mother, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law (the son’s wife, living with them).

Father against son … mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law. An echo of Micah 7:6, describing the breakdown of society in a time of judgement. Jesus says it will happen because of loyalty to him.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should seek conflict, or be needlessly divisive, or neglect their families. As far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). But when others reject Christ, conflict may come, and loyalty to Christ must come first (14:26).

In a sentence. Jesus said he came not to bring peace but division, which would split even families as people responded differently to him.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has divided your family, he foretold it. Love them, pray for them, and stay faithful.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the crowds: when you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, a shower is coming. And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, there will be scorching heat, and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?

When you see a cloud rising in the west. Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain (1 Kings 18:44).

When you see the south wind blowing. The south wind blew from the desert, bringing scorching heat.

You hypocrites! Because they claim not to be able to see, when they can see perfectly well; they just don’t want to.

You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky. They were good at reading the weather.

But why do you not know how to interpret the present time? “The present time” (kairon): this decisive moment, the time of God’s visitation. The signs were all around: the Messiah was among them, healing, preaching, casting out demons. But they would not read them (19:44).

In a sentence. Jesus called the crowds hypocrites, because they could read the weather but would not read the signs of the time in which God was visiting them.

On a Tuesday. Can you read the signs of what God is doing? Don’t be skilled in everything except spiritual discernment.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?

Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? You have the evidence. You don’t need anyone to tell you. Use your own judgement, honestly, and you will see who I am, and what you must do. The time for decision is now. This leads into the parable that follows.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they could not judge for themselves what was right.

On a Tuesday. Don’t wait for others to decide for you. Weigh the evidence about Jesus for yourself, and act.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.

As you go with your accuser before the magistrate. A man on his way to court, with a debt he cannot pay. The case is certain to go against him.

Make an effort to settle with him on the way. Settle out of court while you still can. Once you reach the judge, it will be too late.

And the officer put you in prison. Debtors’ prison.

You will never get out until you have paid the very last penny. The “penny” (lepton) was the smallest coin in circulation. Every last coin.

The meaning. In context (vv. 54–57), this is a parable about the coming judgement of God. We are all on our way to court, with a debt we cannot pay. Now, on the way, is the time to be reconciled with God, through Christ. Once we stand before the Judge, it will be too late. And the debt cannot be paid by us; we would never get out.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. Roman Catholic teaching has sometimes cited this verse in support of purgatory, a place where souls pay for their sins after death before entering heaven. Verdict: the parable is about urgent reconciliation before judgement, not about a process of purification after death. Scripture teaches that Christ’s sacrifice has paid the debt of believers in full (Colossians 2:13–14; Hebrews 10:14), and that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). For those who reject Christ, the debt can never be paid.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to settle with their accuser on the way to court, before it was too late, a picture of the urgency of being reconciled to God before judgement.

On a Tuesday. Today is the day to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2). Don’t wait until you stand before the Judge.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered.
