Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is structured around the call to repentance and its refusal — three overlapping statements that together describe what happens when the opportunity for repentance closes. It opens with Jesus's response to news of a Galilean massacre and the fall of the tower of Siloam — two disasters that the crowd assumes were punishments for exceptional sinfulness. Jesus refuses the assumption and turns both events into a summons to universal repentance: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Then he tells the parable of the fruitless fig tree — one more year of patient cultivation before the axe comes. Then on a Sabbath he heals a woman bent double for eighteen years, and the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus names the synagogue ruler's hypocrisy before the entire crowd.

The middle section (vv. 18–30) moves through the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven — the kingdom's hidden but irresistible growth — to the question about the number of the saved, and Jesus's answer: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” The door will close. The day will come when the master of the house rises and shuts the door, and those who knock and say “we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” will hear “I do not know where you come from.” Familiarity with Jesus is not relationship with Jesus; proximity to the gospel is not reception of it.

The chapter ends with one of the most heartrending passages in the Gospel: the lament over Jerusalem. Some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him; Jesus refuses to be deflected (“I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem”). And then he speaks to the city itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” The willingness is on his side; the unwillingness is on theirs. And the house will be left desolate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The massacre Pilate carried out on Galilean pilgrims is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature — which is itself telling, since this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about the man.

The crowd assumes the victims' fate was a verdict on their exceptional sinfulness, and Jesus brings the assumption into the open before they can state it: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners…? No, I tell you.” Flat, immediate, unqualified.

That was not a fringe view he was demolishing. It was the working theology of the ancient world — Job's friends spent most of a book on it, and the disciples will ask it about a blind man (John 9:2). It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

He then supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate because it is a different kind of disaster. The first was murder; the second is an accident — masonry giving way near the pool of Siloam. Between them the two cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. And the answer is identical, word for word, twice, so that neither case is left open.

The parable of the fig tree extends the urgency and adds the intercession. The tree is planted in a vineyard — prime cultivated ground, occupying space that would otherwise carry vines. Three years is not impatience: a fig takes about three years to bear at all, and the law required the first three years' fruit to be left untouched (Lev. 19:23), so the owner has waited the full statutory period and then come three times on top of it.

And the charge is precise. Not that the tree has done harm, but that it is “using up the ground.” Barrenness here is not a neutral condition; a tree that produces nothing is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else.

The vinedresser disputes none of it. He accepts the whole case and asks for time — and offers to do the work himself: digging round compacted roots, and dunging. Heavy, unpleasant labour on a tree that has given him nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's answer refuses both the question and the assumption behind it. He does not say “God never punishes” — the Old Testament would contradict that. He says this is not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners; all face mortality; all need to repent.

So the disasters are not explanations of why those particular people died. They are reminders to the living that they are not exempt from the mortality those people have just experienced. The right response to someone else's death is not theological analysis of their sins but examination of one's own soul while there is time.

The fig tree and the vineyard together would have been unmistakable. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5 — “he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes” — and Israel is the fig tree in which God came looking and found nothing (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; Mic. 7:1). The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year and offering to do the digging himself, is standing in that room saying it.

But the intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period and concedes the outcome. Which puts this parable in its proper relation to the two disasters: those verses said the axe is real, and this one says the axe is being held — and by whom. Separating the two halves ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered and this passage forbids them both.

The first is the one Jesus is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either — he does not remove these deaths from his Father's world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts.

Between those two errors is where a Christian must stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it. The honest answer to why them? is that we are not told; the answer we are given instead is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs was.

And there is a sting in the wording. “You will all likewise perish” was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple courts and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. It came true in the very forms they had just been discussing.

The vinedresser's response to three barren years is the model of patient labour with an apparently hopeless case — a church that has not grown, a child who will not turn. He neither writes the tree off nor pretends there is fruit. He asks for another year and goes and gets the spade.

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. He answered them: do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Setting. Jesus had just urged the crowds to read the signs of the times and be reconciled to God before judgement (12:54–59). Some in the crowd respond with a news item.

The Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Josephus records several incidents where Pilate’s soldiers killed Jewish crowds. Some Galileans, perhaps suspected of rebellion, were killed in the temple courts while offering sacrifices, probably at Passover, when laymen slaughtered their own lambs. Their blood mixed with the blood of the animals. A sacrilege and an atrocity.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? The common assumption: disaster is God’s punishment for particular sins. Job’s friends thought this (Job 4:7). The disciples did too (John 9:2). Perhaps those who told the story wanted Jesus to condemn Pilate, or to say the victims deserved it.

No, I tell you. Suffering is not always a sign of special guilt. The victims were not worse than others.

But unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Jesus turns the question back on his hearers. Don’t speculate about others’ sins. Look to your own. The real question is not why they died, but whether you are ready to die. Everyone is a sinner, and everyone will perish unless they repent. “Likewise”: perhaps also literally. Forty years later, many Jews died at Roman hands in the temple during the siege of Jerusalem.

In a sentence. When told of Galileans killed by Pilate in the temple, Jesus denied that they were worse sinners than others, and warned that all must repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of disasters, don’t ask what the victims did. Ask whether you are ready to meet God.
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell. Jesus adds a second example, this time not a human atrocity but an accident. Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem (John 9:7). Perhaps a tower in the city wall collapsed, possibly during construction work on an aqueduct that Pilate built. Again, not recorded elsewhere.

Were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? “Offenders” (opheiletai): debtors (11:4). Were they greater debtors to God?

No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. The same warning, repeated for emphasis. Whether by human evil or natural disaster, death comes to everyone, often unexpectedly. The only safety is repentance.

Disasters and God. Scripture teaches that God is sovereign over all things, including disasters (Amos 3:6; Isaiah 45:7). But it does not teach that every disaster is a punishment for the particular sins of those who suffer. Rather, every disaster is a reminder that we live in a fallen world under the curse of sin (Romans 8:20–22), that life is short and death is certain, and that all of us need to repent.

In a sentence. Jesus also denied that those killed when a tower fell in Siloam were worse sinners than others in Jerusalem, and repeated his warning to repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. Every news report of sudden death is a call to repentance. Are you ready?
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told this parable: a man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser: look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?

The parable of the barren fig tree. Only Luke records it. It explains the warning to repent.

A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Fig trees were often planted in vineyards, in the best soil. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). God had planted Israel in the best place, with every privilege (Isaiah 5:1–7).

And he came seeking fruit on it and found none. Fruit: righteousness, justice, repentance, faith (3:8).

For three years now. A fig tree that had not borne fruit after three years probably never would. Some see a reference to the length of Jesus’ ministry, though that is uncertain.

Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground? “Use up” (katargei): waste, exhaust. A fruitless tree took nutrients and space from others. Judgement was deserved.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a vineyard owner who came for three years seeking fruit on a fig tree, found none, and ordered it cut down.

On a Tuesday. God has planted you in good soil, with every privilege. What fruit is he finding in your life?
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he answered him: sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.

Sir, let it alone this year also. The vinedresser pleads for the tree. A picture of intercession, and of God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9). Jesus intercedes for his people.

Until I dig around it and put on manure. Special care: loosen the soil, add fertiliser. Every possible help. God gives every opportunity to repent: his word, his messengers, his Son.

Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good. The sentence in Greek is broken off: “if it bears fruit next year …”, as if the outcome is left open. Will it?

But if not, you can cut it down. Patience has an end. The time of grace is limited. Judgement is delayed, not cancelled.

The point. God’s patience is great, but it is not endless. The extra year is a gift: use it to repent (Romans 2:4). The parable ends without telling us what happened, because the hearers must decide.

In a sentence. The vinedresser pleaded for one more year to tend the tree, after which, if it still bore no fruit, it would be cut down.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience with you is a call to repent, not a reason to delay. This may be your extra year.

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke notes almost in passing that Jesus is teaching in a synagogue — the last time in this Gospel he is recorded doing so. The doors are closing.

The woman had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten herself. Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line. Consider what it means: she has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body, and has not looked another adult in the face in nearly two decades. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming — eighteen years of asking and receiving nothing, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict — and she is in her place. She asks for nothing when he arrives, which is what makes everything that follows one-sided.

Three things happen and all three are his: he saw her, in a crowded room, teaching, with a woman folded double probably out of everyone's sightline; he called her over, which made her healing public when it could have been quiet; and he touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time. “You are freed from your disability” — released, and the release stands; four verses later he calls it being “loosed from this bond.”

She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

The synagogue ruler is indignant, and he does not address Jesus. He addresses the people — public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. And his argument is not stupid: the fourth commandment says what he quotes. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which produces the sentence that gives the whole thing away: “come on those days and be healed.” He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, to a woman who has not been healed on any working day of any week for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
“A disabling spirit” should not be flattened either way. Luke does not call her possessed or record a demon being cast out; Jesus says Satan had bound her — and chapter 11 showed a stronger one overpowering the strong man (11:21-22). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

“Daughter of Abraham” occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Luke will pair it later with Zacchaeus — “he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9).

The argument from lesser to greater is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and leaving it thirsty for a whole day was not an option any farmer would entertain; the rulings of the period permitted untying and leading, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem: “on the Sabbath day.” Not in spite of it. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler's manoeuvre is worth naming because it is recognisable. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the target — the sermon everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And underneath it is the real failure, which is not legalism exactly: he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem. There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure, and it does not feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

The woman glorifies God before anyone can tell her what she should feel — not the carefully considered religious expression calibrated for an audience, but the overflow of a life that has just been changed.

Two responses close the section, set side by side in a single verse: the adversaries put to shame, the people rejoicing. Nothing in the evidence separated them. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up, and what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end. Being put to shame is not the end of a man; shame is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.

Only Luke. Only Luke records this healing. It is the last time in Luke that Jesus is in a synagogue.

A woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. Literally “a spirit of weakness”. Her condition was caused by Satan (v. 16), though she is not described as possessed. Satan can cause physical affliction (Job 2:7; 2 Corinthians 12:7). Not all illness is caused directly by Satan, but some is.

She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. Luke the doctor describes it precisely. Perhaps a fusion of the spine. For eighteen years she had looked at the ground, unable to look up. Yet she came to the synagogue on the Sabbath.

In a sentence. While Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, a woman was there who had been bent double by a spirit of weakness for eighteen years.

On a Tuesday. Faithful in worship despite long suffering. Keep coming to God, whatever your burden.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her: woman, you are freed from your disability. And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.

When Jesus saw her. She did not ask. He saw her, and took the initiative, as at Nain (7:13).

Woman, you are freed from your disability. “Freed” (apolelysai): released, set loose, the perfect tense: you have been freed. The language of liberation (4:18: liberty to the captives).

And he laid his hands on her. A healing touch.

And immediately she was made straight. After eighteen years, she could stand upright and look up. Psalm 146:8: the Lord lifts up those who are bowed down.

And she glorified God. The first thing she did. She kept on praising.

In a sentence. Seeing her, Jesus called her, declared her free, laid his hands on her, and she was straightened at once and praised God.

For worship. Jesus lifts up those who are bowed down. Whatever is bending you low, bring it to him, and look up.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people: there are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.

The ruler of the synagogue. The man responsible for organising its services (8:41).

Indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. Not glad that a woman was freed after eighteen years, but angry that a rule had been broken. Religion without love.

Said to the people. Too cowardly to rebuke Jesus directly, he lectures the congregation.

There are six days in which work ought to be done. Quoting the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:9; Deuteronomy 5:13). True, but misapplied. He counts healing as work.

Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day. As if healing were a service to be booked on weekdays. And as if a woman who had waited eighteen years could not wait one more day.

In a sentence. The synagogue ruler, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, told the people to come for healing on the other six days.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let love for rules make you angry at God’s grace.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Lord answered him: you hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?

You hypocrites! Plural: the ruler and those who agree with him.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath. Animals could not go a day without water. Untying and leading were allowed.

And ought not this woman. “Ought” (edei): must, it was necessary. Divine necessity. It was not merely permitted to heal her; it was required.

A daughter of Abraham. A member of God’s covenant people, an heir of the promises. Like Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham (19:9). Of more value than an ox.

Whom Satan bound for eighteen years. The real cause.

Be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day? A play on words: you untie your animals; should I not untie this woman? And the Sabbath was the most fitting day for it. The Sabbath was given as a sign of God’s rest and of his liberation of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). What better day to free a captive of Satan? The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s liberation.

In a sentence. Jesus called them hypocrites, since they untie their animals to water them on the Sabbath, and argued that a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan for eighteen years should certainly be freed on the Sabbath.

For worship. The Lord’s Day is the day of liberation. Rejoice in the freedom Christ gives.
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.

All his adversaries were put to shame. They had no answer. An echo of Isaiah 45:16 (in Greek): all who are incensed against him shall be put to shame.

And all the people rejoiced. The ordinary people saw it rightly.

At all the glorious things that were done by him. “Glorious things” (endoxois): the word used of God’s mighty acts at the exodus (Exodus 34:10, in Greek). Jesus’ works are God’s works.

In a sentence. His opponents were humiliated, but the people rejoiced at all the glorious things Jesus did.

For worship. Rejoice today at the glorious things Christ has done, including for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties the parables to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, been attacked for it, and sent a happy crowd home — and it is a fair question whether that is what the kingdom of God amounts to.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled. And it is sowed in his garden — deliberately put in the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort. Black mustard grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet; calling it a tree is a stretch, and probably meant to be.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's and Daniel's, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins; this starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The leaven parable ought to bring a reader up short, since one chapter ago leaven was the picture of everything that ruins (12:1). That is its usual role in Scripture — scoured out before Passover (Ex. 12:15), and Paul's image for malice and evil (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

But the sentence refuses the warning reading. Jesus does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says it is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading, and everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy makes it a good image for the kingdom.

Then someone asks whether the saved will be few, and gets no number. “Strive to enter through the narrow door” — strain, exert everything, as an athlete does in a contest. And the door is narrow: not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question “will those who are saved be few?” was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and notice how it is framed — a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has placed himself outside the calculation.

That is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. There is a particular safety in the general: as long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing. And Jesus's reply is to them, plural, though one man asked.

If striving is required, is salvation earned? No — and notice what the striving is for. Not to become worthy, and not until enough has been done. Strive to enter. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is told “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Nobody buys this door open — but plenty intend to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

“I do not know where you come from” is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational (Amos 3:2), and “where you come from” is a householder's question about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The closing vision fulfils Isaiah's feast on the mountain for all peoples (Isa. 25:6-8) and the gathering from far off (Isa. 49:12). The seats do not stand empty; the table is full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.
verseByVerse.examples:
The plea of those outside is entirely true and entirely beside the point. They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording — and he had taught in their streets and they were there. These are not people making things up.

But every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you — and a modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

Which raises the question that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing the entering all along in ordinary people. The centurion who says “say the word” (7:7). The woman told “your faith has saved you; go in peace” (7:50). The leper who came back (17:19). The blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39). Not one was admitted for being impressive; each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

And “some are last who will be first” should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage but grace — and grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore: what is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.

He said therefore. In the light of the healing, and the opposition: the kingdom is present, in small beginnings, and it will grow.

It is like a grain of mustard seed. Mustard seed was proverbially tiny (17:6). The kingdom began with one man from Nazareth and a handful of followers, and seemed insignificant.

And it grew and became a tree. The mustard plant can grow taller than a man, ten feet (3 m) or more, by the Sea of Galilee. A huge result from a tiny seed.

And the birds of the air made nests in its branches. An echo of Daniel 4:12, 21 and Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6, where a great tree with birds nesting in it pictures a world-wide kingdom, sheltering the nations. The birds are the Gentiles, who will find shelter in God’s kingdom. And so the church has grown from a handful in Jerusalem to every nation on earth.

In a sentence. Jesus compared the kingdom of God to a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds nest, a small beginning that becomes great and shelters the nations.

On a Tuesday. Don’t despise small beginnings in God’s work (Zechariah 4:10). He makes great things from tiny seeds.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again he said: to what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.

It is like leaven. Usually in Scripture, leaven pictures a corrupting influence (12:1; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here, unusually, it is a positive picture: a small amount, working invisibly, spreading through the whole.

That a woman took and hid. A man in the first parable, a woman in the second: Luke’s pairing again. “Hid”: the kingdom works hiddenly, invisibly, from within.

In three measures of flour. A very large batch, about 50 pounds (22 kg) of flour, enough to feed a hundred people. About what Sarah baked for her heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:6). An extravagant quantity.

Until it was all leavened. The whole lump is transformed.

The two parables together. The mustard seed shows the kingdom’s outward growth, from small to great. The leaven shows its inward power, transforming from within. The kingdom changes people and societies from the inside out, quietly, steadily, until its work is complete.

What it does not mean. Not that the whole world will gradually become Christian before Christ returns (postmillennialism), though some have read it that way. The parables promise growth and transformation, not universal conversion, and other passages speak of persecution and apostasy until the end (18:8; 21:12; 2 Timothy 3:1–5).

In a sentence. Jesus compared the kingdom to yeast that a woman hid in a large batch of flour until it had worked through the whole.

On a Tuesday. God’s kingdom is at work in your life and in the world, often invisibly. Trust its quiet power.
verseByVerse.note: Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him: Lord, will those who are saved be few? And he said to them:

Journeying toward Jerusalem. Luke reminds us of the journey (9:51). Everything happens on the way to the cross.

Lord, will those who are saved be few? A theological question, perhaps from curiosity. Jewish teachers debated it. Some said all Israel would be saved; others said few. The questioner wants to discuss others.

And he said to them. “Them”: Jesus answers the crowd, and turns the question from theory to personal urgency.

In a sentence. As Jesus travelled toward Jerusalem, someone asked him whether only a few would be saved.

On a Tuesday. The question is not how many will be saved, but whether you will be.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.

Strive to enter through the narrow door. Jesus does not answer the question directly. He tells the questioner what to do. “Strive” (agōnizesthe): struggle, agonise, as an athlete in a contest. Make every effort. The door is narrow: it is Jesus himself (John 10:9). There is one way in, through repentance and faith in him.

For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. Why? Not because they wanted Christ and were refused, but because they came too late (v. 25), or on their own terms, wanting to enter without going through the narrow door. They seek, but not in the right way or at the right time.

What it does not mean. Not that we must earn salvation by effort. Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). But entering requires urgency and wholeheartedness: repentance, faith, turning from sin, coming to Christ now. It is not a casual affair.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to strive to enter by the narrow door, for many will seek to enter and not be able.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be casual about your salvation. Make sure you have come through the narrow door, Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, open to us, then he will answer you: I do not know where you come from. Then you will begin to say: we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets. But he will say: I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!

When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door. The day of judgement. There comes a time when the door is shut, and the opportunity is over (Matthew 25:10). Now it is open; one day it will be shut.

Lord, open to us. They call him Lord, but too late (6:46).

I do not know where you come from. You do not belong to my household. I have no relationship with you. The worst words anyone could hear (Matthew 7:23).

We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets. Their claim: we knew you; we were there. They had contact with Jesus, but not a relationship. Proximity is not faith. Hearing sermons, attending church, being near Jesus, is not the same as belonging to him.

Depart from me, all you workers of evil! Psalm 6:8. Their lives showed they were not his.

In a sentence. When the door is shut, those outside will plead that they ate with Jesus and heard him teach, but he will say he does not know them and send them away as evildoers.

On a Tuesday. Being familiar with Jesus is not enough. Does he know you as his own?

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.

Weeping and gnashing of teeth. Grief and anguish, and perhaps rage. A picture of the misery of those shut out of the kingdom, for ever (Matthew 8:12; 13:42).

When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God. The patriarchs and prophets, whose descendants Jesus’ hearers were proud to be.

But you yourselves cast out. The shock: Abraham’s children shut out, because they did not share Abraham’s faith (3:8).

And people will come from east and west, and from north and south. From all four points of the compass: the Gentiles, from every nation (Isaiah 49:12; 59:19; Psalm 107:3).

And recline at table in the kingdom of God. The messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6–8; Revelation 19:9), where Gentiles will sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11).

Some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last. The great reversal. Gentiles, last in privilege, will be first in the kingdom; Israel, first in privilege, many of them last. And within the church too: the proud will be humbled, and the humble exalted.

In a sentence. Those shut out will weep in anguish when they see the patriarchs and prophets in the kingdom, and people from every nation feasting there, for the last will be first and the first last.

For worship. If you are a Gentile believer, you are one of those who have come from east and west. Thank God for your seat at his table.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him — the only occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain. Not every Pharisee was an enemy; Luke records three who invite him to dinner. But Herod ruled Galilee, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, where his real opponents were waiting.

“That fox” is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage the fox was not primarily crafty but the small predator set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power, which is what he was: Rome never let him be king, and he ended his days exiled to Gaul.

The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Herod does not set the date. “I finish my course” is the language of completion — the same English as the word from the cross, “it is finished” (John 19:30). And the last clause is grim irony: he is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous but that it is the appointed place, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Then the lament. “How often” is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

The image has a long history in Israel's Scriptures: the eagle stirring her nest (Deut. 32:11), the wings under which Ruth took refuge (Ruth 2:12), the shadow of the wings in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 91:4). But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight; what she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way she saves her chicks in a fire is to spread them and stay where she is. Farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, on the road on which he had set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Your house is forsaken” — and the first two words are the devastating ones. It had never been their house — Solomon built it and God filled it, and it is called “my house” in every prophet, as Jesus himself will say in that very building (19:46). To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say the owner has moved out.

Israel had seen it before. Ezekiel watched the glory rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple; it is masonry.

The closing quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters (19:38). Some read the promise as fulfilled there, and the words very nearly match; but the entry is one day, not an era, and what follows it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out (Rom. 11:26). The second fits the words better, since “Blessed is he who comes” is a welcome, not a cry of terror.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lament is the model of prophetic grief — the sorrow a faithful preacher feels for those who hear the word and do not receive it. It is not anger; it is love that has been refused, and the grief of knowing what the refusal costs.

Every pastor who has watched someone hear the gospel clearly and walk away, every parent who has prayed for a child who will not turn, every evangelist who has seen the door closing on someone who came so close, has tasted something of it.

“And you were not willing” is five words and the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other. He does not say they were unable; he says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

And what matters most about the last verse is its shape. It ends with until. He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him: get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you. And he said to them: go and tell that fox, behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course. Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.

Some Pharisees came. Not all Pharisees were hostile. Perhaps these were genuinely concerned. Or perhaps they wanted him out of their area, or were sent by Herod to scare him away.

For Herod wants to kill you. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, who had executed John (9:9). Jesus was probably in Perea at the time.

Go and tell that fox. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructive slyness, a small, crafty predator, not a lion. Not a compliment. Jesus is not afraid of Herod.

I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course. “Today and tomorrow and the third day”: a fixed, short time, determined by God, not by Herod. “I finish my course” (teleioumai): I am brought to completion, perfected. His work will be completed at his death and resurrection (on the third day!) in Jerusalem (Hebrews 2:10; 5:9; John 19:30). Jesus’ timetable is set by his Father.

Nevertheless, I must go on my way. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Herod’s threats cannot change God’s plan.

For it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. Bitter irony. Jerusalem, the holy city, had a long history of killing the prophets (Jeremiah 26:20–23; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22). Jesus would not die in Herod’s Galilee, but in Jerusalem.

In a sentence. Warned that Herod wanted to kill him, Jesus called Herod a fox and said he would continue his work until his appointed time, for a prophet must die in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. No human power can cut short what God has planned for your life. Don’t be ruled by fear.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double address shows deep emotion, grief and love (10:41; 22:31).

The city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! Jerusalem’s history. And it is about to kill the greatest of the prophets.

How often would I have gathered your children together. “How often”: Jesus had visited Jerusalem many times, as John records (John 2:13; 5:1; 7:10; 10:22). And beyond that, God had called Jerusalem through all the prophets. Jesus speaks as God, who longed to gather his people.

As a hen gathers her brood under her wings. A tender, motherly image. A hen spreads her wings over her chicks to protect them from danger, from a hawk or a fire, even at the cost of her own life. In the Old Testament, God shelters his people under his wings (Ruth 2:12; Psalm 36:7; 91:4).

And you were not willing! Jerusalem refused. The tragedy of unbelief.

Where Christians differ: God’s will and human refusal. Arminians take this verse to show that God wills all to be saved but that human free will can finally resist his saving purpose. Verdict: Scripture teaches both that God is sovereign in salvation (John 6:37, 44; Ephesians 1:11) and that he sincerely calls sinners and grieves over their refusal (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11). Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will, what he commands and desires (that people repent and come), from his secret decree, what he has determined will happen. Jesus’ lament is genuine: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The responsibility for refusal lies entirely with those who refuse. Both truths stand; we should not cancel one by the other.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented over Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, because he had longed to gather its people like a hen gathering her chicks, and they would not come.

For worship. Jesus longs to shelter you under his wings. Don’t refuse him. Come.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!

Behold, your house is forsaken. “Your house”: the temple, or the city, or the nation. No longer “my Father’s house” (2:49), but “your house”, abandoned by God. As in Jeremiah 12:7 (I have forsaken my house) and 22:5. God’s presence will leave, and the temple will be destroyed (19:43–44; 21:6). Fulfilled in AD 70.

You will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26. When Jesus enters Jerusalem, the crowds will sing these words (19:38). But the deeper fulfilment is at his return. Does this mean a future turning of Israel to Christ? Paul teaches that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–27), which many understand as a future conversion of large numbers of the Jewish people before Christ returns. Others take it of the full number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. Either way, the verse holds out hope as well as judgement.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that Jerusalem’s house was forsaken, and that they would not see him until they welcomed him as the one who comes in the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Jewish people, that they would welcome Jesus as their Messiah.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
this house shall become a desolation

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is built around a dinner table — and it is one of the most dramatically productive dinner tables in the Gospels. Jesus is at a meal in the house of a prominent Pharisee, being watched carefully. A man with dropsy appears; Jesus heals him on the Sabbath and challenges the watching lawyers and Pharisees. He observes the guests scrambling for the best seats and tells a parable about table manners that is really about the kingdom's reversal of honour. He turns to the host and tells him who to invite to dinner — not the friends and family who will reciprocate, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, who cannot repay. And when a guest at the table says “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God,” Jesus responds with the parable of the great banquet — the most complete statement of grace and rejection in the Gospel.

The chapter's second movement (vv. 25–35) shifts from the dinner table to the crowd following Jesus on the road, and the tone shifts from parable to direct confrontation. “Whoever does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple.” Two parables of counting the cost — the tower-builder and the king going to war — press the same point. “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” This is not the Christianity of added benefits; it is the Christianity of total claim. The banquet of grace and the cross of discipleship belong to the same Gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the Sabbath Jesus goes to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees — the third such invitation Luke records, and every one of them ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

“They were watching him carefully.” The verb is one used of keeping something under observation for a purpose; Luke uses it in Acts of men watching the gates day and night to kill Paul (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity but surveillance. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

A man with dropsy is “before him.” Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing organs. And the ancient world understood something about it we might miss — a man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty, which made it the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Worth holding, in a chapter about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note the staging, too. Luke does not say how he came to be there; he may well have been put there to see what Jesus would do.

Jesus does not wait for the trap; he springs it himself, asking the question out loud before touching anybody — and framing it exactly as they would have framed it. Their silence is not puzzlement. They cannot say yes without undercutting their own position, and cannot say no with a swollen man standing in the room.

Then he heals him and sends him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand there for the argument that follows.

And the second question silences them completely — “a son or an ox” put in one sentence, as items in the same category, because that is where their practice puts them. They could not reply.
verseByVerse.theology:
The silence of the lawyers and Pharisees — both times — is the silence of people who know they have no answer and will not give the answer they do have. It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form cowardice takes among religious people: not denial, not opposition, but a careful and dignified silence held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter but sharpened in two ways. There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water; here something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

The manuscripts vary slightly at v.5 and some read “a donkey or an ox,” which is the more expected pair and very likely why some copyists produced it. “Son or ox” is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote — and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

They are beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text or appealed to his own authority; he has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals the man before making the argument. That is not bad pedagogy but the right order: the principle of Sabbath mercy is not established by syllogism and then applied — it is demonstrated in flesh and blood and then defended. The compassion leads the argument.

And there is a hard general truth in the second silence. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.

The two-tier system is the thing being dismantled: their own emergencies justify Sabbath flexibility, and somebody else's does not. That instinct did not die out in the first century. It is at work wherever a rule is applied rigorously to people at a distance and generously to oneself and one's own — and it is almost never noticed by the person doing it, because the exceptions feel like common sense.

Note also that Jesus sends the healed man away before the debate begins. He will not have a person used as an exhibit, even in an argument he is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.

Setting. Chapter 14 is set at a meal. The whole chapter is about banquets: who is invited, where they sit, who comes, and the great banquet of the kingdom. Jesus turns a dinner party into a lesson on grace and discipleship.

A ruler of the Pharisees. A leading Pharisee, perhaps a member of the Sanhedrin. Sabbath meals were often occasions for entertaining guests, prepared the day before.

They were watching him carefully. Spying on him (6:7). The invitation was a trap.

A man before him who had dropsy. Dropsy (oedema) is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness of the heart, liver or kidneys. Only Luke, the doctor, records this healing. Was he planted there to test Jesus? He was “before him”, prominently placed.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath, at the house of a leading Pharisee, with everyone watching him closely, Jesus was faced with a man suffering from dropsy.

On a Tuesday. Jesus went into hostile places, and still did good. Don’t avoid people because they watch you critically.
verseByVerse.note: Dropsy is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying: is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not? But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.

Jesus responded. To their unspoken thoughts.

Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not? A direct question to the experts in the law. If they say yes, they cannot object. If they say no, they show themselves heartless.

But they remained silent. They would not commit themselves. Silence when they should have spoken.

Then he took him and healed him. “Took him”: laid hold of him, a healing touch.

And sent him away. Perhaps to spare him further embarrassment as a pawn in their game.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and when they said nothing, he healed the man and sent him home.

On a Tuesday. When doing good is right, don’t wait for others’ approval. Do it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out? And they could not reply to these things.

Having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son”. Either way, an emergency. Even strict Jews would rescue a son, or an animal, from a well on the Sabbath. A man with dropsy was full of water; a man in a well was surrounded by it.

Will not immediately pull him out? Of course you would. And will you not let me rescue a man?

And they could not reply to these things. Silenced again (13:17).

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of them would not rescue a son or an ox from a well on the Sabbath, and they had no answer.

On a Tuesday. Show others at least the same compassion you would show your own family, or your property.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus has been watching the guests arrive. Seating at such a meal was not casual — guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement graded by proximity to the host, a visible ranking of the room that everybody could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself. These men have just come from a Sabbath service, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The parable begins as pure social advice, and the scenario would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite, gained and lost in front of witnesses. Follow the mechanics of the humiliation: the man is not merely demoted but has to get up and walk the whole length of the room, because the only seat left is the last one. And “begin with shame” is exact — the shame is not a moment; it starts, and goes on all evening.

Then the reversal, which would be shrewd manoeuvring if it stopped there. What closes the trap is the last verse: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Neither verb says who does the humbling and the exalting, and neither needs to: God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes; it is about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself, and the verse has already seen it.

Jesus then turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. The four categories he names are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: “lest they also invite you in return.” Hospitality in that world ran on reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

The alternative list is the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving — it is that they “cannot repay you.” The inability is the qualification.
verseByVerse.theology:
“He who humbles himself will be exalted” appears repeatedly in Luke (14:11; 18:14; and in substance in the Magnificat). It is the law of the kingdom inverting the law of the world, and it is grounded eschatologically: “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” The accounts are not settled in this life, but they are settled.

The parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat; he is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation rather than merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening at the bottom of the table costs him nothing.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is, and Paul describes the outcome in the same two movements: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Read flatly, the instruction to the host bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No — and the same chapter shows why.
