A dozen verses on, Jesus says a disciple must “hate” his father and mother (v.26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends but do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves: the guests who will have you back, or the guests who cannot. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so — and this is a command with a doorbell, not a principle to admire.

The host who invites only those who will invite him back has not given; he has traded. The host who invites those who cannot repay has given, and in doing so has imitated the God who invites sinners to his table knowing they have nothing to offer him. And note that the account is not cancelled but moved: what is on offer is a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honour, saying to them: when you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honour, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, give your place to this person, and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.

When he noticed how they chose the places of honor. The Pharisees watched Jesus; Jesus watched them. He saw them jostling for the best seats.

A parable. Not just social advice, but a picture of how God deals with people.

Do not sit down in a place of honor. Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host. Guests reclined on couches arranged around tables, with the most important nearest the host.

Lest someone more distinguished than you be invited. And arrive later. Important guests often arrived last.

Give your place to this person. Public humiliation.

And then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. By then, all the middle places are taken. You go to the very bottom. Proverbs 25:6–7: Do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence … for it is better to be told, Come up here, than to be put lower in the presence of a noble.

In a sentence. Seeing guests choose the best seats, Jesus told them not to take the place of honour, in case someone more important came and they were moved down in shame.

On a Tuesday. Don’t push yourself forward for recognition. Let others, and God, do the honouring.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you: friend, move up higher. Then you will be honoured in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

Go and sit in the lowest place. Choose humility.

Friend, move up higher. The host honours the humble.

Then you will be honored. Real honour comes from the host, not from self-promotion.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The principle. The passive voice means: humbled by God, exalted by God. A central truth of the kingdom, repeated in 18:14 (the Pharisee and the tax collector). Mary sang it (1:52). Jesus himself lived it: he humbled himself to the cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:5–11).

What it does not mean. Not false humility, a clever tactic to be noticed. Taking the lowest place in order to be promoted is pride in disguise. True humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less, and leaving your honour to God (1 Peter 5:5–6).

In a sentence. Take the lowest place, so that the host may call you higher, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

On a Tuesday. Where can you take the lower place today, and leave your honour in God’s hands?

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said also to the man who had invited him: when you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbours, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

He said also to the man who had invited him. Now to the host.

Do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors. Not a prohibition of ever inviting family and friends. A Hebrew way of saying: not only these, but rather.

Lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return. Hospitality was a social exchange, building status and alliances. That is not grace; it is business (6:32–34).

Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. Those who could never repay, and who were often excluded from religious gatherings, as the Qumran community excluded the lame and blind from its meals. The very people God will bring to his banquet (v. 21).

And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. The blessing is in giving without return. This is how God gives: to those who cannot repay.

For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. God will repay. “The resurrection of the just”: the resurrection to life of the righteous at the last day (Acts 24:15; John 5:29).

In a sentence. Jesus told his host to invite to his feasts not those who could repay, but the poor and disabled who could not, and God would repay him at the resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Who could you invite to your home who could never invite you back?
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something entirely correct: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The picture he invokes was the settled hope of Israel — the feast on the mountain, rich food for all peoples, death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8).

So why does Jesus answer with a parable about people who refuse an invitation? Listen to the sentence again. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense, and nobody in the room is implicated by it. Jesus has just told them to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them — both remarks about this table, tonight — and what comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The parable changes the tense. And it turns on a custom: a formal banquet involved two invitations, the first well in advance so the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals, the second on the day to say it was ready. So these guests are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They accepted weeks ago, and the host has slaughtered on the strength of it.

“Come, for everything is now ready” is the gospel in six words. Not would you consider coming? The work is done, the cost has been met, and the only thing missing is the guests. And notice who carries it — not the host but a servant, sent on foot to men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

Then the excuses, and not one is disreputable. A field already bought; five yoke of oxen already bought; a new marriage. Property, work, family — every one a good thing, and not one a sin. Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

Which is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say “I refuse Christ.” A great many say “not now — there is something I have to deal with first,” and go on saying it politely for forty years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The master's anger is the only emotion attributed to him, and it is easily made into something it is not. It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He has been given his guests' word and spent accordingly — and in that economy a great banquet meant slaughtered animals that could not be kept, so the cost was already unrecoverable. What has been refused is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved.

But the anger does not cancel the banquet; it redirects it. And the four categories the servant is sent to fetch are the same four Jesus gave the host eight verses earlier (v.13) — which is the parable's quiet accusation to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. God does exactly what he told them to do.

The parable's geography follows the movement of Acts: the original guests, then the streets and lanes of the city, then the highways and hedges outside it — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. The original guests are the religious establishment that has had the invitation through the whole Old Testament and is declining it with polite excuses; the poor and lame of the city are the tax collectors and sinners responding to his ministry; the people beyond the walls are the Gentiles.

And the exclusion is stated without qualification: “none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.” The feast does not wait indefinitely, and the door does not stay open after the house is full.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room” is the most hopeful sentence in the parable. The servant has swept every street and every alley and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

One phrase has done real damage and should be handled plainly: “compel people to come in.” Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used it to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms and penal laws.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will. If the verse presses anything on the church, it is urgency in persuading the people who assume the gospel cannot possibly be for them.

And “that my house may be filled” is the heart of it. Not that the food may not be wasted. He wants the room full.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him: blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!

Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God! A pious remark, perhaps to ease the tension, or to show his own piety. The messianic banquet, the great feast at the end of the age (Isaiah 25:6–8; 13:29). He assumes he will be there. The parable that follows asks: will you?

In a sentence. One of the guests exclaimed how blessed are those who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to speak warmly about heaven. Make sure you have accepted the invitation.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to him: a man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited: come, for everything is now ready.

A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. God, preparing the feast of the kingdom. A great banquet, for many.

And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant. Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready, since there were no clocks. The first invitation had been accepted. Israel had been invited long ago, through the prophets.

Come, for everything is now ready. The servant is Jesus, or those who preach the kingdom. The kingdom is ready now. Everything has been prepared. All they need to do is come. The gospel invitation.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who gave a great banquet and, when it was ready, sent his servant to tell the invited guests to come, for everything was prepared.

For worship. God has prepared everything for your salvation. Come, for everything is now ready.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him: I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused. And another said: I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused. And another said: I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.

But they all alike began to make excuses. To refuse after accepting an invitation was a grave insult. And their excuses are flimsy.

I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Who buys a field without seeing it first? And it would still be there tomorrow. Possessions.

I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Ten oxen: a wealthy man. Again, you would test them before buying. Business.

I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. The law excused a newly married man from war for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5), but not from a feast. And he does not even say “please excuse me”. Family.

The point. Possessions, work, and family: all good things. But they become excuses for refusing God’s invitation. Not wicked things, but good things put first, keep people out of the kingdom (8:14; 9:57–62).

In a sentence. The invited guests all made excuses: one had bought a field, another oxen, and another had just married.

On a Tuesday. What good thing in your life is your excuse for not coming fully to God?
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year — but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant: go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.

Then the master of the house became angry. Rightly. His generosity had been insulted.

Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city. The town’s back streets, where the outcasts lived. Within Israel: the tax collectors, sinners, the poor, those excluded by the religious elite.

And bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame. Exactly the list of verse 13. God does what he told the host to do. The kingdom is filled with those who have nothing to offer.

In a sentence. The angry master sent his servant to bring in the poor and disabled from the city streets instead.

For worship. You were invited when you had nothing. Thank God for his grace to the poor and broken.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant said: sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. And the master said to the servant: go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.

And still there is room. God’s house is large. There is room for more.

Go out to the highways and hedges. Outside the town altogether: the country roads and hedgerows, where travellers and vagrants sheltered. The Gentiles, outside Israel. This is the mission of Acts, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8; 13:46).

And compel people to come in. “Compel” means urge them strongly, press them to come. Strangers would not believe such an invitation, and would be reluctant. In Middle Eastern culture, a guest would politely refuse and have to be urged. The invitation is so generous it must be pressed on people.

Where Christians differ: “compel them to come in”. Augustine used this verse to justify using the power of the state to force heretics (the Donatists) back into the church, and it was later used to justify forced conversions and persecution. Verdict: this is a grievous misreading. The compulsion is the urgency of love and persuasion, not force. Faith cannot be coerced. The gospel is to be pressed on people earnestly, but never by violence (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20).

That my house may be filled. God is determined that his banquet will be full. His purpose will not be thwarted by refusal.

None of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet. Those who refused will be shut out (13:28). By their own choice.

In a sentence. When there was still room, the master sent his servant to the country roads to urge people to come in until his house was full, declaring that none of the first guests would taste his banquet.

On a Tuesday. There is still room. Urge others to come to Christ, earnestly and lovingly.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come — the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds are travelling with him, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel — which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a following.

“Hate” is Semitic idiom for loving less by comparison, and the usage is well attested: Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah,” and in the next verse Leah is described as “hated” (Gen. 29:30-31). Matthew records the same saying in the plainer form — “whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

The idiom explains the word, but the softer reading is not a rescue operation; it is the only one the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity — when the scribes devised Corban to avoid supporting aged parents, he called it making void the word of God (Mark 7:9-13), which is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license. He kept the commandment himself in his last hours, giving his mother to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states it flatly: a man who does not provide for his household “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

And note the last name on the list, which governs the rest: “and even his own life.” Family is not being singled out for sacrifice; the self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation.

The cross image was not a metaphor to that crowd. A cross-bearer was a specific sight: a condemned man, already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets, with the jeering going on around him. It carries finality, shame, and submission — and the man saying it was going to do it himself within the year.

Then two parables, both beginning “sit down first.” The tower is probably a farm watchtower, not a monument, and the failure is public and permanent: an abandoned foundation sits in the field for as long as anybody remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say. The king's case adds a third option the builder does not have — sue for peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost teaching is addressed to those already following, already enthusiastic, already in the crowd. They are not being warned before they commit; they are being warned that what they think they have committed to may not be what discipleship requires. The danger is not the uncommitted outsider but the enthusiastic follower who has not counted the cost.

He is not recruiting. He has just watched thousands attach themselves to his procession and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate — the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used. A crowd that has not counted the cost is not an asset; it is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen.

The king's parable changes the register. The builder's alternatives are to finish or be mocked; the king can send a delegation and ask for terms. And who is the greater king in that picture? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. What is left is the delegation — going out, while there is still distance, and asking for terms. That is not defeat in this parable; it is the only wise move on the board, and it is what the counting of the cost is actually for.

“Renounce” is not primarily get rid of but let go of: a man at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind.
verseByVerse.examples:
What the hate-saying means is a matter of collision, not everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, husband and father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table.

If you are living inside that collision, take two things from it. The cost is real and Jesus never pretends otherwise — he has already said he came to divide households (12:51-53), and he says this to a crowd, not to specialists; the grief you feel is not a sign you have done something wrong. And the command does not license coldness. Nothing here permits writing your family off, arguing at every meal, or making your faith a weapon. You go on loving them, and usually better than before; you simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

“Renounce all that he has” is comprehensive in a way that goes past property — reputation, plans, the rights a man believes his circumstances have granted him, the future he has drawn up. Here is a test that is not about percentages: think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the hardest to lose — the thing quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced.

And the salt saying is the chapter's last word on what a half-committed disciple is for. The salt of Palestine was gathered from Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum; if the sodium leached out with damp it left a white powder that looked exactly like salt and did nothing. Still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt — and it has stopped working.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them: if anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

Great crowds accompanied him. Popular. But Jesus is not interested in crowds; he wants disciples.

He turned and said to them. Deliberately, to the whole crowd.

If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother. A shocking statement. “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less, a comparison (Genesis 29:30–31, where Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Leah was “hated”; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13). Matthew’s parallel says: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). Jesus demands first place, above every other love.

And wife and children and brothers and sisters. The closest relationships.

Yes, and even his own life. Even self.

He cannot be my disciple. Not “may not be a very good disciple”, but “cannot be”. Jesus claims a loyalty that only God has the right to claim. Either he is God, or this is outrageous.

What it does not mean. Not literal hatred, or neglect of family. Jesus commands honouring parents (18:20) and loving wives (Ephesians 5:25). But when love for family conflicts with loyalty to Christ, Christ must win. Compared with our love for him, every other love should look like hatred. And in fact, loving Christ most makes us love others better.

In a sentence. Jesus told the crowds that anyone who does not love him more than family and even his own life cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. Who or what do you love more than Jesus? Put him first, and every other love will find its right place.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

Whoever does not bear his own cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. To bear your cross is to accept rejection, shame and death for Jesus’ sake, as a way of life (9:23).

And come after me. Follow him on the road to Jerusalem and the cross.

Cannot be my disciple. The second “cannot”. There is no cross-less discipleship.

In a sentence. Whoever does not carry his own cross and follow Jesus cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. What cross are you carrying for Jesus today?
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying: this man began to build and was not able to finish.

Desiring to build a tower. A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm (Isaiah 5:2), or be a farm building.

Does not first sit down and count the cost. Wise planning. Do I have enough to finish?

This man began to build and was not able to finish. A half-built tower was a monument to foolishness, mocked by all.

The point. Before you follow Jesus, think about what it will cost. Don’t start enthusiastically and give up halfway (8:13). The crowds were following without thinking.

In a sentence. As a builder first counts the cost of a tower to make sure he can finish it, so a would-be disciple must count the cost of following Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Have you counted the cost of following Jesus? It is everything, and he is worth it.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

What king, going out to encounter another king in war. A second parable. A greater matter: a war, not a building.

Whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Outnumbered two to one.

He sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. Wise surrender, while there is still time.

The point. Two possible readings, both true. First, as with the tower: count the cost of discipleship. Second: God is the king coming against you with superior force. You cannot win against him. Make peace with him now, while he is still far off, by surrendering everything to him (12:58).

In a sentence. As a king facing a stronger army sits down to consider whether he can win, and if not, seeks peace while there is time, so a person must consider the cost and make peace with God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot fight God and win. Surrender to him on his terms, and find peace.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.

Who does not renounce all that he has. “Renounce” (apotassetai): say goodbye to, part with, give up. Not necessarily literally sell everything, but give up ownership of everything to Christ, holding it all at his disposal. Everything you have belongs to him.

Cannot be my disciple. The third “cannot” (vv. 26, 27, 33). Three conditions: Christ above family, above self, and above possessions.

What it does not mean. Not that discipleship earns salvation, or that only those who take a vow of poverty can be saved. But a disciple is someone who has surrendered everything to Christ, and will let go of anything he asks.

In a sentence. Anyone who does not give up everything he has cannot be Jesus’ disciple.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you have not yet surrendered to Christ? Give it to him today.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Salt is good. Salt preserved, flavoured, and was used as a fertiliser in small amounts.

But if salt has lost its taste. Impure salt, collected from the Dead Sea marshes, could have its salt leached out by moisture and lose its taste, leaving a useless white powder.

It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. Not even good enough to be mixed with manure as fertiliser.

It is thrown away. Worthless.

The point. A disciple who loses what makes him a disciple, his wholehearted commitment to Christ, is useless, like saltless salt. Discipleship that is not costly is not discipleship. And a church that has lost its distinctiveness is useless to the world.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Pay attention. This is serious.

In a sentence. A disciple who loses his distinctiveness is like salt that has lost its taste: useless and thrown away.

On a Tuesday. Is your discipleship salty: distinctive, costly, wholehearted? Don’t lose your saltiness.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological heart of Luke's Gospel — the chapter that more than any other earns Luke the title “the Gospel of grace.” It contains three parables told in response to a single complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The three parables are Jesus's answer to the grumbling — not an argument but a story, or rather three stories that together form a single, overwhelming answer to the question: why does the Son of God eat with sinners? Because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. He is the woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house until she finds the one lost coin. He is the father who runs to meet his returning son while he is still a long way off.

The three parables form a crescendo: from a sheep (something lost through its own wandering nature), to a coin (something lost through its owner's carelessness, possibly), to a son (someone lost through deliberate, calculated rebellion). The lostness becomes more personal, more chosen, more culpable at each step — and the joy at the finding becomes more extravagant, more communal, more absolutely centred on grace rather than on the condition of the lost. The sheep does nothing to return; it is carried home. The coin does nothing; it is found. The son turns around and prepares a speech about his unworthiness — and the father interrupts the speech with the best robe and the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. The grace always exceeds the repentance.

The chapter's most searching moment is the elder son (vv. 25–32) — the one who has never left, who has served faithfully, who is furious at the welcome given to the prodigal. He is the Pharisees in the parable — the ones whose complaint prompted all three parables. And the father's final words to him are the most tender and most open-ended in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The chapter ends without the elder son's response. Luke does not tell us whether the Pharisees came in to the feast. The question is left open — which is where Jesus leaves the invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this chapter depends on the first two verses. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear him — a settled pattern rather than one occasion — and the Pharisees and scribes grumble.

Grumbling is what Israel did over and over in the wilderness (Ex. 16:2, 7-8). It is not argument; it is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

“This man receives sinners and eats with them” is meant as an accusation and is completely accurate. The charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners — nobody objected to that. It is the table. A shared meal in that world was the single clearest social statement a person could make about who his people were, and he was making it, often enough for everyone to have noticed.

What follows is his answer: three parables, all about something lost, all ending in a party — and the charge is never denied. Luke calls them one parable (v.3), singular, which is worth noticing. They are one argument in three movements.

He begins by putting his critics inside the story. “What man of you” compels agreement: any shepherd here would do this. He is not defending an eccentric practice but describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to.

The detail is realistic. A hundred sheep is a substantial flock, likely with hired help, so leaving the ninety-nine “in the open country” is not the recklessness it sounds. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will lie down and refuse to move.

“Until he finds it” governs the whole search — there is no clause allowing the shepherd to come home empty. And he does not drive the animal back; an exhausted sheep cannot be herded, so he hoists seventy or eighty pounds across his shoulders and carries it home over the same country he searched, rejoicing.

Then he throws a party, over one sheep out of a hundred, quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.
verseByVerse.theology:
The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine is the most dramatic possible image of divine initiative. The sheep does not seek the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep. This is the consistent pattern of grace: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19); “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The lost sheep contributes nothing to its rescue — it is found, lifted, carried.

Note also where the word repents falls. It appears in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. The repentance and the being-found are the same event seen from two sides.

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended.

But remember who Jesus is answering. On the lips of the men grumbling at verse 2, “righteous persons who need no repentance” is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house. Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge: there is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ninety-nine left “in the open country” looks irresponsible, and it reveals something about the community that belongs to the shepherd: they are safe in his care even while he is searching for the one. The gathered community is not threatened by the shepherd's pursuit of the wanderer; it is the context from which he goes and to which he brings the found sheep.

The church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has misunderstood its own situation. It was once the one, and is now among the ninety-nine.

And the arithmetic of the parable is the thing to sit with, because it is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the sum the shepherd did. One sheep out of a hundred, and the whole neighbourhood is called in.

If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself. The men it was told to were quite certain they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was constructed so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment it closed on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying: this man receives sinners and eats with them.

The gospel within the gospel. Chapter 15 has been called the heart of Luke’s Gospel. Three parables of lost things found: a sheep, a coin, and a son. Each ends with joy. All three answer one complaint: why does Jesus welcome sinners?

The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. “All”: in large numbers. “To hear him”: they came to listen. The outcasts were drawn to Jesus. Something in him made sinners feel welcome.

And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled. “Grumbled” (diegongyzon): muttered among themselves, the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8).

This man receives sinners and eats with them. “Receives” (prosdechetai): welcomes, accepts. Eating together signalled acceptance and friendship; that was the offence. To the Pharisees, a holy man should keep away from sinners. Their complaint is the gospel: Jesus receives sinners. It is the most wonderful thing about him.

In a sentence. When tax collectors and sinners crowded to hear Jesus, the Pharisees and scribes grumbled that he welcomed sinners and ate with them.

For worship. This man receives sinners. Thank God that he received you.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he told them this parable: what man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.

So he told them this parable. To the grumblers. A parable in three parts, perhaps (some say one parable with three panels).

What man of you, having a hundred sheep. A modest flock, for a family. Shepherds were despised by the Pharisees, but Jesus asks them to imagine being one. And God is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34).

If he has lost one of them. One percent. Hardly worth worrying about, you might think. But every sheep matters to the shepherd.

Does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country. Presumably with other shepherds, or safely gathered.

And go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? Key words. The shepherd takes the initiative. The sheep does not find its way back; the shepherd seeks it. “Until he finds it”: he does not give up. This is God’s seeking love. Ezekiel 34:11, 16: I myself will search for my sheep … I will seek the lost. And Jesus: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. A lost sheep is often frightened, exhausted, and lies down and refuses to move. The shepherd carries it home. No scolding, no punishment, only joy. Isaiah 40:11: he will gather the lambs in his arms.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of them, losing one sheep out of a hundred, would not leave the ninety-nine to search for it until he found it, and carry it home with joy on his shoulders.

For worship. Jesus is the shepherd who came looking for you, and carries you home. Rejoice that you have been found.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbours, saying to them: rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.

He calls together his friends and his neighbors. Joy must be shared.

Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. “My sheep”: it belonged to him all along.

Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven. “In heaven”: in God’s presence, a reverent way of saying God himself rejoices. The Pharisees grumble; heaven celebrates. God’s heart is the opposite of theirs.

Over one sinner who repents. Repentance is the sheep being found. Notice: in the parable, the shepherd does all the work. In reality, repentance is the sinner’s response to being found by God.

Than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. Irony. There are no righteous people who need no repentance (Romans 3:10, 23). But the Pharisees thought they were such people (18:9). So heaven has no joy over them, because they will not repent.

In a sentence. As the shepherd calls his friends to rejoice with him, there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ninety-nine who think they need no repentance.

For worship. When a sinner repents, heaven rejoices. Share in God’s joy when someone comes to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman — deliberate, and not likely to be accidental in the Gospel that records more about women than any other. God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a housewife on her hands and knees.

The coins are drachmas, each roughly a day's wage. Ten is not a fortune, but for a peasant household it is ten days' living. It may be more serious still: in some parts of that world a woman's ten coins were her dowry, strung together and worn on her headdress — both her security and the visible sign of her marriage, so that the lost coin is a gap in something she wears.

Every detail of the search is exact for the house she lived in. A peasant home had few windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark — hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying; it is dragging a broom across the floor to hear the coin move, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

“Until she finds it” is the shepherd's clause again, and the same refusal to stop. And the ending is the same: friends and neighbours called in, and a party quite possibly costing more than a drachma.

One difference from the first parable deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin can do nothing at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found — and it made almost none — the coin makes less.

The application changes in two small ways. The tense moves from future to present: not “there will be joy” but “there is joy,” now, and every time. And the location becomes “before the angels of God” — which puts the angels in the position of onlookers, watching somebody else be glad.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whose joy are the angels watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already answered it. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted.

So the picture is this: somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round — and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

That is a very long way from the God the grumblers at verse 2 were defending, and a long way from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable, and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

The angels are elsewhere described as “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). They are not detached observers of the gospel; they are invested in its outcomes. The finding of one lost sinner is a cosmic event, celebrated at every level of the created order that understands what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's method is the model of the kind of prayer and pastoral work that refuses to give up. She does not glance round and conclude it is not there. She lights the lamp — creating the conditions for seeing clearly. She sweeps — removing what might be covering it. And she seeks diligently until the finding.

Intercession for the lost follows the same method: create the conditions for light, remove what obscures the gospel, and keep at it. And the sweeping is worth holding on to, because it is the least glamorous part and the part that actually finds the coin. It is repetitive, unremarkable work done on hands and knees in a dark room, and it is how the thing was recovered.

And the completeness of the coin's helplessness is a comfort rather than an insult. Anyone who has watched a person they love become entirely unable to help themselves — through addiction, or illness of the mind, or a hardness they cannot seem to break — is looking at the coin. It cannot call out. It cannot move towards the light.

What the parable says is that this changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbours, saying: rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.

Or what woman. Luke’s pairing again: a man and a woman (13:18–21). God is pictured as a shepherd and as a woman searching her house.

Having ten silver coins. The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius, a day’s wage. Ten coins: perhaps her savings, or her dowry, worn on a headdress. Losing one was a real loss for a poor woman.

Does not light a lamp and sweep the house. A poor house had few or no windows, and a dirt floor covered with straw. Finding a small coin meant lighting a lamp and sweeping carefully, listening for the clink.

And seek diligently until she finds it. Again, persistent searching, “until”.

Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost. The same joy, the same sharing.

The difference. A sheep wanders away by its own folly; a coin is lost through no will of its own; a son will walk away deliberately. All lost; all sought; all found.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a woman who lost one of her ten silver coins and searched her house carefully until she found it, then called her friends to rejoice with her.

On a Tuesday. God searches diligently for the lost. Be part of his search: pray for and seek those who are lost.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius — about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.

Joy before the angels of God. Not exactly that the angels rejoice, though they surely do, but that there is joy in their presence, the joy of God himself.

Over one sinner who repents. Every single one matters.

In a sentence. There is joy in the presence of God’s angels over every single sinner who repents.

For worship. Heaven rejoiced when you repented. Let that thought fill you with joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“There was a man who had two sons.” The story is announced as being about two — worth remembering, since it is usually preached as though it were about one.

The younger son's request is difficult to convey in its full shock. An estate passed at the father's death; a son had no standing to ask early, and the request carried an unmistakable meaning: I want what I will get when you are dead, and I do not want to wait for you to die. And he calls it “the share that is coming to me” — not a gift but something owed.

The father grants it without a recorded word. Note the plural: “he divided his property between them.” Two-thirds went to the elder son on the spot, and he never asked — which will matter enormously when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything.

Liquidating that land was a public act. Land in Israel was the family's portion in the inheritance of God's people, with laws to keep it in the family (Lev. 25:23-28), so the whole district watched the transactions and drew the obvious conclusion. And the far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved.

The descent is calibrated: the money goes, then a famine removes any possibility of recovery, then he attaches himself to a Gentile who sends him out of sight to feed pigs — the floor, for a son of Israel — and then he is hungry enough to envy the carob pods and cannot get them. “No one gave him anything.” The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

“He came to himself” is exact. He does not become someone else; he comes round, the way a man does after a blow to the head — which says that everything from verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and repentance is sanity returning.

His prepared speech gets two things right and one wrong. He names it as sin, against God first and his father second. Then he proposes to work his way back as a hired labourer — he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

And the father, seeing him a long way off, runs.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father running is the most shocking thing in the parable. An elderly man of standing in a Middle Eastern village did not run; it required gathering up the robe and exposing the legs, which was humiliating, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. He deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village.

And he may have had a further reason. The boy had sold family land to Gentiles and lost it, and could expect a hostile reception. The father reaches him first, on the road, before anyone else can get to him. The same logic runs through the fattened calf: everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father's verdict on his son, and it is very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Every gift is a specific restoration. The best robe is the finest in the house and probably the father's own — so anyone entering afterwards sees a son of the house and nothing else. The signet ring is authority, the instrument for sealing contracts in the father's name, handed to the one member of the family who has proved beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money. Slaves went barefoot; the shoes settle the question the boy had rehearsed all the way home.

An objection has to be met here, because it is raised by critics and by thoughtful believers alike: there is no atonement in this parable. No sacrifice, no blood, no mediator — the father simply forgives. Some have built on that silence the claim that the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel.

But the parable is not costless; we have been reading it from the son's side. The younger son's portion was real property, squandered and not coming back — the father is permanently poorer for having let him go. And the robe, the ring, the sandals and the calf all come out of what remains. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the entire cost himself, in silence, and never once mentions it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry, and the text is entirely candid about it — so a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold. I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real?

Watch what the father does with it. He does not interrogate the motive or wait at the gate to establish whether the boy has come for love or for supper. He sees him a long way off and runs. Luke has been showing this all through: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes came out of sheer misery and went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else on earth to try (23:42-43).

Nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards.

Then the elder brother, and the parable's real target. He describes his life in his father's house as service — “these many years I have served you” — and thinks he is stating a credential. He wanted a goat to celebrate with his friends; even his imagined party does not have his father in it. And the complaint is false: two-thirds of that estate had been legally his since verse 12, and he could have killed a goat any week he liked.

He cannot say “my brother.” The servant managed it without effort; the elder son says “this son of yours.” And he supplies the prostitutes, which Luke never mentioned and which he was several days' journey away from witnessing — resentment filling in the blanks in the worst available way and calling it honesty.

The parable then stops. A man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing. Jesus told this to the men who grumbled at verse 2, and left them on the doorstep. The ending was theirs to write.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: there was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father: father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. And he divided his property between them.

The parable of the two sons. Often called the prodigal son, but it is really about a father and two sons. The younger son represents the tax collectors and sinners (v. 1); the older son represents the Pharisees and scribes (v. 2). The father represents God. The story is left open at the end, because the older son, the Pharisees, must decide.

There was a man who had two sons. Only Luke records this parable.

Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive one-third (the elder received a double portion, Deuteronomy 21:17). To ask for it now was shocking. It was like saying: I wish you were dead. I want your things, not you. A son making this request would expect his father to strike him and throw him out.

And he divided his property between them. Astonishingly, the father agrees. He does not force his son to stay. He lets him go, though it breaks his heart. And the elder son receives his share too, and says nothing in defence of his father.

The picture. This is what every sinner does to God: takes his gifts (life, health, abilities) and wants to live without him. Sin is not first breaking rules, but breaking a relationship, wanting God’s gifts without God.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man with two sons, the younger of whom insulted his father by demanding his inheritance at once, and the father divided his property between them.

On a Tuesday. Are you enjoying God’s gifts while keeping him at a distance? That is the heart of sin.
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third — the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.

Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had. He sold his share of the estate, turning land into cash, as quickly as possible. Selling family land was itself shameful.

And took a journey into a far country. Gentile land, far from his father, his family, his people, and his God.

And there he squandered his property. “Squandered” (dieskorpisen): scattered, wasted, like seed thrown to the wind.

In reckless living. “Reckless” (asōtōs): wastefully, without restraint. His brother will say: with prostitutes (v. 30). Freedom from his father became slavery to his appetites.

In a sentence. The younger son soon turned his inheritance into cash, went to a distant country, and wasted it all on reckless living.

On a Tuesday. The far country promises freedom, but delivers emptiness. Where is your far country?
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.

When he had spent everything. The money ran out, and so did his friends.

A severe famine arose in that country. Circumstances turned against him. God often uses hardship to bring sinners to their senses.

And he began to be in need. From wealth to want.

He hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country. Literally “glued himself”, clung to him. Desperate, he attached himself to a Gentile.

Who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. The lowest point imaginable for a Jew. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7). A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as a person could go: cut off from his people, his religion and his God. A rabbinic saying: cursed is the man who raises pigs.

And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate. Carob pods, the fruit of the carob tree, fed to animals and eaten by the very poorest. He envied the pigs.

And no one gave him anything. No one cared. The far country does not care for its slaves.

In a sentence. When his money was gone and famine struck, he hired himself out to a Gentile to feed pigs, and was so hungry he longed to eat their food, but no one gave him anything.

On a Tuesday. Sin promises much and leaves you envying pigs. If you are at the bottom, the way home is still open.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he came to himself, he said: how many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.

But when he came to himself. Literally “came to himself”: came to his senses, woke up. Sin is a kind of madness; repentance is coming back to sanity. It begins with seeing clearly: where I am, and where I could be.

How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread. He remembers his father’s goodness. Even the lowest servants are well fed. Remembering God’s goodness draws sinners back (Romans 2:4).

But I perish here with hunger! Honest about his condition.

I will arise and go to my father. Repentance is a decision, followed by action: turning around, going back.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. “Against heaven”: against God. All sin is first against God (Psalm 51:4). And against his father. Genuine confession, without excuses or blaming others. He does not blame the famine, or his friends, or his father.

I am no longer worthy to be called your son. True. He has forfeited every right.

Treat me as one of your hired servants. Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family. Not even a household slave. He plans to work off his debt, to earn his way back. His repentance is real, but he still thinks in terms of earning. He has not yet understood his father’s heart.

In a sentence. Coming to his senses, he remembered that even his father’s hired workers had plenty, and resolved to go home, confess his sin, and ask to be treated as a hired worker.

On a Tuesday. Come to your senses. Confess your sin to God, honestly and without excuse. And then go home.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

And he arose and came to his father. He did what he said.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him. The father had been watching, waiting, looking down the road every day. He saw his son before his son saw him.

And felt compassion. Esplanchnisthē: moved in his innermost being. The word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the good Samaritan (10:33).

And ran. In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run. He would have to hike up his robe and show his legs, a disgrace. And the village would have seen the son coming back in rags, and might have abused him; according to some customs, a son who lost his inheritance among Gentiles could be cut off by the village. The father ran to reach him first, taking the shame on himself, protecting his son.

And embraced him. Literally “fell on his neck”, as Esau embraced Jacob (Genesis 33:4) and Joseph his father (Genesis 46:29).

And kissed him. Again and again. A sign of acceptance, forgiveness and reconciliation (2 Samuel 14:33). Before the son could say a word of his confession.

The heart of God. This is the centre of the parable, and the answer to the Pharisees’ complaint. God is not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to forgive. He is a father who runs to meet repentant sinners, while they are still far off. This is why Jesus receives sinners.

In a sentence. While the son was still far off, his father saw him, was filled with compassion, ran to him, threw his arms around him and kissed him.

For worship. This is how God receives you when you turn to him: he runs to you, embraces you and kisses you. Worship the running Father.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the son said to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. He makes his confession. Repentance is still necessary, even after the embrace.

I am no longer worthy to be called your son. True.

What he does not say. He leaves out the last line of his prepared speech: Treat me as one of your hired servants (v. 19). Perhaps the father interrupts him. Perhaps, embraced and kissed, he realises he cannot bargain. Grace does not negotiate. You cannot earn your way back to a father who has already forgiven you. He comes as a son, or not at all.

In a sentence. The son confessed his sin and unworthiness to his father, but did not finish his offer to become a hired worker.

For worship. Confess your sins to God, and then stop trying to earn his favour. He has already welcomed you as a son.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the father said to his servants: bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.

But the father said to his servants. He does not even reply to the confession. He acts.

Bring quickly. No delay, no probation period, no conditions.

The best robe. Literally “the first robe”: the finest in the house, perhaps the father’s own. The robe honoured him. It covered his rags, and showed everyone in the village that he was restored to honour. A picture of the righteousness of Christ, with which God clothes the sinner (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5; Galatians 3:27).

And put a ring on his hand. A signet ring, used to seal documents, gave him authority to act on his father’s behalf (Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:10). Full restoration as a son, with a son’s rights.

And shoes on his feet. Sandals marked a free man; slaves went barefoot. Not a servant, but a son.

In a sentence. The father ordered the best robe, a ring and sandals for him at once, restoring him fully to honour, authority and sonship.

For worship. God does not just forgive you; he restores you fully, clothing you in Christ’s righteousness and making you his child. Rejoice in your robe.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to celebrate.

And bring the fattened calf and kill it. A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations. Enough meat to feed the whole village. The father throws a feast, not for the son only, but for the community, to restore him publicly.

Let us eat and celebrate. Eating together: the very thing the Pharisees complained about (v. 2). Jesus eats with sinners because God celebrates their return.

For this my son was dead, and is alive again. “My son”: not a hired servant. Dead and alive: the language of resurrection. Repentance is passing from death to life (Ephesians 2:1–5; Colossians 2:13).

He was lost, and is found. Like the sheep and the coin.

And they began to celebrate. Joy, as in the first two parables.

Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross? Some liberal theologians have argued that this parable shows God forgives freely, without any need for atonement: the father simply forgives, with no sacrifice. Verdict: a parable teaches one main point, not every doctrine. This one shows God’s welcome to repentant sinners, in answer to the Pharisees. It does not explain how forgiveness is possible for a holy God. The rest of Scripture does: Jesus came to give his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (22:20; Matthew 26:28), and Luke ends with the Christ who must suffer so that forgiveness may be proclaimed (24:46–47). The father’s running, at cost to his own honour, is a hint of the cost God himself bore. And the one telling the story was on his way to Jerusalem to die.

In a sentence. The father ordered the fattened calf killed for a feast, because his son had been dead and was alive, lost and was found, and they began to celebrate.

For worship. You were dead and are alive, lost and found. Join heaven’s celebration.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him: your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.

The second half. The story could have ended with the feast. But Jesus tells it to the Pharisees (v. 2). Now comes their part.

Now his older son was in the field. Working, dutiful, as always.

He heard music and dancing. Celebration.
