And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. He does not go in. He stands outside and asks.

Your brother has come. The servant says “your brother”.

Because he has received him back safe and sound. “Safe and sound” (hygiainonta): healthy, whole. The father’s joy is simply that his son is back.

In a sentence. The older son, returning from the field, heard music and dancing, and was told his brother had come home and his father was celebrating his safe return.

On a Tuesday. When others come to Christ, do you join the celebration or stand outside asking questions?

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him.

But he was angry and refused to go in. Anger, like the Pharisees’ grumbling (v. 2). He refused to join the feast. To refuse to attend a father’s feast was a public insult, as great as the younger son’s demand. Now he is the one who is shut out, by his own choice. The lost son is inside; the “good” son is outside.

His father came out and entreated him. The father goes out again, this time to the older son. He humbles himself a second time, leaving his guests. He pleads. “Entreated” (parekalei): urged, begged. God’s love pursues the self-righteous as well as the openly sinful. Jesus is pleading with the Pharisees, through this very parable.

In a sentence. The older son was angry and refused to go in, so his father came out and pleaded with him.

For worship. God pursues the respectable as well as the rebellious. If you have been standing outside, he is pleading with you too.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he answered his father: look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!

Look. No respectful “Father”. The younger son began “Father”; the older son does not.

These many years I have served you. “Served” (douleuō): slaved for you. He thinks of himself as a slave, not a son. He has been working for wages, not living in love. The younger son wanted to come back as a hired servant; the older son had been living like one all along.

And I never disobeyed your command. Outward obedience, like the rich ruler (18:21) and Paul before conversion (Philippians 3:6). But his heart was far from his father. He was as lost as his brother, though he never left home.

Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. He wanted to celebrate, but with his friends, not his father. He feels he has earned more, and been cheated. Self-righteousness is always resentful of grace.

But when this son of yours came. Not “my brother”, but “this son of yours”. He disowns his brother.

Who has devoured your property with prostitutes. The worst interpretation, perhaps exaggerated, publicly announced. He wants his brother’s sin remembered.

You killed the fattened calf for him! He cannot bear grace being given to someone who does not deserve it. This is the Pharisees’ complaint: this man receives sinners.

In a sentence. The older son complained that he had slaved for his father for years without reward, while the father had killed the fattened calf for this son of his who had wasted everything on prostitutes.

On a Tuesday. Do you resent God’s grace to others? Do you obey God as a slave seeking wages, or as a son who loves him? Self-righteousness can keep you out of the feast as surely as rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.

Son. “Child” (teknon), a tender word. Despite the insult, the father speaks with love.

You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. Everything he wanted, he already had: his father’s presence, and the whole estate. He did not need to earn it. He only had to enjoy it as a son. The Pharisees had the Scriptures, the covenants, the temple, God’s presence (Romans 9:4–5). All theirs. But they lived as servants, not sons.

It was fitting to celebrate and be glad. “It was fitting” (edei): it was necessary, it was right. Divine necessity. How could anyone not celebrate this?

For this your brother. Not “this son of yours”, but “your brother”. The father reminds him of the relationship he has disowned.

Was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found. The refrain repeated.

The open ending. Jesus does not tell us whether the older son went in. The story stops. Because the Pharisees and scribes, listening, had to decide: would they come in to the feast, and rejoice that sinners were coming home? Or would they stay outside? Every self-righteous person faces the same choice.

In a sentence. The father told his older son that he had always been with him and owned everything, but they had to celebrate, because his brother had been dead and was alive, lost and was found.

For worship. If you are a Christian, all that is God’s is yours. Enjoy it as a son or daughter, and rejoice whenever a lost brother or sister comes home.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is one of the most challenging chapters in all the Gospels. It contains two sustained teachings — the Parable of the Dishonest Manager and the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus — that bracket a cluster of sayings about the law, divorce, and divine valuation. What holds it together is money as a spiritual diagnostic: how a person handles wealth reveals the true condition of their heart before God.

The Parable of the Dishonest Manager shocks its hearers because Jesus appears to commend a fraudster. The commendation, however, is carefully qualified: the manager is praised not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness — his ability to think clearly about the future and use present resources to secure it. Jesus turns the parable into an indictment of disciples who exercise less practical wisdom in spiritual things than worldly people do in material ones.

The story of the Rich Man and Lazarus is the only parable in which a character has a proper name, and it closes the chapter with one of Scripture's most sobering statements: if people will not be persuaded by Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. This is both a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy about the response to Jesus's own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this to his disciples while the Pharisees are also listening (v.14), which is why the chapter ends where it does.

The manager is an oikonomos — the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts and ran the property in his master's name. And what he had been doing is what the prodigal did in the far country (15:13). The parable opens with a second man squandering another man's property.

Note the order of the dismissal: he is sacked first and the audit demanded second, which means he is finished and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap — no longer trusted, not yet stripped of authority, the debtors not yet told, the seal still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

His options are closed: he cannot dig, and he will not beg — and the difference in the two clauses is a fair sample of the man. He is not able to dig; he is ashamed to beg. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

What he then buys is not money. He does not embezzle; what he wants is houses — an open door somewhere when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth can be converted into them while he still controls it.

The reductions are uneven — fifty per cent on oil, twenty on wheat — which is the clue. If he were simply defrauding his master the discounts would be arbitrary; that they differ by commodity suggests he is removing something that varied by commodity, and the obvious candidate is his own commission. On that reading he waives his fee and takes a large personal loss, which would explain the otherwise baffling commendation.

It cannot be settled with certainty and the parable does not require it. What is commended is neither the honesty nor the dishonesty but the structure of the act: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would outlast the deadline.
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager. What is praised is his shrewdness: practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act. A commander can admire an enemy's manoeuvre without approving the war.

“Sons of light” was a term the devout used of themselves — the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at reading a situation and acting in time.

The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will plan a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep. Set beside that the way the same qualities are deployed in the things of God by people who genuinely believe they will stand before him: the forward thinking stops, and a man who would never let a financial decision drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it.

The three descriptions of money in vv.10-12 are each deflating. It is unrighteous — the currency of a fallen order, and nobody's money is clean all the way back. It is a very little, said to people for whom it was the difference between eating and not eating. And it is another's. But the promise on the other side is easily missed: the true riches, and that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 9 is the hardest sentence in the chapter and needs facing. Read flatly it appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven — and it has been read that way in defence of almsgiving as accumulated merit.

Who are “they”? Three readings are held by careful Christians: the friends themselves, the angels, or — most likely — God himself, whose name the wording leaves unspoken.

And on whether salvation is for sale, the verse answers itself in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails. The money is explicitly the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity — and in this very chapter a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water.

What the verse teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with “you cannot serve God and money,” which is where the saying is travelling.

And that closing sentence is a statement about what is possible, not advice about priorities. A man may hold two jobs; nobody has ever had two owners. Note too that both outcomes are the same outcome — whichever way it falls, one master gets the loyalty and the other the contempt. Most people serving money would sincerely say they love God, and the conflict only becomes visible when the two masters give conflicting orders.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the disciples: there was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him: what is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.

Setting. Chapter 16 is about money: a dishonest manager (vv. 1–13), the money-loving Pharisees (vv. 14–18), and a rich man and a poor man (vv. 19–31). The parable of the dishonest manager is one of the most puzzling in the Gospels. Read carefully, its point is clear.

He also said to the disciples. Though the Pharisees were listening (v. 14).

A rich man who had a manager. A manager (steward, oikonomos) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers: making contracts, lending, collecting rents. Absentee landlords were common in Galilee.

That this man was wasting his possessions. “Wasting” (diaskorpizōn): the same word used of the younger son squandering his inheritance (15:13). Incompetence or dishonesty.

Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager. He is fired. He must hand in the books. But he still has a short time before the dismissal takes effect.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who, hearing that his manager was wasting his property, fired him and demanded his accounts.

On a Tuesday. Everything you have belongs to God; you are only its manager. One day you will give an account.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manager said to himself: what shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.

What shall I do. A crisis, like the rich fool (12:17). But this man thinks ahead.

I am not strong enough to dig. Manual labour was hard and poorly paid.

And I am ashamed to beg. Pride.

I have decided what to do. A sudden idea.

So that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses. He will use his last days in office to make friends who will look after him when he is out of a job. He plans for his future.

In a sentence. The manager, unable to dig and ashamed to beg, came up with a plan to make people welcome him into their homes after he lost his job.

On a Tuesday. Are you planning ahead for your future, your eternal future?

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Summoning his master’s debtors one by one, he said to the first: how much do you owe my master? He said: a hundred measures of oil. He said to him: take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. Then he said to another: and how much do you owe? He said: a hundred measures of wheat. He said to him: take your bill, and write eighty.

Summoning his master’s debtors one by one. Tenant farmers who paid rent in produce, or merchants who had bought on credit.

A hundred measures of oil. The ESV notes the size: a hundred measures of oil was about 875 gallons (3,300 litres), the yield of perhaps 150 olive trees. A large debt.

Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. “Quickly”: before the master finds out. The debtor writes in his own hand, so the change cannot be traced to the manager. A reduction of fifty measures, worth about 500 denarii, more than a year and a half’s wages.

A hundred measures of wheat. About 1,000 bushels, the yield of about 100 acres.

Write eighty. A reduction of twenty, worth about the same as the oil reduction.

Was it dishonest? Some scholars suggest the manager was simply removing his own commission, or the interest, which the law forbade charging to fellow Jews (Deuteronomy 23:19). But Jesus calls him “dishonest” (v. 8). The simplest reading: he cheated his master to make friends of the debtors, who would now be grateful and in his debt.

In a sentence. The manager called in his master’s debtors and quickly had them reduce their bills, making them indebted to him.

On a Tuesday. The world is clever about its own interests. Are you as thoughtful about the things of God?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. The surprise of the parable. The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty. He is still a scoundrel (“dishonest manager”). But he was clever. He saw the crisis coming, and acted decisively to secure his future. The master, a man of the world, recognised a clever move when he saw one, even at his own expense.

For the sons of this world. Worldly people, who live for this age.

Are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. “Sons of light”: God’s people (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). The rebuke: worldly people are often wiser in pursuing their worldly goals than believers are in pursuing eternal ones. They think ahead, plan, take decisive action, use money cleverly. Christians are often careless about eternity.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not commending dishonesty, or teaching that the end justifies the means. A parable can use a bad man to make a good point (18:1–8, the unjust judge). The point is the manager’s urgency and foresight, not his ethics.

In a sentence. The master praised the dishonest manager for his shrewdness, for worldly people are often shrewder in their affairs than God’s people are in theirs.

On a Tuesday. Be as thoughtful, decisive and wise in eternal matters as worldly people are about money and career.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth. The application. “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions. Literally “mammon of unrighteousness”. Not necessarily wealth gained dishonestly, but wealth that belongs to this unrighteous world, which so often leads to sin. Use it wisely: to make friends, by giving to the poor and supporting the work of God.

So that when it fails. When money runs out, or when you die and it is useless to you.

They may receive you into the eternal dwellings. The manager made friends who would receive him into their houses; you can make friends who will welcome you into eternal homes. Those you have helped with your money, the poor and those who came to faith through the gospel you supported, will be there to welcome you. Or “they” may mean God. Either way: use money now with an eye on eternity. Lay up treasure in heaven (12:33).

What it does not mean. Not that you can buy your way into heaven. Salvation is by grace. But how you use money shows where your heart is, and true faith is generous.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends, so that when it runs out they will be welcomed into eternal homes.

On a Tuesday. How could you use your money this week in a way that will matter in eternity?
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much. Character shows in small things. Faithfulness is not a matter of the size of the task.

And one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. Small dishonesty reveals a dishonest heart.

If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth. Money is “a very little” compared with eternal things.

Who will entrust to you the true riches? The spiritual riches of the kingdom: God’s word, his grace, responsibility in his kingdom, eternal reward. How we handle money is a test of whether we can be trusted with greater things.

If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s. Money is not ours; it belongs to God. We are managers.

Who will give you that which is your own? The eternal inheritance that will truly be ours (1 Peter 1:4).

In a sentence. Faithfulness in small things like money shows whether someone can be trusted with the true riches of the kingdom, which will be their own.

On a Tuesday. Be faithful in small things: your money, your time, your promises. They reveal and shape your character.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

No servant can serve two masters. “Servant” (oiketēs): a household slave. A slave was owned completely by one master. Two owners would make impossible, conflicting demands.

Either he will hate the one and love the other. “Hate” and “love”: the Hebrew idiom for preference (14:26). One will always come first.

You cannot serve God and money. The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon. Money is personified as a rival god, a master demanding service. It promises security, power and happiness, the things only God can give. Money is a wonderful servant, but a terrible master. You must choose.

In a sentence. No one can be a slave to two masters, and so you cannot serve both God and money.

On a Tuesday. Which master do you serve? Your bank statement and your diary will tell you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees are described as lovers of money, which is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. But it was not a secret vice among them and did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

Their response is not argument. They ridiculed him, and that is the tell. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective: it requires no reasoning and lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Jesus goes past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. “You justify yourselves before men” describes the exhausting business of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience. And “abomination” is a heavy word, not chosen loosely — in the Old Testament it is a standard word for idols. He is not saying human and divine values sometimes differ. He is putting visible success, honour and social standing in the same category as an idol.

Then two verses that must be held together. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” dates an era, and John stands on the seam — the last of the old order and the herald of the new (cf. 7:28). But “not one dot of the Law” will become void: the dot is the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

The word holding them together is fulfilment. The Law's era as the way God's people related to him has closed; the Law itself has been kept — by the man saying this — and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it.

Which is why the divorce saying follows, and the placing is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things, by the party of permissive divorce rulings. He takes the point where their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law and shows who is actually relaxing it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Everyone forces his way into it” is a strange phrase and the translations divide: everyone is pressing in, or, as the ESV margin gives it, everyone is forcefully urged into it. Either way the point stands and it is not gentle: since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door (cf. Matt. 11:12).

There is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are shoving their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

The two verses guard against two opposite errors that are always with the church. One man reads “the Law and the Prophets were until John” and concludes the commandments no longer trouble him — that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes nothing has changed at all — that he is still under a covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him: the good news is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

And the permanence of the Law is why the sexual ethic is not negotiable. The Pharisees were known for liberal divorce interpretations — Hillel's school allowed it for almost any reason — and Jesus reaffirms the original design of Genesis 2:24 as the Law's continuing moral claim, not as something the kingdom relaxes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke gives the divorce saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and remarriage is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in: Matthew records the same teaching twice with an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds, and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Luke leaves the exception out because he is giving the rule, not the case law — which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says “never take this on an empty stomach” is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. The exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church: what about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18) — he calls them husbands, names the truth exactly, and does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that exists and carries real obligations.

Where there was sin it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross rather than dragged out every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: “and such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them: you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money. Not all Pharisees were wealthy, but many saw wealth as a sign of God’s blessing on the righteous (Deuteronomy 28:1–14). Money and piety went together, they thought.

And they ridiculed him. Literally “turned up their noses at him”, sneered. A poor teacher telling them about money!

You are those who justify yourselves before men. They made themselves look righteous in people’s eyes. Their wealth and religious reputation impressed others.

But God knows your hearts. He sees through appearances (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. “Abomination” (bdelygma): something detestable, used of idolatry. The things people admire, wealth, status, religious reputation, are often detestable to God when they flow from pride and self-love (Proverbs 16:5).

In a sentence. When the money-loving Pharisees sneered at him, Jesus said that they justified themselves before people, but God knows their hearts, and what people prize is detestable to God.

On a Tuesday. What do you admire most? Ask whether God values it.

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.

The Law and the Prophets were until John. The Old Testament era, the time of promise, lasted until John the Baptist. He was the last of the old-covenant prophets, the bridge between the ages (7:28).

Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached. A new era has begun: the time of fulfilment. The kingdom has come in Jesus.

And everyone forces his way into it. A difficult phrase. Possibly: everyone is pressing urgently to enter, with the earnest striving of 13:24, as the tax collectors and sinners do. Or: everyone is urged, pressed, to come in (14:23). Or (as in Matthew 11:12): the kingdom is suffering violence from its opponents. In Luke’s context, the first is most likely: people of all kinds are pressing into the kingdom, while the Pharisees stay outside.

In a sentence. The era of the Law and the Prophets lasted until John; since then the good news of the kingdom is preached, and people are pressing into it.

On a Tuesday. Enter the kingdom with urgency. Don’t stand at the door.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.

But. In case anyone thought the new era meant the law was abolished.

It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away. The most permanent things imaginable.

Than for one dot of the Law to become void. The “dot” (keraia, “little horn”) is a tiny stroke of a Hebrew letter, the smallest distinguishing mark, like the difference between letters. The law stands for ever. Not one word of God’s law will fail.

How the law continues. Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17–18). Its moral demands remain, summed up in love for God and neighbour. Its ceremonial laws, such as the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ, who is their reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). Its promises are kept in him. Nothing of God’s word is lost; it all reaches its goal.

In a sentence. Heaven and earth would sooner pass away than the smallest stroke of God’s law fail.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is more permanent than the universe. Build your life on it.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

Why here? An example of the permanence of God’s law (v. 17), against the Pharisees, who used the law to allow easy divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1). They justified themselves (v. 15) by quoting Moses, while breaking the deeper intent of God’s law for marriage. And perhaps a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias (3:19).

Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery. In God’s eyes, the marriage bond still holds, so remarriage is adultery (Mark 10:11–12).

And he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. The second husband too.

The exceptions. Luke, like Mark, gives the principle without exception. Matthew records the exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15).

Where Christians differ. As at Mark 10:10–12. Verdict: the Westminster position (Confession 24.5–6) is best: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery and wilful, irremediable desertion are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and remarry. Those who have sinned in divorce and remarriage can find full forgiveness in Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, as does the man who marries a divorced woman.

On a Tuesday. Honour marriage as God designed it. And if you have failed here, there is forgiveness in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The most extended treatment of life after death in the Synoptics, told as the direct sequel to the teaching on money.

Every detail of the opening is a price tag. Purple came from the murex shellfish and took thousands of them to colour a garment; the fine linen was a costly luxury cloth, and he feasted every day, not on feast days when ordinary people ate meat.

Lazarus was laid at the gate — passive, because he could not get there himself — and the gate is the great portal of a walled estate, which means the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He wanted what fell: not a place at the table but the scraps on the floor. And he did not get them. The dogs are not a comfort but the final degradation — scavenging pariah animals reaching him when no human being would.

Then the reversal, and it is total. Lazarus is carried — the same passivity as at the gate, and he does nothing in either case. “Abraham's side” is, as the ESV margin gives it, his bosom: at a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the guest of honour lay with his head near the host's chest, which is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple (John 13:23). The beggar who longed for what fell from a table is in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man is buried — a few words, and the last good thing that happens to him. And the first thing he sees from Hades is Lazarus: the one face he had trained himself not to register, and he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Everything he then says shows that nothing has been learned. He pleads descent — “Father Abraham,” exactly what John the Baptist warned against (3:8) — and twice says “send Lazarus,” still treating him as somebody who ought to be running errands.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story teaches several interlocking truths. There is conscious existence after death, prior to the resurrection: the rich man sees, recognises, feels pain and argues. This is consistent with 23:43 and with Paul (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23). The final state of the wicked involves real torment. And it is irreversible — the chasm “has been fixed,” established and standing established, and it is described as working in both directions. That second clause rules out something a sentimental reading would like: it is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him.

One caution on reading the scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

But the warning must not be softened by that caution — and the gulf of verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well. It was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to. One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did.

Abraham's “Child, remember” is tender and it is not an accusation. Nothing new is introduced; no list of sins is produced. He simply asks the man to recall a life in which he received his good things — got exactly what he had chosen, all of it, for as long as he lasted.
verseByVerse.examples:
One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything, and the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns.

That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was wealthy. Note also the one name in the story: the rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous, and the beggar is called Lazarus — named, and known. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily; what saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

“They have Moses and the Prophets” is one of the most important sentences in Luke. They had not been left without warning: the Law commands provision for the poor at your gate (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 15:7-11), and the Prophets say almost nothing more often — Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved, Isaiah on fasting that does not share bread with the hungry (Amos 6:4-6; Isa. 58:6-7). The rich man heard it read every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner.

And the final line is devastating for two reasons. The problem is never a shortage of evidence but an unwillingness to hear — miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it. And somebody did rise from the dead. When another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him too (John 12:10). The test was run, and it went exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.

The rich man and Lazarus. Only Luke records this story. It illustrates the danger of wealth (v. 13), the reversal of the beatitudes and woes (6:20–26), and the sufficiency of Scripture (vv. 29–31).

There was a rich man. Unnamed. Tradition calls him Dives, Latin for “rich”. He has no name before God.

Clothed in purple and fine linen. Purple dye was costly, and fine linen a luxury: the clothing of the very rich and of royalty.

And who feasted sumptuously every day. Not just on feast days. Constant luxury.

And at his gate was laid a poor man. “Laid”: thrown down, dumped there, perhaps by others, too disabled to walk. At the rich man’s gate, impossible to miss.

Named Lazarus. The only character in any of Jesus’ parables to be given a name. Lazarus, from Eleazar, means “God helps”. No one else did. The poor man has a name; the rich man does not. God knows the poor by name.

Covered with sores. Ulcerated, perhaps from malnutrition.

Who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Like the prodigal longing for pig food (15:16). Scraps. Diners used pieces of bread to wipe their hands, and threw them under the table. Even those were not given to him.

Even the dogs came and licked his sores. Street dogs, scavengers, unclean animals. He was too weak to keep them off. Perhaps the dogs showed him more attention than the rich man did.

The rich man’s sin. Not that he was rich, nor that he had done anything to Lazarus. He did nothing. He walked past the poor man at his gate every day and ignored him. His sin was neglect, indifference, the failure to love his neighbour.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who lived in daily luxury while a poor, sick man named Lazarus lay at his gate, longing for scraps, with dogs licking his sores.

On a Tuesday. Who is lying at your gate: someone in need whom you see every day and ignore?
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury — the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

The poor man died. No mention of a burial. Perhaps his body was thrown in a pauper’s grave.

And was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom”, the place of honour at a banquet, reclining next to the host (John 13:23). A picture of paradise, the blessed rest of the righteous with the father of the faithful, at the messianic banquet (13:28–29). Angels carried him.

The rich man also died and was buried. A grand funeral, no doubt. But death came to him too, and his wealth could not save him.

And in Hades, being in torment. Hades is the realm of the dead, here the place of punishment for the wicked. “Torment” (basanois): torture, agony. The reversal is complete: the rich man has nothing, Lazarus has everything (6:20–26; 1:53).

He lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. He can see what he has lost.

Where Christians differ: parable or history? And what happens after death? Some argue this is a literal description of the afterlife; others that it is a parable using popular imagery, and should not be pressed for details. Some (soul sleep, annihilationism) deny conscious existence after death. Verdict: it is a parable, and its details (seeing across the chasm, speaking, a drop of water) are pictures, not a map of the afterlife. But Jesus would not use a picture that taught falsehood. The story teaches clearly that at death there is conscious existence, that the righteous are comforted and the wicked suffer, immediately after death, that there is a fixed separation, and that destiny is settled at death. The fuller picture comes at the resurrection and final judgement.

In a sentence. When Lazarus died, angels carried him to Abraham’s side, but when the rich man died, he found himself in torment in Hades, seeing Lazarus far off with Abraham.

On a Tuesday. Death reveals what was true all along. Where you spend eternity is decided by how you respond to God now.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom” — the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called out: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame. But Abraham said: child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.

Father Abraham. He claims Abraham as his father (3:8). Physically, yes. But not in faith.

Have mercy on me. He never showed mercy to Lazarus. Now he begs for it.

Send Lazarus. Even now, he thinks of Lazarus as a servant to run his errands. He has not changed.

To dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue. A single drop. He who feasted every day now begs for one drop of water. The reversal of the scraps from his table.

For I am in anguish in this flame. Fire is a picture of the suffering of the lost (3:17; Mark 9:43–48).

Child. Abraham speaks gently. But the answer is no.

Remember. Memory remains. A torment in itself.

You in your lifetime received your good things. “Your good things”: he had his comfort in this life, and chose it as his portion (6:24). He lived for himself, and got what he lived for.

And Lazarus in like manner bad things. Not that Lazarus was saved because he was poor. His name, “God helps”, suggests he trusted God. But in this life, he received evil.

But now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. The great reversal.

In a sentence. The rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water, but Abraham reminded him that he had received his good things in life, and now Lazarus was comforted and he was in anguish.

On a Tuesday. If your good things are all in this life, you have nothing left for eternity. Store up treasure in heaven.

parallels.desc: men whose portion is in this life

verseByVerse.quote: And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.

A great chasm has been fixed. “Fixed” (estērktai): firmly established, perfect tense, permanent. By God.

So that those who would pass from here to you may not be able. Not even out of compassion.

And none may cross from there to us. No escape from punishment.

No second chance. After death, destiny is fixed. There is no crossing, no purgatory, no second chance (Hebrews 9:27: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgement). The time to repent is now. The rich man had a chasm at his gate, between himself and Lazarus, which he could have crossed any day. Now a chasm separates them that cannot be crossed.

In a sentence. A great chasm has been fixed between the blessed and the lost, so that no one can cross from one side to the other.

On a Tuesday. Now is the time to cross the chasm between you and those in need, and between you and God. After death, it will be too late.

parallels.desc: to die once, and after that comes judgment

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment. But Abraham said: they have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.

Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house. Still treating Lazarus as an errand boy. But now he shows some concern, for his family.

For I have five brothers. Living as he had lived.

So that he may warn them. “Warn” (diamartyrētai): testify earnestly. A hint of self-justification: if only I had been warned properly, I would not be here.

They have Moses and the Prophets. “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures. They have everything they need. The law commanded care for the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Isaiah 58:6–7; Amos 6:4–7, which describes the rich lying on ivory beds while ignoring the ruin of others). And the Scriptures point to repentance and faith.

Let them hear them. Listen and obey.

The sufficiency of Scripture. God’s word is enough to bring people to repentance and salvation (2 Timothy 3:15–17). They do not need a special messenger from the dead.

In a sentence. The rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers, but Abraham said they had the Scriptures and should listen to them.

On a Tuesday. You have the Scriptures. Listen to them. They are all you need.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures.

parallels.desc: if you believed Moses, you would believe me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: no, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent. He said to him: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.

No, father Abraham. He contradicts Abraham. Scripture is not enough, he thinks.

If someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent. A spectacular sign would convince them. The common belief that if only there were more evidence, people would believe.

If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets. The problem is not lack of evidence, but hardness of heart.

Neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead. A haunting prophecy. Someone did rise from the dead: Jesus himself. And the Pharisees and leaders were not convinced. They bribed the soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). And in John’s Gospel, when another Lazarus was raised from the dead, the leaders plotted to kill him and Jesus (John 11:43–53; 12:10–11). Miracles do not create faith in those who reject God’s word. Faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), by the work of the Spirit.

In a sentence. When the rich man insisted that someone returning from the dead would make his brothers repent, Abraham replied that if they would not listen to Scripture, they would not be convinced even by someone rising from the dead.

For worship. Someone has risen from the dead. Listen to the Scriptures that point to him, and believe.

parallels.desc: after Lazarus of Bethany is raised, they plot to kill Jesus

16.text: <sup>1</sup> He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. <sup>2</sup> And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ <sup>3</sup> And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. <sup>4</sup> I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’ <sup>5</sup> So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ <sup>6</sup> He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ <sup>7</sup> Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ <sup>8</sup> The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. <sup>10</sup> “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. <sup>11</sup> If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? <sup>12</sup> And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own? <sup>13</sup> No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.” <sup>14</sup> The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 gathers teachings that might appear loosely connected but share a common thread: the shape of life in the kingdom as it moves toward its final consummation. Disciples are warned about causing others to stumble, commanded to forgive repeatedly, confronted about the nature of faith, and then — after the extraordinary healing of ten lepers — taught about gratitude. The chapter then pivots to sustained teaching about the coming of the Son of Man: apocalyptic instruction that would be at home in the Olivet Discourse.

The healing of the ten lepers is one of the most poignant episodes in Luke, precisely because of what does not happen: nine healed men simply walk away. The one who returns is a Samaritan — an outsider — and his return becomes the occasion for Jesus to say something remarkable: “your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” The nine received physical healing; the one received something more.

The eschatological teaching (vv. 20–37) is deliberately disorienting. The kingdom does not come with observable signs (v. 20); it is already in your midst (v. 21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come with lightning-like sudden visibility (v. 24). The tension is not a contradiction: the kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus, but its final manifestation remains future — and when it comes, it will be unmistakable, inescapable, and final.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Four short teachings, each pressing the disciples on a different part of their calling.

The ESV margin gives “temptations to sin” as “stumbling blocks” — not primarily an enticement but an obstacle set in somebody's path. Drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew who expected burial in his own ground, and it is offered as the preferable outcome.

The weight of the saying falls on the influential, because nobody trips a person who is not following them. The “little ones” include children and reach wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The forgiveness command opens with “pay attention to yourselves,” and the order governs everything after it — a man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not. Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic: anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere, and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself. The test is not whether the repentance convinces but whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

The apostles respond “Increase our faith!” — and note when. Not before a storm or a demon. They have been told to forgive, and they say they have not got enough of whatever it takes. The answer is not what they asked for: he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

Then the servant parable, which checks the pride that obedience produces. And note the condition: “when you have done all that you were commanded” — this is the sentence for the best possible day, with nothing outstanding. Even then there is no credit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching anticipates the Lord's Prayer — “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes the effect of justification on a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The mulberry saying needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and made into a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once about the tumour and the child. It cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where it sits: the apostles asked for help to forgive, and this is his answer about that. Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel — if this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed, and men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer offered in perfect faith: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). Nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

Achreioi — “unworthy” — means unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. And it must be guarded from the opposite error, because the same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage; there is a Master who pays anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents and leaves the other case open. What if he never says “I repent”? That silence is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and Jesus attaches it to “if he repents.” You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally; you cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

That protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

And the servant parable has a reader for whom the whole scene will sting: anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement, doing the work that is simply expected and eating after everybody else. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to his disciples: temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.

Setting. After the parables about money and the Pharisees, Jesus turns to his disciples with four short teachings on life in the community of faith: do not cause others to stumble, forgive, have faith, and serve without seeking credit.

Temptations to sin are sure to come. “Temptations” (skandala): stumbling blocks, traps, anything that trips someone into sin or out of faith. In a fallen world they are inevitable.

But woe to the one through whom they come! Inevitability does not excuse responsibility. Each person who causes another to fall is accountable.

A millstone … cast into the sea. The heavy upper stone of a mill, turned by a donkey. Drowning with it would be a terrible death, and a body that could not be buried. Yet that would be better than the judgement that awaits whoever destroys the faith of another.

One of these little ones. Humble, ordinary, perhaps young or new believers, the tax collectors and sinners just come to Jesus (15:1).

In a sentence. Stumbling blocks are inevitable, but woe to the person who causes one of Jesus’ little ones to fall, for drowning would be a better fate.

On a Tuesday. Your example is watched by others. Never be the reason a weaker believer falls.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you must forgive him.

Pay attention to yourselves! Watch yourselves: your own example, and your own heart.

If your brother sins, rebuke him. Love does not ignore sin. A fellow believer who sins should be lovingly confronted, privately first (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Silence is not always kindness.

And if he repents, forgive him. The goal of rebuke is restoration, not humiliation.

Seven times in the day. Seven: completeness. Not a limit, but limitless forgiveness (Matthew 18:21–22: seventy-seven times). Even if his repentance seems unconvincing, if he says “I repent”, forgive.

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong, or always restoring full trust at once, or removing all consequences. But it means letting go of the debt and of revenge, and being ready to restore the relationship.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to rebuke a sinning brother and to forgive him whenever he repents, even seven times in a day.

On a Tuesday. Is there a brother or sister you need to confront lovingly, or forgive again?

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles said to the Lord: increase our faith! And the Lord said: if you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it would obey you.

Increase our faith! The response to the demand to forgive without limit. They feel unable. A good prayer.

If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed. The smallest seed (13:19). Jesus does not say they need more faith, but real faith. The size of faith matters less than its object. Tiny faith in a great God can do great things.

This mulberry tree. The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system and was very hard to uproot. It was said to live six hundred years.

Be uprooted and planted in the sea. A deliberately impossible picture: a tree growing in the sea. Faith does the impossible, because God does. Forgiving seven times a day may feel like uprooting a mulberry tree; faith in God makes it possible.

In a sentence. When the apostles asked for more faith, Jesus said that even faith as small as a mustard seed could uproot a tree and plant it in the sea.

For worship. Bring your small faith to a great God. He does the impossible.
verseByVerse.note: The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any one of you who has a servant ploughing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field: come at once and recline at table? Will he not rather say to him: prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterwards you will eat and drink?

A servant ploughing or keeping sheep. A slave who worked in the field by day and in the house in the evening. A small farmer with one slave.

Come at once and recline at table? No master would serve his slave first. That was not how things worked.

Prepare supper for me. The slave’s duty continued.

The point. Not about how masters should treat slaves, but about the disciple’s attitude to God. A slave does not expect special reward for doing his duty. Elsewhere Jesus says the Master will serve his faithful servants (12:37): that is grace, not obligation.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether a master would invite his slave to sit and eat when he came in from the field, rather than expecting him to prepare and serve his master’s meal first.

On a Tuesday. Serve God without expecting thanks or reward for doing what you should.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say: we are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.

Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? No. A slave doing his job puts no one in his debt.

When you have done all that you were commanded. And no one has (Romans 3:23).

We are unworthy servants. “Unworthy” (achreioi): not deserving special merit, owed nothing. Not worthless, but with no claim on the master.

We have only done what was our duty. Obedience to God is our duty, not a favour to him. We cannot put God in our debt (Romans 11:35). This destroys the idea of earning salvation or merit by good works. Even our best obedience earns nothing; we owe God everything. Any reward he gives is pure grace.

Where Christians differ: merit. Medieval theology developed a doctrine of merit, including “works of supererogation”, good works beyond what is required, which built up a treasury of merit in the church. Verdict: this verse refutes it. No one can do more than duty requires. Even after doing everything, we are unworthy servants. Reward is grace.

In a sentence. When disciples have done everything commanded, they should say they are unworthy servants who have only done their duty.

For worship. You can never put God in your debt. Serve him gladly, and receive his rewards as gifts of grace.

parallels.desc: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is in the border country where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory — a detail that will matter in five verses.

The ten stand at a distance because the law required it: a man with the disease lived outside the camp, in torn clothes, calling “unclean” as anyone approached (Lev. 13:45-46). “Leprosy” covered a range of skin conditions, but the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis — total exclusion from worship, family, work, and touch.

And ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever each had been before, the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. Which is what makes verse 16 so striking: one of these ten is a Samaritan. Nine Jews and a Samaritan are living together outside a village, because the disease has done to their divisions what nothing else could.

“Master” is, everywhere else in this Gospel, on the lips of disciples. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, leaving the content of it to him.

He does not touch them and does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand that only makes sense afterwards — the inspection of Leviticus 14 is what you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence.

“And as they went they were cleansed.” Not before they went. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed.

One turns back — and it is worth being clear that the other nine were obeying. Until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them stops.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story illustrates the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one responded to the Giver. And the nine were not ingrates by worldly standards — their failure was not defiance but distraction. They moved from the gift to the system without pausing to return.

The Samaritan's outsider status is theologically loaded in Luke, who shows Samaritans in a positive light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5).

And the point is sharper than it first appears. The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem — to the temple, the sacrifices, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place open to him, and it turned out to be the right one.

“Foreigner” at v.18 is allogenēs, a word found only here in the New Testament — and it is the word carved on the stone barrier in the temple court warning Gentiles not to pass beyond on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him, and the only man in the story fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
