“Your faith has made you well” — or, as the ESV margin gives it, “has saved you.” Luke has used those words to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48).

Which answers the obvious difficulty: all ten were cleansed, so what is left for this man to receive? Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved. A man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

And notice what his faith actually consisted of, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men, obeyed an instruction that made no sense, and when he saw what had happened, turned round and went back to the one who did it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in his story.

The three questions at v.17 are among the few places where Jesus expresses something like disappointment at how he has been treated. He does not do it elsewhere for himself — not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner.

And the nine are not villains but ordinary. Nobody in that group decided to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers; within weeks the thankfulness has given way to relief and resumed normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance.

On the way to Jerusalem. The journey continues (9:51). Only Luke records this healing.

Between Samaria and Galilee. Along the border, where Jews and Samaritans lived near each other.

He was met by ten lepers. Lepers lived together outside towns, cut off from society (Leviticus 13:46). Shared misery had joined Jews and a Samaritan together.

Who stood at a distance. Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning (Leviticus 13:45). They could not approach.

In a sentence. On the way to Jerusalem, on the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus was met by ten lepers who kept their distance as the law required.

On a Tuesday. Suffering often breaks down barriers that pride builds. Jesus meets the outcasts on the edges.
verseByVerse.note: Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And lifted up their voices, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. When he saw them he said to them: go and show yourselves to the priests. And as they went they were cleansed.

Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. “Master” (epistata), a word only Luke uses, elsewhere only from disciples. The cry for mercy (18:13, 38).

Go and show yourselves to the priests. A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin society (Leviticus 14:2–32; 5:14). Jesus tells them to go before they are healed. A test of faith: will they go, still leprous, trusting his word?

And as they went they were cleansed. As they obeyed. Faith acts on Christ’s word before seeing the result, like Naaman, who was healed when he obeyed and washed (2 Kings 5:14).

In a sentence. The lepers cried for mercy, and Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went, they were healed.

On a Tuesday. Obey Christ’s word before you see the result. Blessing often comes on the way.
verseByVerse.note: A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin the community.

parallels.desc: he shall be brought to the priest

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.

When he saw that he was healed, turned back. Before reaching the priest. He could not wait to give thanks.

Praising God with a loud voice. Loudly, as loudly as he had cried for mercy.

And he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet. Worship. He gives glory to God, and does so at Jesus’ feet. Praising God and thanking Jesus are the same act.

Giving him thanks. “Thanks” (eucharistōn), from which comes “Eucharist”.

Now he was a Samaritan. The punchline, delayed for effect. The despised outsider, the heretic, is the only one who returns (10:33). Samaritans and Jews despised each other.

In a sentence. One of the ten, seeing he was healed, came back praising God loudly and fell at Jesus’ feet to thank him, and he was a Samaritan.

For worship. Have you come back to thank Jesus for what he has done? Do it now.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other; shared misery had joined these ten.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus answered: were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?

Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Jesus notices. He notices our gratitude, and our ingratitude. The nine were probably doing what they were told, going to the priests. Perhaps rushing home to their families. But they did not return.

Except this foreigner? “Foreigner” (allogenēs): the word on the temple inscription that warned foreigners not to enter the inner courts on pain of death. The outsider, excluded from the temple, comes to Jesus, the true temple, to worship.

The lesson. Ingratitude is common. Many receive God’s blessings and never return to thank him (Romans 1:21: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him). And outsiders often respond better than insiders.

In a sentence. Jesus asked where the other nine were, and why only this foreigner had returned to give praise to God.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of God’s blessings this week, and thank him for each one.

parallels.desc: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.

Rise and go your way. Go on to the priests, and to your new life.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken): has saved you. All ten were cleansed; this one was saved. The nine received physical healing; the Samaritan received more: salvation, a restored relationship with God through Christ. The difference was faith that returned in worship. Physical blessing is not the same as salvation.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Samaritan to rise and go, for his faith had saved him.

For worship. The greatest gift is not healing but salvation. If you have it, thank him with your whole life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, and the question assumes a datable event that can be worked out by people currently standing outside it.

“Not coming in ways that can be observed” rules out surveillance for signs, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

“The kingdom of God is in the midst of you” has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it “within you,” and that has been carried off to mean that the kingdom is an inner glow native to every human heart. The ESV margin allows “within you,” so the translation is not dishonest — what settles it is who he is addressing. He is answering the Pharisees, who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53-54). He is not telling them the kingdom is glowing inside their hearts; he is telling them it is standing in the room.

Turning to the disciples, he warns of days when they will long to see one ordinary day of his presence and will not. The longing is named and allowed — and then he deals with the danger it creates, because a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will travel to where somebody says he has. The lightning settles it: nobody has ever been told where the lightning was.

Then, dropped into the middle of it, verse 25: first he must suffer. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man about to be spat at and hung up outside a city wall, and he will be that first.

The Noah and Lot examples select, out of everything available, the ordinary: eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting and building. Not one is a sin. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tension between “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” and “the days of the Son of Man are coming” is the foundation of the New Testament's already-not-yet. The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus; it has not yet come in fullness. Believers live in the overlap.

“Revealed” at v.30 means unveiled — which says something precise about what is coming. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from elsewhere like a visitor; he will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen. The day does not change where he is; it changes what can be seen.

On the missing verse 36: your Bible may go straight from 35 to 37, or may print a verse 36 reading “two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who borrowed Matthew's “two men in the field” to bring Luke's two examples up to three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the chapter, which is why the gap is visible — honest bookkeeping, with the workings printed rather than tidied away.

On “taken”: popular retellings fix the picture so that the taken are caught up to safety. But two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both it was the judgement that did the taking — the flood swept them all away, and the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Remember Lot's wife” is one of the shortest verses in Luke, and it does not need the story told. She had been brought out by the hand — the angels seized Lot and his wife and set them outside the city, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Gen. 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back.

Her looking back was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town — her house, her daughters, the whole shape of a life. She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her.

Which is worth taking personally rather than eschatologically. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward; he is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say “remember Sodom.” He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it” is a statement about how reality is constructed rather than a piece of moral advice, and everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the man who protects his reputation above everything is left with nothing but a reputation. The grip is what loses the thing.

And the disciples' “Where, Lord?” is our instinct exactly. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want is the geography. He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them: the kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, look, here it is! or there! For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.

When the kingdom of God would come. The Pharisees expected a visible, political kingdom, with signs announcing it: the defeat of Rome and the restoration of Israel.

The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed. “Observed” (paratērēseōs): watched for by signs, as astronomers watch the sky. You cannot calculate it by signs.

Nor will they say, Look, here it is! or There! It is not a place you can point to on a map.

For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you. The ESV notes the alternative: “within you”. Most scholars prefer “in the midst of you” or “among you”, because Jesus was speaking to Pharisees, in whose hearts the kingdom certainly was not. The kingdom is present in the person of Jesus, the King, standing among them, and in his works (11:20). They are looking for signs, and the King is in front of them. And the kingdom is also present wherever God reigns in human hearts.

In a sentence. Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom would come, Jesus said it would not come with observable signs, for the kingdom of God was already in their midst.

On a Tuesday. Don’t look for the kingdom in political movements or spectacular signs. It is found where Jesus reigns.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the kingdom of God is within you”; “in the midst of you” fits the setting — the King stood among them.

parallels.desc: the kingdom has come upon you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to the disciples: the days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, look, there! or, look, here! Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

Now to the disciples. The kingdom is present (v. 21), but its fullness is still to come, at the return of the Son of Man.

You will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. After Jesus’ departure, in times of persecution and waiting, his disciples will long for his presence, or for his return, and it will not come as soon as they wish.

Look, there! or Look, here! False claims about Christ’s return, or false messiahs (21:8; Matthew 24:23–26).

Do not go out or follow them. Don’t be deceived.

For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other. His return will be sudden, visible to all, unmistakable, universal. No one will need to tell you where he is. Every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples that they would long for his coming and should not be deceived by claims that he had appeared somewhere, for his coming would be as visible as lightning across the sky.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be taken in by anyone who claims to know where or when Christ will return. When he comes, everyone will know.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

But first. Before the glory, the cross.

He must suffer many things. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, God’s plan (9:22). The way to glory goes through suffering (24:26).

And be rejected by this generation. By the people of his own time.

In a sentence. But before his glorious coming, the Son of Man must first suffer and be rejected by his generation.

For worship. The one who will come like lightning first came to suffer for you. Worship him for both.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

Just as it was in the days of Noah. Genesis 6–7. Jesus treats Noah and the flood as real history.

They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage. Ordinary life. Nothing wrong with any of these things. The problem was that they were absorbed in them, and ignored God’s warnings through Noah, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Life went on as normal, as if judgement would never come.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Sudden. Too late. The door was shut (Genesis 7:16).

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the flood in Noah’s day, when people carried on with ordinary life until the flood suddenly destroyed them.

On a Tuesday. Are you so absorbed in ordinary life that you have forgotten Christ is coming?

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot (they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all), so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.

In the days of Lot. Genesis 19. Sodom was notorious for its wickedness, but Jesus emphasises its ordinariness.

Eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. Business as usual: commerce, agriculture, construction. The busyness of a prosperous city, with no thought of God.

On the day when Lot went out from Sodom. The moment the righteous were removed, judgement fell.

Fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. Sudden and complete.

So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. “Revealed” (apokalyptetai): unveiled. He is present now, hidden; then he will be revealed in glory. And judgement will be as sudden and complete.

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the destruction of Sodom, which fell suddenly on people busy with everyday business the day Lot left.

On a Tuesday. Business and building are not wrong. But don’t let them make you forget the day of the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife.

Let the one who is on the housetop … not come down to take them away. Similar words in 21:21 and Mark 13:15–16 concern flight from Jerusalem. Here the point is different: on the day of Christ’s coming, there will be no time to save possessions, and no point. Attachment to things will be fatal.

And likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Don’t look back to what you are leaving (9:62).

Remember Lot’s wife. The shortest verse in Luke. She looked back to Sodom as she fled, and was turned into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). Her heart was still in Sodom, with her possessions and her old life. She was saved from the city, but lost because she could not let go of it. A warning to those who follow Jesus but whose hearts are attached to this world.

In a sentence. On that day, no one should go back for possessions or turn back, but remember Lot’s wife, who looked back and was destroyed.

On a Tuesday. What are you tempted to look back to? Remember Lot’s wife, and fix your heart on Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.

Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it. Lot’s wife tried to hold on to her old life, and lost everything. Those who cling to this world will lose it, and their souls.

But whoever loses his life will keep it. “Keep” (zōogonēsei): preserve alive, keep it alive. Those who give up their lives to Christ gain eternal life (9:24).

In a sentence. Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will preserve it.

On a Tuesday. What are you clinging to? Let go of it for Christ, and you will find true life.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left. And they said to him: where, Lord? He said to them: where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.

In that night there will be two in one bed. The coming of the Son of Man will divide people who were closest: husband and wife, or two companions.

There will be two women grinding together. Two women working side by side at a hand mill, grinding grain, a daily task done in the morning. Night and day: whenever he comes.

One will be taken and the other left. A sudden separation, with no warning. Outwardly the same, inwardly different.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36: Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left. Probably added from Matthew 24:40.

Where, Lord? Where will they be taken?

Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. A proverb. As certainly as vultures gather around a dead body, judgement will fall wherever there is spiritual death. The question “where?” is pointless; judgement will come where it is deserved, as visibly as vultures circling. Those “taken” are taken to judgement, to the vultures.

Where Christians differ: one taken, one left. Dispensationalists teach that “one will be taken” describes the secret rapture of believers before a tribulation, as in the novels and films about being “left behind”. Verdict: in context, the comparisons with Noah and Lot (vv. 26–30) show that those taken are taken in judgement, like those swept away by the flood, while those left are like Noah and Lot, spared. And the vultures (v. 37) show that being taken means death. There is no secret rapture here. Christ’s coming will be visible like lightning (v. 24), and will bring both the gathering of his people and judgement, at one public return.

In a sentence. At the Son of Man’s coming, people side by side will be separated, one taken and one left, and judgement will come wherever it is due, as surely as vultures gather over a corpse.

On a Tuesday. Being near a believer will not save you. Make sure you are ready for his coming yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36, “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” and that “vultures” may also be rendered “eagles.”

17.text: <sup>1</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! <sup>2</sup> It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin. <sup>3</sup> Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan. <sup>17</sup> Then Jesus answered, “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. <sup>35</sup> There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.” <sup>37</sup> And they said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is constructed around a series of contrasts: persistent widow versus unjust judge; Pharisee versus tax collector; those who would keep children from Jesus versus Jesus who receives them; a rich ruler who becomes very sad versus disciples who have left everything; a blind beggar who cries out versus those who rebuke his cry. In each pair, the unexpected person receives what they need — and the principle is always the same: those who come to God with empty hands receive; those who come convinced they already have what is required leave empty.

Luke tells us explicitly why Jesus told the opening parables. The widow-and-judge parable is told to show that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). The Pharisee-and-tax-collector parable addresses “those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Together they define authentic prayer: persistent, humble, directed entirely toward a God who can do what we cannot.

The final section (vv. 31–43) contains the third passion prediction — which the disciples cannot understand — and closes with a blind beggar, a man who cannot see physically but sees Jesus with perfect spiritual clarity: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us the point before the story starts — something he rarely does — which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed. And the two halves of the purpose are the same thing from two sides: “always to pray” and “not lose heart,” where the second word means to grow weary, to give out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting.

Note where it sits. The previous paragraph closed with a discourse about a day that comes without warning after a long wait. This parable is what to do in the meantime.

The judge is described comprehensively: he neither feared God nor respected man, which is the whole of the Old Testament's requirement for the office (cf. 2 Chr. 19:6-7). He is not corrupt — a bribe would be a lever, and a lever would work. He simply does not care, and Luke says so twice, once as narrator and once in the man's own mouth, so nobody can call it a hostile characterisation.

The widow is the other end of the scale. Without husband, father or male relative she had no standing in a court at all, no money for a lawyer and no influence. And the law was emphatic about her: God “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deut. 10:18), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deut. 27:19). The one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

What she asks for is not charity but a verdict — “give me justice” — vindicate me. And the judge's phrase for what she is doing to him is violent: she will beat him down. He is not worn down by sympathy or shamed into it. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place.

So justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, by a man who cared nothing about it, because one powerless woman would not go away. Which is the setup for the argument, and the argument runs by contrast: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a mechanism for overcoming divine reluctance. The unjust judge is the contrast, not the model — this is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and every term in v.7 is set against him. He had no fear of God; this is God. The widow was a stranger; these are “his elect.” She was a nuisance at a door; they “cry to him day and night,” which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile.

And Jesus raises the delay himself rather than pretending it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming a long time. What is denied is not the delay but its meaning: the widow's problem was that her judge did not care, and that was the only reason for her wait. Whatever the reason for yours, it is not that one — because the one you are asking chose you.

“Speedily” does not promise a quick answer. It means without dawdling — that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And notice what the elect are crying for: not relief but justice, the setting right of all things, which arrives in full at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life; every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come asking whether God will keep faith with us; he settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us — and he leaves it open, which is more unsettling than any answer would have been.

The “nevertheless” is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is not. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address: the risk is not an unanswering God but a widow who stops coming.

So if you are still praying after eleven years and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

And there is a word here for the man whose prayer life has quietly collapsed — who prays in a crisis but finds sustained daily prayer pointless, since God knows what he needs anyway. The purpose of persistent prayer is not to overcome divine ignorance. It is to keep the heart oriented toward the right Source, and to sustain the posture of a person who genuinely believes help is coming from outside himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said: in a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.

The link. Jesus has just spoken of the days before the Son of Man comes, when disciples will long for him and not see him (17:22). How should they live while waiting? By prayer.

To the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. Luke tells us the point before the parable begins. “Always”: persistently, continually. “Lose heart” (enkakein): give up, grow weary, become discouraged. The great danger in the long wait is to stop praying.

A judge who neither feared God nor respected man. A corrupt, godless judge, accountable to no one, moved by nothing. In Israel, judges were to judge fairly, fearing God (2 Chronicles 19:6–7; Deuteronomy 16:18–20). This one feared nothing and no one.

In a sentence. Jesus told a parable to teach that his disciples should always pray and not give up, about a judge who neither feared God nor cared about people.

On a Tuesday. Have you given up praying for something? This parable is for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying: give me justice against my adversary. For a while he refused, but afterwards he said to himself: though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.

A widow. Widows had no one to plead their case. The law singled them out for protection (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17, 23). A widow without money for a bribe or a man to speak for her was helpless before a corrupt judge.

Who kept coming to him. The tense means repeated, continual coming. Her only weapon was persistence.

Give me justice against my adversary. Perhaps a debt, or her inheritance being stolen. She asks not for revenge but for justice.

For a while he refused. He had no reason to help her.

Because this widow keeps bothering me. Not justice, not compassion, but annoyance.

So that she will not beat me down by her continual coming. “Beat me down” (hypōpiazē): literally “give me a black eye”, a boxing term. Perhaps he means: wear me out, or shame me publicly. Either way, he gives in, to get rid of her.

In a sentence. A widow kept coming to the judge for justice, and though he refused for a while, he finally gave it to her just to stop her pestering.

On a Tuesday. Keep coming to God, as this widow kept coming. Persistence is not wasted.
verseByVerse.note: Widows had no one to plead their case; the law singled them out for protection.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord said: hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?

Hear what the unrighteous judge says. Listen to the point.

And will not God give justice to his elect. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater (11:13): if even this unjust judge gives justice to a widow he cares nothing for, how much more will God give justice to his chosen people, whom he loves? God is not like the judge. He is just, and he cares. The contrast is the point. “His elect” (eklektōn): his chosen ones (Romans 8:33: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?).

Who cry to him day and night? The persistent prayer of God’s people, suffering in a hostile world, longing for justice and for Christ’s return (Revelation 6:10: how long, O Lord?).

Will he delay long over them? Or: will he be patient with them, or keep them waiting? God is patient (2 Peter 3:9), but he will not abandon his people.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if an unjust judge gave justice, how much more will God give justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night.

For worship. You are not pleading with an unjust judge, but with your loving Father, who chose you. Pray with confidence.
verseByVerse.note: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge acts, how much more God.

parallels.desc: I cry out day and night before you

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?

He will give justice to them speedily. “Speedily” (en tachei): quickly, or suddenly. From our point of view, it may seem long. From God’s, it is soon (2 Peter 3:8). And when justice comes, at Christ’s return, it will come suddenly.

Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? A searching question. God will certainly be faithful. The question is whether we will be. “Faith”: literally “the faith”, this kind of persistent, praying faith. Will his people still be praying, still trusting, when he returns, or will they have given up? The question is not answered. It is put to each reader.

In a sentence. God will give his people justice quickly, but when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?

On a Tuesday. When Christ comes, will he find faith in you: still praying, still trusting? Keep praying today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke names the target before the story begins, and the two clauses belong together as cause and effect. “Trusted in themselves that they were righteous” places confidence in something that can be inspected — and a righteousness that has to be maintained needs a scale, and a scale needs other people on it. The contempt is not an unfortunate trait attached to an otherwise sound position; it is generated by the position.

Note too that Luke does not say “to the Pharisees.” He says “to some who” — a description rather than a party, which leaves the door open for anybody to walk through.

The pairing is as wide as first-century Judaism could make it. A Pharisee was a serious man who took the law seriously enough to organise his life around it. A tax collector had contracted with the occupying power to extract money from his own people and was barred from giving evidence in court.

A word about the wording at v.11, since translations differ and something has been built on the difference. The phrase can attach either to the standing or to the praying — the ESV text has “standing by himself, prayed,” and its margin “standing, prayed to himself”; some older versions take the second, and preachers have made much of the idea that his prayer never got past his own ears. It is a fair possibility and not certain, and it should not carry weight the text will not bear.

What is certain is the content. The prayer opens correctly — thanksgiving, addressed to God — and then turns into a list of other people, the fourth of whom is standing in the same courtyard. And both claims are almost certainly true and both exceed what was required: the law commanded one fast a year, and he does two a week; the tithe was on produce, and he tithes everything.

This is not a fraud. He is doing more than God asked. Which is what makes the parable uncomfortable, because the natural reading is that his problem was insincerity, and it was not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is a pre-Pauline statement of justification by faith alone. The tax collector contributes nothing except his need and his cry — no promise of reformation, no religious performance, no favourable comparison — and he goes home justified.

His plea is worth pausing on. It is not “overlook my sin.” He is standing in the temple, very possibly at the hour when a lamb was being killed, asking for mercy on the only terms that building knew — sin dealt with by sacrifice. Paul will name what he was reaching for: Christ, “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Rom. 3:25).

And he names himself without qualification: “a sinner.” Which is what a man says when he has stopped comparing: the Pharisee could see four categories of people and himself above them, and this man cannot see anybody else in the building.

“Justified” is a courtroom word — a verdict entered in his favour, by somebody else, and standing. So a man who had defrauded his neighbours for a living walked out with a legal standing before God that the most religious man in the country did not have.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rather than the other” is not “more than.” The Pharisee went home exactly as he arrived, which is the quiet tragedy of the parable: nothing happened to him at all. He came with a balance and took it away again.

And the closing principle needs one guard, because it can be turned into a technique. A man who humbles himself in order to be exalted has exalted himself, and the verse has already seen him. The tax collector was not performing humility; he was telling the truth, and it happened to be devastating — which is the only humility that has ever done anybody any good.

The parable also exposes what religious confidence actually costs. The Pharisee's problem was not that his facts were wrong but that his arithmetic required a comparison, and comparison requires somebody underneath. He had looked around the courtyard, found the tax collector, and put him in the prayer.

A man in a small group shares prayer requests — articulate, theologically sophisticated, focused on what he is doing for God. A woman prays: “Lord, I don't know what to say. I'm a mess. Have mercy.” Authentic prayer is measured not by eloquence but by honesty about need, and one of those two is a good deal closer to going home justified.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: 'Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.

The second prayer parable. The first parable was about persistence in prayer; this one is about humility in prayer. And it is one of the clearest pictures of justification in the Gospels.

To some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous. Luke again gives the point first. Self-righteousness: trusting in one’s own goodness to be right with God.

And treated others with contempt. “Treated with contempt” (exouthenountas): despised, considered as nothing. Self-righteousness always looks down on others.

Two men went up into the temple to pray. Probably at the hours of prayer, the morning or afternoon sacrifice, when people gathered to pray (Acts 3:1).

One a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. Pharisees were respected for their devotion to the law; tax collectors were despised as traitors and cheats (3:12; 19:7). To Jesus’ hearers, the Pharisee was the obvious hero, the tax collector the obvious villain.

In a sentence. To those who trusted in their own righteousness and despised others, Jesus told of a Pharisee and a tax collector who went up to the temple to pray.

On a Tuesday. Do you trust in your own goodness? Do you look down on anyone? This parable is aimed at you.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were respected for their devotion to the law; tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats. Public prayers were offered at the temple morning and afternoon.

parallels.desc: the hour of prayer, the ninth hour

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.

Standing by himself. Or “standing, prayed to himself”. Either he stood apart, so as not to be defiled by others, or his prayer was really addressed to himself. Probably both.

God, I thank you that I am not like other men. It sounds like a prayer of thanks. But he thanks God for himself, not for God’s mercy. He asks for nothing; he does not think he needs anything. He uses “I” five times in two verses.

Extortioners, unjust, adulterers. He compares himself with notorious sinners, and of course comes off well.

Or even like this tax collector. He looks at the man behind him with contempt.

I fast twice a week. The law required only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Strict Pharisees fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. He did more than required.

I give tithes of all that I get. Tithes even of what others should already have tithed (11:42). Again, more than required.

The problem. He was probably telling the truth about his outward life. His problem was not his deeds but his heart: he trusted in them, compared himself with others rather than with God, and despised sinners. He came to God to report his goodness, not to seek mercy.

In a sentence. The Pharisee prayed, thanking God that he was not like sinners or the tax collector, and listing his fasting and tithing.

On a Tuesday. When you pray, do you compare yourself with others? Compare yourself with God, and you will have nothing to boast about.
verseByVerse.note: The law required only one yearly fast (the Day of Atonement); the Pharisee fasted twice a week and tithed even what the law did not require.

verseByVerse.quote: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner!

Standing far off. At a distance from the sanctuary, and from the Pharisee. He feels he has no right to come near.

Would not even lift up his eyes to heaven. Jews normally prayed standing, looking up, with hands raised. He could not bring himself to look up. Shame (Ezra 9:6).

But beat his breast. Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse (23:48). He beats his heart, the source of his sin.

God, be merciful to me, a sinner! Seven words in English, six in Greek. The whole gospel in a prayer. “Be merciful” (hilasthēti): be propitiated, be reconciled to me. The word is related to the “mercy seat” (hilastērion), the lid of the ark where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Hebrews 9:5; Romans 3:25). He is asking God to accept the atoning sacrifice on his behalf, and to turn away his wrath. And “a sinner” is literally “the sinner”: not one among many, but the sinner, as if he were the only one. He does not compare himself with anyone. He brings nothing but his need.

In a sentence. The tax collector stood far off, unable to look up, beat his breast and prayed: God, be merciful to me, the sinner.

For worship. This is the prayer that God answers. Pray it today: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
verseByVerse.note: Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

I tell you. On Jesus’ authority. A shocking verdict for his hearers.

This man went down to his house justified. Key word. “Justified” (dedikaiōmenos) means declared right with God, acquitted, accepted as righteous. Not made morally perfect, but declared righteous by God the Judge. The tax collector was declared righteous, not because of anything he had done, but because he cast himself on God’s mercy. The perfect tense: he went home in a state of being justified.

Rather than the other. The Pharisee was not justified. All his good works did not make him right with God, because he trusted in them.

The doctrine of justification. Here, in a parable, is the doctrine Paul would set out in Romans and Galatians: a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). Not by our righteousness, but by his mercy, through the atoning sacrifice that Christ would offer. The tax collector prayed for propitiation; Christ provided it (Romans 3:24–26; 1 John 2:2).

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification is a process in which God makes us inwardly righteous by infusing grace, received through baptism and increased by good works and the sacraments; it can be lost through mortal sin and restored through penance. Verdict: the Reformers rightly taught that justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed (credited) to him, received by faith alone (Romans 4:3–8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). The tax collector went home justified that day, at once, not after a long process of becoming righteous. Good works follow as the fruit of justification, never as its ground.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted. The principle of 14:11. The proud Pharisee is humbled; the humble tax collector is exalted.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified before God, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself exalted.

For worship. If you trust in Christ, you are justified: declared righteous before God, now and for ever. Rejoice, and never trust in yourself again.
verseByVerse.note: “Justified” means declared right with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's word is infants, and it is precise: not children generally but babies. Matthew and Mark say children; Luke narrows it. These are infants in arms, and the parents want nothing except that he should touch them.

The disciples deserve a fair hearing. In this chapter he has been teaching about prayer, justification and the coming of the Son of Man, and in the last one he told them he must suffer many things and be rejected (17:25). The pressure is enormous and the time is visibly short — and a queue of mothers has formed with babies who cannot understand a word he says.

They are protecting his diary, and by every reasonable measure of importance they are right. Which is the thing worth sitting with, because the same judgement gets made constantly and never feels like a fault. The people with no standing, no urgency and nothing to contribute are the ones edged out of the schedule — not by hard men, but by conscientious ones with a great deal to get through.

“Do not hinder them” uses kōluein, a word with a history in Luke's second volume: the Ethiopian asks “What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36); Peter asks “can anyone withhold water?” (Acts 10:47). It is the word used when somebody is being kept out who should be let in.

And the reason given is not what sentiment expects. Children are not held up as innocent, and Scripture nowhere claims it. What an infant in that world had was nothing — no legal standing, no property, no achievements, no capacity to give anything back. It can only be carried and received.

That is the model. Which is why the paragraph sits exactly where it does, between a tax collector who had nothing and a ruler who had a great deal.
verseByVerse.theology:
One further question needs asking, since this is one of the two texts most often brought to it: does “let the children come to me” support the baptism of infants? Honestly, it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it.

Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who can offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them — and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Gen. 17:7; cf. Acts 2:39, “the promise is for you and for your children”). They add that the disciples who sought to exclude them are explicitly rebuked.

Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that Jesus blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith. That second point is the weightier, and the believer’s-baptism view is the better reading (see on Acts 2:39).

The text will not carry the whole argument by itself, and Christians who love the same Lord have divided over it for centuries without either side being able to close the case from this verse alone.

What the passage does say, and says with force, is the thing both sides should agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing. If an infant can be blessed by Christ, then the door is not opened by understanding, or by maturity, or by anything a person brings — and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother's arms.
verseByVerse.examples:
The verb Luke uses for the disciples' rebuke is a strong one; he used it of Jesus silencing a demon (4:35) and rebuking a fever (4:39). These men are not being gentle with the parents — and they are corrected in front of them.

Which is worth noticing again two dozen verses later, when the crowd tells a blind beggar to be quiet (v.39) using the same verb. The people nearest to Jesus are the ones clearing the road of those with nothing to offer, and it happens twice in one chapter.

A family brings their newborn to be presented at church, and the pastor wonders whether to spend time explaining the theological weight of it. This passage gives the content: this child is being presented to Jesus, exactly as the infants were in v.15, and Jesus's posture is not reluctance but welcome.

And the placing is the sermon. One verse after Jesus says the kingdom belongs to people who can do nothing, a ruler arrives asking what he must do — and ends very sad, still holding everything he came with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.

The placing. Luke now rejoins Mark’s order (Mark 10:13). The story follows naturally after the tax collector: the kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing, like children.

Even infants. Only Luke says “infants” (brephē), babies. Mark and Matthew say children.

That he might touch them. To bless them, as Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing.

And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. Perhaps thinking Jesus was too busy or too important for babies.

In a sentence. People were bringing even babies to Jesus for him to touch them, and the disciples rebuked them.

On a Tuesday. Never think a child is too small to be brought to Jesus in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus called them to him, saying, 'Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus called them to him, saying: let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.

But Jesus called them to him. He calls the children, and their parents.

Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them. Nothing must stand between a child and Jesus.

For to such belongs the kingdom of God. To children, and to all who are like them: dependent, helpless, receiving as a gift.

Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it. A child receives without thinking he has earned it. That is the point of the tax collector. The Pharisee came as an adult with his achievements; the tax collector came as a child, empty-handed. The kingdom is received, not achieved.

Where Christians differ. As at Mark 10:14. Verdict: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, but does not mention baptism and cannot settle that question. The New Testament pattern of baptism following repentance and faith fits the credobaptist position, held charitably.

In a sentence. Jesus called the children to him, saying the kingdom belongs to such as these, and that whoever does not receive it like a child will not enter it.

For worship. Come to God today as a child, receiving his kingdom as a gift.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke calls him a ruler, a man of official standing; Matthew tells us he was young, and all three Gospels that he was rich. He asks the best question in the Gospel, sincerely — Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap.

But listen to the shape of it: “what must I do to inherit?” The same collision Luke recorded from the lawyer at 10:25, a doing-word and a receiving-word in one breath. And it comes one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

“Why do you call me good?” has been used to argue that Jesus denied his own deity, and it will not do the work. He does not say “I am not good”; he asks a question about a word. Either the title is loose — flattery paid to an admired teacher — or it is exact, and the ruler has said far more than he intended. Jesus does not resolve it. He leaves the man holding both halves.

The commandments he lists are all from the second table, and all observable. What is not quoted is the first table — nothing about other gods or idols — and nothing about the tenth commandment, the only one that is entirely interior. That omission is filled in at verse 22.

The man's claim deserves to be taken seriously, because Jesus does. Mark records that he looked at him and loved him. By any measure a first-century community could apply, this is an exemplary man — and that is precisely why the passage is so uncomfortable. He is not a warning about scandalous living but about a life that passes every test a person can be set. A man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

“One thing you still lack” sounds like a small outstanding balance, which is how he would have heard it. It is not. The one thing is the whole thing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Is Jesus prescribing poverty as a universal requirement? No — the command was specific to this man, whose particular idol was wealth. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8-9); he does not say it to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3). What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses earlier, has been applied: you shall have no other gods before me, tested in the one area where it would cost him. It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

The camel and the needle should not be softened, and two softenings should be set aside. There is no evidence that “the eye of the needle” was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall — that story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. And the suggestion that a copyist confused the word for camel with the word for rope is speculation about a text nobody has; a rope will not go through a needle either. Jesus picked the largest animal in the country and the smallest opening in common life, and the sentence means what it appears to mean.

The crowd's reaction — “then who can be saved?” — surprises modern readers, and the surprise is important. They shared the assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16, that prosperity evidenced God's approval. On that theology the rich were at the front of the queue.

“What is impossible with man is possible with God” is the pivot of the whole chapter. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did. The infants could not come; they were carried.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's “we have left our homes” is easy to hear as boasting, and it is fairer to hear it as a question with the question mark missing. He has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions, and heard that entry is impossible for such a man — and Peter has done the thing the ruler would not. And “our homes” is understated: Luke has recorded boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

Note the qualifying phrase in the answer: “for the sake of the kingdom of God.” This is not a promise attached to loss in general, and certainly not a licence for abandoning a family — Luke has already ruled that out (cf. 1 Tim. 5:8).

And what is returned is not usually the same currency. Mark's version specifies houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30), which is not a promise of replacement relatives but a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. Anyone who has watched a convert lose his relations and gain a congregation has seen this verse work.

But Mark adds two words Luke omits — with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable, and Luke's silence should not be read as a promise of an easier settlement than his brother evangelist offers.

A wealthy member of a congregation serves faithfully — on the board, in generous giving, in every visible way — and there is one area he has never submitted to Christ's scrutiny. The rich ruler was, by most measures, exemplary. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler asked him: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? And Jesus said to him: why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

The contrast. After the child who receives, a man who wants to achieve.

A ruler. Luke calls him a ruler, perhaps a synagogue leader or member of a council; Matthew adds that he was young (Matthew 19:20). Rich (v. 23), powerful, respectable.

Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? The lawyer’s question (10:25). “Do”: he thinks of eternal life as something to be earned.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. Jesus makes him think. If only God is good, then either the ruler is speaking carelessly, or he is recognising who Jesus is. And if only God is good, then the ruler is not good either. Jesus is not denying his own goodness or deity, but challenging the ruler’s shallow understanding of goodness.

In a sentence. A ruler asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus challenged his use of “good”, since only God is good.

On a Tuesday. Only God is truly good. Stop measuring yourself by your own standards.
verseByVerse.note: Luke calls him a ruler; Matthew adds that he was young.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments: do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honour your father and mother. And he said: all these I have kept from my youth.

You know the commandments. Jesus points him to the law, the second table, about duty to neighbour.

The list. The seventh, sixth, eighth, ninth and fifth commandments. Jesus leaves out the first table (about God) and the tenth (do not covet). That is where the ruler’s problem lies: his wealth is his god (Exodus 20:3), and he covets.

All these I have kept from my youth. Sincere, and outwardly perhaps true. But he has not understood how deep the law goes: to the heart (Matthew 5:21–28). He has never seen himself as a sinner, unlike the tax collector.

In a sentence. Jesus listed the commandments about others, and the ruler claimed to have kept them all since childhood.

On a Tuesday. Have you kept God’s law in your heart, not just outwardly? Ask God to show you.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard this, he said to him: one thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.

One thing you still lack. His wealth had his heart. He broke the first commandment.

Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor. Not a universal rule for all disciples, but the specific cure for this man’s idol. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing he loved more than God.

And you will have treasure in heaven. Not a loss, but an exchange (12:33).

And come, follow me. The real goal. Not poverty, but discipleship. Eternal life is found in following Jesus.

But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. “Very sad” (perilypos): deeply grieved. He wanted eternal life, but not more than his money. Luke does not say he went away, but the implication is clear (Mark 10:22). The contrast with the tax collector, and with the disciples who left everything (5:11, 28), and with Zacchaeus, who will give half his goods away (19:8).

In a sentence. Jesus told the ruler that he lacked one thing: he must sell all, give to the poor, and follow him, but the ruler became very sad, because he was very rich.

On a Tuesday. What is the one thing that stands between you and wholehearted discipleship? Give it to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said: how difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

Seeing that he had become sad. Jesus watches him with compassion (Mark 10:21).

How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! Wealth gives self-sufficiency, security, and attachment to this world. It makes it hard to come as a child, empty-handed.

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The camel was the largest animal in the land; the needle’s eye the smallest opening. Deliberate, comic exaggeration, meaning: impossible. Luke, the doctor, uses the word for a surgeon’s needle (belonēs). Theories about a small gate called “the needle’s eye”, which a camel could squeeze through on its knees, have no historical basis and miss the point.

In a sentence. Seeing his sadness, Jesus said how hard it is for the rich to enter God’s kingdom, harder than for a camel to go through the eye of a needle.

On a Tuesday. By the world’s standards, you are probably rich. Don’t let your wealth keep you from the kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who heard it said: then who can be saved? But he said: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

Then who can be saved? If the rich, who seemed so blessed and could afford to do so much good, cannot be saved, who can? The right question.

What is impossible with man is possible with God. Salvation is humanly impossible, for anyone, rich or poor. No one can save himself. But God can, and does. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9). The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through. In the next chapter, a rich man is saved: Zacchaeus (19:1–10).

In a sentence. When people asked who then could be saved, Jesus said that what is impossible for people is possible for God.

For worship. Your salvation was impossible for you, and possible for God. Praise him for doing what you could not.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said: see, we have left our homes and followed you. And he said to them: truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.

See, we have left our homes and followed you. We did what the ruler would not.

There is no one who has left house or wife. Only Luke includes “wife” (also 14:26). Peter was married (4:38), and his wife later travelled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Leaving here means putting the kingdom first, sometimes literally leaving family behind for mission.

For the sake of the kingdom of God. The motive.

Who will not receive many times more in this time. In the family of God, the church: brothers, sisters, mothers, homes (Mark 10:30). The losses are more than made up.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the ruler’s question (v. 18). Those who give up everything for Christ gain eternal life.

In a sentence. When Peter said they had left everything, Jesus promised that anyone who leaves home and family for the kingdom will receive far more now and eternal life in the age to come.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you, look at the family of believers he has given you. And look ahead to eternal life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third and fullest of the passion predictions, and the only one that explicitly grounds the events in Scripture: “everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.” What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan; it is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before.

Every item can be traced. Isaiah's Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6); he was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:3-5). The psalmist is mocked and surrounded (Ps. 22:7-8). And “delivered over to the Gentiles” is new: the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

Notice how much of the list concerns humiliation rather than pain — mocked, shamefully treated, spat on — and Luke will record every one of them happening.

Then the incomprehension, stated three times in one verse so the reader cannot soften it. Jesus has given six specific things in plain language with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him three years took in nothing.

And the juxtaposition that follows is deliberate and devastating. The disciples, who have eyes, cannot see what he has just told them plainly. A blind beggar outside Jericho, working from one sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right — and “Son of David” is a messianic title, the first time in this Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud.

The crowd tells him to be silent, using the same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the babies two dozen verses earlier. And the people doing it are “those who were in front” — the ones nearest to Jesus.

He cries out all the more, and the widow at the top of the chapter would have recognised him exactly.
verseByVerse.theology:
A reader with three Gospels open will stop at v.35, and the difficulty is worth facing because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke has the healing “as he drew near to Jericho” and then has Jesus entering the town (19:1); Matthew and Mark both have it as he was going out (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew reports two blind men where the others report one, and only Mark supplies a name.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives a name and a father's name — “Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus” — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask.

The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart: the ancient city standing as a ruin on its old mound, and the splendid new town Herod the Great had built to the south with his winter palace, with the road running between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there produce exactly these.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's threefold statement that the disciples understood nothing is a mercy to the reader as well as astonishing. These are the men who would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this stupid, and nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would write down that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word.

And there is something here for anyone who has read a passage repeatedly and got nothing from it. They heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity; it arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45).

“And Jesus stopped” is worth the whole paragraph. He is on the last stretch to Jerusalem, has just described in detail what is waiting there, and the entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for a beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

“What do you want me to do for you?” is on the face of it unnecessary — anybody could name the need. But being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. And the mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

He was not told to follow, and he followed. The first thing he does with working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the Twelve, he said to them: see, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.
