Luke explains the meaning for Gentile readers. Fulfilled when the Romans surrounded Jerusalem, first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66, and then under Titus in AD 70.

Then know that its desolation has come near. “Desolation”: the destruction and abandonment of the city (Daniel 9:27).

Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Don’t try to defend the city. Flee. The church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophecy, fled to Pella, in the hills east of the Jordan, when Cestius Gallus withdrew in AD 66, and so escaped.

And let not those who are out in the country enter it. Many Jews fled into the city for refuge, and were trapped.

In a sentence. When they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies, they would know its destruction was near, and must flee rather than take refuge in the city.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ warnings are given in love, so that his people can obey in time.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, as the Romans did in AD 66–70; Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation.”

verseByVerse.quote: for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For these are days of vengeance, to fulfil all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.

For these are days of vengeance. God’s judgement on Jerusalem for rejecting her Messiah (19:43–44). The day of vengeance that Jesus left unread at Nazareth (4:19) would come.

To fulfill all that is written. The prophets had warned of judgement on unfaithful Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 28:49–57; Daniel 9:26; Micah 3:12).

Alas for women who are pregnant. Jesus’ compassion.

Great distress upon the earth. Or “upon the land”, the land of Israel.

And wrath against this people. God’s wrath. Josephus describes horrors of famine and slaughter during the siege.

In a sentence. These would be days of God’s vengeance, fulfilling Scripture, terrible for pregnant women and nursing mothers, with great distress and wrath on the people.

On a Tuesday. God’s judgement on sin is real. Take refuge in the one who bore wrath for us.

parallels.desc: the days of punishment have come

verseByVerse.quote: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

They will fall by the edge of the sword. Josephus says over a million died in the siege (probably an exaggeration, but the scale was vast).

And be led captive among all nations. Josephus says 97,000 were taken captive, many sold as slaves or sent to die in the arenas.

Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles. Under Gentile control. After the second Jewish revolt (AD 132–135), the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city, Aelia Capitolina, and banned Jews from entering it.

Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Only Luke. A period of Gentile domination of Jerusalem, and perhaps also the period of the Gentile mission (Romans 11:25: until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in). It has an end, set by God. Jerusalem’s judgement is not the end of God’s purposes for Israel.

Where Christians differ: the times of the Gentiles. Dispensationalists see the founding of the modern state of Israel (1948) and the capture of Jerusalem (1967) as the end of the times of the Gentiles, and a sign of the imminent end. Verdict: Jesus gives no such timetable, and warns against date-setting (vv. 8–9). The times of the Gentiles is the age of Gentile mission and Gentile dominance between the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s return. Paul holds out hope of a future turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27), but that is a work of grace through the gospel, not a political event to be calculated.

In a sentence. Many would die by the sword or be taken captive, and Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are complete.

On a Tuesday. God is working out his purposes in history, for Jews and Gentiles. Pray for the gospel to reach both.

parallels.desc: the nations have come into your inheritance
until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in

verseByVerse.quote: 'And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

Now the end. After the fall of Jerusalem and the times of the Gentiles, Jesus speaks of his return.

Signs in sun and moon and stars. Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgement (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:30–31).

And on the earth distress of nations in perplexity. Worldwide anguish, not knowing where to turn.

Because of the roaring of the sea and the waves. The sea, in Scripture, is a picture of chaos and evil (Psalm 46:3; Isaiah 17:12; Revelation 13:1). Creation in turmoil.

People fainting with fear and with foreboding. Terror at what is coming.

For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26–27. The whole created order shaken by the coming of its maker.

In a sentence. There will be signs in the heavens, nations in anguish at the roaring sea, people fainting with fear, as the powers of heaven are shaken.

On a Tuesday. When everything is shaken, those who belong to Christ have an unshakeable kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.

And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud. Daniel 7:13. The visible, glorious return of Christ. Everyone will see it (Revelation 1:7). There is no secret coming.

With power and great glory. In contrast to his first coming in weakness.

Straighten up and raise your heads. While others faint with fear, believers lift their heads in hope. Like the woman bent double for eighteen years, straightened by Jesus (13:11–13). The posture of confident expectation.

Because your redemption is drawing near. “Redemption” (apolytrōsis): full and final deliverance, including the resurrection of the body (Romans 8:23; Ephesians 4:30). What is terror for the world is hope for the church. Christ comes to complete the salvation he began.

In a sentence. Then all will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and glory, and when these things begin, believers should stand up and lift their heads, because their redemption is near.

For worship. Lift up your head. Your redemption is drawing near. Pray: come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–38 — The Fig Tree, the Weight on the Heart, and the Daily Rhythm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable is deliberately ordinary. Trees come into leaf, and everybody knows summer is near; nobody consults an expert about it. Luke adds a phrase the others do not — and all the trees — which quietly rules out reading the fig tree as a coded symbol requiring decipherment. The signs are meant to be legible from your own doorstep. And note what the application says is near: not the end, not the judgment, but the kingdom of God.

Then the most debated sentence in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Taken with v. 24, Luke’s structure is straightforward — the things the disciples asked about in v. 7 all happened within forty years, and v. 24’s interval of Gentile times stands between that and the Son of Man’s appearing. And the ground under everything is v. 33: heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not. The visible is the perishable thing; his speech is not.

Then, after the cosmos, the kitchen. Watch yourselves — not the sky. Three weights are named, running from the obvious to the invisible: dissipation, the heaviness of the morning after; drunkenness, the night that produced it; and the cares of this life. The third is not a sin in the ordinary sense, which is exactly why it is the deadliest. Nobody will ever be rebuked for it.

The verb is physical — weighed down, like a ship low in the water or eyes too heavy to stay open, as the disciples' were on the mountain (9:32). An overloaded heart does not become wicked. It becomes slow. And a trap works on one principle: the animal is looking at something else.

The remedy is not detachment but prayer: stay awake at all times, praying for strength to escape and to stand before the Son of Man. That is the entire practical conclusion of the discourse.

Then Luke closes with a timetable. Teaching in the temple by day, sleeping on Olivet by night, and the people coming early to hear him. The mount that had seen his tears (19:41) would see his agony (22:39), his arrest, and his ascension (Acts 1:12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Watchfulness in the New Testament is not scanning the news for prophetic fulfilment. It is the settled attention of people who know that today is lived under eternity. That is why Jesus ends a discourse about the end of the world with two verbs — stay awake, pray — and no preparations, no place to go, no date.

The phrase at all times rules out the pattern every generation falls into: intense watchfulness when the news is bad, and none when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness; it is nerves.

And to stand before the Son of Man is courtroom language. The Psalms ask it directly: if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, who could stand (Ps. 130:3)? The answer of this verse is that the strength to stand is not mustered but asked for, and asked of the very one before whom we shall stand. He is not the examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. Jude puts the ground plainly: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for v. 34, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Count the hours of the last week spent turning over a practical worry — money, a diagnosis, a difficult colleague. Then count the minutes spent thinking about the return of Christ. The ratio is the answer.

None of this is a call to care less about your family or your work. It is a diagnosis: what will finally leave a Christian unready for glory is very unlikely to be a scandal. It will be a diary.

And vv. 37–38 give the pattern for anyone overwhelmed by what is coming — not a technique but a rhythm. This man has just announced the fall of the temple, the arrest of his friends, the shaking of the heavens and his own return in glory, and he knows he will be crucified within the week. What he does with the days that remain is teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again. No frenzy, no last campaign, no scramble to secure the movement. Work in the day, withdraw at night, be found where the people who need you can find you, and do the next ordinary faithful thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable: look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.

Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. Only Luke adds “and all the trees”, for readers outside Palestine.

As soon as they come out in leaf … summer is already near. Signs are readable.

When you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. “These things”: the events described, beginning with the fall of Jerusalem. “The kingdom of God”: Luke’s phrase for its full arrival. Each event in history is a reminder that the end is approaching.

In a sentence. As the leaves on trees show that summer is near, so the events Jesus described would show that God’s kingdom is near.

On a Tuesday. Read the signs of the times, not to calculate dates, but to stay ready.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

This generation will not pass away until all has taken place. “This generation”: Jesus’ contemporaries. “All”: the events leading to and including the fall of Jerusalem, which happened within forty years.

Verdict. As at Mark 13:30: some take “this generation” to mean the Jewish race, or the generation alive at the end. Some critics claim Jesus was mistaken. The best reading: Jesus’ contemporaries would see the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, the event the disciples had asked about (v. 7), and they did. The day of his coming remains unknown (Mark 13:32).

Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. A claim only God could make (Isaiah 40:8). His words are more permanent than the universe. Everything he has said will come true.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly said his generation would not pass away before all these things happened, and that his words would outlast heaven and earth.

On a Tuesday. Everything else will pass away; Jesus’ words will not. Stake your life on them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.

But watch yourselves. The practical application, only in Luke.

Lest your hearts be weighed down. Made heavy, dull, sluggish.

With dissipation. “Dissipation” (kraipalē): the hangover after a drinking bout, or carousing.

And drunkenness. Self-indulgence.

And cares of this life. Anxieties about ordinary things (8:14; 12:22). Two opposite dangers, self-indulgence and anxiety, both make the heart heavy and blind it to eternity.

And that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. Like an animal caught in a snare it did not see.

For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. No one will escape it. Isaiah 24:17.

In a sentence. Jesus warned them not to let their hearts be dulled by self-indulgence or the worries of life, so that the day would not catch them suddenly like a trap, for it will come on everyone.

On a Tuesday. Is your heart heavy with indulgence or with worries? Lift it to God and be ready.

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.

Stay awake at all times. Watchfulness: spiritual alertness, every day.

Praying that you may have strength to escape all these things. Not escape from the world, but from the judgement, and from being swept away by deception and fear. Prayer is the means of watchfulness (22:40, 46).

And to stand before the Son of Man. To stand before him at his coming, unashamed, accepted (1 John 2:28; Jude 24). Not to fall in judgement, but to stand in his presence.

In a sentence. Stay alert and pray always for strength to escape what is coming and to stand before the Son of Man.

For worship. Pray today for strength to stand before Christ when he comes. He will hold you up (Jude 24).

verseByVerse.quote: And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

Every day he was teaching in the temple. His last week.

But at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside. Jesus may have stayed at Bethany (Mark 11:11) or in the open, at Gethsemane (22:39), which is where Judas found him.

And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him. Eager crowds, at dawn. The leaders could not touch him in public.

In a sentence. Each day Jesus taught in the temple and each night stayed on the Mount of Olives, and early each morning all the people came to hear him.

On a Tuesday. Begin your day by hearing Jesus in his word.
verseByVerse.note: Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside it.

parallels.desc: as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives

21.text: <sup>1</sup> Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, <sup>2</sup> and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. <sup>3</sup> And he said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. <sup>4</sup> For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.” <sup>5</sup> And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said, <sup>6</sup> “As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>7</sup> And they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?” <sup>8</sup> And he said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them. <sup>9</sup> And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.” <sup>10</sup> Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. <sup>11</sup> There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. <sup>12</sup> But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. <sup>13</sup> This will be your opportunity to bear witness. <sup>14</sup> Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, <sup>15</sup> for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. <sup>16</sup> You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. <sup>17</sup> You will be hated by all for my name's sake. <sup>18</sup> But not a hair of your head will perish. <sup>19</sup> By your endurance you will gain your lives. <sup>20</sup> “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. <sup>21</sup> Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it, <sup>22</sup> for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. <sup>23</sup> Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. <sup>24</sup> They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. <sup>25</sup> “And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, <sup>26</sup> people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>27</sup> And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <sup>28</sup> Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” <sup>29</sup> And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. <sup>30</sup> As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. <sup>31</sup> So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. <sup>32</sup> Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. <sup>33</sup> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>34</sup> “But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. <sup>35</sup> For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. <sup>36</sup> But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” <sup>37</sup> And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. <sup>38</sup> And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

22.title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest
22.overview:
Luke 22 covers the most theologically concentrated night in human history. It begins with Judas's betrayal agreement and the preparation of the Passover meal, moves through the institution of the Lord's Supper, includes a remarkable dispute among the disciples about greatness, records Jesus's prediction of Peter's denial and his commissioning of Peter to strengthen the brothers, narrates the agony in Gethsemane, and ends with the arrest, Peter's denial, and Jesus before the Sanhedrin.

Luke's account of the Last Supper has several distinctive features: he records two cups (v. 17 and v. 20), emphasises the kingdom dimension of the meal (“I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”), and includes the unique account of the disciples' dispute about greatness followed immediately by Jesus's teaching about servant leadership. The contrast between the disciples' argument about rank and Jesus washing their feet (in John) — and more immediately, serving them with his body and blood — could not be sharper.

The Gethsemane account in Luke is distinctive for the appearance of an angel strengthening Jesus (v. 43) and for the detail that “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (v. 44) — a possible description of hematidrosis, a rare condition in which extreme distress causes capillaries to rupture into the sweat glands. Luke the physician may be noting what he understood as a medical phenomenon of extreme psychological anguish. The cup Jesus prays about is not merely the physical suffering of crucifixion but the cup of God's wrath that he will drink on behalf of sinners.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Conspiracy, Preparation, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke lays two sentences on top of each other and makes the reader hold both. The Passover — the feast of the lamb whose blood turned the destroyer aside in Egypt — draws near; and in that week the chief priests are looking for a way to kill the Lamb of God. Their reasoning is entirely practical: they feared the people. A crowd-control problem, being managed during a busy festival, by men who had no idea what they were aiming at and hit it exactly.

Then the most disturbing sentence in the chapter: Satan entered into Judas — who was of the number of the twelve. Luke offers no psychology. But his next sentence makes the responsibility plain: Judas went, conferred, agreed a figure, consented, and began looking for a moment without a crowd. Every verb is his. Matthew gives the price, and it is the compensation the law set for a slave killed by an ox, and the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah.

The preparation is handled the way the colt was handled in chapter 19 — two disciples sent, a sign described in advance, everything found just as he said. A man carrying a water jar would stand out in that crowd, since water-carrying was women's work. Whether Jesus had arranged it quietly or knew it prophetically, the effect is the same: nothing about this night is happening to him.

At the table he says he has earnestly desired this meal, and then looks past his suffering to a Passover still owing in the kingdom of God. He takes the Passover cup and the unleavened bread, both of them fifteen centuries old, and fills them with himself: this is my body, which is given for you; this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. Jeremiah's promise, unfulfilled for six hundred years, is claimed at a supper table.

And then, only after the bread and the cup have been handed round, the betrayer is named — his hand on the same table. The Son of Man goes as it has been determined, and woe to the man by whom he is betrayed. Both, in one breath, unreconciled.

The disciples begin questioning one another, and not one of them looks at Judas.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper is memorial, proclamation and anticipation at once. Memorial: do this in remembrance of me — remembrance of the kind Passover itself was, never bare recollection but an act that brought a past deliverance into the present of the people keeping it (cf. Exod. 12:14). Proclamation: you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor. 11:26). Anticipation: he will not eat or drink it again until the kingdom of God comes, so every communion table is an unfinished meal.

Four views are held on what happens at that table. Rome teaches transubstantiation — the substance becomes the body and blood while the appearances remain. Luther held the body is present in, with and under the elements. Zwingli held the elements purely symbolic, the Supper a remembrance and a pledge. The Reformed position, with Calvin and the Westminster standards, is that the bread remains bread and Christ is nonetheless truly given: by his Spirit the believer really feeds on Christ, not with the teeth but by faith. The strongest argument for it is that his body was in front of them, unbroken, when he said the words — and he habitually spoke this way: I am the door, I am the vine.

Note the two words in both sayings: for you — on behalf of, in the place of. Substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before he was substituted.

And vv. 21–22 set divine determination and human guilt side by side without reconciling them. This is the settled pattern of Scripture — Joseph's you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, and Peter's delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 3 frightens some believers, who wonder whether they could be handed over like Judas. The fear is itself the answer. Judas is never recorded as afraid of what he was becoming; he was calm, he negotiated, he ate the supper, he came with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not being handed over — it is being held. And the man in this chapter who did deny his Lord out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it.

Verses 4–6 supply a test that needs no theological training. Every part of that transaction required the absence of a crowd. Is there any part of what you are arranging that has been arranged so that it happens where you will not be seen?

Verse 20 answers the fear that keeps some believers away from the table — that they are not good enough to come. The cup does not commemorate anyone's fitness. It was poured out for a table that contained a traitor, a denier, and ten men who would run before morning.

And v. 23 is quietly searching. When a sin is named from a pulpit, notice who comes to mind first. The eleven looked inward before they looked around, and they were right to. When Judas asked it, he already knew the answer (Matt. 26:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.

The passion narrative. Chapters 22–23 tell the story of Jesus’ last supper, arrest, trials and death. The early church told this story more than any other.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover (Exodus 12:15–20). Luke explains for Gentile readers that the two were spoken of as one. Passover recalled Israel’s deliverance from Egypt through the blood of the lamb (Exodus 12). Jesus will die as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death. The plot has been building (19:47; 20:19).

For they feared the people. They needed a quiet arrest, away from the crowds who hung on his words (21:38).

In a sentence. As Passover approached, the leaders looked for a way to kill Jesus without provoking the people.

On a Tuesday. Behind human plots stands God’s plan. Jesus would die at Passover, as the true Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; the two names were used together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the Twelve.

Then Satan entered into Judas. Satan had left Jesus after the temptation “until an opportune time” (4:13). Now is that time. Satan works through Judas. John says the same, at the supper (John 13:2, 27).

Who was of the number of the twelve. The horror: one of the chosen inner circle.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was not responsible. Satan does not possess those who resist him. Judas had already given way to greed (John 12:6), and opened the door. He chose. And yet even Satan’s work serves God’s purpose (v. 22; Acts 2:23). The cross that Satan plotted would be his defeat (Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. Satan entered into Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve.

On a Tuesday. Sin left unchecked opens the door to Satan. Close the door today, by repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.

And conferred with the chief priests and officers. The officers were the captains of the temple police, Levites responsible for order in the temple, who would make the arrest (v. 52).

How he might betray him to them. “Betray” (paradoi): hand over.

And they were glad. Their problem solved.

And agreed to give him money. Matthew says thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Matthew 26:15; Exodus 21:32; Zechariah 11:12).

In the absence of a crowd. At night, in a quiet place, with an insider to show them where.

In a sentence. Judas went to the chief priests and temple officers to arrange to betray Jesus, and they gladly agreed to pay him, so he looked for a chance to hand Jesus over away from the crowds.

On a Tuesday. Beware the love of money. It led an apostle to sell his Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the captains of the temple police. Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, 'Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying: go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.

On which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal, on 14 Nisan, by the thousands. “Had to be”: the law required it, and the true Lamb too must be sacrificed.

So Jesus sent Peter and John. Only Luke names them. The two who would later be partners in Acts (Acts 3–4).

Go and prepare the Passover for us. Buying a lamb, having it sacrificed at the temple, roasting it, and preparing the unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine and sauce.

In a sentence. On the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal.

On a Tuesday. Jesus planned his last meal with his disciples. He wanted to be with them.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, 'Where will you have us prepare it?' He said to them, 'Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: where will you have us prepare it? He said to them: behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters.

A man carrying a jar of water. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out. Jesus knew it, by foreknowledge or by arrangement.

Follow him into the house that he enters. A secret arrangement, perhaps so that Judas would not know the place in advance and could not betray Jesus before the meal.

In a sentence. Jesus told them that in the city they would meet a man carrying a water jar, and should follow him into the house he entered.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is in control of every detail. Follow his directions step by step.
verseByVerse.note: Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And tell the master of the house: the Teacher says to you, where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.

The Teacher says to you. The owner knew him.

Where is the guest room. “Guest room” (katalyma): the same word as the “inn” at Bethlehem where there was no room (2:7). At his birth there was no room; at his death, a room is ready.

A large upper room furnished. Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair. “Furnished”: with couches for reclining. Perhaps the same upper room where the disciples gathered after the ascension (Acts 1:13), and possibly the house of Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12).

In a sentence. They were to ask the owner, on the Teacher’s behalf, for the guest room, and he would show them a large furnished upper room.

On a Tuesday. Make room for Jesus in your home and life.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

Just as he had told them. As with the colt (19:32). Every word of Jesus comes true. If he could be trusted about a man with a water jar, he could be trusted about his death and resurrection.

And they prepared the Passover. They obeyed.

In a sentence. They found everything just as Jesus had said, and prepared the Passover.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word is always true. Trust it today.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.

And when the hour came. After sunset, when the Passover began. And “the hour” of his suffering (22:53; John 13:1).

He reclined at table. The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining, as free people, not slaves. Originally it was eaten standing, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11), but by Jesus’ time reclining had become the custom, to celebrate freedom.

And the apostles with him. The Twelve, including Judas.

In a sentence. When the hour came, Jesus reclined at the table with the apostles.

For worship. Jesus still invites his people to his table. Come.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.

I have earnestly desired. Literally “with desire I have desired”, a Hebrew way of expressing intensity. Jesus longed for this meal with his friends. Only Luke records this.

To eat this Passover with you before I suffer. This was a Passover meal, and the last before his suffering. He knew.

For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. The Passover pointed forward. Its meaning would be fulfilled in his death, the true Passover sacrifice, and finally in the messianic banquet of the kingdom (13:29; 14:15; Revelation 19:9). The meal looks back to Egypt, forward to the cross, and beyond to the feast of the kingdom.

In a sentence. Jesus told the apostles how deeply he had longed to eat this Passover with them before his suffering, for he would not eat it again until it was fulfilled in God’s kingdom.

For worship. Jesus longs for fellowship with his people. Come to his table with longing too.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, 'Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said: take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.

He took a cup. The Passover meal included several cups of wine, traditionally four. Luke mentions two cups (vv. 17, 20). This first cup is probably one of the early cups of the meal, before the bread; the second (v. 20) is the cup after supper.

And when he had given thanks. The Jewish blessing over wine: Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.

Take this, and divide it among yourselves. Shared fellowship.

I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes. His last meal before death. A vow of abstinence until the kingdom’s fulfilment. He will drink again with his people at the messianic banquet.

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks over a cup and told them to share it, for he would not drink wine again until the kingdom of God came.

For worship. Every communion looks forward to the day we will drink with Christ in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover meal included several cups of wine; Luke mentions a cup before the bread and another after supper.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying: this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.

He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them. The four actions of the feeding (9:16) and of Emmaus (24:30).

This is my body. At the Passover, the head of the household explained the elements: this is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in Egypt. Jesus gives a new meaning: this bread represents my body, about to be given in death.

Which is given for you. Only Luke (and Paul, 1 Corinthians 11:24) records these words. “For you” (hyper hymōn): on your behalf, in your place. His death is a sacrifice for his people. Substitution.

Do this in remembrance of me. Only Luke and Paul record the command. Jesus institutes an ongoing practice. As Israel remembered the exodus at Passover, the church remembers Christ’s death at his supper. “Remembrance” (anamnēsin) is more than mental recall; it is a living proclamation of his death (1 Corinthians 11:26) and a renewal of the covenant.

Where Christians differ: the Supper. As at Mark 14:22–24. Roman Catholics hold transubstantiation and the Mass as a sacrifice; Lutherans a real bodily presence; Zwinglians a memorial; Calvin a real spiritual presence by the Spirit. Verdict: Calvin’s view is best. “This is my body” is a sacramental sign, spoken while his body was at the table. The Supper is more than a memory: believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 10:16). And it is not a repeated sacrifice: Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14). “Do this in remembrance of me” does not mean “offer this sacrifice”, as some medieval theologians argued.

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks for bread, broke it and gave it to them, saying it was his body given for them, and told them to do this in remembrance of him.

For worship. When you eat the bread at communion, remember: his body was given for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying: this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

The cup after they had eaten. Probably the third Passover cup, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the main meal.

This cup that is poured out for you. “Poured out”: like the blood of a sacrifice poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7). “For you”: in your place.

Is the new covenant in my blood. Key words. The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31–34: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people … For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Covenants were sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8). The old covenant at Sinai was sealed with the blood of animals; the new covenant is sealed with Jesus’ own blood. His death establishes a new relationship between God and his people, based on complete forgiveness and a new heart (Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:15–22).

In a sentence. After supper Jesus took the cup, saying it was the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them.

For worship. You belong to the new covenant, sealed in Jesus’ blood. Your sins are forgiven and remembered no more.

verseByVerse.quote: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!

The hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. In Luke, Judas is apparently present for the Lord’s Supper itself. The betrayer shares the meal (Psalm 41:9).

For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined. “Determined” (hōrismenon): decreed, appointed by God. Jesus’ death is God’s plan (Acts 2:23; 4:28).

But woe to that man by whom he is betrayed! God’s plan does not excuse Judas. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility together: God determined it, and Judas is guilty.

In a sentence. Jesus said that his betrayer was at the table, and that though the Son of Man goes as God has determined, woe to the one who betrays him.

On a Tuesday. God’s sovereignty never excuses your sin. You are responsible for your choices.

parallels.desc: according to the definite plan of God

verseByVerse.quote: And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.

Which of them it could be. None suspected Judas. He had hidden it well. And each knew he was capable of it.

In a sentence. The disciples began to ask each other which of them would do this.

On a Tuesday. Don’t assume betrayal is something only others are capable of. Examine yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–38 — Greatness, Sifting, and the Turning Season
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The bread has been broken and the betrayal announced, and in that room an argument breaks out about rank. It was a love of winning, and they had done it before (9:46). It is not a failure peculiar to them: a congregation can have a moving communion service and a dispute about who was asked to serve at it in the car park afterwards.

Jesus describes the world they know. Gentile kings play the lord, and those in authority are called benefactors — a formal honorific, voted by cities and inscribed on stone, claimed by rulers who had done real good and intended it remembered. So the mechanism of worldly power is not brute force. It is force that has arranged to be thanked.

But not so with you. He does not abolish leadership — he distinguishes the greatest from the rest in the same sentence in which he redefines them. The greatest becomes as the youngest, who in that world ran the errands and was interruptible. And then: I am among you as the one who serves, said while reclining at his own table, having handed round the bread himself.

Then he satisfies the ambition he has just corrected. You are those who have stayed with me in my trials — said to men who will scatter within hours, and said accurately, because three years of staying is not cancelled by one night of failure. He assigns them a kingdom on the same terms his Father used with him: a table to eat at, and thrones.

To Peter, by his old name and doubled: Satan demanded to have you — the plural you, the whole barn — that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, singular, that your faith may not fail. Not that the sifting be cancelled, nor the fall prevented, but that the faith itself hold. And the commission comes before the failure, with when and not if: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

Peter contradicts him and is told the number and the deadline. Then the season turns: the disciples who once went out with no moneybag and lacked nothing are told to take the bag, and the sword saying arrives — which the next two verses immediately defuse.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 32 is the doctrine of perseverance in one sentence, and it is not a claim about the strength of Christians. Peter's faith survived because Christ was praying, and he prays still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). The scene behind Satan's demand is Job 1 — the accuser must ask, is given a limit, and cannot exceed it.

The teaching on greatness in vv. 25–27 is not a management philosophy but the application of the incarnation to the question of authority. The one holding the basin is the eternal Son by whom all things were made, and within a day the serving goes further than a towel. Authority in the kingdom is real and it exists for those under it.

Verses 35–38 must be read as a unit or they will be abused. Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 — numbered with the transgressors — which is precisely why the swords must go: a man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one. Two swords for a band of disciples facing an armed detachment is absurd for a fight, and it is enough is not a quartermaster approving the arsenal but a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong. Both the crusading reading and the absolute-pacifist reading are more than the passage will carry.
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for anyone who leads anything, and it is sharper than asking whether you serve, since everyone believes they serve. When did you last do something for your church that carried no credit whatever, that nobody would notice was done, and that could not be mentioned afterwards without losing the point? That is the youngest man's work, and Jesus took it.

Verse 28 is one of the most reassuring things in the Gospel about how Christ assesses a life. He is not scoring the worst night. He looks at eleven men hours from failing him completely and says: you stayed.

Verses 33–34 are for anyone who has made God a promise they did not keep — the resolve after a hospital ward, the change that lasted eleven days. Peter's sincerity was real, his self-confidence was misplaced, his failure was total, and none of it surprised Jesus or altered anything he had decided about the man. Being told in advance is what made restoration possible: the denial could only ever mean he knew, and prayed for me anyway.

And v. 35 is worth answering out loud, as the disciples had to. Not has life been easy, but the narrower question: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word they used.

verseByVerse.quote: A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them: the kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.

A dispute also arose among them. At the Last Supper, immediately after Jesus spoke of his body given and his blood poured out, and of betrayal. Only Luke places the dispute here. A tragic contrast. And probably about seating: who was nearest Jesus.

Which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. The old argument (9:46).

The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them. The world’s model: power over others.

And those in authority over them are called benefactors. “Benefactor” (euergetēs) was an official title that rulers loved to claim, inscribed on coins and monuments. Rulers presented their domination as generosity. Ptolemy III of Egypt was called Euergetes. Human leaders love to be honoured for the good they claim to do.

In a sentence. When the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus said that Gentile kings lord it over their people and like to be called benefactors.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the desire to be recognised as great, even in serving.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefactor” was an official title that rulers loved to claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.

But not so with you. The kingdom’s way is different.

Let the greatest among you become as the youngest. In that culture, the youngest had the lowest status and did the menial jobs.

And the leader as one who serves. Leadership is service (Mark 10:43–45).

Who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? By the world’s standards, the guest is greater than the waiter.

But I am among you as the one who serves. At this very meal, Jesus served. John tells us he washed their feet (John 13:4–15). And he was about to serve them supremely, by giving his body and blood. The Lord of all is the servant of all. His followers must be the same.

In a sentence. Jesus told them not to be like that: the greatest must become like the youngest and the leader like a servant, for he himself was among them as one who serves.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus served, how can you refuse to? Who can you serve today?

verseByVerse.quote: 'You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom,
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom.

You are those who have stayed with me in my trials. Despite their failures and arguments, they had stayed with him through the opposition and difficulties. Jesus honours their loyalty. Grace sees the good in weak disciples.

And I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom. “Assign” (diatithemai): appoint, grant, as by covenant or will. The Father has given the kingdom to the Son (Daniel 7:14); the Son gives it to his disciples (12:32). They will share his reign. They argued about greatness; Jesus gives them a kingdom.

In a sentence. Jesus told the apostles that because they had stood by him in his trials, he was granting them a kingdom, as his Father had granted one to him.

For worship. Christ shares his kingdom with his faithful people. What a gift for such weak disciples.

parallels.desc: he himself has suffered when tempted
if we endure, we will also reign

verseByVerse.quote: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom. The messianic banquet, fellowship with Christ for ever (v. 16).

And sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The Twelve correspond to the twelve tribes. They will share in Christ’s rule and judgement over the renewed people of God (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 21:12–14). “Judging” may mean ruling, as the judges of Israel ruled. And all believers will share in some way in his reign (1 Corinthians 6:2–3; Revelation 3:21).

In a sentence. They would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

For worship. You are invited to Christ’s table in his kingdom. Live today in that hope.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

Simon, Simon. The double name, tender and urgent (10:41). Not “Peter”, the rock, but Simon, his old name, as he is about to fail.

Satan demanded to have you. The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural: Satan asked for all of them. As with Job, Satan has to ask permission (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6). He cannot touch God’s people without God’s permission.

That he might sift you like wheat. Sifting shook grain violently in a sieve to separate it from the chaff. Satan wanted to shake them until their faith fell apart, to show them to be chaff.

But I have prayed for you. Here “you” is singular: for Peter specifically, who was about to fall most heavily. Jesus intercedes for his people, now at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25).

That your faith may not fail. Not that Peter would not fall: he would deny Jesus three times. But that his faith would not finally fail. Peter fell, but did not fall away. Judas fell away. The difference: Jesus prayed for Peter. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints: not the strength of our faith, but the prayer of our Saviour (John 17:11–15).

And when you have turned again. Repented, returned. Jesus knows Peter will fall, and will come back.

Strengthen your brothers. His failure will become the means of his usefulness. Restored, he will strengthen others (John 21:15–17; 1 Peter 5:8–10, where he warns about the devil prowling).

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon that Satan had asked to sift them all like wheat, but that he had prayed for Simon that his faith would not fail, and when he turned back, he must strengthen his brothers.

For worship. Jesus prays for you, that your faith will not fail. That is why you are still standing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural — Satan asked for all of them — while in verse 32 it is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter. Sifting shook wheat in a sieve to separate it.

parallels.desc: Satan asks leave to test Job
shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, 'Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.' Jesus said, 'I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him: Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. Jesus said: I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.

Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. Sincere, and brave. Peter would later go to prison (Acts 12:3–5) and, by tradition, to death by crucifixion in Rome (John 21:18–19). But not yet. Now he relied on his own strength.

I tell you, Peter. The only time in the Gospels Jesus calls him “Peter” directly. The rock is about to crumble.

The rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me. Before dawn. Three times.

In a sentence. Peter declared he was ready to go to prison and death with Jesus, but Jesus told him that before the rooster crowed that day, he would deny three times that he knew him.

On a Tuesday. Don’t trust your own strength. Trust the one who prays for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?' They said, 'Nothing.' He said to them, 'But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: when I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything? They said: nothing. He said to them: but now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.

When I sent you out with no moneybag. The mission of 9:3 and 10:4.

Did you lack anything? Nothing. God had provided through people’s hospitality.

But now. Things are changing. After his death, they will face hostility, not welcome. They will need to provide for themselves.

Let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance. The cloak was the most essential possession, used as a blanket at night (Exodus 22:26–27). Selling it for a sword means: things will be desperate. Jesus is speaking figuratively of the danger they will face.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that on their earlier mission they had lacked nothing, but said now they would need money, supplies, and even a sword, so great would the hostility be.

On a Tuesday. Be prepared for opposition. Following Christ in a hostile world is not always welcome.
verseByVerse.note: The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance, as verses 38 and 51 show.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.' And they said, 'Look, Lord, here are two swords.' And he said to them, 'It is enough.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: and he was numbered with the transgressors. For what is written about me has its fulfilment. And they said: look, Lord, here are two swords. And he said to them: it is enough.

This Scripture must be fulfilled in me. “Must” (dei): divine necessity.

And he was numbered with the transgressors. Isaiah 53:12, the suffering servant, who poured out his soul to death … yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors. The only direct quotation of Isaiah 53 by Jesus in the Gospels. He will be treated as a criminal, crucified between two criminals (23:32–33). And he identifies himself as the servant of Isaiah 53, who bears sin for others.

For what is written about me has its fulfillment. Literally “has its end”: is reaching its goal. Everything written about him is being fulfilled.

Look, Lord, here are two swords. They take him literally. Two short swords or large knives, perhaps for preparing the Passover lamb.

It is enough. Not “two swords are enough to fight”, which would be absurd against a Roman cohort. Rather: “Enough of this!”, ending a conversation they had misunderstood (Deuteronomy 3:26). When Peter uses a sword, Jesus will stop him (vv. 50–51).

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Scripture about being counted among the lawless must be fulfilled in him, and when the disciples produced two swords, he said: enough.

For worship. Jesus was numbered with the transgressors so that transgressors like you could be numbered with the righteous.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes to the Mount of Olives as was his custom — which is why Judas knew where to look, and why he had a path to walk on the worst night of his life. The habit was already worn smooth. And his instruction to the disciples is not that they pray for him but that they pray for themselves: pray that you may not enter into temptation, the petition from the prayer he taught them.

A stone's throw away he kneels, which was not the customary posture, and prays Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. The cup is not a general image of suffering. In the prophets it is fixed: the cup of the wrath of God, which the wicked drain to the dregs (Ps. 75:8; Jer. 25:15; Isa. 51:17).

Luke adds two details the others do not: an angel strengthening him, and sweat like great drops of blood. Both verses carry a note in modern Bibles — some manuscripts omit them, as the ESV margin says — because the manuscript evidence is genuinely divided — including the real possibility that early scribes removed them because a Christ who trembled embarrassed them.

He finds the disciples asleep, and Luke alone says why: for sorrow. They were not indifferent; grief of that weight shuts a body down. He wakes them without rebuke and gives them the smallest possible next action: rise and pray.

Then, while he is still speaking, the torches. Judas leads them and comes to kiss him, and Jesus names it to his face — using his name, in a question, which is a door held open to the last second. A disciple strikes and takes an ear, and Jesus stops his own arrest to heal a member of the arresting party.

To the officials who came out at night with clubs, he points out that he had been in their temple every day that week and they had not touched him. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness — real authority, genuinely theirs, and lasting exactly an hour.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not my will, but yours, be done is the perfect alignment of a human will with the divine, and it required agony to reach — which is what makes it obedience rather than indifference. Both wills are real: he genuinely did not want the cup. Gethsemane is the counterpart of Eden. In one garden a man said my will, not yours and the world broke; in another the second Adam said it the other way round.

The unanswered request is itself doctrine. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of that cup, there was no other way for sinners to be saved. The silence after if you are willing is the measure of what the cross was for.

Verse 51 is the last healing before the cross and it is performed on an enemy, unasked, by the prisoner. He had said love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (6:27), and here he does it with his own disciple's blade still wet.

And this is your hour, and the power of darkness concedes two things and withholds a third. The hour is genuinely theirs; the authority is real and belongs to darkness. What is withheld is any suggestion that it is more than an hour. Luke has used that clock before — the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 39 is for anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there. The crisis is a terrible time to begin; what carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, and paths are made in the ordinary weeks when nothing is wrong.

Verse 42 settles a question many carry: is if you are willing a failure of faith? A woman facing a diagnosis, told that Christian prayer should always be confident and specific, wonders whether her honest conditional is weakness. The Son of God prayed exactly that prayer, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is the highest thing faith ever does.

Verse 44 ends another argument — the idea that visible distress proves weak faith. The sinless Son, in perfect communion with his Father and doing exactly his will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it.

And vv. 45–46 name one of the least-discussed experiences in the Christian life: the point at which grief makes prayer impossible. Bereavement, depression, exhaustion after months of caring — and the believer finds the one thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do, with the accusation following that a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through worse, and he wakes them gently and tells them to pray. They were kept that night, and it was not by their own watchfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, 'Pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them: pray that you may not enter into temptation.

As was his custom. He went there every night (21:37). Judas knew where to find him. Jesus did not hide.

When he came to the place. Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives. Luke does not name it.

Pray that you may not enter into temptation. The Lord’s Prayer (11:4). “Temptation” (peirasmon): the trial that is coming, which could make them fall. Their only defence is prayer. Jesus says it at the beginning and end of the scene (v. 46).

In a sentence. Jesus went as usual to the Mount of Olives with his disciples, and told them to pray that they would not enter into temptation.

On a Tuesday. What testing are you facing? Pray before it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, 'Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

About a stone’s throw. A short distance, perhaps thirty yards. Near enough to be seen and heard.

And knelt down. Jews usually prayed standing. Kneeling showed intensity and submission. Mark says he fell on the ground (Mark 14:35).

Father. Even in agony, the intimate address.

If you are willing, remove this cup from me. The “cup” pictures God’s wrath poured out on sin (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus was about to drink the cup of God’s judgement against sin in the place of sinners. A real human shrinking from the horror.

Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. The heart of the prayer. Total submission. His human will submitted to the Father’s. Where Adam said “my will” in a garden, Christ says “your will” in a garden. This obedience is our salvation (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 10:7–10).

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew a short distance, knelt and prayed that, if the Father was willing, the cup would be taken from him, yet asked that not his will but the Father’s be done.

For worship. Jesus drank the cup of God’s wrath for you. Pray as he did: not my will, but yours.
verseByVerse.note: A stone’s throw is a short distance. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44. They are missing from some early and important manuscripts, but are present in many others, and were known to early writers like Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the second century. Some scribes may have omitted them because they seemed to make Jesus too weak. Many scholars think they are original. They are true in any case to what we know of Gethsemane.

An angel from heaven, strengthening him. As after the temptation in the wilderness (Mark 1:13). God did not remove the cup, but gave strength to drink it. That is often how God answers prayer: not by removing the trial, but by strengthening us in it (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

In a sentence. An angel from heaven appeared to Jesus and strengthened him.

On a Tuesday. God may not take away your trial, but he will give you strength to bear it. Ask him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44.

verseByVerse.quote: And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

And being in agony. “Agony” (agōnia): the struggle of an athlete in a contest, anguish, intense conflict. A battle of the will.

He prayed more earnestly. Strengthened by the angel, he prayed harder. Strength from God leads to deeper prayer, not less.

And his sweat became like great drops of blood. Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish. “Like great drops of blood” may mean the sweat fell like drops of blood, thick and heavy. Or there may have been actual blood: hematidrosis, a rare condition where extreme stress causes capillaries near the sweat glands to burst, mixing blood with sweat. Either way, it shows the intensity of his anguish as he faced the wrath of God.

Falling down to the ground. In a garden, on the ground, like Adam cursed to labour by the sweat of his face (Genesis 3:17–19). The curse of Adam’s sin is borne by the second Adam.

In a sentence. In his anguish, Jesus prayed even more earnestly, and his sweat fell to the ground like great drops of blood.

For worship. This is the cost of your salvation. Worship the Saviour who sweated blood for you.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish; “like great drops of blood” may be a comparison or describe a rare medical condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, 'Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them: why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.

And found them sleeping for sorrow. Only Luke gives the reason: sorrow. Grief exhausts. Luke is gentle with the disciples, mentioning only one return (Mark has three).

Why are you sleeping? A gentle rebuke.

Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The same command as v. 40. The testing is about to come. They will fail, because they did not pray.

In a sentence. Rising from prayer, Jesus found the disciples asleep from grief, and told them to get up and pray that they would not enter into temptation.

On a Tuesday. Sorrow can make you spiritually sleepy. When you are grieving, pray all the more.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?

While he was still speaking. The temptation arrives.

The man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. At the head of the arresting party. The one who had followed Jesus now leads his enemies.

He drew near to Jesus to kiss him. A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher, a sign of respect and love. Judas used it as a signal to identify Jesus in the dark.

Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Only Luke records these words. Jesus names him, and exposes the obscenity: betrayal with a sign of love. And still he calls himself the Son of Man, the one who will come in glory (Daniel 7:13). A last appeal to Judas’ conscience.

In a sentence. Judas arrived leading a crowd and came to kiss Jesus, and Jesus asked whether he would betray the Son of Man with a kiss.

On a Tuesday. Outward signs of love for Jesus can hide betrayal. Let your love for him be real.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, 'No more of this!' And he touched his ear and healed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When those who were around him saw what would follow, they said: Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said: no more of this! And he touched his ear and healed him.

Lord, shall we strike with the sword? They had two swords (v. 38). They misunderstood.

And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus (John 18:10). Only Luke and John say it was the right ear.

No more of this! Or “Let them do this”, allowing the arrest. Either way, Jesus stops the violence. His kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36).

And he touched his ear and healed him. Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. His last miracle of healing before the cross, done for an enemy, one of those arresting him. He loves his enemies (6:27), even at the moment of betrayal.

In a sentence. When a disciple cut off the right ear of the high priest’s servant, Jesus stopped the violence, touched the man’s ear and healed it.

For worship. Even as he was arrested, Jesus healed his enemy. He loved you when you were his enemy (Romans 5:10).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. John names the servant Malchus and the swordsman Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, 'Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him: have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

The chief priests and officers of the temple and elders. The leaders themselves had come.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? A bandit or a rebel. They treat him as a dangerous criminal.

When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. Their night-time arrest exposed their cowardice.

But this is your hour, and the power of darkness. Only Luke records these words. “Your hour”: the time God has permitted for them to act. The power of darkness means the authority of Satan (Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18). Satan, who left Jesus “until an opportune time” (4:13), has his hour. Darkness seems to triumph. But it is only an hour, and it is God who has given it.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the leaders why they came against him with weapons as if he were a bandit, when they had not arrested him in the temple, and said this was their hour, and the power of darkness.

On a Tuesday. Evil has its hour, but only an hour, and only by God’s permission. Light will win.
