verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–71 — The Denial and the Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter follows at a distance — more than anyone else managed, and still far enough to be nobody. In the courtyard a fire is kindled and he sits down among the men who arrested his Lord. It was cold, and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm; but this is how a fall actually happens. He did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm.

The accuser is a servant girl, the person of least standing in that yard, and her charge is about as mild as an accusation can be: this man also was with him. Peter answers, Woman, I do not know him — denying not a fact but a person.

Luke keeps the clock running: a little later, then an interval of about an hour. This is not a moment of panic; Peter had an hour to get up and leave. And the denials deteriorate — first the person, then the fellowship (I am not), then the subject itself (I do not know what you are talking about). The third accuser has evidence nobody can argue with: his accent. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

Then the rooster, mid-sentence — the most ordinary sound in the world, and enough, because it had been named in advance. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. It was not a look of contempt; a man looked at with contempt remembers the contempt, and Peter remembered the saying of the Lord — which included I have prayed for you and when you have turned again. He went out and wept bitterly.

Inside, the guards fill the night with a game: blindfold him, strike him, and demand he name the hand. While they demand a prophecy, three of his prophecies are being fulfilled in that building.

At daybreak the council reconvenes to give the night's work a lawful appearance, and asks its one question. He declines to perform — if I tell you, you will not believe — and then makes a claim larger than the question: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They ask if he is the Son of God. He affirms it, and they need nothing further.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's fall and Judas's ruin are the two halves of the same night, and the difference between them is the most important distinction in the chapter. Both men were sorry. Matthew says Judas was seized with remorse and threw the money back; then he hanged himself. Peter wept and lived. Paul named the difference exactly: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The test is not the intensity of the grief but its direction.

Verse 69 is one of the most explicit claims of identity in the Synoptic Gospels, and it welds two Scriptures together: Psalm 110:1, the Lord seated at God's right hand, and Daniel 7:13, the Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion. The right hand is not geography but authority, and the sitting means the work is finished — under the old covenant the priests stood, because it never was (Heb. 10:11–12). And the timing is the audacity: from now on, said with his hands tied.

The council's reaction disposes of the notion that Jesus never claimed divinity and the church invented it. His enemies, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion and put it to him, and he affirmed it in the recognised idiom of assent. They convicted him under exactly the right law. They got one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 54 gives a better test than a resolution. Not would I deny Christ under pressure — everyone answers no, and Peter answered no out loud a few hours earlier. Ask instead: where do I habitually sit, whose fire am I warming myself at, and what have I already agreed, without saying so, never to bring up there? The distance always comes before the denial.

A Christian leader fails publicly — not a considered defection but a collapse of nerve under social pressure — and concludes he has forfeited his calling. Peter is the specific answer. The man who denied Jesus three times within earshot of him was restored, commissioned, and preaching Christ in that same city within seven weeks. The look did not end his ministry; it began it.

Verses 63–65 describe the commonest kind of cruelty, which has nothing ideological in it: a man who was available and could not retaliate, and it passed the time. He could have named every man in that room and the day of each one's death. He said nothing, and the power that made the hands striking his face was restrained by nothing but his own will to be struck.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest’s house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.

Bringing him into the high priest’s house. John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest (John 18:13), then before Caiaphas. Luke records the denial first, then the mocking, then the morning council.

And Peter was following at a distance. Braver than the others, who had fled. But at a distance.

They had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard. Jerusalem nights in spring can be cold.

Peter sat down among them. Among the servants and guards. In the light of the fire.

In a sentence. They seized Jesus and took him to the high priest’s house, and Peter followed at a distance and sat down with others around a fire in the courtyard.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus at a distance puts you in danger. Stay close.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, 'This man also was with him.' But he denied it, saying, 'Woman, I do not know him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said: this man also was with him. But he denied it, saying: woman, I do not know him.

A servant girl. The lowest person there, with no power over him.

Seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him. “Looking closely” (atenisasa): staring intently.

This man also was with him. “With him”: the very essence of discipleship (8:1).

Woman, I do not know him. The first denial. A flat lie. A few hours earlier he had said he was ready to go to prison and death (v. 33).

In a sentence. A servant girl stared at Peter in the firelight and said he had been with Jesus, but Peter denied knowing him.

On a Tuesday. Denials of Christ often happen in small moments, before unimportant people. Watch your words.

verseByVerse.quote: And a little later someone else saw him and said, 'You also are one of them.' But Peter said, 'Man, I am not.' And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, 'Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.' But Peter said, 'Man, I do not know what you are talking about.' And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little later someone else saw him and said: you also are one of them. But Peter said: man, I am not. And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying: certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean. But Peter said: man, I do not know what you are talking about. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

You also are one of them. The second accusation.

Man, I am not. The second denial.

After an interval of about an hour. Only Luke notes the time. An hour to think, to leave, to repent. He stayed.

For he too is a Galilean. Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent (Matthew 26:73).

Man, I do not know what you are talking about. The third denial.

And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (v. 34).

In a sentence. Peter denied it twice more, the last time an hour later, when someone noticed his Galilean accent, and while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ words always come true, both his warnings and his promises.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.' And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him: before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Only Luke records this. Jesus was perhaps being led across the courtyard, or could see Peter from where he was held. A look. Not of anger or contempt, surely, but of grief and love. A look Peter never forgot. He calls him “the Lord”: even as a prisoner, he is Lord.

And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord. The word of Jesus came back to him.

And he went out and wept bitterly. Bitter tears of repentance. Peter went out into the night, like Judas (John 13:30). But Judas went out to despair; Peter went out to weep. Godly grief leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). And Jesus had prayed for him (v. 32). His faith did not fail. He would turn again, and be restored (24:34; John 21:15–19).

In a sentence. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered his words, went out and wept bitterly.

For worship. When you have failed Jesus, his look is not one of rejection but of love. Weep, repent, and come back.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, 'Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?' And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him: prophesy! Who is it that struck you? And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.

Mocking him as they beat him. The temple guards. As Jesus had foretold (18:32).

They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, Prophesy! Who is it that struck you? A cruel game. They mock him as a prophet. The irony: at that very moment, his prophecy about Peter had just been fulfilled (vv. 34, 61). He is a true prophet. Isaiah 50:6: I gave my back to those who strike.

And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. “Blaspheming” (blasphēmountes): they would condemn him for blasphemy (v. 71), but they are the blasphemers, insulting the Son of God.

In a sentence. The guards mocked and beat Jesus, blindfolded him and taunted him to prophesy who hit him, and insulted him in many other ways.

For worship. The Son of God endured mockery and blows in silence, for you. Worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, 'If you are the Christ, tell us.' But he said to them, 'If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said: if you are the Christ, tell us. But he said to them: if I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.

When day came. A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at dawn to confirm the verdict.

The assembly of the elders of the people … chief priests and scribes. The Sanhedrin.

If you are the Christ, tell us. The direct question.

If I tell you, you will not believe. They had already decided (20:1–8).

And if I ask you, you will not answer. As they refused to answer about John (20:7).

In a sentence. At dawn the council met and demanded that Jesus tell them if he was the Christ, and he said they would not believe him if he did.

On a Tuesday. If you have already decided against Jesus, no evidence will convince you. Open your heart.
verseByVerse.note: A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at daybreak.

verseByVerse.quote: But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.

But from now on. From this very moment, through his death, resurrection and ascension.

The Son of Man. Daniel 7:13–14: the one who receives everlasting dominion.

Shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. Psalm 110:1 (20:42). Jesus claims the place of supreme authority, beside God, sharing his throne. The prisoner before them is the judge of all. Luke omits the coming on the clouds (Mark 14:62), emphasising the present enthronement, which begins at the ascension (Acts 2:33–36; 7:55–56).

In a sentence. Jesus declared that from now on the Son of Man would be seated at the right hand of God’s power.

For worship. Jesus is seated at God’s right hand now. Worship your enthroned Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: So they all said, 'Are you the Son of God, then?' And he said to them, 'You say that I am.' Then they said, 'What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they all said: are you the Son of God, then? And he said to them: you say that I am. Then they said: what further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.

Are you the Son of God, then? They draw the right conclusion. The one seated at God’s right hand must be God’s Son.

You say that I am. A Hebrew way of saying yes: you have said it (Matthew 26:64). The words are yours, and they are true.

What further testimony do we need? They have their charge: blasphemy.

We have heard it ourselves from his own lips. Jesus was condemned for telling the truth about who he is. Either he was a blasphemer, or he is the Son of God. There is no third option.

In a sentence. When they asked whether he was the Son of God, Jesus said that they said he was, and they declared they needed no more testimony, having heard it from his own lips.

For worship. Jesus is the Son of God. He was condemned for saying so. Confess him.

22.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. <sup>2</sup> And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people. <sup>3</sup> Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve. <sup>4</sup> He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. <sup>5</sup> And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. <sup>6</sup> So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd. <sup>7</sup> Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. <sup>8</sup> So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.” <sup>9</sup> They said to him, “Where will you have us prepare it?” <sup>10</sup> He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters <sup>11</sup> and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>12</sup> And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.” <sup>13</sup> And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>14</sup> And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <sup>16</sup> For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” <sup>17</sup> And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <sup>18</sup> For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” <sup>19</sup> And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” <sup>20</sup> And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. <sup>21</sup> But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. <sup>22</sup> For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” <sup>23</sup> And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this. <sup>24</sup> A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors. <sup>26</sup> But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. <sup>27</sup> For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves. <sup>28</sup> “You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, <sup>29</sup> and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, <sup>30</sup> that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>31</sup> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, <sup>32</sup> but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” <sup>33</sup> Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” <sup>34</sup> Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.” <sup>35</sup> And he said to them, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” <sup>36</sup> He said to them, “But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. <sup>37</sup> For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.” <sup>38</sup> And they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “It is enough.” <sup>39</sup> And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. <sup>40</sup> And when he came to the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>41</sup> And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” <sup>43</sup> And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. <sup>44</sup> And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. <sup>45</sup> And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, <sup>46</sup> and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>47</sup> While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, <sup>48</sup> but Jesus said to him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” <sup>49</sup> And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” <sup>50</sup> And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. <sup>51</sup> But Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he touched his ear and healed him. <sup>52</sup> Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? <sup>53</sup> When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” <sup>54</sup> Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. <sup>55</sup> And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. <sup>56</sup> Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, “This man also was with him.” <sup>57</sup> But he denied it, saying, “Woman, I do not know him.” <sup>58</sup> And a little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” <sup>59</sup> And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” <sup>60</sup> But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. <sup>61</sup> And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.” <sup>62</sup> And he went out and wept bitterly. <sup>63</sup> Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. <sup>64</sup> They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>65</sup> And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. <sup>66</sup> When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, <sup>67</sup> “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe, <sup>68</sup> and if I ask you, you will not answer. <sup>69</sup> But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” <sup>70</sup> So they all said, “Are you the Son of God, then?” And he said to them, “You say that I am.” <sup>71</sup> Then they said, “What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.”

23.title: The Trial, the Cross, and the Tomb
23.overview:
Luke 23 is the passion narrative — the most carefully and deliberately structured chapter in the Gospel, in which every detail carries theological weight. Jesus is tried before Pilate, sent to Herod, returned to Pilate, condemned, led to Golgotha, crucified between two criminals, and buried in a borrowed tomb. Through it all, Luke maintains a single consistent emphasis: Jesus is innocent. Pilate declares it three times (vv. 4, 14, 22). Herod finds no crime worthy of death (v. 15). The criminal on the cross confesses it (v. 41). The centurion declares it at his death (v. 47). This is the innocent One dying for the guilty.

Luke's crucifixion account is distinctive in several ways. He records Jesus's prayer for his killers: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (v. 34). He preserves the remarkable conversion of the dying criminal — the most compressed account of salvation in the Gospels: a man with minutes to live, who can offer nothing but a confession and a request, receives from Jesus the promise of paradise this very day. And he records the moment of Jesus's death as a prayer of trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” — drawn from Psalm 31:5, later used in Jewish tradition as a prayer before sleep, now spoken by the Son into the Father's hands in the sleep of death.

The chapter ends in mourning and waiting. The women from Galilee follow and see the tomb; they return and prepare spices and ointments; they rest on the Sabbath. The darkness before the dawn of resurrection is total — and in the silence, everything depends on whether the one who said “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” was speaking to Someone who was listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Trial before Pilate and Herod
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sanhedrin cannot execute — only Rome can — so the charge has to change. In their own chamber they convicted him of blasphemy; before Pilate they produce three fresh charges built for a Roman ear: subversion, tax revolt, and a claim to a throne. The middle one is a flat lie, and they knew it when they said it: they had asked him that very question in the temple and heard him answer render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (20:25). The third is not a lie at all, and it is the one that will kill him.

Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him, hears a qualified affirmation, and reaches the correct verdict at once: I find no guilt in this man. He was not a soft man — Judea had already made him notorious for handling unrest badly — and he had crucified rebels before. He looks at this one and says there is nothing here.

The accusers press, mentioning Galilee as an aggravating detail, and Pilate hears in it an escape route: Galilee is Herod's jurisdiction. It is not a legal necessity; it is a door. Herod is delighted, because he has wanted to see Jesus for a long time (9:9) and is hoping for a sign. He questions him at length and gets nothing — the one occasion in Luke on which Jesus is asked a direct question by a ruler and answers not a word. Herod counts him as nothing, has him arrayed in a bright robe as a joke, and sends him back. And two enemies become friends over him that day, which is the world's unity at its truest: a peace built on a shared contempt.

Pilate then convenes a public assembly and states his finding for the record — not guilty of any charge, and neither did Herod find anything — and follows it, in the same breath, with I will therefore punish and release him. Flogging an innocent man as a concession is the hinge of the chapter, and it fails, as such compromises do.

The crowd asks for Barabbas: an insurrectionist and a murderer, guilty of precisely what Jesus was falsely accused of. Three times Pilate declares the innocence; three times the shouting overrules him. And their voices prevailed. He releases the guilty man and delivers Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke's repeated declarations of innocence are the theological spine of the chapter: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod by implication (v. 15), the dying criminal (v. 41), the centurion (v. 47). This is not a deserved death, and the innocence is not a tragic detail — it is the point, because a guilty man dying settles nothing for anybody. Only an innocent one has a life to spare.

The Barabbas exchange is the atonement enacted in the street before it is accomplished on the hill. He is not pardoned and not reviewed; nothing about him changes. He is guilty when he goes into the cell and guilty when he walks out, and he goes free because another man dies in his place that day. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21).

Verses 23–25 must hold two truths at once. These men are entirely guilty — Peter says so to their faces at Pentecost. And behind the crowd stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32) — and Paul can say of the Father's act what Luke says of Pilate's: he was delivered up for our trespasses (Rom. 4:25). Pilate surrendered him to pressure; the Father gave him in love. The same handing over, and the difference is everything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Pilate's sin is not brutality but procedure. He never once says he believes Jesus guilty; he simply never gets round to acting on the fact that he is not. Every institution has that move and most of us have used it — refer it upward, wait for the review, ask for another opinion. The test is simple: is the referral a way of finding the right answer, or a way of not having to act on the answer you already have? Responsibility does not transfer. The man who tried hardest not to be involved has had his name said in the creed every Sunday for eighteen centuries.

Verse 5 is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people, and it alleges no crime — only disturbance. Honesty requires admitting that some of the trouble Christians attract is their own manner and not the gospel, and it is worth asking which before claiming this verse. But when the charge is that a man taught the truth and people were changed, the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment.

Herod is the frightening figure here, and not for the reason people assume. He had already had his word from God in John the Baptist and had killed him; what he wanted now was a trick. But the believer who fears that God has gone silent on him is answered by the shape of the case: Herod was not troubled about it. He was very glad. Anxiety about God's silence is itself evidence that he has not gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, 'We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying: we found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.

The whole company of them. The Sanhedrin.

And brought him before Pilate. Under Roman rule, the council could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). They needed the governor.

Three charges. The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and treason. Blasphemy, their real charge, would mean nothing to Pilate.

Misleading our nation. Stirring up rebellion.

And forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar. A lie. Jesus had said the opposite (20:25).

And saying that he himself is Christ, a king. They translate “Messiah” into “king”, a rival to Caesar. Half-true, deliberately twisted. Jesus is a king, but not the kind Pilate feared.

In a sentence. The council brought Jesus to Pilate and accused him of subverting the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be the Messiah, a king.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was falsely accused, and bore it. When you are falsely accused, entrust yourself to God.
verseByVerse.note: The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and a rival king. The tax charge was false.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pilate asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' And he answered him, 'You have said so.' Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, 'I find no guilt in this man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asked him: are you the King of the Jews? And he answered him: you have said so. Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds: I find no guilt in this man.

Pilate. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, known for brutality and contempt for the Jews (13:1).

Are you the King of the Jews? The political charge.

You have said so. A guarded yes: true, but not in the sense you mean. John records more of the conversation: My kingdom is not of this world (John 18:33–38).

I find no guilt in this man. The first of three declarations of Jesus’ innocence by Pilate (vv. 4, 14, 22). Luke emphasises that Jesus was innocent of every charge, as the Roman authorities themselves acknowledged. He died not for his own crimes, but for the sins of others (1 Peter 3:18). And Luke’s readers in the Roman world would learn that Christianity was not a political threat.

In a sentence. Pilate asked Jesus if he was King of the Jews, Jesus said “you have said so”, and Pilate declared he found no guilt in him.

For worship. The Judge declared him innocent, and yet he died. He died for you.
verseByVerse.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, saying, 'He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, saying: he stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.

But they were urgent. Insistent, refusing to accept the verdict.

He stirs up the people. A rabble-rouser.

Teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place. “Judea” here means the whole Jewish land (4:44). From Galilee to Jerusalem: the whole course of his ministry. Ironically, they summarise Luke’s Gospel. And the mention of Galilee gives Pilate an idea.

In a sentence. They insisted that he was stirring up the people with his teaching throughout the land, from Galilee to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Faithful teaching of God’s word will sometimes be called stirring up trouble. Don’t be silenced.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.

Only Luke records the trial before Herod. Perhaps from Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward (8:3), or Manaen (Acts 13:1).

He asked whether the man was a Galilean. A way out of a difficult case.

He belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover.

He sent him over to Herod. Pilate tries to pass the problem to someone else. Also, perhaps, a diplomatic courtesy.

In a sentence. Learning Jesus was a Galilean, under Herod’s jurisdiction, Pilate sent him to Herod, who was in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. You cannot pass Jesus off to someone else. You must decide about him yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.

He was very glad. Not for Jesus, but for entertainment.

For he had long desired to see him. Since 9:9. He had beheaded John, and wondered who Jesus was.

He was hoping to see some sign done by him. A miracle, a magic trick, a performance. Curiosity, not faith.

So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. The only person in the Gospels to whom Jesus says nothing at all. Herod had silenced the voice of God in John; now God is silent to him. Isaiah 53:7: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent. Jesus will not perform for the curious.

In a sentence. Herod was delighted to see Jesus, hoping to see a miracle, and questioned him at length, but Jesus said nothing.

On a Tuesday. If you come to Jesus only for entertainment or curiosity, he may be silent. Come in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.

Vehemently accusing him. Fiercely, relentlessly.

And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Disappointed, Herod turned to mockery. “Treated with contempt” (exouthenēsas): regarded him as nothing (Isaiah 53:3: despised and rejected).

Arraying him in splendid clothing. A bright robe, mocking his claim to be king.

He sent him back to Pilate. Herod found no grounds to condemn him either (v. 15).

In a sentence. As the priests and scribes fiercely accused him, Herod and his soldiers mocked him, dressed him in a splendid robe, and sent him back to Pilate.

For worship. The King of kings was mocked with a king’s robe. Worship him as the true King.

parallels.desc: a similar mockery by Pilate’s soldiers

verseByVerse.quote: And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.

Became friends with each other that very day. United by their contempt for Jesus. Perhaps Pilate’s courtesy in sending Jesus to Herod healed their quarrel.

For before this they had been at enmity. Perhaps because of Pilate’s massacre of Galileans (13:1).

The fulfilment. The early church saw this as a fulfilment of Psalm 2:1–2: The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Anointed. In Acts 4:25–28, they pray: truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.

In a sentence. That day Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies, became friends.

On a Tuesday. Opposition to Christ unites strange allies. But God rules over them all.

parallels.desc: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, 'You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them: you brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.

And the people. Now the people are involved.

After examining him before you. A formal Roman hearing.

I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. The second declaration of innocence (v. 4).

In a sentence. Pilate summoned the leaders and the people and told them that after examining Jesus, he found him not guilty of any of their charges.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was innocent. He did not deserve death; you and I do. He took our place.

parallels.desc: I find no guilt in him

verseByVerse.quote: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.

Neither did Herod. Two rulers, two verdicts of innocence. Two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Nothing deserving death has been done by him. The verdict.

I will therefore punish and release him. To “punish” here means a flogging, a lighter beating, as a warning. Unjust: why punish an innocent man? A compromise, to appease the crowd.

In a sentence. Pilate said that neither he nor Herod found Jesus guilty of anything deserving death, so he would have him flogged and release him.

On a Tuesday. Compromise with injustice never satisfies. Stand for what is right.
verseByVerse.note: To “punish” here means a flogging.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all cried out together, 'Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas'— a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all cried out together: away with this man, and release to us Barabbas, a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.

Away with this man. Literally “take this one”. The same cry the crowd raised against Paul (Acts 21:36; 22:22).

And release to us Barabbas. The Passover amnesty (Mark 15:6). The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.

A man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. Ironically, exactly the crime Jesus was falsely accused of: insurrection. The guilty rebel goes free; the innocent man is condemned in his place. A picture of substitution: Barabbas could say, literally, Jesus died for me.

In a sentence. The crowd shouted for Jesus to be taken away and for Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, to be released.

For worship. You are Barabbas. The innocent died so the guilty could go free.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, 'Crucify, crucify him!' A third time he said to them, 'Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting: crucify, crucify him! A third time he said to them: why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.

Desiring to release Jesus. Luke emphasises Pilate’s wish to free Jesus.

Crucify, crucify him! The repetition shows the frenzy. Crucifixion: the most shameful death, for slaves and rebels.

A third time. Three times Pilate declared him innocent (vv. 4, 14, 22). As Peter denied him three times. The innocence of Jesus is established beyond doubt.

Why? What evil has he done? No answer is given. There was none.

In a sentence. Pilate appealed again to release Jesus, but they kept shouting “Crucify him”, and a third time he asked what evil Jesus had done, declaring him not guilty.

On a Tuesday. The crowd had no answer to “what evil has he done?” He did none. He bore yours.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.

And their voices prevailed. The mob won. Justice lost.

So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. “Decided” (epekrinen): pronounced sentence. The judge gave in to the crowd, against his own verdict. Pilate chose his position over justice (John 19:12). He bears real guilt, though the plan was God’s (Acts 4:27–28).

In a sentence. They kept loudly demanding crucifixion, their shouts won, and Pilate gave the sentence they demanded.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let the crowd decide what you do with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.

He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder. Luke repeats the crimes, to make the injustice plain.

For whom they asked. They chose a murderer (Acts 3:14: you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you).

But he delivered Jesus over to their will. “Delivered over”: the word used throughout the passion predictions (9:44; 18:32). The Son of Man handed over into the hands of men. And behind it, the Father’s will (Romans 8:32).

In a sentence. Pilate released the rebel and murderer they asked for, and handed Jesus over to their will.

For worship. Jesus was handed over to the will of sinners, according to the will of God, for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — The Way of the Cross and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Simon of Cyrene is seized out of the crowd — coming in from the country, with plans for the day, compelled by a soldier as any provincial could be. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus, which is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship in 9:23. He did not volunteer. He is the only human being who ever carried the cross of Christ, and Mark's readers in Rome evidently knew his sons by name.

Women follow, mourning and wailing, and Jesus turns round on the way to his own execution to speak to them about their future: do not weep for me, but for yourselves and your children. What is coming to Jerusalem will be so terrible that barrenness — the standard image of shame in that world — will be called a blessing, and people will ask the mountains to fall on them (Hos. 10:8). Then the proverb: if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

At the place called The Skull he is crucified between two criminals, one on his right and one on his left — the arrangement two disciples had once requested for themselves (Mark 10:37), and the fulfilment of numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Luke records the execution in four words and describes none of it.

The first word from the cross is a prayer for the men driving the nails: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, while the squad gambled for his clothes exactly as Psalm 22:18 had said they would.

Three groups mock, and all three say the same thing: the rulers (let him save himself), the soldiers (if you are the King of the Jews — the wilderness temptation in its original form), and one of the criminals. Above his head Pilate's notice states the only charge ever proved against him: that he is the King of the Jews.

And the other criminal turns. He fears God, agrees with his own sentence, declares Jesus innocent, and asks only to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied — today you will be with me in paradise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do raises the question of how far ignorance mitigates. It is real and partial: they knew they were killing a man, not that they were killing the Author of life. The plea is not an acquittal — if it acquitted them no forgiveness would be needed — but a ground on which to ask. And Luke shows the prayer answered in his own second volume: Peter tells that same city you acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and three thousand are forgiven in a day.

The mockery of v. 35 states the atonement with perfect accuracy and no understanding. He could not save himself and save others; not for lack of power, since legions were available for the asking, but because the two were mutually exclusive. To come down would leave the work undone and everyone he came for still under sentence. He saved others; himself he did not save.

The dying criminal answers works-based salvation and deathbed scepticism at once. He cannot be baptised, cannot make restitution, cannot demonstrate any fruit, and has no time in which to try. He brings a verdict on himself, a recognition of who Jesus is, and a request. And the reply exceeds it at every point: not someday but today; not somewhere but with me. There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 26 is one of the most useful in the chapter, because most crosses in a Christian life are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as a decision, and sometimes it is — but the diagnosis was not chosen, nor the redundancy, nor the decade of caring for a parent. It was laid on. Simon is not recorded as willing, and he may have resented every step, and he is the man who walked closest behind the Son of God.

Verses 27–28 correct the commonest sentiment attached to the cross: a devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, dwelling on the physical agony, producing much sympathy and no repentance. He declines it on the road. And grief that fastens on someone else's situation can be a way of not looking at your own — it is far easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face one's own household.

Verses 39–40 demolish the assumption that suffering makes people better. Two men, identical pain, identical distance from Jesus and from death, and Matthew says both began by reviling him. One changed. Proximity to Christ saved neither of them; one of them looked at him.

And v. 43 is for anyone who thinks it is too late — the man in a hospice, raised near the church and never committed, wanting to know whether there is time. There was no baptism, no restitution, no probation, no changed life, because there was no life left in which to change. There was a confession and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.

As they led him away. Out of the city to the place of execution.

They seized one Simon of Cyrene. Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Perhaps a pilgrim. Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, apparently known Christians (Mark 15:21; Romans 16:13).

And laid on him the cross. The crossbeam. Jesus, weakened by the flogging, could not carry it further.

To carry it behind Jesus. Only Luke says “behind Jesus”. A picture of discipleship: take up your cross and follow me (9:23; 14:27). Simon literally did it.

In a sentence. As they led Jesus away, they forced Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross behind him.

On a Tuesday. Carry your cross behind Jesus today.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said: daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

A great multitude of the people. Not all were hostile.

And of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. Only Luke records this. Women beating their breasts and wailing, as at a funeral. Perhaps the women of Jerusalem who traditionally mourned for the condemned.

Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me. Even on the way to the cross, Jesus thinks of others. Not self-pity.

But weep for yourselves and for your children. Weep for the judgement coming on Jerusalem (19:41–44; 21:20–24). Their children would see the siege and destruction of AD 70.

In a sentence. A large crowd followed, including women who mourned for him, but Jesus turned and told them not to weep for him but for themselves and their children.

On a Tuesday. Don’t just feel sorry for Jesus. Weep for your own sin, and for those who face judgement.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, the days are coming when they will say: blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed! Then they will begin to say to the mountains, fall on us, and to the hills, cover us.

Blessed are the barren. A terrible reversal. In Israel, barrenness was a grief and shame (1:25). But in the coming catastrophe, women without children would be counted fortunate, not having to watch their children suffer and die.

They will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us. Hosea 10:8. A cry of despair: better to be crushed than to face what is coming. Revelation 6:16 uses the same words of the last judgement.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that days would come when childless women would be called blessed, and people would beg the mountains to fall on them.

On a Tuesday. The judgement of God is terrible. Take refuge in Christ, who bore it for his people.

parallels.desc: they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us”

verseByVerse.quote: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

A proverb. If this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will be done to the guilty (dry wood)? Green wood does not burn easily; dry wood burns fast. If the Romans do this to Jesus, an innocent man, what will they do to the guilty nation in rebellion? Or: if God allows this to happen to his innocent Son, what will happen to those who reject him? (1 Peter 4:17–18).

In a sentence. If they do this to green wood, what will happen to dry?

On a Tuesday. If the innocent Son suffered so, how serious is the judgement on the guilty. Flee to him.
verseByVerse.note: A proverb: if this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will happen to the guilty (dry wood, ready to burn)?

parallels.desc: every green tree and every dry tree

verseByVerse.quote: Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

Two others, who were criminals. Fulfilling Isaiah 53:12 (22:37): he was numbered with the transgressors.

The place that is called The Skull. Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha, and the Latin, Calvary.

There they crucified him. Luke, like the other Gospels, describes it in a single word. His readers knew what it meant: nailed to a cross, left to die slowly in agony and public shame.

One on his right and one on his left. The places James and John had asked for (Mark 10:37).

In a sentence. Two criminals were led out with him, and at the place called the Skull they crucified Jesus between them.

For worship. He was crucified among criminals, counted as one of them, so that sinners could be counted righteous.
verseByVerse.note: Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' And they cast lots to divide his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. And they cast lots to divide his garments.

Father, forgive them. The first of Jesus’ words from the cross in Luke. “Father”: even on the cross. “Forgive them”: the soldiers, the leaders, the crowd, all who had a part. He practises what he taught: love your enemies, pray for those who abuse you (6:27–28). Stephen would pray the same as he died (Acts 7:60).

For they know not what they do. They did not understand who he was (Acts 3:17; 1 Corinthians 2:8). Ignorance does not remove guilt; they needed forgiveness. But it made forgiveness possible. And the prayer was answered: at Pentecost thousands of those who crucified him repented and were forgiven (Acts 2:36–41), and a centurion confessed him (v. 47).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer. It is missing from some important early manuscripts. But it is very early, widely attested, and fits Luke perfectly. Some scribes may have omitted it because they thought the Jews should not be forgiven, after the destruction of Jerusalem. Most scholars accept it as an authentic saying of Jesus.

And they cast lots to divide his garments. Psalm 22:18. The soldiers gambled for his clothes at the foot of the cross. The very ones he prayed for.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed for his Father to forgive those crucifying him, for they did not know what they were doing, while the soldiers gambled for his clothes.

For worship. Jesus prayed for his killers. He prayed for you. Who do you need to forgive?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer “Father, forgive them.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying: he saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!

And the people stood by, watching. Luke distinguishes the people from the rulers. The people watch; the rulers scoff.

But the rulers scoffed at him. “Scoffed” (exemyktērizon): turned up their noses, sneered. Psalm 22:7: All who see me mock me.

He saved others; let him save himself. The great irony. They admit he saved others. And because he would save others, he would not save himself.

If he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One! They use Peter’s confession (9:20) and the Father’s word at the transfiguration (9:35), in mockery. Their words are true. He is God’s Chosen One, the servant in whom God delights (Isaiah 42:1), and he is saving others by not saving himself.

In a sentence. While the people watched, the rulers sneered that he saved others and should save himself if he was God’s Christ, his Chosen One.

For worship. He did not save himself, so that he could save you.

verseByVerse.quote: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, 'If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying: if you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!

The soldiers also mocked him. Jews and Gentiles together.

Offering him sour wine. Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank. Offered as mockery: a toast to the king. Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself! The same taunt. Three times he is told to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39), as he was tempted three times in the wilderness. The last temptation: to come down from the cross.

In a sentence. The soldiers also mocked him, offering him sour wine and taunting him to save himself if he was the King of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. The world mocks the idea of a crucified king. But this is our King.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

verseByVerse.quote: There was also an inscription over him, 'This is the King of the Jews.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was also an inscription over him: this is the King of the Jews.

An inscription over him. The charge, posted on the cross, as was the Roman custom.

This is the King of the Jews. Meant as mockery and a warning. But true. Pilate proclaimed to the world who Jesus is. He reigns from the cross.

In a sentence. Above him was the notice: this is the King of the Jews.

For worship. The sign was meant as a mockery, and it told the truth. Bow to the crucified King.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him, saying, 'Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying: are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us! But the other rebuked him, saying: do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?

One of the criminals … railed at him. “Railed” (eblasphēmei): blasphemed. Even a dying criminal joins the mockery. Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first (Mark 15:32). Perhaps the second changed his mind as he watched Jesus die and heard him pray for his enemies. Only Luke records what follows.

Save yourself and us! He wants rescue from the cross, not from sin.

Do you not fear God. The beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Facing death, he fears God.

Since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? We are all dying. How can you mock?

In a sentence. One of the criminals mocked Jesus to save himself and them, but the other rebuked him for not fearing God when he was under the same sentence.

On a Tuesday. Facing death clarifies what matters. Do you fear God?
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first.

verseByVerse.quote: And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.' And he said, 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong. And he said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

And we indeed justly. He confesses his guilt. No excuses. True repentance.

For we are receiving the due reward of our deeds. He accepts that he deserves his punishment.

But this man has done nothing wrong. Another witness to Jesus’ innocence, alongside Pilate and Herod.

Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Astonishing faith. He calls him by his name, Jesus, “the Lord saves”. He sees a dying man on a cross and believes he is a king, who will come into his kingdom. Not even the disciples believed that at this moment. He asks only to be remembered, as Joseph asked the cupbearer (Genesis 40:14). He has nothing to offer, no good works, no time to do any, no baptism. Only faith in Jesus.

In a sentence. The second criminal admitted they deserved their punishment, declared that Jesus had done nothing wrong, and asked Jesus to remember him when he came into his kingdom.

For worship. Pray the thief’s prayer: Jesus, remember me. It is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn promise.

Today. Not at some distant future day, but today. Luke’s great word of present salvation (2:11; 4:21; 19:9).

You will be with me. The heart of heaven: being with Jesus (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

In paradise. “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the garden of Eden in the Greek Old Testament (Genesis 2:8), and for the place of the blessed dead with God (2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). Eden restored. The thief would be with Christ that very day, in the presence of God.

What it shows. Salvation is by grace through faith alone. The thief had no good works, no baptism, no communion, no time for any of them. He was saved by trusting Jesus. And at death, believers go immediately to be with Christ, conscious and blessed, awaiting the resurrection of the body.

Where Christians differ: purgatory and soul sleep. Roman Catholic teaching holds that most of the saved must pass through purgatory to be purified before entering heaven. Others teach soul sleep, an unconscious state until the resurrection. Some have tried to move the comma: “I say to you today, you will be with me”. Verdict: “today” goes naturally with “you will be with me”, as Luke uses the word elsewhere. The thief, a criminal with no time for penance, went straight to paradise with Christ. There is no purgatory: Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient (Hebrews 10:14). And believers who die are with the Lord at once, consciously (Philippians 1:21–23).

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised the criminal that he would be with him in paradise that very day.

For worship. No one is too late to be saved. And for every believer, death means: today, with Christ in paradise.
verseByVerse.note: “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the dwelling of God’s people after death.

parallels.desc: the tree of life in the paradise of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–56 — The Death of Jesus and the Burial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From noon until three the land goes dark — not an eclipse, which is impossible at Passover full moon and never lasts three hours, and Luke names no mechanism, only that the sun's light failed. The Old Testament supplies the meaning: I will make the sun go down at noon (Amos 8:9), and the three-day darkness over Egypt, the plague just before the night the firstborn died. This is the sign of judgment, falling this time on one man.

And the temple curtain tears — a woven hanging some sixty feet high, guarding the room nobody entered but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Matthew and Mark record the direction: from top to bottom, where no hand could reach.

Then, with a loud voice — which is not how crucified men died — Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. It is Psalm 31:5, which later Jewish tradition used as a prayer before sleep, with one word added: Father. And he breathes his last.

The centurion praises God and says certainly this man was innocent. The crowds who came for a spectacle go home beating their breasts — the gesture of the justified tax collector in 18:13. And his acquaintances and the women from Galilee stand at a distance, watching, having been there through all of it.

Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented to the verdict and who was waiting for the kingdom of God, goes to Pilate and asks for the body — a request that publicly identifies him with a man executed for treason. He takes it down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock-cut tomb where no one had ever been laid.

It is the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath is beginning. The women see the tomb and how the body was laid, go home and prepare spices against the clock — and then, with the jars ready by the door, rest according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.theology:
The darkness is judgment language, not grief. The blow that fell on Egypt and was promised on Israel falls here on the Lamb, in the middle of the day, in the dark, so that it need not fall on anyone else.

The tearing of the veil is the architecture of the atonement. For fifteen centuries the message of that room was not yet, and not you. Hebrews states the consequence exactly: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20). It was torn from the top and has never been mended.

A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice that Luke has no cry of dereliction. He has not softened the death. No Gospel records the horror more directly — the agony, and the sweat like blood and the strengthening angel that are Luke's alone. He shows the abandonment in Gethsemane and chooses trust for the last moment, and both are true. Stephen would die with almost the same words on his lips (Acts 7:59).

And the burial is not an appendix. Paul lists it among the four facts of first importance — died, was buried, was raised, appeared (1 Cor. 15:3–5) — because it proves he was dead and supplies the address at which he stopped being dead. A rock-cut tomb with one entrance, previously unused, its location known to a named councillor and to the women watching. Isaiah had written it: and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 47 rewards a reader who compares Gospels. Mark's centurion says truly this man was the Son of God; Luke's says certainly this man was innocent. A man watching an execution says more than one sentence, and each writer keeps the one that serves his account. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader who will shortly read a second volume full of Christians before magistrates: the founder of this movement was examined by every competent authority, pronounced innocent by all of them, and executed anyway.

Verse 49 is for anyone whose service to Christ has been the kind nobody records. The women who had followed him from Galilee had been funding the ministry out of their own means (8:2–3). The twelve are gone; the women are still on the hillside. They see him die, they see where he is buried and how, and they are the first human beings on earth to hear that he is alive — and in that world their testimony would not have been admitted in a court.

Verse 54 leaves a gap that the church has never quite known what to do with, and a great deal of Christian life is lived in it: not the crisis and not the deliverance, but the flat interval afterwards when nothing whatever is moving and prayers appear to land nowhere. Nothing here suggests that gap means abandonment. The most decisive work in history had just been finished, and from the outside on the Saturday it looked exactly like defeat.

And vv. 55–56 describe faithfulness with no feeling left in it. The spices are made up, the tomb is a walk away, every instinct says go — and the commandment says rest, so they rest a whole day with the jars by the door. Anyone who has kept turning up, praying with nothing in it, holding the line in the dark, is standing where those women stood, and should notice how their Saturday ended.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun’s light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.

About the sixth hour … until the ninth hour. The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m.

Darkness over the whole land. A sign of God’s judgement (Amos 8:9). The judgement against sin was falling on the Son.

While the sun’s light failed. Not an eclipse, which cannot happen at Passover full moon. A supernatural darkness.

And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. The curtain separating the Most Holy Place, God’s presence, from the rest of the temple, which only the high priest could pass once a year (Leviticus 16). Torn: the way into God’s presence is open through the death of Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22). And a sign that the temple system was ending. Luke places the tearing before Jesus’ death, Mark after (Mark 15:38); Luke groups the signs together.

In a sentence. From noon until three, darkness covered the land as the sun failed, and the temple curtain was torn in two.

For worship. The way into God’s presence is open. Come boldly through the torn curtain of Christ’s flesh.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' And having said this he breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! And having said this he breathed his last.

Calling out with a loud voice. Not the faint whisper of a dying man, but in strength. He chose the moment of his death (John 10:18).

Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! Psalm 31:5. Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer, said by children before sleep. Jesus dies with a bedtime prayer, trusting his Father. “Father”: the relationship unbroken. Luke records only this last word, not the cry of dereliction (Mark 15:34). It is the word of perfect trust, the work finished. Stephen would pray similarly (Acts 7:59).

And having said this he breathed his last. He died. Truly.

In a sentence. Jesus called out loudly, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit, and died.

For worship. Because Jesus committed his spirit to the Father, you can too, in life and in death. Pray his prayer tonight.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer.

parallels.desc: into your hand I commit my spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, 'Certainly this man was innocent!' And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying: certainly this man was innocent! And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.

When the centurion saw what had taken place. A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers. He was in charge of the execution.

He praised God. A Roman soldier praising God at the cross.

Certainly this man was innocent! Or “righteous” (dikaios). Mark has “Son of God” (Mark 15:39). Luke emphasises the innocence, completing the chain of witnesses: Pilate, Herod, the thief, and now the executioner. The righteous one has died for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18; Isaiah 53:11).

And all the crowds … returned home beating their breasts. Beating the breast: grief and remorse, like the tax collector (18:13). The beginning of repentance, which would bear fruit at Pentecost (Acts 2:37).

In a sentence. The centurion, seeing what had happened, praised God and declared Jesus innocent, and the crowds went home beating their breasts.

For worship. Stand at the cross with the centurion and the crowd. Praise God, and beat your breast in repentance.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers but in practice about eighty. Beating the breast was a sign of grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.

All his acquaintances. His friends, perhaps including some of the disciples. Psalm 38:11: my friends and companions stand aloof; my nearest kin stand far off.

And the women who had followed him from Galilee. The women of 8:2–3, who had supported him. They will be witnesses of his death, burial and resurrection (vv. 55–56; 24:1–10).

Stood at a distance watching these things. Watching: eyewitnesses.

In a sentence. All who knew him, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness sometimes means simply staying, watching, not running away.

parallels.desc: my friends stand aloof from my plague

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.

A man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. Arimathea was a town of Judea, perhaps Ramathaim, Samuel’s birthplace.

He was a member of the council. The Sanhedrin.

A good and righteous man. Like Simeon (2:25) and Zechariah (1:6).

Who had not consented to their decision and action. Only Luke records this. Not every member of the council agreed. Perhaps he was absent from the night hearing, or voted against it.

And he was looking for the kingdom of God. Waiting for it, like Simeon and Anna (2:25, 38). The Gospel begins and ends with faithful people waiting.

In a sentence. Joseph from Arimathea, a member of the council, a good and righteous man who had not agreed to their decision, was waiting for the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. You don’t have to go along with the crowd. Stand for what is right, even alone.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.

This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. A brave act, identifying himself with a condemned man (Mark 15:43).

And wrapped it in a linen shroud. A burial cloth.

And laid him in a tomb cut in stone. A rock-cut tomb, the kind wealthy families had. Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone. Isaiah 53:9: with a rich man in his death.

Where no one had ever yet been laid. A new tomb (John 19:41). No confusion possible about whose body it held. And like the colt that had never been ridden (19:30), set apart for him.

In a sentence. Joseph asked Pilate for Jesus’ body, took it down, wrapped it in linen and laid it in a new tomb cut from rock.

For worship. Jesus truly died and was buried. His tomb was real, and it would be empty.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone.

verseByVerse.quote: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.

It was the day of Preparation. The day of Preparation was Friday, when preparations were made for the Sabbath.

And the Sabbath was beginning. The Sabbath began at sundown. Literally “was dawning”, perhaps referring to the lamps being lit, or the evening star. The burial had to be done quickly, before sunset.

The Sabbath rest. On the seventh day God rested from creation (Genesis 2:2). Now the Son rests in the tomb on the seventh day, his work finished (John 19:30). On the first day of the week, the new creation would begin.

In a sentence. It was Friday, the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.

For worship. Jesus rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, his work complete. Rest in his finished work.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday; the Sabbath began at sundown.

verseByVerse.quote: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
