Followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Eyewitnesses of the burial. They knew the right tomb. On Sunday they would not go to the wrong one.

Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. To anoint the body properly after the Sabbath. They expected a dead body. They did not expect a resurrection.

On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment. Faithful Jews, keeping the law (Exodus 20:10). Even in grief, they obeyed God.

In a sentence. The women from Galilee saw where and how the body was laid, went home to prepare spices, and rested on the Sabbath as the law commanded.

On a Tuesday. Love for Jesus serves him even when hope seems gone. And God was about to astonish them.

23.text: <sup>1</sup> Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. <sup>2</sup> And they began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” <sup>3</sup> And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>4</sup> Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no guilt in this man.” <sup>5</sup> But they were urgent, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.” <sup>6</sup> When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. <sup>7</sup> And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time. <sup>8</sup> When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. <sup>9</sup> So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. <sup>10</sup> The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. <sup>11</sup> And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. <sup>12</sup> And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other. <sup>13</sup> Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, <sup>14</sup> and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. <sup>15</sup> Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. <sup>16</sup> I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>18</sup> But they all cried out together, “Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas”— <sup>19</sup> a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. <sup>20</sup> Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, <sup>21</sup> but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!” <sup>22</sup> A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>23</sup> But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. <sup>24</sup> So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. <sup>25</sup> He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will. <sup>26</sup> And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus. <sup>27</sup> And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. <sup>28</sup> But turning to them Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. <sup>29</sup> For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ <sup>30</sup> Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ <sup>31</sup> For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” <sup>32</sup> Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. <sup>33</sup> And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” And they cast lots to divide his garments. <sup>35</sup> And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” <sup>36</sup> The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine <sup>37</sup> and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” <sup>38</sup> There was also an inscription over him, “This is the King of the Jews.” <sup>39</sup> One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” <sup>40</sup> But the other rebuked him, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? <sup>41</sup> And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” <sup>42</sup> And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” <sup>43</sup> And he said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” <sup>44</sup> It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, <sup>45</sup> while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. <sup>46</sup> Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And having said this he breathed his last. <sup>47</sup> Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” <sup>48</sup> And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. <sup>49</sup> And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things. <sup>50</sup> Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, <sup>51</sup> who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God. <sup>52</sup> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>53</sup> Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid. <sup>54</sup> It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning. <sup>55</sup> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <sup>56</sup> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

24.title: Resurrection, Recognition, and Commission
24.overview:
Luke 24 is one of the most carefully constructed chapters in the New Testament. It moves through three episodes — the empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and the appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem — each building on the last, each advancing the disciples' understanding from confusion to recognition to burning conviction to mission. The chapter does not merely report the resurrection; it shows how the resurrection makes sense of everything that has come before and commissions everything that comes after.

The Emmaus account (vv. 13–35) is Luke's unique contribution to resurrection narrative, and it is one of the most theologically rich passages in the entire Gospel. Two disciples, walking away from Jerusalem in bewilderment, encounter the risen Jesus — who does not reveal himself immediately but walks with them, opens the Scriptures to them, and is recognised only in the breaking of bread. The entire sequence is a model of Christian formation: Scripture opened, heart burning, Jesus recognised in the meal, and immediate return to the community to testify.

The final appearance in Jerusalem includes Jesus's most explicit post-resurrection teaching: that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms has been fulfilled; that repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations; that the disciples are witnesses; and that they must wait in Jerusalem for the power from on high. The chapter — and the Gospel — ends with the ascension and with the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God. Luke's Gospel that began in the temple (Zechariah at the altar of incense, 1:9) ends in the temple. The story is complete — and about to begin again in Acts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The previous chapter ended with jars of spices standing ready while the Sabbath was kept. This one opens with them being carried out at first light. Nobody grinds spices for a man they expect to be alive — which disposes of the theory that the resurrection was something wishful people talked themselves into. These women were carrying embalming materials, and their only practical worry was who would move the stone.

It was already moved. Luke describes no rolling, no earthquake, no angel heaving at it; he simply reports the state of things on arrival. And the stone was not moved to let him out — a body that would enter a locked room that evening needed no doorway. It was moved to let them in.

Then the first fact of the Christian faith, arriving as an absence: they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. Luke uses that full title here for the first time in the Gospel, and writes it over an empty shelf.

Two men in dazzling apparel ask the finest opening question in the New Testament: Why do you seek the living among the dead? It is not a rebuke but a reorientation — they have come to the right place with the wrong category. And the phrasing claims more than he is alive again: the living is a class, a permanent condition.

The remedy the angels give for bewilderment is not new information. It is old information that was not believed: remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee. He had — three times, plainly, with the details (9:22; 9:44; 18:31–33).

They remember, and that is the first act of Easter faith on record: they believe a promise before any appearance at all. Then they run to the eleven — the men who had abandoned him — and hand over the best news in the world, and are told it is an idle tale.

Peter gets up and runs. He sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, which no grave-robber ever left behind, and goes home marvelling — which Luke is careful not to call believing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The resurrection is a bodily event in space and time, and Luke is meticulous about the physical detail — the stone, the body, the cloths — because what is claimed is not the survival of a spirit but the raising of the one who died. Paul builds everything on it: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile; if he has, death is defeated and the future of the universe is different (1 Cor. 15:14–20).

That women are the first witnesses is one of the strongest historical arguments the Gospels contain. In that world a woman's testimony carried little weight in court, and pagan critics would later sneer at a religion resting on it. Every instinct of a forger would put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke names the women, reports that the apostles dismissed them as hysterical, and leaves it standing. Nobody invents a story that embarrasses their own leadership and undermines their own witnesses.

And the angels' remember is the hermeneutical key to the whole chapter. The failure to understand the resurrection is a failure to have believed the word already given. Everything that happened had been announced in advance; the only question was whether those who heard it would take it seriously.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women's walk to the tomb is obedience with no expectation attached. They were not going out to meet a risen Lord; they were going to finish a burial. A great deal of faithful Christian service has exactly that shape, and it does not make it less faithful — it was the people carrying the spices who were first at the empty tomb.

Verses 6–8 supply the most practical test in the chapter. Think of the thing that frightens you most at present, and ask what God has actually said about it in Scripture — not what you feel, but the words. Most Christians discover they know the verse, could quote it, and have not once thought of it since the trouble began. Faith rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory.

Verse 11 is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree.

And v. 12 names a real place on the road that is not a disqualification. Peter looked at the strongest evidence anyone had yet seen and went home wondering. Marvelling is not believing — but nobody who ran to the tomb stayed outside it for long.

verseByVerse.quote: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

The resurrection chapter. All of Luke 24 takes place on one day, the first Easter Sunday: the empty tomb (vv. 1–12), the road to Emmaus (vv. 13–35), the appearance to the disciples (vv. 36–49), and the ascension (vv. 50–53). It is the climax of the Gospel.

On the first day of the week. The first day of the week is Sunday. From then on, the day of resurrection became the Lord’s Day, when Christians gather (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

At early dawn. As soon as possible after the Sabbath.

Taking the spices they had prepared. To anoint a dead body (23:56). They did not expect a resurrection.

And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb. Rolled away by God (Matthew 28:2), not to let Jesus out, but to let the witnesses in.

But when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. The empty tomb. “The Lord Jesus”: the only time in the Gospels this full title is used. The crucified one is the Lord.

In a sentence. At dawn on Sunday, the women went to the tomb with spices, found the stone rolled away, and went in but did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

For worship. The tomb was empty. Every Lord’s Day celebrates that fact.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them: why do you seek the living among the dead?

While they were perplexed about this. Confused, at a loss. Their first thought was not resurrection.

Two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. Angels (v. 23). Two: the two witnesses required by the law (Deuteronomy 19:15). Like Moses and Elijah at the transfiguration, “two men” in glory (9:30), and like the two men at the ascension (Acts 1:10). Mark and Matthew mention one; Luke two. Mark and Matthew focus on the spokesman.

And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground. Awe before heavenly messengers.

Why do you seek the living among the dead? A gentle rebuke. A tomb is for the dead. Jesus is alive. He is “the living one” (Revelation 1:18).

In a sentence. As the women stood perplexed, two angels in dazzling clothes appeared and asked why they were looking for the living among the dead.

For worship. Don’t look for Jesus among the dead. He is the Living One.

verseByVerse.quote: He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.

He is not here, but has risen. “Has risen” (ēgerthē): literally “has been raised”, by God. The heart of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee. Jesus had foretold it (9:22, 44; 18:31–33). The women were among those who heard. Remember his words. The resurrection fulfils his promise.

The Son of Man must be delivered. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, God’s plan.

Into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise. All of it happened exactly as he said.

In a sentence. The angels said Jesus was not there but had risen, and reminded them of his words in Galilee that he must be handed over, crucified and raised on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Remember Jesus’ words. Every one of his promises will come true.

verseByVerse.quote: And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.

And they remembered his words. The beginning of faith: remembering what Jesus said, and seeing it fulfilled.

They told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. The first witnesses of the resurrection were women. They became the first messengers of the risen Lord.

In a sentence. The women remembered his words, returned from the tomb, and told everything to the eleven and the others.

On a Tuesday. Tell what you know of the risen Christ, even if you are not sure you will be believed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.

Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James. Named eyewitnesses (8:2–3). Joanna, from Herod’s household, is named only by Luke.

But these words seemed to them an idle tale. “Idle tale” (lēros): nonsense, delirious chatter, a medical term for the ravings of the feverish. The apostles were not gullible. They did not believe.

And they did not believe them. A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time. No one inventing a resurrection story would have made women the first witnesses, or shown the apostles refusing to believe. These details are marks of truth.

In a sentence. The women told the apostles, but the apostles thought their words were nonsense and did not believe them.

On a Tuesday. The apostles were sceptics. They had to be convinced by evidence. Their faith rests on facts.
verseByVerse.note: A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time; no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marvelling at what had happened.

But Peter rose and ran to the tomb. Peter, who had denied Jesus, ran. John tells us John went with him (John 20:3–10). Some manuscripts omit this verse, but it is well attested.

Stooping and looking in. Tomb entrances were low.

He saw the linen cloths by themselves. The burial cloths, lying there, without the body. Not the scene of a robbery: thieves would have taken the body with its wrappings. Something had happened.

And he went home marveling at what had happened. Wondering, not yet believing fully. Later that day, the Lord would appear to him (v. 34).

In a sentence. Peter ran to the tomb, looked in, saw only the linen cloths, and went home amazed.

On a Tuesday. Go and look at the evidence for yourself. It will lead you to wonder, and to faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the same Sunday, two disciples walk seven miles out of Jerusalem, going over the events again and again the way grief does. Jesus draws near and walks with them, and their eyes are kept from recognising him — deliberately and temporarily, until in v. 31 they are opened.

He asks what they are discussing, and they stop dead in the road, downcast. Cleopas's reply is one of the great ironies in Scripture: are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened? He is addressing the only person alive who knows what actually took place on that hill, and Jesus does not correct him.

Their summary of him is entirely accurate and completely insufficient: Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet mighty in deed and word, delivered up by our own chief priests, crucified. Every clause is true. The sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home. And then the saddest tense in any language: we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel — followed by it is now the third day, the very fact that should have sent them running back, offered as the closing argument for despair.

They have the empty tomb, the angelic message and independent corroboration, and they are walking away. So he gives them not more evidence but the key: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interprets in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself — making a foreign language intelligible.

At the village he acts as if he were going farther. He will not force the door. They press him — stay with us, for it is toward evening — and at their table the guest becomes the host: he took the bread, blessed, broke and gave it, the same four actions as on the hillside and in the upper room. Their eyes are opened, they recognise him, and he is gone.

Then, and only then: did not our hearts burn within us? And they rise that same hour and walk the seven miles back in the dark — to find the room already alight with news that the Lord has appeared to Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Necessary — the divine must that governs this Gospel. Their whole difficulty inverts here: they thought the crucifixion was the reason he could not be the Christ, and are told it is the reason they should have known he was. The suffering was never a detour from the plan; it was the plan, and the glory is entered through it rather than after it.

Verse 27 is the hermeneutical claim on which the church has read its Bible ever since. The Old Testament is not religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book with one subject: the seed of the woman, the ram in the thicket, the lamb at the door, the serpent on the pole, the goat driven out, the servant who said nothing, the son of man receiving a kingdom. To read it without him is to miss what it is about.

And the sequence of the afternoon is the pattern the church has followed since: Scripture opened, then bread broken, and Christ known in both. This is not the Lord's Supper — it is an ordinary meal in a private house — but the Reformers' insistence stands: Word and Table belong together, and neither is complete without the other.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 16 describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is nearer than at any point you could identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is preparation rather than abandonment. These men later said their hearts had burned the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger.

Verse 21 is for anyone currently living inside a we had hoped. Their hope was not disappointed; it was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked, on the very day they gave it up, and the redemption they wanted for Israel turned out to be a redemption for the world.

Verses 19–20 describe a position a great many decent people hold: Jesus was remarkable, his teaching profound, his death unjust, the world would be better if people lived as he said. All true, all sincere, and it is a description of a corpse.

And v. 32 answers a question honest Christians carry privately — what do I do when the Bible feels dead? Not try harder, and not a better method. The burning came from a person, and the response is a prayer he grants: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Ps. 119:18). Note also the reverse error: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is a gift, not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.

The Emmaus road. Only Luke records this story, one of the most beautiful in the Bible.

Two of them. Not apostles, but disciples. One is named Cleopas (v. 18); the other is unnamed, perhaps his wife.

A village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location is uncertain. Going home, away from Jerusalem, perhaps in disappointment.

Talking with each other about all these things. The crucifixion, the empty tomb, the women’s story. Trying to make sense of it.

In a sentence. That same day two disciples were walking to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about everything that had happened.

On a Tuesday. Talk about Jesus with other believers, especially when you are confused. He often draws near in such conversations.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location of Emmaus is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognising him.

Jesus himself drew near and went with them. The risen Lord comes alongside two discouraged disciples on a dusty road. He takes the initiative.

But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. A divine passive: God kept them from recognising him, until the right moment (v. 31). So that they would learn to know him first through the Scriptures. Mary Magdalene also did not recognise him at first (John 20:14). His risen body was the same, yet changed.

In a sentence. As they talked, Jesus himself came and walked with them, but they were kept from recognising him.

For worship. Jesus walks with you, even when you don’t recognise him.

parallels.desc: the disciples did not know that it was Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?' And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: what is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk? And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him: are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?

What is this conversation. Jesus asks, to draw them out.

And they stood still, looking sad. “Sad” (skythrōpoi): gloomy, downcast.

One of them, named Cleopas. Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25, whose wife Mary stood at the cross. If so, perhaps she was the other disciple. Early tradition says Clopas was Joseph’s brother.

Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know. Irony: he is the only one who truly knows.

In a sentence. Jesus asked what they were discussing, and they stopped, downcast, and Cleopas asked if he was the only visitor in Jerusalem who did not know what had happened.

On a Tuesday. Tell Jesus what is troubling you. He already knows, but he wants you to tell him.
verseByVerse.note: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What things?' And they said to him, 'Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: what things? And they said to him: concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.

What things? He lets them tell the story.

Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word. A good description, but limited. A prophet like Moses (Acts 7:22). Not yet the Son of God.

Before God and all the people. Approved by God, recognised by the people.

And how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. The facts, accurately told. But they do not understand them.

In a sentence. They told him about Jesus of Nazareth, a mighty prophet in word and deed, whom their leaders had handed over to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Knowing the facts about Jesus is not the same as understanding them. Ask him to open your eyes.

parallels.desc: a man attested to you by God

verseByVerse.quote: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

But we had hoped. The saddest words in the story. Past tense: hope had died.

That he was the one to redeem Israel. To set Israel free, as Zechariah and Anna had hoped (1:68; 2:38). They understood redemption as political liberation from Rome. A crucified Messiah seemed a contradiction.

It is now the third day. The very day Jesus said he would rise (9:22). They mention it without seeing its significance.

In a sentence. They said they had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel, and now it was the third day since it all happened.

On a Tuesday. When your hopes in Christ seem dashed, perhaps your hopes were too small. He is doing something greater.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.

Some women of our company amazed us. They report the evidence: the empty tomb, the angels, the message that he was alive.

Who said that he was alive. The message they had heard, but could not believe.

Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said. Peter and John (v. 12; John 20:3–10). Confirmed.

But him they did not see. The evidence was there, but not yet faith. They had everything except sight of Jesus himself, and the understanding that only he could give.

In a sentence. They told him that some women had found the tomb empty and seen angels saying he was alive, and others had confirmed the tomb was empty, but had not seen him.

On a Tuesday. The evidence for the resurrection is strong. But faith needs Christ himself to open your eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?

O foolish ones. “Foolish” (anoētoi): without understanding, thoughtless (Galatians 3:1).

And slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Not slow of mind, but slow of heart. They believed parts of the prophets, the glorious parts, not all, especially not the suffering parts. Selective reading of Scripture leads to misunderstanding.

Was it not necessary. “Necessary” (edei): divine necessity. The cross was not a defeat that ruined God’s plan; it was the plan.

That the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Suffering first, then glory (1 Peter 1:11). The pattern of the whole Bible. The Messiah had to suffer to redeem Israel, not by defeating Rome, but by dying for sin.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked them for being slow to believe all the prophets had said, asking whether it was not necessary for the Messiah to suffer and then enter his glory.

On a Tuesday. Believe all of Scripture, not just the parts you like. The cross is at its centre.

parallels.desc: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

He interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. The greatest Bible study ever given. “Interpreted” (diermēneusen): explained, translated. The whole Old Testament is about Jesus. Not just a few prophecies, but all of it: the promises (Genesis 3:15; 12:3), the sacrifices and Passover, the priesthood and temple, the kings and the Son of David, the suffering servant (Isaiah 53), the psalms of suffering and vindication (Psalm 22; 16; 110), and the whole history of God’s saving acts. Jesus is the key that unlocks the Scriptures (John 5:39, 46).

How to read the Old Testament. This verse teaches Christians how to read the Bible: with Christ at the centre. Not by forcing Jesus into every verse, but by seeing how every part points to him, prepares for him, or is fulfilled in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

In a sentence. Starting with Moses and all the prophets, Jesus explained to them what all the Scriptures said about himself.

For worship. Read your Old Testament looking for Jesus. He is there on every page.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, 'Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.' So he went in to stay with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying: stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent. So he went in to stay with them.

He acted as if he were going farther. He does not force himself on them. He waits to be invited (Revelation 3:20).

But they urged him strongly. Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty. But more: they wanted him to stay. Their hearts were burning (v. 32).

Stay with us, for it is toward evening. The words of a famous hymn: Abide with me, fast falls the eventide.

So he went in to stay with them. He accepts the invitation.

In a sentence. When they reached their village, Jesus made as if to go on, but they urged him to stay with them because evening was coming, and he went in.

For worship. Invite Jesus to stay with you. He will come in.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognised him. And he vanished from their sight.

He took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. The guest becomes the host. The same four actions as at the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and the Last Supper (22:19).

And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. Another divine passive: God opened their eyes. Perhaps they recognised the way he broke bread, or saw the wounds in his hands. Recognition came in fellowship at the table, after the Scriptures had prepared them.

And he vanished from their sight. His risen body was not bound by ordinary limits. And once they knew him, they did not need to see him. He would be known through the Scriptures and the breaking of bread.

Word and table. The pattern of Emmaus became the pattern of Christian worship: the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken. Christ is known in word and sacrament.

In a sentence. At table Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened to recognise him, and he vanished.

For worship. At the Lord’s table, after the word is preached, ask God to open your eyes to know Christ.

parallels.desc: he took bread and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: They said to each other, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to each other: did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?

Did not our hearts burn within us. Even before they recognised him, his words had set their hearts on fire. Jeremiah 20:9: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire. The Scriptures, opened by Christ, warm cold hearts.

While he opened to us the Scriptures. “Opened” (diēnoigen): the same word as “their eyes were opened” (v. 31) and “he opened their minds” (v. 45). Christ opens the Scriptures, opens eyes, and opens minds.

In a sentence. They said to each other that their hearts had burned within them as he talked on the road and opened the Scriptures to them.

For worship. Ask Christ to open the Scriptures to you, until your heart burns.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, 'The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!' Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the Eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying: the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon! Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.

They rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. Seven miles, at night, without hesitation. Their sadness turned to joy, their direction reversed.

The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon! Simon is Peter. A private appearance to Peter, the one who had denied him, is mentioned here and by Paul (1 Corinthians 15:5), but not described. The Lord went first to Peter to restore him. “Risen indeed” (ontōs): really, truly. The ancient Easter greeting: The Lord is risen! He is risen indeed!

And how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. “The breaking of the bread” would become Luke’s term for the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:42, 46; 20:7).

In a sentence. They immediately returned to Jerusalem and found the disciples saying the Lord had really risen and appeared to Simon, and they told how they had recognised him when he broke the bread.

For worship. The Lord is risen indeed! Say it to another believer today.
verseByVerse.note: Simon is Peter.

parallels.desc: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–53 — Jerusalem, the Commission, and the Ascension
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He arrives mid-sentence into a locked room, and the first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church is peace — spoken to men who had failed him in the garden and the courtyard, by the one who bought it on Friday. Their response is not faith: they think they are seeing a ghost. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was apparitions, not resurrection. Nobody in that room was expecting this.

So he offers evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. See my hands and my feet — the identification runs through the wounds. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And then, while they are disbelieving for joy, he asks whether there is anything to eat, and eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

Then he sends them back to the book. The Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms is the standard threefold division of the Hebrew Scriptures — the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections. And he opened their minds to understand it: the third opening of the day, after their eyes at the table and the Scriptures on the road, all three by the same hand.

The commission follows, and it is still inside thus it is written: repentance for the forgiveness of sins, in his name, to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem — the city that had just killed him. You are witnesses of these things. And then a command nobody expects at the end of a commission: stay in the city and do nothing until you are clothed with power from on high.

Finally Bethany, and hands lifted in the priestly posture of Leviticus 9:22 — hands with holes in them. He parts from them while he blessed them, in the middle of the blessing, and is carried up.

They worship him — Jewish monotheists, on their faces, before a man they had eaten with in those forty days — and return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 39–43 close off an entire family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, nor a vision granted to grieving friends, nor a cause living on. It is a body, with hands and feet, that can be handled and that eats. A reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty, since Paul calls it a spiritual body — but Paul is describing not what it is made of but what governs it, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning immaterial. Paul's argument is that ours will be like his, and Luke has just shown his eating fish.

And the wounds are kept. He did not leave the marks in the tomb as an unpleasantness now finished with; the Lamb in John's vision stands in the middle of the throne looking as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6).

Verse 45 carries a whole doctrine. These men had the text, had heard it since childhood, and had just spent an evening with the risen Christ expounding it — and still needed their minds opened before they could take it in. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence or access (1 Cor. 2:14; Acts 16:14). That is humbling, and it is freeing: the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask the one who opens it.

And the ascension is not the end of the story but the beginning of the reign — seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:3), exactly as he told the council would begin from that moment (22:69). The disciples' worship of him is the first unambiguous worship of the risen Jesus in this Gospel, given by monotheists, with nobody correcting them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Disbelieved for joy is the commonest form of unbelief among genuine Christians: not doubt that the gospel is true, but the inability to take it personally — believers who can recite justification and cannot quite accept that they are forgiven. Jesus neither rebukes it nor argues with it. He asks for something to eat. Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

Beginning from Jerusalem is the measure of the thing announced. Any ordinary movement starts where it is welcome and works back to hostile ground later. The risen Christ orders the reverse: the first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it, carried by men who watched. Three thousand of them took it in a day.

Verse 48 defines what any Christian is actually asked for. Not to have the answers to every question, and not to argue anyone into the kingdom — simply to say what he has seen of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed. And it was entrusted to eleven men who had all failed him within the previous seventy-two hours.

Verse 49 is for anyone in a season of enforced waiting. There is a stillness that is disobedience and a stillness that is obedience, and the difference is not how it feels — both feel like wasting time. These men went nowhere and did nothing, on orders, until the power came. Zeal without the Spirit was what Peter had already shown in the garden with a sword.

And v. 52 speaks to anyone who half wishes he had been there instead of here. These men had the choice between seeing him in the room and having him enthroned with the Spirit about to come, and they went home with great joy.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, 'Peace to you!' But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them: peace to you! But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.

Jesus himself stood among them. Suddenly, through locked doors (John 20:19).

Peace to you! The ordinary greeting, shalom. But from the risen Lord, more: the peace he made by his death, peace with God (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17). The angels had announced peace at his birth (2:14).

But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. A ghost. They had seen him die. The disciples were not expecting a resurrection, and their first thought was not resurrection but a ghost.

In a sentence. As they talked, Jesus stood among them and greeted them with peace, but they were terrified, thinking he was a ghost.

For worship. The risen Lord speaks peace to you. Receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.

Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Gently, he deals with their doubts.

See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. The wounds of the crucifixion. The risen Lord is the same Jesus, the crucified one. His scars remain, eternally (Revelation 5:6).

Touch me, and see. Physical evidence. Not just a vision.

For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. The resurrection was bodily, not spiritual only. Jesus’ body was raised, transformed but real (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Not a ghost, not a vision, not a myth, not merely his “spirit living on”.

Where Christians differ: a spiritual or bodily resurrection? Some modern theologians speak of the resurrection as spiritual, a vision, or the disciples’ renewed faith. Verdict: Luke goes out of his way to insist on bodily resurrection: flesh and bones, wounds, touch, eating. The empty tomb, and Jesus’ own words, rule out a merely spiritual resurrection. As he rose bodily, so will his people (Philippians 3:21).

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they doubted, showed them his hands and feet, told them to touch him, and said a ghost does not have flesh and bones as he had.

For worship. Jesus rose in his body, with his scars. Your body too will be raised. Worship the risen Lord.

parallels.desc: which we have looked upon and touched

verseByVerse.quote: And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marvelling, he said to them: have you anything here to eat? They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.

While they still disbelieved for joy. Too good to be true. Joy and doubt mixed.

Have you anything here to eat? More evidence.

They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them. A ghost cannot eat. Peter would later preach: we … ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:41). The risen body is real, and can eat, though it does not need to.

In a sentence. While they were still struggling to believe for joy, Jesus asked for food, and ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is a fact you can stake your life on. Jesus gave abundant evidence.

parallels.desc: who ate and drank with him

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to them: these are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you. He had told them, many times (9:22, 44; 18:31–33).

Everything written about me. Not a few verses, but everything.

In the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three parts of the Hebrew Bible. The whole Old Testament.

Must be fulfilled. “Must” (dei): divine necessity again. Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that he had told them that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

For worship. The whole Bible is about Jesus, and all of it is fulfilled in him. Read it so.
verseByVerse.note: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

Then he opened their minds. What was hidden from them before (9:45; 18:34) is now revealed. Understanding Scripture is a gift of the risen Christ, by his Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:12–14; 2 Corinthians 3:14–16). Without it, the Bible remains a closed book.

To understand the Scriptures. The Old Testament, read in the light of Christ.

In a sentence. Then Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

For worship. Pray before you read the Bible: Lord, open my mind to understand.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to them: thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead.

Thus it is written. The heart of what the Scriptures teach.

That the Christ should suffer. Isaiah 53; Psalm 22; Zechariah 12:10; 13:7.

And on the third day rise from the dead. Psalm 16:10 (Acts 2:25–31); Isaiah 53:10–12; Hosea 6:2; Jonah 1:17. The death and resurrection of the Messiah are the centre of the Bible.

In a sentence. He told them that Scripture says the Messiah would suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.

For worship. Christ died and rose, as the Scriptures said. This is the gospel you stand on (1 Corinthians 15:1–4).

parallels.desc: on the third day he will raise us up

verseByVerse.quote: and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

And that repentance for the forgiveness of sins. The message to be preached. Repentance: turning from sin to God. Forgiveness of sins: the gift won by Christ’s death (1:77; 3:3). The same words as John the Baptist’s preaching, now grounded in the cross.

Should be proclaimed. Also written: the mission is part of the Scriptures’ plan (Isaiah 49:6).

In his name. On his authority, by his power, through faith in him (Acts 2:38; 4:12).

To all nations. The climax of Luke’s great theme: all flesh shall see the salvation of God (3:6). Simeon’s song: a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32).

Beginning from Jerusalem. The book of Acts follows this exact plan: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

In a sentence. Scripture also says that repentance for the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. You are part of this mission. How are you helping the gospel reach the nations?

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses of these things.

You are witnesses. The apostles were eyewitnesses of his life, death and resurrection. Their testimony is the foundation of the church (Acts 1:8, 22; 2:32). We believe through their word (John 17:20). And every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done for them.

Of these things. His suffering and resurrection, and the message of forgiveness.

In a sentence. Jesus told them they were witnesses of these things.

On a Tuesday. Be a witness today. Tell someone what Jesus has done.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.

I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; 2:1–4, 33). Promised in the prophets (Joel 2:28–29; Ezekiel 36:26–27). Notice that Jesus himself sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7). Another claim to divine authority.

But stay in the city. Wait in Jerusalem.

Until you are clothed with power from on high. “Clothed”: as with a garment. “Power” (dynamin): the power of the Spirit (Acts 1:8). They cannot be witnesses in their own strength. Mission needs the Spirit.

In a sentence. Jesus promised to send them what the Father had promised, and told them to wait in the city until they were clothed with power from on high.

For worship. The Spirit of the risen Christ is given to his people. Depend on his power, not your own.
verseByVerse.note: The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.

He led them out as far as Bethany. Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. Acts 1:9–12 gives a fuller account, forty days later. Luke here compresses the time.

And lifting up his hands he blessed them. As the high priest blessed the people (Leviticus 9:22; Numbers 6:24–26). The Gospel began with Zechariah the priest, unable to speak the blessing (1:22). It ends with Jesus, the great high priest, blessing his people.

While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. The ascension. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven”. His last act on earth was blessing. And he goes to the Father’s right hand, from where he intercedes for us (Hebrews 7:25) and will return (Acts 1:11). His hands are still raised in blessing over his people.

In a sentence. Jesus led them out to Bethany, lifted his hands and blessed them, and while blessing them he left them and was taken up into heaven.

For worship. The ascended Christ’s hands are raised in blessing over you. Live under his blessing.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven.”

parallels.desc: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed them

verseByVerse.quote: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they worshipped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.

And they worshiped him. The first time in Luke that anyone worships Jesus (proskynēsantes). They now know who he is: the Lord, to be worshipped as God. Worship belongs to God alone (4:8), and they give it to Jesus.

And returned to Jerusalem with great joy. Not grief at his departure, but great joy. The good news of great joy the angel announced at his birth (2:10) is now theirs. They know he is alive, reigning, and coming back, and that his Spirit is coming.

And were continually in the temple blessing God. The Gospel began in the temple, with Zechariah offering incense (1:9), and ends in the temple, with the disciples blessing God. The circle is complete. Praise is the right response to the gospel.

The end of Luke, the beginning of Acts. Luke’s first volume ends in worship and joy, waiting for the Spirit. His second volume, Acts, tells what the risen Lord continued to do through his Spirit and his church (Acts 1:1).

In a sentence. They worshipped Jesus and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, spending their time in the temple praising God.

For worship. Worship the risen, ascended Lord with great joy, and bless God continually.

24.text: <sup>1</sup> But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. <sup>5</sup> And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” <sup>8</sup> And they remembered his words, <sup>9</sup> and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. <sup>10</sup> Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, <sup>11</sup> but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. <sup>12</sup> But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened. <sup>13</sup> That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup> and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. <sup>15</sup> While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. <sup>16</sup> But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. <sup>17</sup> And he said to them, “What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, looking sad. <sup>18</sup> Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to them, “What things?” And they said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <sup>20</sup> and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. <sup>21</sup> But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. <sup>22</sup> Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, <sup>23</sup> and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. <sup>24</sup> Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.” <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! <sup>26</sup> Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” <sup>27</sup> And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. <sup>28</sup> So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, <sup>29</sup> but they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. <sup>30</sup> When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight. <sup>32</sup> They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” <sup>33</sup> And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, <sup>34</sup> saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” <sup>35</sup> Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. <sup>36</sup> As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace to you!” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. <sup>38</sup> And he said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” <sup>40</sup> And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Have you anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> They gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate before them. <sup>44</sup> Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” <sup>45</sup> Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, <sup>46</sup> and said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, <sup>47</sup> and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. <sup>48</sup> You are witnesses of these things. <sup>49</sup> And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” <sup>50</sup> And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. <sup>51</sup> While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. <sup>52</sup> And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, <sup>53</sup> and were continually in the temple blessing God.
